# Majmu' al-Fatawa - Tome 7

## Page 3040

Volume Seven
The Book of Faith

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Praise be to Allah alone, and blessings and peace be upon the one after whom there is no prophet.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah bless his resting place—said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Praise be to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whoever He leads astray, none can guide. We bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, and we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon him and his family.

Know that “faith and Islam” together encompass the whole religion. There has been much discussion, disagreement, and confusion concerning “the true nature of faith and Islam.” Volumes have been written on the subject, and disagreement over it has existed among the various groups ever since the Kharijites emerged.

---

## Page 3041

And we shall set out what may be learned from the words of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—together with what may be learned from the words of Allah Most High, so that the believer may arrive at this understanding directly from the words of Allah and His Messenger, for this is the objective. We shall therefore not begin by discussing people’s disagreements. Rather, while explaining what may be learned from the words of Allah and His Messenger, we shall mention those disagreements insofar as they demonstrate that referring disputed matters to Allah and the Messenger is better, affords a better resolution, and leads to a better outcome in this world and the Hereafter.

We say:

In the hadith of Gabriel, peace be upon him, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—distinguished between what is meant by “Islam,” “faith,” and “excellence.” He said:

“Islam is that you testify that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House if you are able to make the journey.”

And he said:

“Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

This distinction is mentioned in the hadith of Umar recorded by Muslim alone, and in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Both relate that Gabriel came to him in the form of a Bedouin man and questioned him. The hadith of Umar states that he came to him in the form of a Bedouin.

He likewise explained “Islam” in the well-known hadith of Ibn Umar, saying:

“Islam is built upon five: testifying that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, establishing prayer, giving zakat, performing pilgrimage to the House, and fasting Ramadan.”

The hadith of Gabriel makes clear that “Islam, which is built upon five,” is Islam itself

---

## Page 3042

—what is built is not distinct from that upon which it is built. Rather, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—established three levels of religion: the highest is “excellence,” the middle is “faith,” and below it is “Islam.” Everyone who attains excellence is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim; but not every believer attains excellence, nor is every Muslim a believer. This will be explained—Allah willing—through the other hadiths, such as the hadith narrated by Hammād ibn Zayd, from Ayyūb, from Abū Qilābah, from a man of Syria, from his father, who reported that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to him:

“Embrace Islam and you will be safe.”
He asked, “What is Islam?”
He replied, “That you submit your heart to Allah, and that the Muslims be safe from your tongue and hand.”
He asked, “What is the best form of Islam?”
He replied, “Faith.”
He asked, “What is faith?”
He replied, “That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and resurrection after death.”
He asked, “What is the best form of faith?”
He replied, “Migration.”
He asked, “What is migration?”
He replied, “That you abandon evil.”
He asked, “What is the best form of migration?”
He replied, “Jihad.”
He asked, “What is jihad?”
He replied, “That you strive against—or fight—the unbelievers when you encounter them, neither misappropriating the spoils nor showing cowardice.”

Then the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Two deeds are the best of deeds, except when someone performs their like”—he said this three times—“an accepted Hajj or an umrah.”

This was narrated by Ahmad and Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī. For this reason, he mentions these “four ranks,” saying:

“The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe. The believer is the one whom people trust with their lives and property. The migrant is the one who abandons evil deeds. The one who strives is the one who strives against his own soul for Allah’s sake.”

This is narrated from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—through the reports of Abd Allāh ibn Amr, Fadālah ibn Ubayd, and others, with a good chain of transmission. It appears in the Sunan collections, and part of it appears in the two Sahīh collections.

---

## Page 3043

It has also been established through several chains of transmission that he said:

“The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the believer is the one whom people trust with their lives and property.”

Clearly, anyone trusted with lives and property is someone from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe. Were they not safe from him, they would not trust him. The same is found in the hadith narrated by Ubayd ibn Umayr from Amr ibn Abasah, and also in the hadith narrated by Abd Allāh ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, from his father, from his grandfather:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was asked, ‘What is Islam?’
He replied, ‘Feeding others and speaking kindly.’
He was asked, ‘What, then, is faith?’
He replied, ‘Generosity and patience.’
He was asked, ‘Which Muslim is best in his Islam?’
He replied, ‘The one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.’
He was asked, ‘Which believer is best in his faith?’
He replied, ‘The one with the best character.’
He was asked, ‘What is the best migration?’
He replied, ‘That of someone who abandons what Allah has forbidden him.’
The questioner asked, ‘Which prayer is best?’
He replied, ‘Prolonged standing.’
He asked, ‘Which charity is best?’
He replied, ‘Giving what one can despite having little.’
He asked, ‘Which jihad is best?’
He replied, ‘That you strive with your wealth and your life, so that your steed is struck down and your blood is shed.’
He asked, ‘Which time is best?’
He replied, ‘The depths of the remaining night.’”

Clearly, all these are ranks, some higher than others; a migrant must in any case be a believer, as must one who strives in jihad. Hence he said:

“Faith is generosity and patience.”

And of Islam he said:

“Feeding others and speaking kindly.”

The former entails the latter: someone whose character is marked by generosity will do these things. The converse, however, does not hold, for a person may do them by deliberately adopting such behaviour without generosity and patience being part of his character.

He likewise said:

“The best of Muslims

---

## Page 3044

is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”

He also said:

“The believers most complete in faith are those with the best character.”

Clearly, this includes the former: whoever has good character will act accordingly. Al-Hasan al-Basrī was asked, “What is good character?” He replied, “Giving generously, refraining from harm, and having a cheerful countenance.” Thus, refraining from harm is part of good character.

Authentic hadiths will follow in which he counted outward deeds as part of faith, such as his saying:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

And his saying to the delegation of Abd al-Qays:

“I enjoin upon you faith in Allah alone. Do you know what faith in Allah alone is? Testifying that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, establishing prayer, giving zakāh, and paying one-fifth of whatever spoils you acquire.”

Clearly, he did not mean that these deeds constitute faith in Allah without faith in the heart, for he stated on numerous occasions that faith in the heart is indispensable. It is therefore evident that these deeds, together with faith in the heart, constitute faith.

In al-Musnad, Anas narrates that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Islam is outwardly manifest, while faith is in the heart.”

He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—also said:

“Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the rest of the body is sound; and if it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”

Thus, whoever has a sound heart will certainly have a sound body, but the reverse does not hold.

Sufyān ibn Uyaynah said:

“The scholars of earlier times used to write these words to one another: Whoever sets right his inward state, Allah will set right his outward state; and whoever sets right what lies between him

---

## Page 3045

and Allah, Allah will set right what lies between him and other people; and whoever works for his Hereafter, Allah will take care of his worldly affairs.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā related this in Kitāb al-Ikhlās (The Book of Sincerity).

Thus, when the heart is sound through faith, the body becomes sound through Islam, which is itself part of faith. This is indicated by his words in the hadith of Gabriel:

“This is Gabriel; he came to teach you your religion.”

He thus identified religion as Islam, faith, and excellence (ihsān). It is therefore clear that our religion encompasses all three, but consists of three degrees: a Muslim, then a believer, then one who attains excellence. As Allah Most High says:

“Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Some of them wrong themselves, some follow a middle course, and some are foremost in good deeds, by Allah’s permission.”

Both those who follow a middle course and those foremost in good deeds enter Paradise without punishment, unlike those who wrong themselves. Likewise, whoever outwardly observes Islam, together with belief in the heart, but does not fulfill the inward faith required of him is liable to the threatened punishment, as will be explained, Allah willing.

Excellence is more comprehensive in its content than faith, but applies to a narrower group of people. Faith, in turn, is more comprehensive in its content than Islam, but applies to a narrower group of people. Thus, excellence includes faith, and faith includes Islam; those who attain excellence form a narrower group than the believers, and the believers form a narrower group than the Muslims.

The same distinction is made regarding messengership and prophethood. Prophethood is included within messengership, while messengership is more comprehensive in its content but applies to a narrower group of people. Every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger. Prophets therefore constitute the broader group, while prophethood itself is part of messengership. Messengership encompasses prophethood and more, whereas prophethood does not encompass messengership.

---

## Page 3046

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained “Islam and faith” through the answers he gave, just as something is explained by giving its definition: when asked, “What is such-and-such?” one answers, “It is such-and-such.” Thus, in the authentic hadith:

“When asked, ‘What is backbiting?’ he said, ‘Your mentioning your brother in a way he dislikes.’”

And in another hadith:

“Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.”

Rejecting the truth means denying and refusing to accept it; looking down on people means despising and belittling them. We shall explain, if Allah Most High wills, why his answers varied and how they are all true.

The (point), however, is that his statement, “Islam is built on five,” is equivalent to saying, “Islam consists of the five,” as mentioned in the hadith of Gabriel. For when something consists of several parts, its overall structure is built upon those parts and composed of them. Thus, Islam is built upon these pillars. We shall explain, Allah willing, what distinguishes these five such that they constitute Islam and form the foundations upon which it is built, and why they, rather than the other obligations, have been singled out in this way.

In the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, he explained “faith” in the same terms with which he explained Islam here, except that he did not mention Hajj. This hadith is reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim. He said:

“I command you to have faith in Allah alone. Do you know what faith in Allah alone is?”

They replied, “Allah and His Messenger know best.”

He said, “To testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakat, to fast Ramadan, and to pay a fifth of what you acquire as spoils—or a fifth of the spoils.”

Some chains of transmission give the wording:

“Faith in Allah and testifying that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah.”

---

## Page 3047

But the first wording is better known.

In Abū Saʿīd’s narration:

“I command you to do four things and forbid you four things: worship Allah and associate nothing with Him.”

In the hadith about the branches of faith, he explained faith in terms of this and other things, saying:

“Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

It is also authentically reported from him through several chains of transmission, in narrations from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, and ʿImrān ibn Husayn, that he said:

“Modesty is a branch of faith.”

He also said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father, and all people.”

And he said:

“None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”

He said:

“By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe!”

He was asked, “Who, O Messenger of Allah?”

He replied, “The one whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”

He said:

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest level of faith.”

He said:

“Whenever Allah sent a prophet, there were among his people those who followed his guidance and adhered to his sunnah. Then successors arise after them who say what they do not do and do what they have not been commanded to do. Whoever strives against them with his hand is a believer; whoever strives against them with his tongue is a believer; and whoever strives against them with his heart is a believer. Beyond that there is not even a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

This is reported by Muslim alone. Likewise, Muslim alone reports his words:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not direct you to something which, if you do it, will make you love one another?

---

## Page 3048

Spread the greeting of peace among yourselves.”

In the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, and also reported by al-Bukhārī from Ibn ‘Abbās, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is a believer while committing it; no one who drinks wine is a believer while drinking it; no thief is a believer while stealing; and no one who seizes plunder, causing people to raise their eyes towards him, is a believer while doing so.”

Thus, the term “faith” is sometimes mentioned on its own, without being coupled with the term “Islam,” righteous deeds, or anything else. At other times it is mentioned alongside something else: either Islam, as in the questions in the hadith of Gabriel:

“What is Islam, and what is faith?”

And as in the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women.”

And His words, mighty and majestic:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted.”’”

And the words of the Most High:

“So We brought out the believers who were there.”

“But We found there only one household of Muslims.”

Likewise, faith is mentioned alongside righteous deeds in various passages of the Quran, as in the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

Or it is mentioned alongside those who have been given knowledge, as in the words of the Most High:

“And those who were given knowledge and faith said.”

And His words:

“Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.”

Wherever those who believe are mentioned, those who have been given knowledge are included among them, for they are the best of them. The Most High says:

“And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, ‘We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.’”

And He says:

“But those among them who are firmly grounded in knowledge, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you.”

---

## Page 3049

And the term “believers” is also mentioned alongside the Jews, Christians, and Sabians. Then He says:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

The believers mentioned at the beginning of the passage are distinct from the other three groups, whereas faith as mentioned later encompasses them, just as it encompasses them in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation.”

We shall explain this at length, if Allah Most High wills.

(The point here) concerns the broader and narrower senses of faith in relation to its inward and outward aspects. Its broader scope in relation to religious communities, however, is “a separate matter.” Thus, when he mentioned faith alongside Islam, he defined Islam as the outward deeds: the two testimonies of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting, and Hajj. He defined faith as what is in the heart of belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day.

Likewise, in the hadith Ahmad narrated from Anas, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.”

When the term “faith” is mentioned on its own, it includes Islam and righteous deeds, as in his words in the hadith concerning the branches of faith:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

The same applies to all the other hadiths in which righteous deeds are counted as part of faith. Furthermore, when “faith” is negated in their absence, this indicates that they are obligatory. If, however, he mentions the excellence of the faith of one who performs them—without negating his faith—this indicates that they are recommended. For Allah and His Messenger

---

## Page 3050

do not negate the designation of anything commanded by Allah and His Messenger unless some of its obligatory requirements have been omitted, as in his words:

“There is no prayer without the Mother of the Quran.”

And his words:

“There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy, and no religion in one who does not keep his covenant.”

The same applies to similar statements. But when an act is recommended within an “act of worship,” he does not negate that worship because the recommended act is absent. If this were permissible, it would be permissible to deny faith, prayer, zakat, and Hajj to most believers. For there is no deed but another is better than it, and no one performs righteous deeds as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did—or even as Abū Bakr or ʿUmar did. If it were permissible to negate these acts of worship for someone who had not attained their recommended completeness, it would be permissible to negate them for most Muslims, earlier and later alike. No reasonable person would say this.

Thus, if someone says that what is negated is completeness, then if he means “obligatory completeness,” the omission of which makes a person blameworthy and liable to punishment, he has spoken correctly. But if he means “recommended completeness,” this has never occurred in the speech of Allah and His Messenger, nor could it properly occur. For when someone fulfills an obligation as required, omitting none of its obligatory requirements, it is not permissible to say that he has not fulfilled it, whether literally or figuratively.

Thus, when he said to the Bedouin who prayed improperly:

“Go back and pray, for you have not prayed,”

and said to the man who prayed behind the row—having ordered him to repeat the prayer:

“There is no prayer for one who stands alone behind the row,”

this was because an obligatory requirement had been omitted. Likewise, the words of the Most High:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are the truthful,”

make clear that striving in Allah’s cause is obligatory and that refraining from doubt is obligatory.

---

## Page 3051

Although jihad is a collective obligation, its command is initially addressed to all believers. They must therefore all believe it to be obligatory and resolve to undertake it if it becomes individually binding upon them. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever dies without having fought in a military campaign and without having contemplated doing so dies with a trait of hypocrisy.”

Reported by Muslim. He thus stated that anyone who has not entertained the intention of doing so has a trait of hypocrisy. Moreover, jihad encompasses various kinds, and some kind of it must necessarily be obligatory upon every believer.

The same applies to His words:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord; those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them. It is they who are truly believers.”

All of this is obligatory. Reliance upon Allah is indeed among the greatest obligations, just as sincerity to Allah is obligatory, and love for Allah and His Messenger is obligatory.

Allah has commanded reliance upon Him in numerous verses, with greater emphasis than His command to perform ablution and to bathe after sexual impurity. He has also forbidden reliance upon anyone other than Allah. The Most High says:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And the Most High says:

“Allah—there is no god but He. And in Allah let the believers put their trust.”

And the Most High says:

“If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who can help you after Him? And in Allah let the believers put their trust.”

And the Most High says:

“Moses said, ‘My people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.’”

As for His words:

“Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them,”

we say: Among the states and actions of the heart are those that necessarily accompany faith and are firmly established within the heart, such that, if a person is a believer, they necessarily follow without his intending them or deliberately bringing them about

---

## Page 3052

and if they are absent, this indicates that the obligatory faith has not been attained in the heart. This is like the words of the Most High:

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

He thus states that you will not find a believer showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. Faith itself is incompatible with such affection, just as either of two opposites excludes the other. When faith is present, its opposite—allegiance to Allah’s enemies—is absent. If a man gives allegiance to Allah’s enemies in his heart, this indicates that his heart lacks the obligatory faith.

Similar are His words in another passage:

“You see many of them taking those who disbelieve as allies. Evil indeed is what their souls have sent ahead for them: Allah is angry with them, and they will abide in punishment forever.”

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient.”

He thus sets out a “conditional statement,” which entails that when the condition is fulfilled, the consequent follows, using the particle law (“if”), which, together with the condition, entails the negation of the consequent. He says:

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

This indicates that the faith mentioned excludes taking them as allies and is incompatible with it: faith and taking them as allies cannot coexist in the heart. It also indicates that whoever takes them as allies has not fulfilled the obligatory faith in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him. Similar are the words of the Most High:

“Do not take the Jews and Christians as allies; they are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies is indeed one of them.”

For in those verses He states that whoever gives them allegiance cannot be

---

## Page 3053

a believer. Here He states that whoever gives them allegiance is one of them. Thus, the passages of the Quran confirm one another. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse: a Book consistent in its parts and oft-repeated, at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver”—to the end of the verse.

Likewise, His words:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

This shows that leaving in the circumstances mentioned without asking his permission is impermissible, and that one must not leave until one has asked permission. Whoever leaves without asking permission has therefore neglected part of the faith obligatory upon him. This is why faith is negated in his case: the particle “innamā” affirms what is mentioned and excludes everything else.

Some scholars of legal theory say that “inna” expresses affirmation and “mā” expresses negation, so that combining them conveys both negation and affirmation. This, however, is not the view of Arabic grammarians or those who discuss the matter with knowledge. This “mā” is the restraining particle that attaches to “inna” and its sister particles, preventing them from exercising their grammatical effect. They exercise that effect only when restricted to nominal clauses. Once restrained, both their grammatical effect and their restriction cease, so that either verbal or nominal clauses may follow them. Thus, adding “mā” changes both their meaning and their grammatical effect. The same applies to “ka’annamā” and other such combinations.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away after that. Such people are not believers.

“When they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, a group of them turns away.

“But if the right is theirs, they come to him in submission.

“Is there a disease in their hearts? Or have they doubted? Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.

“The only response of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, is to say, ‘We hear and we obey.’ It is they who are successful.”

---

## Page 3054

If it is objected: If the true believer is one who performs the obligations and avoids what is forbidden, Allah has said:

“Those are the believers in truth,”

although He mentioned only five things. Likewise, He says in another verse:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger.”

There are two answers to this:

(First): What He mentions may entail what He leaves unmentioned. He mentions their hearts trembling when Allah is mentioned, their faith increasing when His verses are recited to them, together with their reliance upon Him and their establishment of prayer as commanded, both inwardly and outwardly, as well as their giving of wealth and benefits. These things therefore entail the rest, for the heart’s trembling when Allah is mentioned entails awe and fear of Him. They have explained wajilat (“trembled”) as meaning “were afraid.” In Ibn Masʿūd’s reading:

“When Allah is mentioned, their hearts are afraid.”

This is correct, for wajal in Arabic means fear. Thus, one speaks of “the flush of embarrassment and the pallor of fear.” Another example is Allah Most High’s saying:

“And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord.”

ʿĀ’ishah said: “O Messenger of Allah, is this a man who commits fornication and steals, and fears being punished?”

He replied: “No, daughter of al-Siddīq. It is a man who prays, fasts and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

Al-Suddī said concerning Allah Most High’s words, “Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned”: “This refers to

---

## Page 3055

a man who intends to do wrong or contemplates a sin, but then refrains from it.”

This is like His saying, Most High:

“But as for one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from its desires, Paradise will surely be his refuge.”

And His saying:

“For whoever fears standing before his Lord there will be two gardens.”

Mujāhid and other Quran commentators said: “This refers to a man who contemplates a sin, then remembers his standing before Allah and abandons it out of fear of Allah.” If “the heart’s trembling at His mention” entails awe and fear of Him, then this prompts a person to do what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: “No veil between the servant and Allah is thicker than the claims he makes for himself, and no path to Him is shorter than need of Him. The foundation of all good in this world and the Hereafter is fear of Allah.” This is indicated by His saying, Most High:

“When Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the tablets; their inscription contained guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord.”

He thus declares that guidance and mercy are for those who stand in awe of Allah.

Mujāhid and Ibrāhīm said: “This refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers his standing before Allah and abandons the sin.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated this from Ibn al-Jaʿd, from Shuʿbah, from Mansūr, from them both, concerning His saying, Most High:

“For whoever fears standing before his Lord there will be two gardens.”

These are the successful ones mentioned in His saying, Most High:

“They are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is they who are successful.”

They are “the believers” and “the God-fearing” mentioned in His saying, Most High:

“Alif Lām Mīm. This is the Book in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing.”

Likewise, He says in the verse concerning righteousness:

“Those are the ones who are truthful, and it is they who are God-fearing.”

These are the ones who follow the Book, as in His saying, Most High:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.”

And if he does not go astray, he is a rightly guided follower,

---

## Page 3056

and if he does not suffer misery, he is a recipient of mercy. These are the people of the straight path, whom Allah has blessed—the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous—not those who have incurred His anger, nor those who have gone astray. Those who receive mercy have not incurred His anger, and those who are guided have not gone astray. Thus it becomes clear that those who stand in awe of Allah are mindful of Him and deserving of His Paradise without punishment. These are the ones who have fulfilled the requirements of obligatory faith.

Among the passages indicating this meaning is His saying, Most High:

“It is only those of His servants who have knowledge who fear Allah.”

This means that none fears Him except one who has knowledge. Allah has thus declared that everyone who fears Him has knowledge, as He says in another verse:

“Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for his Lord’s mercy, like one who is not? Say, ‘Are those who know equal to those who do not know?’”

Fear always includes hope; otherwise, it would be despair. Likewise, hope necessarily entails fear; otherwise, it would be a sense of security. Those who fear Allah and place their hope in Him are therefore the people of knowledge whom Allah has praised.

It is reported that Abū Hayyān al-Taymī said: “Scholars are of three kinds.” One knows Allah but does not know Allah’s commands; another knows Allah’s commands but does not know Allah; and another knows both Allah and His commands. The one who knows Allah is the one who fears Him, while the one who knows Allah’s commands is the one who knows what He commands and forbids.

In al-Sahīh (The Authentic Collection), it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Allah, I hope to be the one among you who fears Allah most and knows His limits best.”

Since those who fear Allah are the scholars praised in the Book and the Sunnah, they cannot be deserving of blame. This can only be the case if they fulfil their obligations. This is also indicated by His saying, Most High:

---

## Page 3057

“Then their Lord revealed to them: ‘We will surely destroy the wrongdoers and settle you in the land after them. This is for whoever fears standing before Me and fears My warning.’”

And His saying:

“But whoever fears standing before his Lord will have two gardens.”

Thus He has promised those who fear Him victory in this world and reward in the Hereafter. This can only be because they have fulfilled their obligations, indicating that fear necessarily entails fulfilling one’s obligations. Hence the wicked person is described as someone who does not fear Allah. This meaning is also indicated by His saying, Most High:

“Allah only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterwards.”

Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: “I asked the Companions of Muhammad about this verse, and they told me: ‘Everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant, and everyone who repents before death has repented soon afterwards.’” The other Quran commentators likewise said this.

Mujāhid said: “Every sinner is ignorant at the time of his sin.” Al-Hasan, Qatādah, ʿAtāʾ, al-Suddī, and others said: “They were called ignorant because of their sins, not because they lacked discernment.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “The verse does not mean that they do not know the act is evil, for if a Muslim committed an act without knowing it was evil, he would be like someone who had committed no evil. Rather, it admits of two meanings:

“(First): They committed it without knowing the harm it entailed.

“Second: They embarked upon it with full awareness and knowledge that its consequences would be harmful, preferring the immediate to the hereafter. They were therefore called ignorant for preferring so little to abundant ease and lasting well-being.”

Al-Zajjāj thus understood ‘ignorance’ to mean either a lack of knowledge of an act’s consequences or a corruption of the will. It may be said that the two necessarily accompany one another. This is discussed at length in the arguments with the Jahmiyyah. The point here is that everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant, and everyone who fears Him has knowledge

---

## Page 3058

and obeys Allah. A person is ignorant only because his fear of Allah is deficient, for if his fear of Allah were complete, he would not disobey Him. Hence the saying of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: “Fear of Allah is sufficient knowledge, and being deluded about Allah is sufficient ignorance.”

This is because conceiving of what is feared prompts one to flee from it, while conceiving of what is loved prompts one to seek it. If someone neither flees from the former nor seeks the latter, this indicates that he has not fully conceived of it. He may, however, conceive of a report about it; but conceiving of a report, accepting its truth, and memorizing its wording are different from conceiving of what it describes.

The same applies when what he conceives of is neither loved nor disliked by him. A person may accept the reality of something that threatens someone else or that someone else loves, without this prompting him either to flee or to seek. Likewise, someone may be told about something he loves or dislikes, and, far from disbelieving the informant, may recognize his truthfulness; yet his heart is too preoccupied with other matters to conceive of what he has been told. Such a person is not moved either to flee or to seek.

Among the well-known sayings of al-Hasan al-Basrī—which is also transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through a disconnected chain—is:

“Knowledge is of two kinds: knowledge in the heart and knowledge on the tongue. Knowledge in the heart is beneficial knowledge, while knowledge on the tongue is Allah’s proof against His servants.”

It is also recorded in the two Sahīhs, on the authority of Abū Mūsā, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believer who recites the Quran is like a citron: its taste is pleasant and its fragrance is pleasant. The believer who does not recite the Quran is like a date: its taste is pleasant, but it has no fragrance. The hypocrite who recites the Quran is like basil: its fragrance is pleasant, but its taste is bitter. The hypocrite who does not recite the Quran is like a colocynth: its taste is bitter, and it has no fragrance.”

This hypocrite who recites the Quran memorizes it and conceives of its meanings, and may even believe that it is

---

## Page 3059

the speech of Allah and that the Messenger is true, yet he is not a believer. Likewise, the Jews recognize him as they recognize their own sons, yet they are not believers. The same applies to Iblīs, Pharaoh, and others. Such a person, however, has not attained complete knowledge and understanding, for these necessarily entail acting accordingly. This is why someone who does not act upon his knowledge is called ignorant, as explained above.

The same applies to the term “reason.” Although it is originally the verbal noun of “to reason,” and many speculative thinkers have classified it as a kind of knowledge, it must also be understood as knowledge upon which one acts. Thus, only someone who recognizes good and pursues it, and recognizes evil and abandons it, is called “rational.” Hence the inhabitants of the Fire will say:

“If only we had listened or reasoned, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.”

And He says of the hypocrites:

“You think they are united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.”

Someone who does what he knows will harm him has no reason. Just as fear of Allah entails knowledge of Him, knowledge of Him entails fear of Him, and fear of Him entails obedience to Him. Whoever fears Allah obeys His commands and avoids His prohibitions. This is what we intended to explain at the outset.

This is also indicated by His words, exalted is He:

“So remind, if the reminder should benefit.”
“He who fears will be reminded.”
“But the most wretched will avoid it.”
“He who will enter the great Fire.”

He thus states that whoever fears Him will heed the reminder. Heeding the reminder here necessarily entails worshipping Him. Allah, exalted is He, says:

“It is He who shows you His signs and sends down provision for you from the sky. But none will heed the reminder except those who turn to Him.”

And He says:

“As insight and a reminder for every servant who turns to Him.”

Hence, concerning His words, they said:

---

## Page 3060

“He who fears will be reminded”: whoever fears Allah will take admonition from the Quran. And concerning His words, “But none will heed the reminder except those who turn to Him,” they said: only those who return to obedience take admonition. This is because fully remembering something necessarily entails being affected by what one remembers: if one remembers something beloved, one seeks it; if one remembers something feared, one flees from it. This is also illustrated by His words, exalted is He:

“It is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them—they will not believe.”

And He, glorified is He, says:

“You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen.”

He thus denies that anyone other than these is warned, despite His saying:

“It is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them—they will not believe.”

He therefore affirms that they are warned in one respect and denies it in another, for warning means informing someone of something to be feared.

Warning is thus like teaching and instilling fear. If you teach someone and he learns, your teaching of him is complete. Yet another person says, “I taught him, but he did not learn.” Likewise, if you instil fear in someone and he becomes afraid, your instilling of fear has achieved its full effect. But if someone is warned of something frightening yet feels no fear, the instilling of fear has not achieved its full effect. Likewise, if you guide someone and he follows that guidance, the guidance given to him is complete. This is illustrated by His words, exalted is He:

“A guidance for the God-fearing.”

But if you guide someone and he does not follow that guidance—as He says, “As for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness to guidance”—the guidance given to him is not complete. This is like saying, “I cut it, and it came apart,” or, “I cut it, but it did not come apart.”

A complete cause necessarily produces its effect: whenever its effect does not occur, the cause is not complete. When an action encounters a receptive subject, it is complete; otherwise, it is not. Knowledge of what one loves gives rise to seeking it, and knowledge of what one dislikes gives rise to abandoning it. This is why such knowledge is called a motive. It is said that a motive, together with the ability to act, necessarily brings about the corresponding action. It is knowledge of the object sought that necessarily entails willing that known and desired object.

All of this occurs only when the innate disposition is sound and unimpaired. When it is corrupted, however, a person may perceive something pleasurable yet find no pleasure in it; rather, it causes him pain. Likewise, he may take pleasure in something painful because his innate disposition is corrupted. And corruption

---

## Page 3061

affects both the cognitive and practical faculties. It is like someone afflicted by bile who finds honey bitter: his very perception has become impaired, so that he perceives it contrary to its true nature because of the bile mingled with it. The same applies to someone whose inward state has become corrupted. Allah, exalted is He, says:

“And what will make you realize that even if it came, they would not believe?”

“And We turn their hearts and eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and leave them wandering blindly in their transgression.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“When they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”

And He says:

“And for their saying, ‘Our hearts are covered.’ Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief.”

And in the other verse He says:

“They said, ‘Our hearts are covered.’ Rather, Allah has cursed them because of their disbelief.”

Ghulf, “covered,” is the plural of aghlaf: something enclosed in a covering, like an uncircumcised person. It is as though they regarded the impediment as something innate—that their hearts were created with coverings over them. Allah, exalted is He, therefore says:

“Rather, Allah has cursed them because of their disbelief,”

and:

“Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief, so they believe but little.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“Among them are those who listen to you, but when they leave your presence, they say to those who have been given knowledge, ‘What did he just say?’ Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has sealed and who follow their own desires.”

Likewise, they said:

“O Shuʿayb, we do not understand much of what you say.”

He says:

“Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear.”

That is, He would have made them understand what they heard. He then says that, had He made them understand while they remained in their present state:

“They would have turned away in aversion.”

Their innate disposition has thus become corrupted: they did not understand, and even if they had understood, they would not have acted. He therefore denies that either their cognitive faculty or their practical faculty is sound. And He says:

“Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; rather, they are even further astray

---

## Page 3062

in their way.”

And He says:

“We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. They are like livestock; rather, they are even further astray. It is they who are heedless.”

And He says:

“The example of those who disbelieve is like that of someone calling to creatures that hear nothing but calls and cries. Deaf, mute and blind, they do not understand.”

And He says of the hypocrites:

“Deaf, mute and blind, they will not return.”

Some people say: “Since they did not benefit from hearing, sight and speech, they were deemed deaf, mute and blind”; or: “Since they turned away from hearing, seeing and speaking, they became like the deaf, blind and mute.” But this is not so. Rather, their very hearts have become blind, deaf and mute, as Allah, exalted is He, says:

“It is not the eyes that become blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

The heart is the king, and the bodily members are its soldiers. When it is sound, the rest of the body is sound; when it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt. A person may still hear sounds with his ears, just as animals do, yet fail to understand their meaning. Even if he understands to some extent, he does not understand fully. For full understanding necessarily produces its effect in the heart: love of what is lovable and hatred of what is hateful. Whenever this does not occur, full apprehension has not been attained. It may therefore be denied, since something incomplete may be spoken of as absent—as in the Prophet’s words to the man who prayed incorrectly:

“Pray, for you have not prayed.”

The negation of faith, wherever it occurs, is of this kind.

Allah has described them both as having hearts that tremble when He is mentioned and as increasing in faith when they hear His verses. Al-Dahhāk said: “They increased them in certainty.” Al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas said: “In reverent fear.” And it is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās: “In affirmation of the truth.”

Allah has likewise mentioned these two principles in various places. He, exalted is He, says:

“Has not

---

## Page 3063

the time come for the hearts of those who believe to be humbled at the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed, and not to be like those who were given the Scripture before, whose hearts hardened as time passed? And many of them are defiantly disobedient.”

Reverent humility encompasses two meanings: first, humility and submissiveness; second, stillness and tranquillity. This necessarily entails a softness of heart that is incompatible with hardness. Thus, the heart’s reverent humility encompasses both its servitude to Allah and its tranquillity. Accordingly, reverent humility in prayer includes both humility and stillness.

Regarding His words:

“Those who are reverently humble in their prayers,”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Submissive and lowly.” Al-Hasan and Qatādah said: “Fearful.” Muqātil said: “Humble.” It is reported from ‘Alī: “Reverent humility is in the heart, and means being gentle toward a fellow Muslim and not turning to the right or left.” Mujāhid said: “Lowering the gaze and humbling oneself.” When a man of knowledge stood to pray, his awe of the Most Merciful kept his gaze from wandering and his mind from dwelling on worldly affairs.

It is reported from ‘Amr ibn Dīnār: “Reverent humility is not bowing and prostrating; rather, it is stillness and a love of maintaining a proper bearing in prayer.”

It is reported from Ibn Sīrīn and others:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions used to raise their eyes toward the sky during prayer and look to the right and left, until these verses were revealed: ‘Successful indeed are the believers, those who are reverently humble in their prayers.’ Thereafter, they directed their gaze toward the place where they prostrated, and none of them was subsequently seen looking anywhere but at the ground.”

It is reported from ‘Atā’: “It means not fidgeting with any part of your body while praying.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw a man playing with his beard during prayer and said: “Had there been humility in

---

## Page 3064

this man’s heart, his limbs would have been humble as well.”

The term “reverent humility” will, Allah willing, be discussed at greater length elsewhere. “Bodily humility” follows from the heart’s humility, provided that a person is not showing off by outwardly displaying what is absent from his heart. As has been reported: “Seek refuge in Allah from hypocritical humility.” This is when the body appears humble while the heart is empty and distracted.

He, glorified be He, reproached the believers for their delay when He said:

“Has the time not come for the hearts of those who believe to be humbled at the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed?”

He thus called them to humility of heart at His remembrance and what He had revealed of His Book, and forbade them to be like those whose hearts hardened as time passed. These believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them.

Likewise, He said in another verse:

“Allah has sent down the best message—a Book consistent in its parts, reiterating its teachings. The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it; then their skins and hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah.”

Those who fear their Lord are those whose hearts tremble when Allah Most High is mentioned.

If it is said, “Then humility of heart at the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed is obligatory,” the answer is: Yes, but people fall into two categories in this regard: “the moderate” and “the foremost.” The foremost distinguish themselves by performing recommended deeds, while the moderate—the righteous—are the general body of believers deserving of Paradise. Whoever belongs to neither category wrongs himself.

In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that brings no benefit, a heart that has no humility, a soul that is never satisfied, and a supplication that goes unanswered.”

---

## Page 3065

Allah has condemned “hardness of heart,” which is incompatible with reverent humility, in several places. He Most High said:

“Then, after that, your hearts hardened and became like stones, or even harder.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “In Arabic, qasat means ‘grew coarse, dry, and hard.’” Hardness of heart is thus the loss of tenderness, mercy, and reverent humility. The words qāsī and ‘āsī mean “extremely hard.” Ibn Qutayba said: “Qasat, ‘asat, and ‘atat all mean ‘grew dry.’”

The praiseworthy strength of the heart differs from its blameworthy hardness: it should be strong without harshness and tender without weakness. A transmitted report states:

“Hearts are Allah’s vessels on His earth; those dearest to Allah are the firmest, tenderest, and purest.”

This is like the hand, which is both strong and supple, unlike the hardened part of the heel: it is dry and lacks suppleness, even though it has strength.

He, glorified be He, mentioned the heart’s trembling at His remembrance, then mentioned the increase of faith—in knowledge and action—when His Book is recited. One must then rely upon Allah in matters beyond one’s power and obey Him in matters within one’s power. The foundation of this is “prayer” and “zakat.” Whoever fulfils these five as commanded will necessarily fulfil all the other obligations. Indeed, “prayer itself,” when performed as commanded, restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing. As reported from Ibn Mas‘ūd and Ibn ‘Abbās:

“Prayer contains a restraint and deterrent against disobeying Allah. Whoever is not restrained by his prayer from indecency and wrongdoing only grows more distant from Allah through his prayer.”

The statement, “only grows more distant,” applies if the obligatory elements of prayer that he omits outweigh those he performs: neglecting the greater obligation distances him from Allah more than fulfilling the lesser obligation brings him near, and this

---

## Page 3066

is as reported in the Sahīh from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! He watches the sun until, when it is between Satan’s two horns, he rises and pecks out four units of prayer, remembering Allah only a little during them.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people and remembering Allah only a little.”

In the Sunan collections, ‘Ammār reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A servant may finish his prayer with only half of it recorded for him, or only a third…”—until he said, “…or only a tenth.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “You have only that portion of your prayer of which you were mindful.” Although most scholars do not require such a person to repeat his prayer, he is instructed to offer voluntary prayers to make up the deficiency in his obligatory prayer.

It is well known that whoever maintains the prayers with their inward reverent humility and outward actions, and fears Allah as He has commanded, will fulfil the obligations and commit no major sin. Whoever commits major sins—such as unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking wine, or the like—must lose that reverent fear, humility, and light from his heart, even if the foundation of belief remains in it. This is part of the “faith” that is taken from him when he commits a major sin, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it, nor is the thief a believer while stealing.”

For the “God-fearing” are as Allah describes them in His words:

“Indeed, when those who fear Allah are touched by a prompting from Satan, they remember, and at once they see clearly.”

Thus, when a prompting from Satan passes through their hearts,

---

## Page 3067

they remember Allah and see clearly.

Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr said: “This refers to a man who becomes angry, then remembers Allah and restrains his anger.”

Layth reported from Mujāhid: “This refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers Allah and abandons it.”

Desire and anger are the source of evil deeds. When a person sees clearly, he turns back. Then Allah says:

“But their brothers are drawn further into error, and they do not desist.”

That is, the devils draw their brothers further into error, and they do not desist. Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Neither do the humans desist from evil deeds, nor do the devils leave them alone.”

Thus, when a person fails to see clearly, his heart remains in error, and Satan draws him further into it, even though belief remains in his heart and he has not denied the truth. That light and insight, and that reverent awe and fear, depart from his heart.

This is like someone who closes his eyes and sees nothing, even though he is not blind. Likewise, the heart cannot see the truth because of the rust of sins covering it, even though it is not blind with the blindness of a disbeliever.

Reports to this effect have also been transmitted. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in his book (Faith): Yahyā narrated to us, from Ash‘ath, from al-Hasan, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Faith is taken away from him; if he repents, it is restored to him.”

He also said: Yahyā narrated to us, from ‘Awf, who said that al-Hasan said:

“Faith stays away from him as long as he remains in that state. If he returns, faith returns to him.”

Ahmad said: Mu‘āwiyah narrated to us, from Abū Ishāq, from al-Awzā‘ī, who said: “When al-Zuhrī mentioned this hadith—‘The one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it’—I said to him: ‘They say: If he is not a believer, then what is he?’” He said: “He objected to that and disliked my asking him about it.”

Ahmad also said: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Ibrāhīm ibn

---

## Page 3068

Muhājir, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ‘Abbās, who said to his young servants:

“Whoever among you wishes to marry, we will arrange his marriage. None of you commits unlawful sexual intercourse without Allah removing from him the light of faith. If He wills to restore it, He restores it; and if He wills to withhold it, He withholds it.”

Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī said: ‘Abd al-Wahhāb ibn Najdah narrated to us: Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd narrated to us: Safwān ibn ‘Amr narrated to us, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rabī‘ah al-Hadramī, who informed him, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that he used to say:

“Faith is like a garment belonging to one of you: he sometimes wears it and sometimes takes it off.”

He likewise transmitted it through his chain from ‘Umar. It was also reported from al-Hasan directly from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, without a Companion named in the chain. In another hadith, Abū Hurayrah reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When a person commits unlawful sexual intercourse, faith leaves him and becomes like a canopy over him. When he ceases, faith returns to him.”

This will be discussed at greater length elsewhere (if Allah wills).

---

## Page 3069

Section

There are hadiths whose authenticity people have disputed, such as his saying:

“There is no prayer without ablution, and no ablution for one who does not mention Allah’s name over it.”

The first statement is equivalent to his saying:

“There is no prayer without purification.”

This is agreed upon among Muslims, for purification is obligatory for prayer. Prayer is thus negated because something obligatory for it is absent. As for mentioning the name of Allah Most High when performing ablution, there is a well-known disagreement over whether it is obligatory. Most scholars do not consider it obligatory. This is the position of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by al-Khiraqī, Abū Muhammad and others.

The second position is that it is obligatory. This is the view of a group of scholars and the other position reported from Ahmad, adopted by Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and his followers.

Another example is his saying:

“There is no prayer for one who lives near the mosque except in the mosque.”

Al-Dāraqutnī narrated it. Some consider its attribution to the Prophet weak and say that it is a statement of ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. Others, such as ‘Abd al-Haqq, affirm its attribution to the Prophet.

Likewise, his saying:

“There is no fast for one who has not formed the intention to fast during the night.”

The compilers of the Sunan narrated it. It has been said that its attribution to the Prophet is not authentic, and that it is authentically established only as a statement of Ibn ‘Umar or Hafsah. Thus, no one may affirm that a particular wording comes from the Messenger while maintaining that it was intended to deny perfection

---

## Page 3070

that is merely recommended. If these wordings are authentic, they conclusively establish that these matters are obligatory. If they are not authentic, they cannot overturn an established principle grounded in the Quran and Sunnah. No one may interpret the words of Allah and His Messenger to suit his own school of thought without evidence from their words establishing their intended meaning. Rather, scholars’ statements must follow the words of Allah Most High and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; the words of Allah and His Messenger do not follow scholars’ statements.

Thus, when scholars disagree over whether something is obligatory, while the Lawgiver’s wording consistently conveys a particular meaning, an established principle derived from the words of Allah and His Messenger cannot be overturned by an opinion disputed among scholars.

Some people, however, are unfamiliar with the views of the scholars. Having grown up knowing only one opinion, they imagine it to be a matter of consensus. For example, someone may imagine that there is consensus that a person who forgoes congregational prayer and prays alone has discharged his obligation. This is not the case. Rather, scholars hold two well-known views on whether such a prayer fulfills the obligation, and there are also two views within Ahmad’s school. A group of his early followers—as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā reports from them in Sharh al-Madhhab (Commentary on the School’s Doctrine)—and some of his later followers, such as Ibn ‘Aqīl and others, say:

Whoever performs an obligatory prayer alone without an excuse permitting him to do so is like someone who performs the noon prayer on Friday. If he can subsequently perform it in congregation, he must do so. Otherwise, he bears the sin of his action, just as one who misses the Friday prayer bears its sin. The door to repentance remains open.

This is the view of more than one scholar, and most of the reports transmitted from the early generations—the Companions and their successors—support it.

They have cited as evidence the authentic report that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever hears the call

---

## Page 3071

but then fails to respond without an excuse has no prayer.” They answered the hadith concerning the greater merit of congregational prayer by saying that it concerns someone whose excuse permits him to pray alone, just as it is authentically reported that he said:

“The prayer of a man sitting is worth half the prayer of one standing, and the prayer of one lying down is worth half the prayer of one sitting.”

This refers to someone with an excuse, as the hadith relates that he came out to them when they were suffering from fever and were praying sitting down, and made this statement. None of the early generations permitted voluntary prayer while lying down without an excuse, nor is anyone among them known to have done so. Its permissibility is one view within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, but no reliable predecessor among the early generations is known for its proponent, even though this is a matter of widespread practical concern. If every Muslim were permitted to offer voluntary prayers lying on his side while healthy and free of illness, just as he may offer voluntary prayers sitting or riding a mount, the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have explained this to his community, and the Companions would have known it. Given their strong eagerness to do good, some of them would inevitably have done so. Since none of them did, this indicates that they did not regard it as prescribed. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that a Muslim should accord the words of Allah and His Messenger their due weight. Indeed, no one may interpret anyone’s words except according to what that person is known to have intended—not according to whatever meaning those words might bear in anyone else’s speech. Many people, when interpreting texts that contradict their own position, proceed as though “interpretation” consisted merely of mentioning a possible meaning of the wording. Their purpose is to fend off the person citing that text against them. This is mistaken. Rather, everything Allah and His Messenger have said

---

## Page 3072

must be believed. We may not believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in another part. Nor is attending to his intended meaning in one text rather than the other any more justified than the reverse. If he believes that he has followed the Messenger’s intent in the text that agrees with his position, he must do likewise with the other text that he has interpreted. His primary aim must therefore be to ascertain what the Messenger intended by his words. This is the purpose of all permissible tafsīr (explanation) and ta’wīl (interpretation), according to those whose terminology distinguishes their meanings. As for those who regard them as synonymous—as is generally the usage of Quran commentators—ta’wīl means tafsīr. But “ta’wīl” in the words of Allah and His Messenger has a third meaning, distinct both from its meaning in the terminology of Quran commentators and from its meaning among later jurists and scholars of legal theory, as explained at length elsewhere.

The point here is that whenever Allah and His Messenger deny the applicability of a designation for obligatory matters—such as faith, Islam, religion, prayer, fasting, purification, Hajj, and so forth—it is only because an obligatory element encompassed by that designation has been omitted. An example is His saying, Most High:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided and submit completely.”

Since He negated faith until this condition is fulfilled, this indicates that fulfilling it is obligatory upon people. Whoever neglects it is among those subject to the threat of punishment: he has not fulfilled the obligatory faith whose possessors have been promised entry into Paradise without punishment. Allah has promised this only to those who do what they have been commanded. As for someone who performs some obligations and neglects others, he is exposed to the threat of punishment.

It is established by the consensus of the Muslims that it is obligatory to “make the Messenger the judge” in every dispute between

---

## Page 3073

people in their religious and worldly affairs, concerning both the fundamentals and the subsidiary matters of their religion. Whenever he gives a judgment, they must all find within themselves no discomfort at what he has decided and submit completely.

Allah Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They wish to seek judgment from false authorities, although they have been commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“And when they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turning away from you in aversion.”

As for His words, “to what Allah has revealed,” Allah has revealed the Book and wisdom, which is the Sunnah. Allah Most High says:

“Remember Allah’s favor upon you and what He has revealed to you of the Book and wisdom, with which He admonishes you.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you did not know. Allah’s favor upon you has been immense.”

Calling people to what Allah has revealed necessarily entails calling them to the Messenger, and calling them to the Messenger necessarily entails calling them to what Allah has revealed. This is like obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger: the two are inseparable. Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah, and whoever obeys Allah has obeyed the Messenger. The same applies to His saying, Most High:

“And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows a path other than that of the believers”.

These two things are inseparable. Everyone who opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him has followed a path other than that of the believers, and everyone who follows a path other than that of the believers has opposed the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him. If someone thinks that he is following the path of the believers but is mistaken, he is like someone who thinks that he is following the Messenger but is mistaken.

This “verse” indicates that the consensus of the believers constitutes authoritative proof, in that opposing them

---

## Page 3074

necessarily entails opposing the Messenger, and that everything on which they have reached consensus must be supported by an explicit text from the Messenger. Thus, every issue on which consensus and the absence of any dissent among the believers are established with certainty is one concerning which Allah has made guidance clear. Whoever opposes such a consensus falls into disbelief, just as someone who opposes an unambiguous text falls into disbelief.

But where consensus is presumed rather than established with certainty, it may likewise be impossible to establish with certainty that the matter is one concerning which guidance has been made clear through the Messenger. Someone who opposes such a consensus may not fall into disbelief. Indeed, the assumption that consensus exists may itself be mistaken, the correct position being contrary to that view. This is the decisive distinction between opposition to consensus that constitutes disbelief and opposition that does not.

Does “consensus” provide conclusive or presumptive evidence? Some people affirm one or the other without qualification, while others deny both without qualification. The correct approach is to distinguish: where consensus is established with certainty, and it is known with certainty that there is absolutely no dissent among the believers, its truth must be affirmed with certainty. It must also concern something on which the Messenger has made guidance clear, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Another aspect is that when what is obligatory is described by inseparable attributes, this indicates that whenever any one of those attributes becomes evident, what it signifies must be followed. This is like “the straight path,” which Allah has commanded us to ask Him to guide us to. It has been described as Islam, as following the Quran, as obeying Allah and His Messenger, and as the path of servitude to Allah. It is well known that what each of these names designates must be followed. They all designate the same reality, although its attributes vary. Thus, whenever any one of these attributes becomes evident, what it signifies must be followed, for it signifies the same thing as the others. Likewise, the names of Allah Most High, the names of His Book, and the names of His Messenger are like the names of His religion.

---

## Page 3075

The same applies to the words of Allah Most High:

“And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.”

It has been said that Allah’s rope is the religion of Islam; that it is the Quran; that it is His covenant; that it is obedience to Him and His command; and that it is the community of Muslims. All of these interpretations are true.

Likewise, when we speak of the Book, the Sunnah and consensus, what all three indicate is one and the same. Everything in the Book accords with what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, taught, and the Muslim community agrees upon it in general terms: every believer considers adherence to the Book obligatory. Likewise, whatever the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, established as Sunnah, the Quran commands us to follow him in it, and the believers unanimously agree upon this. Similarly, whatever the Muslims unanimously agree upon can only be true and consistent with the Book and the Sunnah.

The Muslims, however, receive their entire religion from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, whereas the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, receives the revelation of the Quran and another revelation, which is wisdom. As he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Indeed, I have been given the Book and something like it along with it.”

Hassān ibn ‘Atiyyah said:

“Gabriel would descend to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with the Sunnah and teach it to him just as he taught him the Quran.”

Thus, not everything brought by the Sunnah must be explained in the Quran. This differs from what those who reach consensus affirm: the Book and the Sunnah must provide evidence for it, for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is the intermediary between them and Allah in conveying His commands and prohibitions, and what He makes lawful and unlawful. The purpose here, however, is to discuss faith.

Another example of this is the Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“No man who believes in Allah and the Last Day hates the Ansār.”

And his saying:

“A sign of faith is love for the Ansār, and a sign of hypocrisy is hatred of the Ansār.”

For whoever knows how the Ansār supported Allah and His Messenger from the very beginning of

---

## Page 3076

their mission, and loves Allah and His Messenger, will certainly love them. His love for them is thus a sign of the faith in his heart. Whoever hates them lacks the faith that Allah has required of him. Likewise, anyone whose heart does not hate what Allah and His Messenger hate—the wrongs they have forbidden, including disbelief, wickedness and disobedience—lacks the faith that Allah has required of him. If he has no hatred whatsoever for anything forbidden, then he has no faith whatsoever, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

Likewise, whoever does not love for his fellow believer what he loves for himself lacks the faith that Allah has required of him. Whenever Allah denies faith to someone, it can only be because of a deficiency in the faith required of him. Such a person is liable to the threatened punishment, rather than entitled to the unqualified promise of reward.

The same applies to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Whoever cheats us is not one of us, and whoever takes up arms against us is not one of us.”

All of this falls into the same category. He says this only of someone who has neglected what Allah has required of him or done what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. Such a person has neglected an obligatory aspect of faith on account of which the designation of believer is denied him. He is therefore not among the believers who are entitled to the promised reward and safe from the threatened punishment.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away after that. Those are not believers.”

“When they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, a group of them turns away.”

“But if the right is theirs, they come to him in submission.”

“Is there disease in their hearts? Or have they doubted? Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will treat them unjustly? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.”

---

## Page 3077

“The only response of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, is to say, ‘We hear and we obey.’ It is they who will be successful.”

This, then, is the scope of the term “faith” when used without qualification in the words of Allah and His Messenger: it encompasses performing obligatory duties and refraining from forbidden acts. Anyone whom Allah and His Messenger deny faith must have neglected an obligation or committed something forbidden. He therefore does not fall within the designation whose bearers are entitled to the promised reward and safe from the threatened punishment; rather, he is among those liable to the threatened punishment.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“He has made faith beloved to you and beautiful in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. It is they who are rightly guided.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī said:

Since some sins constitute disbelief while others do not, He distinguished between them, dividing them into three categories: disbelief; wickedness that does not constitute disbelief; and disobedience that constitutes neither disbelief nor wickedness. He stated that He had made all of them hateful to the believers.

Since all acts of obedience fall within faith, with none lying outside it, He did not list them separately by saying, “He has made faith, obligatory duties, and all other acts of obedience beloved to you.” Rather, He encompassed them all in His words:

“He has made faith beloved to you.”

Thus, all acts of obedience are included in this, for He has made prayer, zakat, and all other acts of obedience beloved to the believers as a matter of religious devotion. Allah has stated that He made these things beloved to them and beautiful in their hearts, in His words:

“He has made faith beloved to you.”

They likewise hate all sins—disbelief, wickedness, and all other sins—as a matter of religious devotion, for Allah has stated that He made these things hateful to them.

Among the statements illustrating this are the words of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him:

---

## Page 3078

“Whoever is pleased by his good deed and distressed by his evil deed is a believer.”

This is because Allah has made good deeds beloved to the believers and evil deeds hateful to them.

I say: His making all acts of disobedience hateful to them necessarily entails their loving all acts of obedience.
