Neglecting acts of obedience is itself disobedience; moreover, a person cannot abandon all acts of disobedience unless he engages in their opposite, which he will therefore love—namely, obedience. The heart must necessarily will something; if it hates all evil, it must desire good. A permissible act becomes good through a good intention and evil through an evil intention. No voluntary act occurs without an exercise of will. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in an authentic hadith:

“The names most beloved to Allah are ʿAbd Allāh and ʿAbd al-Rahmān; the truest names are Hārith and Hammām; and the ugliest are Harb and Murrah.”

His statement that the truest names are Hārith and Hammām is because every human being is both a hammām and a hārith. A hārith is someone who earns and works, while a hammām is someone who frequently forms intentions—which are the beginning of volition. A human being is a living creature, and every living creature has sensation and moves by its will. Thus, whenever a person performs a permissible act, there must be some end toward which his intention is directed. Every intended end is sought either for its own sake or for the sake of something else.

If his ultimate aim and desire are to worship Allah alone, without partner—Allah being his God whom he worships, worshipping nothing else, and whom he loves more than anything else—then his will ultimately leads to seeking Allah’s Countenance. He is therefore rewarded for the permissible acts by which he intends to help himself perform acts of obedience. Thus, it is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A man’s spending on his family, when he seeks reward for it, is charity.”

It is also reported from him in the two Sahīh collections that he said to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās when

---

## Page 3079

he fell ill in Mecca and the Prophet visited him: “You will never spend anything seeking Allah’s Countenance without being raised in rank and standing thereby—even the morsel you lift to your wife’s mouth.”

Muʿādh ibn Jabal said to Abū Mūsā:

“I seek reward for my sleep just as I seek reward for my standing in prayer.”

A report states: “A scholar’s sleep is glorification of Allah.”

If, however, a person’s fundamental aim is to worship other than Allah, good things are not lawful for him, for Allah has made them lawful for His believing servants. Indeed, the disbelievers, those who commit crimes and sins, and those who indulge their desires will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection for the blessings they enjoyed without remembering Him or using them to worship Him. They will be told:

“You exhausted your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them. So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation because you were arrogant upon the earth without right and because you were defiantly disobedient.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Then you will surely be asked that Day about the blessings.”

That is, about giving thanks for them. The disbeliever did not give thanks for the blessings Allah bestowed upon him, so He will punish him for that. Allah has made these things lawful only for the believers and commanded them to give thanks for them, as He Most High says:

“O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah.”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah is indeed pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

In Sunan Ibn Mājah and elsewhere, it is reported:

“One who eats and gives thanks holds the same standing as one who fasts and is patient.”

Likewise, He said to the messengers:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.”

And He Most High says:

“Grazing livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you, but hunting is not lawful while you are

---

## Page 3080

in a state of consecration for pilgrimage.”

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, said:

“And provide its people with fruits—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.”

Allah Most High said:

“As for whoever disbelieves, I will grant him brief enjoyment, then compel him to the punishment of the Fire. What a wretched destination!”

Thus, Abraham asked for good things specifically for the believers. Allah made grazing livestock lawful only for those who observe His prohibition on hunting while in a state of consecration for pilgrimage. He commanded the believers to eat of good things and give thanks to Him.

For this reason, He, glorified and exalted be He, distinguished between His address to people in general and His address to the believers. He said:

“O mankind, eat of whatever is lawful and good on earth, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you.”

“He only commands you to commit evil and indecency and to say about Allah what you do not know.”

“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘Rather, we follow what we found our fathers following.’ Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?”

He therefore permitted people to eat of what is on earth on two conditions: that it be good and that it be lawful. Then He said:

“O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.”

“He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah.”

Thus, He permitted the believers to eat of good things without stipulating that they be lawful, and stated that He had forbidden them only what He mentioned. Anything else, therefore, was not forbidden to the believers. Yet He had not made it lawful through His address; rather, it was covered by His pardon, as in the report from Salmān, narrated both as his own statement and as a statement traced back to the Prophet:

“The lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book, and the unlawful is what Allah has forbidden in His Book. Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.”

---

## Page 3081

In the hadith of Abū Tha‘laba, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has set limits, so do not overstep them; He has forbidden certain things, so do not violate His prohibitions; and He has remained silent about certain things out of mercy for you, not forgetfulness, so do not inquire into them.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden for anyone to eat unless it be carrion.’”

He thus negated the prohibition of anything other than what was mentioned. The rest remained unprohibited through His silence, as a matter of pardon, whereas declaring something lawful requires an explicit address. Hence, He said in Sūrat al-Mā’idah, which was revealed later:

“They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say, ‘Lawful for you are good things and the game caught by the hunting animals you have trained.’”

And further on:

“Today good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them.”

Thus, on that day good things were made lawful for them. Before this, nothing had been forbidden to them except what He had specified as exceptions. Moreover, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade every fanged beast of prey and every bird with talons.” This did not abrogate the Book, because the Book had not declared these lawful; rather, it had remained silent about their prohibition. Prohibiting them therefore constituted the introduction of a new ruling. Hence, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith transmitted through several chains from Abū Rāfi‘, Abū Tha‘laba, Abū Hurayrah, and others:

“Let me not find any of you reclining on his couch when an instruction from me reaches him concerning something I have commanded or forbidden, saying, ‘Between us and you stands this Quran: whatever we find lawful in it, we deem lawful, and whatever we find forbidden in it, we deem forbidden.’ Indeed, I have been given the Book and something like it along with it.”

In another wording:

“Indeed, it is like the Quran, or more. Indeed, I

---

## Page 3082

have forbidden every fanged beast of prey.” Thus, he made clear that another revelation had been sent down to him—the Wisdom, distinct from the Book—and that, through this revelation, Allah had forbidden to him the things he declared prohibited. This did not abrogate the Book, for the Book had never declared these things lawful.

It had only declared good things lawful, and these are not among the good things. He said:

“O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you.”

Thus, the general wording of this verse did not encompass these animals. Yet He had not prohibited them: their prohibition had been left unstated as a matter of pardon, rather than their consumption being authorized.

As for “the disbelievers,” Allah has not authorized them to eat anything, declared anything lawful for them, or granted them any exemption regarding what they eat. Rather, He said:

“O mankind, eat of whatever is on earth that is lawful and good.”

He therefore stipulated that what they eat must be lawful—that is, authorized by Allah and His Messenger. Allah has authorized eating only for those who believe in Him; thus, He has not authorized them to eat anything unless they believe.

For this reason, their property was not theirs by ownership recognized under Islamic law. Such ownership means the authority to dispose of property in a manner permitted by the Lawgiver, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Lawgiver has not permitted them to dispose of property except on condition of faith. Their property therefore remained open to acquisition. If one group of them overpowered another in a manner they considered lawful in their religion and took their property, the takers stood in the same relation to it as those from whom it had been taken.

When Muslims gain control of it and take it as spoils of war, they acquire ownership recognized under Islamic law, because Allah has permitted spoils of war to them and has not permitted them to others. They may conduct transactions with disbelievers concerning what some of them have forcibly taken from others in a manner they consider lawful in their religion. It is also permissible to purchase from some of them what

---

## Page 3083

they have taken captive from others, for this is akin to their taking possession of things open to acquisition. This is why Allah called the wealth that passes from them to the Muslims “fay” (restored wealth): Allah has restored it to its rightful recipients—that is, to those who believe in Him, worship Him, and use His provision to help them worship Him. He created His creatures only that they might worship Him, and created provision for them only that they might use it to help them worship Him.

The term “fay” may also encompass spoils of war, as in the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the spoils of Hunayn:

“Of what Allah has restored to you, nothing belongs to me except the fifth, and even the fifth is returned to you.”

However, because Allah Most High said:

“As for what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you spurred neither horses nor riding camels to obtain it,”

the term “fay,” when used without qualification in the terminology of the jurists, came to mean wealth taken from the disbelievers without spurring horses or riding camels into action. Ījāf denotes a form of setting in motion.

When a believer does something permitted to him, intending to turn away from the unlawful to the lawful to meet his need, he is rewarded for that. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“In the sexual intercourse of any one of you there is charity.” They said, “O Messenger of Allah, when one of us satisfies his desire, is he rewarded for it?” He replied, “Tell me: if he were to satisfy it unlawfully, would he bear a sin? Likewise, when he satisfies it lawfully, he receives a reward.”

This resembles his statement in the hadith narrated by Ibn Umar from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He dislikes being disobeyed.”

This was narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahīh, and others. He thus stated that Allah loves the use of His concessions just as He dislikes acts of disobedience to Him. Some jurists narrate it as:

“Just as He loves that His binding commands be observed.”

But this is not the wording of the hadith. Allah has permitted these concessions only because His servants need them, and the believers use them to help them worship Him;

---

## Page 3084

so He loves that they avail themselves of these concessions, for the generous love their kindness and bounty to be accepted. As he said in the hadith:

“Shortening the prayer is a charity Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity.”

It is also because these concessions enable worship and obedience to Him to be fulfilled. Whatever a person says or does without need, merely to no purpose, counts against him, not in his favor, as stated in the hadith:

“Everything the son of Adam says counts against him, not in his favor, except enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, or remembering Allah.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent.”

He thus commanded the believer to do one of two things: either speak good or remain silent. Hence, speaking good is better than remaining silent about it, and refraining from evil speech is better than uttering it. For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Not a word does he utter without an observer ready at hand.”

Quran commentators have differed over whether all a person’s words are recorded. Mujāhid and others said, “The two angels record everything, even his groaning during illness.” Ikrimah said, “They record only that for which he is rewarded or incurs sin.”

The Quran indicates that they record everything, for He says:

“Not a word does he utter.”

Here, “word” is an indefinite noun in a conditional construction, reinforced by the particle min; this therefore encompasses everything he says. Furthermore, whether a person is rewarded for a particular utterance or incurs sin for it requires the recording angel to know what that person has been commanded and forbidden to do. Establishing that the recording angel possesses this knowledge therefore requires transmitted evidence.

Moreover, a person is commanded either to speak good or to remain silent. If he turns away from the silence he has been commanded to observe and instead indulges in needless speech containing no good, this counts against him, for it is disliked, and what is disliked diminishes his standing. Hence the words of

---

## Page 3085

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Part of the excellence of a person’s Islam is leaving what does not concern him.”

When he involves himself in what does not concern him, this detracts from the excellence of his Islam and thus counts against him. Something need not make him deserving of the punishment of Hell and Allah’s wrath in order to count against him; even a reduction in his standing and rank counts against him.

Hence Allah Most High says:

“It will have the good it has earned, and it will bear the evil it has earned.”

Everything a person does counts either against him or in his favor. If it is something he has been commanded to do, it counts in his favor; otherwise, it counts against him, even if it merely diminishes his standing. The soul is active by nature and is never still. However, Allah has pardoned the thoughts that pass through believers’ minds so long as they neither voice them nor act upon them. Once they act upon them, their actions fall within the scope of commands and prohibitions.

If, then, Allah has made all sins hateful to the believers, while making faith beloved to them—faith which, as everyone agrees, impels them toward all acts of obedience when nothing opposes it—then, if He has made the opposing force hateful to them, the impetus toward obedience is free of that opposing force. Even the Murji’ah do not dispute that faith in the heart calls a person to obedience and impels him toward it, and that obedience is among its fruits and results. What they dispute is whether faith necessarily entails obedience. For although it calls a person to obedience, it faces opposition from the soul and Satan.

Furthermore, if they hate all evil deeds, nothing remains but good deeds or permissible things. Permissible things have only been permitted for people of faith who use them to help them perform acts of obedience. Otherwise, Allah has never permitted anyone to use anything to assist him in disbelief, wickedness, or disobedience. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed both the one who presses grapes for wine and the one who has them pressed, just as he cursed the one who drinks it. And the one who presses them

---

## Page 3086

presses grapes into juice that can be put to permissible use. Yet once it is known that the presser intends to turn it into wine, one may not assist him in disobeying Allah by providing something that is, in itself, permissible. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed him for doing so, because Allah has neither permitted assisting a sinner in his sin nor allowed him what he uses to commit it. Thus, these things are permissible for them only when they use them to help them perform acts of obedience. It follows that, in the absence of evil deeds, they do nothing but good deeds. Hence, whoever abandons all sins must necessarily occupy himself with obedience to Allah.

An authentic hadith states:

“Everyone goes out in the morning and sells his soul, either setting it free or bringing it to ruin.”

A believer must love good deeds and hate evil deeds; doing good must please him, and doing evil must distress him. If this is not the case in some matters, his faith is deficient. A believer may commit an evil deed and then repent of it, perform good deeds that erase it, or suffer an affliction that expiates it. Nevertheless, he must hate it, for Allah has told us that He has made faith beloved to the believers and made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to them. Whoever does not hate all three is not among them. However, Muhammad ibn Nasr says: “The sinner hates them out of religious commitment.”

The response is: If this means that he believes his religion has forbidden them, that he loves his religion, and that this prohibition is part of it, then he does hate them. But if he loves his religion in general while having no hatred for them in his heart, then he lacks faith to that extent, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest degree of faith.”

---

## Page 3087

And in another hadith, also recorded in Sahīh Muslim:

“Whoever strives against them with his hand is a believer; whoever strives against them with his tongue is a believer; and whoever strives against them with his heart is a believer. Beyond that, there is not a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

Thus, it is clear that if the heart does not hate what Allah hates, it contains none of the faith for which one merits reward.

His words “of faith” refer to this faith—faith in its unqualified sense. That is, beyond these three, there is nothing that constitutes faith, not even a mustard seed’s weight. The meaning is: this is the furthest limit of faith; beyond this, there is no further degree of faith. He does not mean that whoever fails to do this has no faith left at all. Rather, the wording of the hadith indicates only the former meaning.

---

## Page 3088

Section

The terms “disbelief” and “hypocrisy” also fall into this category. When disbelief is mentioned on its own in warnings concerning the Hereafter, it includes the hypocrites, as in His words:

“Whoever rejects faith—his deeds have become worthless, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.”

And His words:

“Whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has certainly strayed far astray.”

And His words:

“None will burn in it except the most wretched, who denied and turned away.”

And His words:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’ They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error.”’”

And His words:

“Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them, ‘Did messengers from among yourselves not come to you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?’ They will say, ‘Yes, but the decree of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers.’ It will be said, ‘Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein forever.’ How evil is the abode of the arrogant!”

And His words:

“Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?”

And His words:

“Whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.”

And His words:

## Page 3089

“Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever. They are the worst of creation.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. In some passages, however, “disbelief” is mentioned alongside “hypocrisy.” At the beginning of al-Baqarah, He devotes four verses to describing the believers, two verses to describing the disbelievers, and over ten verses to describing the hypocrites. He, the Exalted, says:

And He says in two surahs:

And He says:

“Have you not seen the hypocrites saying to their brothers who disbelieved…”—to the end of the verse.

Likewise, the term “polytheists” is sometimes mentioned alongside the People of the Book alone, and sometimes alongside the five religious communities, as in His words, exalted is He:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Magians, and those who associated partners with Allah—Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things.”

And (the former case) is exemplified by His words:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists

## Page 3090

would not desist until clear evidence came to them.”

And His words:

“Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever. They are the worst of creation.”

And His words, exalted is He:

“And say to those who were given the Scripture and to those without scripture, ‘Have you submitted yourselves to Allah?’ If they submit, they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, your duty is only to convey the message.”

Since Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was sent, everyone belongs either to those who were given the Scripture or to those without scripture. Every nation that is not among those who were given the Scripture belongs to those without scripture. These include the Arabs without scripture, the Khazars, the Slavs, the Indians, the black African peoples, and other nations possessing no scripture. All these are peoples without scripture, and the Messenger was sent to them just as he was sent to the Arabs without scripture.

His words, “And say to those who were given the Scripture”—addressing only those living in the Prophet’s time, after abrogation and alteration—show that whoever professes the religion of the Jews or Christians belongs to those who were given the Scripture. This expression is not restricted to those who adhered to it before abrogation and alteration, nor is there any distinction between their descendants and the descendants of others.

For if their descendants are among those who were given the Scripture after abrogation and alteration, then the same applies to others, when all of them are disbelievers. He has designated them as those who were given the Scripture in His words, “And say to those who were given the Scripture.” This address is directed only to those whom the Prophet’s message has reached, not to those who have died.

This shows that His words, “And the food of those who were given the Scripture,” encompass all these people. This is the position of the majority of the early and later generations, and the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfah. It is also the position explicitly stated by Ahmad in most of his responses. His statements differed only concerning the Christians of Banū Taghlib. According to the later of the two reports from him, it is permissible to marry their women and eat the animals they slaughter, as is the position of the majority of the Companions.

---

## Page 3091

And his statement in “the other report” that this is not permissible, following ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—was not based on lineage. Rather, it was because they had adopted nothing of the religion of the People of the Book except what suited their desires, such as drinking wine and the like. Some of the Successors, however, thought that this was because of lineage, as is reported from ‘Atā’. Al-Shāfi‘ī and those of Ahmad’s followers who agreed with him adopted this view. They derived further rulings from it, concerning, for example, someone with one parent belonging to the People of the Book and the other not, and similar cases. Indeed, some works by Ahmad’s followers contain no other view. Yet this misrepresents his school and contradicts his explicit statements: the ruling in such cases was never made contingent on lineage, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The term “polytheists” also occurs on its own, as in His words:

“Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe.”

Does it include the People of the Book? There are two well-known views on this among the early and later generations.

Among those who hold that it includes them, some say that the verse remains in force, such as Ibn ‘Umar and the majority who permit marriage to women of the People of the Book, as Allah mentions in the verse in Sūrat al-Mā’idah, which was revealed later than this verse. Others say that its prohibition of marriage to women of the People of the Book was abrogated. Still others say that, rather, they are excluded from its scope and were not intended by the general wording.

After the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, Allah Most High revealed His words:

“And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women.”

Regarding this, it may be said that He only forbade those married to disbelieving women from maintaining their marriage bonds. At that time, they were married only to women who were idol-worshipping polytheists, so women of the People of the Book were not included.

The same applies to the terms “disobedience,” “wickedness,” and “disbelief.” When disobedience to Allah and His Messenger is mentioned without qualification, it includes disbelief and wickedness, as in His words:

“Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger will have the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Such were ʿĀd: they rejected the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.”

He described them as disobeying the messengers because their disobedience to Hūd constituted rejection of the messengers as a whole. Their disobedience was thus directed against all the messengers, like the disobedience of those who said:

“So we denied and said, ‘Allah has sent down nothing.’”

It is also like the disobedience of those who denied and turned away. Allah Most High says:

“None will burn in it except the most wretched, who denied and turned away.”

That is, he denied the good and turned away from obeying the command. People are required to believe the messengers in what they report and obey them in what they command.

Likewise, He says concerning Pharaoh:

“But he denied and disobeyed.”

And He says of the disbeliever generally:

“He neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away.”

Denial concerns what is reported, while turning away concerns what is commanded. Faith consists in believing the messengers in what they report and obeying them in what they command. Another example is His statement:

“As We sent a messenger to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

The expression “turning away,” in the sense of turning away from obedience, occurs in several passages of the Quran

---

## Page 3095

as in His words:

“You will be called to face a people of great might, whom you will fight unless they submit. If you obey, Allah will grant you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.”

His condemnation, in several passages of the Quran, of those who turn away shows that obedience to Allah and His Messenger is obligatory, and that an unqualified command requires obedience and entails condemnation of whoever turns away from obeying it. Likewise, He attaches condemnation to disobedience without qualification in such statements as:

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

It has been said that “forever” is mentioned in the Quran only in threats against the disbelievers. Thus He says:

He says concerning those who act unjustly in matters of inheritance:

“Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, abiding therein, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

Here He qualifies disobedience by mentioning the transgression of His limits, rather than speaking of it without qualification. He also says:

“Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.”

This was a particular act of disobedience. Allah Most High also says:

“Until you lost courage, disputed over the command, and disobeyed after He had shown you what you loved.”

He thus describes a specific instance of disobedience: the archers’ disobedience to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He had ordered them to remain at their post even if they saw that the Muslims had won. Those of them who disobeyed did so by violating this command. Their commander continued to give them orders when they saw the disbelievers retreating, while some of them turned to the spoils.

Likewise, in His words:

“And He has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you,”

He distinguishes three levels.

He also says:

“And that they will not disobey you in what is right.”

Here He qualifies disobedience. Hence it has been interpreted as wailing over the dead. This interpretation was given by Ibn ʿAbbās and has also been narrated as a statement of the Prophet. Likewise, Zayd ibn Aslam said that they must not cry out in woe or scratch

---

## Page 3096

their faces, loosen their hair, or tear their clothes.

Some have said: “This encompasses everything the Messenger commands them concerning the ordinances of Islam and its proofs,” as stated by Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī. The wording of the verse is general: they must not disobey him in what is right. Disobedience to him can only concern what is right, for he never commands anything wrong. However, as has been said, this indicates that obedience to those in authority is obligatory only in what is right, as is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Obedience is only in what is right.”

A similar example is His saying:

“Respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.”

He calls only to that. The qualification here carries no contrary implication, since he never calls to anything else or commands anything other than what is right. This resembles the statement of Allah Most High:

“Do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity.”

If they do not desire chastity, compulsion is impossible. Rather, this wording makes clear the characteristic relevant to the ruling. Another example is the statement of Allah Most High:

“Whoever invokes another god alongside Allah, for which he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.”

And His saying:

“And they kill the prophets without right.”

In all these instances, the qualification serves to explain and clarify, not to exclude cases bearing a different description. Hence some grammarians say: “Adjectives qualifying definite nouns serve to clarify, not to restrict, whereas those qualifying indefinite nouns serve to restrict.” They mean definite nouns that need no further restriction, as in His saying:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and fashioned in due proportion.”

And His saying:

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find mentioned in their Torah and Gospel.”

And His saying:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.”

Adjectives qualifying indefinite nouns also serve to clarify when those nouns have already been sufficiently distinguished. Nevertheless, He conjoins disobedience with disbelief and wickedness in His saying:

“And He has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you.”

It is well known that a wicked person is also disobedient.

And he said:

“A person follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you consider whom he befriends.”

The zawj of a thing is its counterpart. A category is called a zawj because its members resemble one another, as in His saying:

“We caused every noble kind to grow therein.”

And He said:

“And of everything We created pairs, so that you may take heed.”

Several Quran commentators explained this as two categories, two distinct kinds: heaven and earth, the sun and the moon, night and day, land and sea, plains and mountains, winter and summer, jinn and humankind, disbelief and faith, felicity and wretchedness, truth and falsehood, male and female, light and darkness, sweet and bitter, and the like.

---

## Page 3099

“So that you may take heed”—and thus know that the Creator of all pairs is One.

What is meant is not that He will gather their wives with them indiscriminately. A righteous woman may have a wicked husband, or even a disbelieving one, as was the case with Pharaoh’s wife. Likewise, a righteous man may have a wicked wife, or even a disbelieving one, as was the case with the wives of Noah and Lot. But when a woman follows her husband’s religion, she falls within the general meaning of “their counterparts.” Hence al-Hasan al-Basrī said: “And their polytheist wives.” There is no doubt that this verse includes the disbelievers, as its context indicates.

The Quran commentators’ statements have already been cited: the verse includes those given to unlawful sexual intercourse being gathered with others given to it, and those given to wine with others given to wine. Similarly, the following report has been narrated:

“When the Day of Resurrection comes, it will be said: ‘Where are the oppressors and their helpers?’—or he said: ‘those like them.’ They will then be gathered into coffins of fire and cast into the Fire.”

More than one of the early generations said: “The helpers of oppressors are those who assist them, even if only by preparing an inkwell or sharpening a pen for them.” Some of them would say: “Indeed, even those who wash their clothes are among their helpers.”

Their helpers are among “their counterparts” mentioned in the verse. Whoever assists in righteousness and piety belongs among those who practise them, and whoever assists in sin and transgression belongs among those who practise them. Allah Most High said:

“Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in it.”

An intercessor is someone who assists another, thereby forming a pair with him where previously there had been only one. Hence “good intercession” has been explained as helping the believers in jihad, and “evil intercession” as helping the disbelievers fight the believers, as mentioned by Ibn Jarīr and Abū Sulaymān. “Good intercession” has also been explained as a person interceding for another to secure some benefit for him

---

## Page 3100

or deliver him from an affliction, as stated by al-Hasan, Mujāhid, Qatāda and Ibn Zayd. Good intercession is thus assistance in something good that Allah and His Messenger love: benefiting someone who deserves that benefit, or averting harm from someone who deserves to be protected from it. “Evil intercession” is helping someone in something that Allah and His Messenger dislike, such as intercession that wrongs someone or deprives him of kindness to which he is entitled.

Good intercession has also been explained as supplicating for the believers, and evil intercession as supplicating against them. Good intercession has likewise been explained as reconciling two people. All these explanations are correct. The intercessor thus forms a pair with the person for whom he intercedes, since the created being to whom the intercession is addressed either assists him in righteousness and piety or assists him in sin and transgression.

Whenever someone came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with a request, he would say to his Companions:

“Intercede, and you will be rewarded; Allah will decree through the tongue of His Prophet whatever He wills.”

The rest of the passage makes clear that, although the verse includes the wrongdoer whose wrongdoing consists in disbelief, it also includes wrongdoing less grave than that, even though it contains the words, “and what they used to worship.” It is authentically reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

It is also authentically reported from him in the Sahīh that he said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then recited this verse:

In another hadith:

“It is made to appear to him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald-headed serpent, which follows its owner wherever he goes while he flees from it: ‘This is your wealth, which you used to withhold out of greed.

ants.” Ibn ‘Abbās and his companions said:

Whatever they command us to do, we will do, and whatever they forbid us to do, we will refrain from, following their word.” Thus they sought counsel from men and cast the Book of Allah behind their backs.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that their worship of them consisted in permitting what was forbidden and forbidding what was lawful—not in praying to them, fasting for them or supplicating to them besides Allah. This is worship of men, whereas the former is worship of wealth. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained it, and Allah described it as shirk in His words:

“There is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.”

This is therefore a form of wrongdoing that

Allah Most High also says:

“If only you could see the wrongdoers, made to stand before their Lord, exchanging accusations! Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, ‘Had it not been for you, we would have been believers.’ Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed, ‘Did we turn you away from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you yourselves were criminals.’ Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, ‘Rather, it was your plotting by night and day, when you commanded us to disbelieve in Allah and set up equals to Him.’ They will conceal their remorse when they see the punishment. We will place shackles around the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed for anything other than what they used to do?”

And His words in the context of the verse:

“Whenever they were told, ‘There is no deity but Allah,’ they grew arrogant.”

and there is no doubt that it encompasses both forms of shirk—minor and major. ## Page 3106

And he said:

And he said:

Now, if the person who declares lawful things forbidden and forbidden things lawful is a scholar exercising independent judgment, whose intention is to follow the Messenger, but the actual truth has eluded him despite his fearing Allah as much as he can, Allah does not hold him accountable for his error. Rather, He rewards him for the scholarly effort through which he obeyed his Lord. But whoever knows that this is an error concerning what the Messenger brought, yet follows that person in his error and turns away from the Messenger’s words, has a share in this shirk which Allah has condemned. This is especially so if he follows his own desires in doing so and supports that person with his words and actions, despite knowing that he is opposing the Messenger. This is shirk for which its perpetrator deserves punishment.

For this reason, the scholars agree that once someone knows the truth, he may not follow anyone in contradicting it. Their disagreement concerns only whether someone capable of examining the evidence may follow another’s scholarly judgment. If he is unable to make known the truth that he knows, he is like someone who knows that Islam is the truth while living among Christians: if he puts into practice as much of the truth as he can, he is not held accountable for what he is unable to do. Such people are like al-Najāshī and others.

Allah has revealed verses in His Book concerning such people, including His words, Exalted is He:

“Indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them.”

And His words:

“Among the people of Moses is a community which guides by the truth and establishes justice by it.”

And His words:

“When they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized.”

But if someone who follows a scholar exercising independent judgment is unable to ascertain the truth in detail and has done

---

## Page 3107

all that someone in his position can do to exercise judgment in choosing whom to follow, then he is not held accountable if he errs, just as when determining the direction of prayer. But if he follows one person rather than another of equal standing merely out of personal desire, and supports him through his actions and words without knowing that the truth is with him, then he belongs to the people of pre-Islamic ignorance. Even if the person he follows is correct, his own action is not righteous; and if the person he follows is mistaken, he is sinful. He is like someone who interprets the Quran according to his own opinion: even if he is correct, he has acted wrongly; and if he is mistaken, let him take his seat in the Fire.

Such people are of the same kind as the person who withholds zakat, concerning whom the warning was mentioned earlier, and as the slave of the dinar, the dirham, plush cloth, and patterned cloaks. For when someone loves wealth so much that it prevents him from worshipping and obeying Allah, he becomes its slave. The same applies to these people: they have an element of minor shirk and are subject to the warning of punishment accordingly.

The hadith states:

This is discussed at length in connection with the texts that describe many sins as disbelief and shirk.

The point here is that the unqualified term “wrongdoing” encompasses disbelief but is not restricted to it; rather, it also encompasses lesser wrongdoing, each according to its degree. The same applies to the terms “sin,” “offence,” and “disobedience”: they encompass disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. Thus, in the two authentic hadith collections, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which sin is the gravest?’

except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds. For them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful. Whoever repents and does righteousness indeed turns to Allah in true repentance.’”

Close friendship entails mutual love and affection. Hence the saying:

“A person follows the religion of his close friend.”

When two people love one another, each loves what the other loves in proportion to their love. If one follows his companion in loving what Allah and His Messenger hate, their religious commitment diminishes accordingly, until it reaches

---

## Page 3109

major shirk (associating partners with Allah). Allah, Exalted is He, says:

These are “those guilty of major shirk.” As for the “slaves of wealth” who hoarded it, and the slaves of men whom they obeyed in disobedience to Allah, they will suffer a punishment less severe than that of those who associated partners with Allah, either on the plains of the Resurrection or in Hell. Whoever loves something other than Allah will be tormented through it.

Allah, Exalted is He, says:

Thus, “absolute disbelief” is absolute wrongdoing. Those guilty of it will therefore have no intercessor on the Day of Resurrection, as He denies intercession in this verse and in His saying:

“So they will be hurled into it, they and those who went astray, and the soldiers of

## Page 3110

Iblīs, all together. They will say, as they dispute therein, ‘By Allah, we were clearly astray when we held you equal to the Lord of all worlds. None led us astray but the evildoers. Now we have no intercessors, nor any close friend. If only we could return, we would be among the believers.’”

Their words, “when we held you equal,” do not mean that they made them equal to Allah in every respect. No human being has ever said this, nor has it ever been reported of any disbelieving people that they said this world has two identical creators. Even the Magians, who affirm “the two principles: light and darkness,” agree that “light” is good and deserves to be worshipped and praised, while “darkness” is evil and deserves to be condemned and cursed. They hold two different views as to whether darkness came into existence or is eternal. In either case, they did not regard it as equal to light in every respect.

Likewise, the “Arab polytheists” agreed that their lords had no share with Allah in creating the heavens and the earth. Rather, they acknowledged that Allah alone created the heavens, the earth, and everything between them, as Allah relates about them in several verses. For example, He, Exalted is He, says:

And He, Exalted is He, says:

and who sends down water from the sky in due measure, with which We revive a dead land—thus will you be brought forth—and who created all pairs and provided for you ships and livestock on which you ride, so that you may settle upon their backs, then remember your Lord’s blessing when you have settled upon them and say, ‘Glory be to Him who subjected this to us, for we could never have brought it under our control. That is: did a god alongside Allah do this? This is a rhetorical question expressing denial, and they acknowledge that no other god alongside Allah did this.

Those commentators who say that the intended meaning is, “Is there another god alongside Allah?” are mistaken. For they did set up other gods alongside Allah, as He, Exalted is He, says:

“Do you truly testify that there are other gods alongside Allah

He thus denied to all besides Him everything to which the polytheists cling. He denied that anyone besides Him possesses dominion, has any share in that dominion, or is a helper to Allah. Only intercession remained, so He explained that it is of no benefit except for one to whom the Lord has given permission, as He, Exalted is He, says:

“Who can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

And He, Exalted is He, says of the angels:

“They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased.”

And He says:

Thus, this “intercession” that the polytheists imagine will not exist on the Day of Resurrection, just as it is denied by

## Page 3113

the Quran. As for what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said would take place, he reported:

“He will come and prostrate before his Lord and praise Him; he will not begin by interceding. Once he has prostrated and praised his Lord with words of praise that He inspires him to utter, he will be told: ‘O Muhammad, raise your head. Speak, and you will be heard; ask, and you will be given; intercede, and your intercession will be accepted.’ He will say: ‘O Lord, my nation!’ Allah will then set a limit for him, and he will admit them to Paradise. The same will happen a second and a third time. Abū Hurayra asked him: ‘Who will be most blessed by your intercession on the Day of Resurrection?’ He replied: ‘Whoever says “There is no god but Allah” sincerely from his heart.’”

That “intercession” is for those sincerely devoted to Allah, by His permission. It is not for those who associate partners with Allah, and it takes place only with His permission. Its reality is that Allah Himself bestows His favour upon those sincerely devoted to Him alone, forgiving them through the supplication of the intercessor whom He has permitted to intercede. He thereby honours him and grants him the Praiseworthy Station, which the first and last generations will long to attain—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Likewise, in this world he would pray for rain for them and supplicate for them. That was intercession on their behalf, and Allah would answer his supplication and accept his intercession.

Since this is so, “wrongdoing is of three kinds”: there is no intercession for wrongdoing that consists of associating partners with Allah. As for people wronging one another, the wronged person must receive his due; his right is not waived through intercession or anything else. Yet the wronged person may receive his due from the wrongdoer, just as one who has wronged himself may be forgiven through intercession. The wrongdoer in the absolute sense has no intercessor whose plea will be heeded. The monotheist, however, is not a wrongdoer in the absolute sense; rather, he remains a monotheist despite wronging himself. In reality, it is his sincere devotion to Allah that benefits him, making him one of those who may benefit from intercession.

The Quran’s purpose in denying intercession is to rule out associating partners with Allah: a person must worship Allah alone

---

## Page 3114

and neither invoke nor ask anyone other than Him, nor place his trust in anyone other than Him, whether concerning intercession or anything else. He must not rely upon anyone to provide for him, even though Allah brings him his provision through various means. Likewise, he must not rely upon anyone other than Allah to forgive him and have mercy on him in the Hereafter, even though Allah grants him forgiveness and mercy through such means as intercession and others. The intercession that the Quran categorically denies is that which involves associating partners with Allah; such intercession is ruled out altogether. Hence, in several passages, He affirms intercession by His permission. The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that this is only for those who worship Allah alone with sincere devotion. It is therefore an aspect of monotheism, and those entitled to it are the people of monotheism.

As for “wrongdoing in a qualified sense,” it may refer specifically to a person wronging himself or to people wronging one another, as in the words of Adam, peace be upon him, and Eve:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

And the words of Moses:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself.”

And His words, exalted is He:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins.”

However, the statements of Adam and Moses describe particular events and have no general scope. It is known, praise be to Allah, that these did not constitute disbelief.

As for His words:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves,”

this is an indefinite expression within a conditional construction, encompassing everything by which a person wrongs himself. If he associates partners with Allah and then repents, Allah accepts his repentance. It has already been explained that, when used without qualification, a person’s wronging himself includes every sin, major or minor. Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds.”

Here, wronging oneself is mentioned alongside other categories, so it does not include major polytheism. In the two Sahīh collections:

“Ibn Mas‘ūd reported that when this verse was revealed—‘Those who believe and do not taint their faith with wrongdoing’—this weighed heavily on the Companions of the Prophet

## Page 3115

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and they said, ‘Which of us has not wronged himself?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘It refers only to associating partners with Allah. Those who found this difficult thought that the wrongdoing mentioned in the condition meant a servant’s wronging himself, and that security and guidance were only for those who had not wronged themselves. Accordingly, security and guidance are attained only by those who do not taint their faith with this wrongdoing. Whoever does not taint his faith with it is among those granted security and guidance, just as he is among those chosen in His words:

through to His words:

He thus explained that a believer, who will enter Paradise if he repents, may be recompensed for his evil deeds in this world through the calamities that befall him. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “The believer is like a tender shoot that the winds sway, setting it upright at one time and bending it at another. The hypocrite is like a cedar tree that remains standing firm

## Page 3116

in place until it is uprooted all at once.”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is also reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No illness, fatigue, anxiety, sorrow, distress or harm afflicts a believer—not even the prick of a thorn—without Allah expiating some of his sins thereby.”

In the hadith of Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, he said:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which people are most severely tried?’ He replied, ‘The prophets, then the righteous, then those nearest to them in virtue, and so on. A man is tried according to his religious commitment. If his commitment is firm, his trials are increased; if it is weak, they are eased. Reported by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī and others.

He also said:

“Illness removes sins from the one afflicted with it, just as a dry tree sheds its leaves.”

There are many hadiths on this subject. Whoever remains free of all three kinds of wrongdoing will have complete security and complete guidance. Whoever does not remain free of wronging himself will have security and guidance in a general sense: he will inevitably enter Paradise, as promised in the other verse. Allah has guided him to the straight path, which ultimately leads him to Paradise. Yet his security and guidance will be diminished in proportion to the diminution of his faith through his wronging himself.

By saying, “It refers only to associating partners with Allah,” the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not mean that whoever avoids major association of partners with Allah will have complete security and complete guidance. His many hadiths, together with the texts of the Quran, make clear that those who commit major sins are exposed to fear. They have attained neither complete security nor the complete guidance by which they would follow the straight path—the path of those whom Allah has blessed among the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous—without suffering any punishment. Rather, they have a basic measure of guidance to

---

## Page 3117

this path, and they possess a basic share of Allah’s favor and will inevitably enter Paradise.

As for the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “It refers only to associating partners with Allah,” if he meant major association of partners with Allah, his intent is that whoever is not guilty of it is safe from the punishment in this world and the Hereafter with which those who associate partners with Allah are threatened, and is guided to that end.

If, however, he meant association of partners with Allah in all its forms, then it may be said: a servant’s wronging himself—for example, by withholding, out of love of wealth, some of what he is obliged to give—is a minor form of associating partners with Allah. Likewise, loving what Allah hates to the point of giving precedence to one’s own desires over love for Allah is a minor form of associating partners with Him, and so on. Whoever does this loses a corresponding measure of security and guidance. This is why the early Muslims included sins within this wrongdoing when considering it in this light.

## Page 3118

Section

The terms “righteousness” and “corruption” also belong to this category. When used without qualification, righteousness encompasses all good; likewise, corruption encompasses all evil, as explained earlier concerning the designation “righteous person.” The same applies to the designations “one who sets things right” and “one who causes corruption.” Allah Most High says in the account of Moses:

“Do you intend to kill me as you killed someone yesterday? You only wish to be a tyrant in the land; you do not wish to be among those who set things right.”

“And Moses said to his brother Aaron, ‘Take my place among my people, set things right, and do not follow the way of those who cause corruption.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“When they are told, ‘Do not cause corruption in the land,’ they say, ‘We are only setting things right.’ Indeed, it is they who cause corruption, but they do not perceive it.”

The pronoun refers to the hypocrites mentioned in His words:

“Among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ yet they are not believers.”

This wording is unrestricted: it includes those who lived in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those who would come after them. Hence Salmān al-Fārisī said that this verse referred to people who had not yet been created when it was revealed. Al-Suddī also reported from his teachers: “Corruption is disbelief and sins.”

Mujāhid explained it as “failing to obey the commands and to avoid the prohibitions.” These two explanations have the same meaning.

Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as “disbelief.” This is also the meaning of the explanation: “The hypocrisy through which they befriended the disbelievers and disclosed the believers’ secrets to them.”

Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Muqātil explained it as “committing sins.” This, too, is comprehensive, like the first two explanations.

---

## Page 3119

Their statement,

“We are only setting things right,”

has been interpreted as a denial of what they had acknowledged—that is: “We only do what the Messenger has commanded us to do.” It has also been interpreted as meaning: “What we do is right, and our intention is to set things right.” Both interpretations are reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and both are true, for they say both things. They say the first to those who have not discovered their hidden intentions, and the second to themselves and to those who have discovered them. The second interpretation, however, encompasses the first, for their actions include concealing the opposite of what they outwardly profess, and they regard this as setting things right.

Mujāhid said: “They meant that befriending the disbelievers was setting things right, not causing corruption.” Al-Suddī is reported to have said: “This conduct of ours is what sets things right, whereas believing Muhammad causes corruption.” It has also been said that they meant this would serve their worldly interests: if the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gained the upper hand, they would have secured their safety by following him; and if the disbelievers gained the upper hand, they would have secured their safety from them by befriending them.

In light of these two interpretations, His words,

“Indeed, it is they who cause corruption, but they do not perceive it,”

have been explained as meaning that they do not perceive that what they have done is corruption, not reform. It has also been said that they do not perceive that Allah discloses their corruption to His Prophet. The first interpretation encompasses the second and is therefore the intended meaning, as the wording of the verse indicates.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who has sent down the Book, and He protects the righteous.”

He also says:

“Moses said, ‘What you have brought is sorcery. Allah will surely bring it to nothing. Indeed, Allah does not make the work of those who cause corruption prosper.’”

And Joseph said:

“Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”

Either of these terms may also be coupled with something more specific than itself, as in His words:

“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption in it and to destroy crops and livestock. And Allah does not love corruption.”

This has been explained as causing corruption through disbelief, or through wrongdoing; both interpretations are correct. Allah Most High also says:

“That home of the Hereafter We grant to those who do not desire

---

## Page 3120

exaltation upon the earth or corruption.” Earlier, Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was one of those who cause corruption.”

Allah Most High also says:

“For that reason, We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a person, unless in retaliation for a life or for corruption in the land, it is as though he has killed all mankind.”

The first-mentioned killing of a person is itself a form of corruption. However, in cases of killing, the right belongs to the victim’s next of kin, whereas in cases of apostasy, waging war, and unlawful sexual intercourse, the right belongs to the public at large. This is why it is called a right belonging to Allah, and why the latter cannot be pardoned as the former can: the corruption it causes affects everyone. Allah Most High says:

“The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides”—to the end of the verse.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the men of ʿUraynah who apostatized, killed, and seized property. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning people under a treaty who broke their treaty and waged war. Another view is that it concerned the polytheists. Thus, He has linked corruption with apostates who wage war, treaty-breakers who wage war, and polytheists who wage war. The majority of the early and later scholars hold that it also covers highway robbers among the Muslims. The verse encompasses all these groups. Thus, whoever among them repents before being apprehended has Allah Most High’s right waived in his case.

Likewise, He has coupled “righteousness and reform with faith” in many passages, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

“Whoever believes and sets things right—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.”

It is well known that faith is the finest form of reform and the finest righteous deed, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which deed is best?’ He replied, ‘Faith in Allah.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“And indeed, I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does

---

## Page 3121

righteous deeds, and then remains rightly guided.”

He also says:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—they will enter Paradise.”

And He says:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—for them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds.”

Concerning accusations of unchastity, He says:

“Except those who repent thereafter and reform, for Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Concerning the thief, He says:

“But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms—Allah will accept his repentance.”

And He says:

“And the two among you who commit it—punish them both. But if they repent and reform, leave them alone.”

For this reason, according to one of their two opinions, the jurists stipulated that an accuser of unchastity must reform before his testimony can be accepted. They set a period of one year for this, just as Umar did when he gave Subaygh ibn Asal a year. Ahmad likewise adopted this approach concerning the repentance of someone who calls others to religious innovation: he is to be given a year, just as Umar gave Subaygh ibn Asal a year.

---

## Page 3122

Section

If it is said:

“What has been stated about how a word’s meaning varies according to whether it is used without qualification or with qualification—in the speech of Allah, His Messenger, and everyone else—is clear, evident, and undeniable. Yet we maintain that the word ‘faith’ refers to deeds figuratively. Thus, the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches, the highest of which is saying “There is no god but Allah,” and the lowest of which is removing something harmful from the road,’ is figurative. His statement, ‘Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His Messengers,’ and so forth, is literal.”

This is the central argument of the Murji’ah, the Jahmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and everyone who excludes deeds from what the term “faith” encompasses.

We offer two answers. The first is a general discussion of the terminology (literal and figurative). The second concerns this particular issue: assuming that one of the two usages is figurative, which is literal and which is figurative? Is the literal usage the unqualified one, the qualified one, or are both literal? This must be established to know how the word “faith” is to be understood when used without qualification.

First, we say: Expressions that signify meanings may be classified as “literal and figurative”; the same classification may also be applied to their signification or to the meanings signified, if the terms “literal” and “figurative” are used to describe either the signified meaning or the signification. All these usages may occur in the writings of later scholars. But the prevalent view

---

## Page 3123

is that literal and figurative usage are properties of expressions. In any event, this classification is a convention introduced after the first three generations had passed. None of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the renowned imams of learning—such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, and al-Shāfi‘ī—spoke in these terms. Nor did the leading scholars of language and grammar, such as al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, Abū ‘Amr ibn al-‘Alā’, and others like them.

[The first person known to have used the term “majāz” was Abū ‘Ubaydah Ma‘mar ibn al-Muthannā in his book. However, by majāz he did not mean figurative usage as distinct from literal usage] (*). Rather, by the majāz of a verse he meant an expression conveying the verse’s meaning. Accordingly, any legal theorist—such as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and others like him—who says, “Literal usage is distinguished from figurative usage through various methods, including an explicit statement by the scholars of language: ‘This is literal, and this is figurative,’” has spoken without knowledge. He has assumed that the scholars of language said this, whereas none of them, nor any of the early generations of the Muslim community and their scholars, said it. This is merely a later convention, most likely originating with the Mu‘tazilah and other speculative theologians like them. It is not found in the discourse of any of the early scholars of jurisprudence, legal theory, Quranic exegesis, hadith, or related disciplines.

Al-Shāfi‘ī, the first to devote a separate treatment to legal theory, did not make this classification or use the terms “literal” and “figurative.” Likewise, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan has well-known discussions in al-Jāmi‘ al-Kabīr and elsewhere concerning questions that hinge on Arabic usage, yet he did not use the terms “literal” and “figurative.” Likewise, regarding the other imams, there is no record of

> **Footnotes:**
> (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 59):
> It appears that the book’s title has been omitted. It is Majāz al-Qur’ān, as the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, stated (12/277): “The very first to use this term was Abū ‘Ubaydah Ma‘mar ibn al-Muthannā, in the book he wrote on majāz in the Quran.”

---

## Page 3124

the term “majāz” in the words of any of them except Ahmad ibn Hanbal. In his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah, concerning the expressions “Indeed, We” and “We” and similar expressions in the Quran, he said: “This is an instance of majāz in the language. A man says, ‘We shall give you; We shall do such-and-such.’” He thus described this as majāz in the language.

Those of his followers who held that the Quran contains figurative usage—such as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn ‘Aqīl, Abū al-Khattāb, and others—cited this as evidence for attributing that position to him. Other followers of his denied that the Quran contains figurative usage, including Abū al-Hasan al-Kharzī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid, and Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, son of Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī. Muhammad ibn Khuwayz Mindād and other Mālikī scholars likewise denied that the Quran contains figurative usage. Dāwūd ibn ‘Alī, his son Abū Bakr, and Mundhir ibn Sa‘īd al-Ballūtī also rejected it; the latter composed a work on the subject. Some have related two differing reports from Ahmad on this issue.

As for the other imams, none of them—neither Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, nor Abū Hanīfah—nor any of Ahmad’s early followers said that the Quran contains figurative usage. The classification of expressions into literal and figurative usage only became widespread in the fourth century AH, with its beginnings appearing in the third. I do not know of its existence in the second century, unless perhaps towards its end.

Those who denied that Ahmad and others had spoken in terms of this classification said that Ahmad’s phrase “an instance of majāz in the language” meant something permissible in linguistic usage: a single person of high standing who has assistants may say, “We have done such-and-such, and we shall do such-and-such,” and similar expressions. They said: “Ahmad did not mean by this that the expression was used in a sense other than the one for which it was coined.”

Some have denied that figurative usage exists in language at all, whether in the Quran or elsewhere, such as Abū

---

## Page 3125

Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī.

Those who disputed his position said: The disagreement with him is merely terminological. If he concedes that language contains expressions used in a sense other than that for which they were coined, whose meaning is conveyed only through a contextual indication, then this is figurative usage, even if he does not call it that.

Those who defend him reply: Those who divided expressions into literal and figurative usage said: “Literal usage” is the use of an expression in the sense for which it was coined, while “figurative usage” is its use in a sense other than that for which it was coined. Examples are the words “lion” and “donkey,” whether they refer to the animals themselves or, respectively, to a brave man and a dull-witted man. This classification and these definitions entail that an expression was first coined for a particular meaning, after which it may be used either in its assigned sense or in another sense. Hence the well-known position among those who adopt this classification is that every figurative usage must have a corresponding literal usage, whereas not every literal usage has a corresponding figurative usage.

One of their later scholars objected, saying: An expression that has been assigned a meaning but has not yet been used is neither literal nor figurative. If it is then used in a sense other than its assigned meaning, it is a figurative usage with no corresponding literal usage.

All of this would be valid only if it were known that Arabic expressions were first assigned meanings and were subsequently used in those meanings, so that their assignment preceded their use. This, in turn, would be valid only according to the view that languages arise through convention: that a group of rational people gathered and agreed to call one thing by one name and another thing by another name, and that this applies to all languages.

We know of no Muslim who expressed this view before Abū Hāshim ibn al-Jubbā’ī. Both he and Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī studied under Abū ‘Alī al-Jubbā’ī. Al-Ash‘arī, however, renounced the Mu‘tazilī school and differed with them concerning divine decree, the threat of punishment, religious designations and rulings, and concerning

---

## Page 3126

the attributes of Allah Most High, and exposed their contradictions and the unsoundness of their views, as is well known. Al-Ash‘arī and Abū Hāshim then disagreed over the origin of languages. Abū Hāshim said, “They arise through convention,” whereas al-Ash‘arī said, “They are divinely taught.” Others subsequently entered into this discussion. Some said, “They are partly divinely taught and partly conventional,” while a fourth group suspended judgment.

The point here is that no one can report that the Arabs—or, indeed, any nation—assembled a group who assigned all the names found in their language and then began using them after that assignment. What is known and established through mass transmission is simply their use of these expressions for the meanings they intended. Anyone who claims to know of an assignment preceding that usage is making a false claim, for no one has transmitted any such account.

It cannot be argued, “We know this by inference: without a prior convention, usage would not have been possible.”

The reply is: This is not so. Rather, we observe that Allah inspires animals to make sounds through which they understand one another’s intentions. Such communication is called “speech” and “saying,” as in Solomon’s words:

“We have been taught the speech of birds.”

And in Allah’s words:

“An ant said, ‘O ants, enter your dwellings.’”

And His words:

“O mountains, echo his praises, and you birds too.”

The same applies to human beings. Once a child begins to discern things, he hears his parents or caregiver utter an expression while pointing to its meaning. He thus comes to understand that the expression is used for that meaning—that is, that the speaker intends that meaning by it. He then hears one expression after another until he learns the language of the people among whom he has grown up, without their having agreed with him upon any prior assignment of meanings. Indeed, they have not even explicitly taught him the meanings of the names

---

## Page 3127

although he may sometimes ask what certain names denote and be told, just as a language someone does not know may be translated for him, acquainting him with the meanings of its words. Yet if he spends some time among its speakers, he learns this without explicit instruction from any of them.

People may indeed give names to new things unknown to those before them. For example, someone may have a child and give him either an existing name or a newly coined one. The person giving the name may act alone, without agreeing with anyone else, or people may coincide in their naming. Likewise, someone may devise a tool for a craft, write a book, build a city, or do something similar, and give it a name, since it does not belong to an already familiar category with a name in the common language.

Allah has said:

“The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, and taught him speech.”

And:

“They will say, ‘Allah, who causes all things to speak, has caused us to speak.’”

And He said:

“Who created and fashioned, and who determined and guided.”

Thus He, glorified be He, inspires human beings to speak just as He inspires other creatures. If He, glorified be He, taught Adam all the names and presented the things named to the angels, as He has told us in His Book, we nevertheless know that He did not teach Adam every language that all people would speak until the Day of Resurrection, with those languages then being passed down to his children so that they spoke only those languages. Such a claim is plainly false. Only Adam’s children could have transmitted anything from him, peace be upon him, and in the year of the Flood Allah drowned all his descendants except those aboard the Ark. The lineages of those aboard the Ark subsequently died out, except for the descendants of Noah. They did not speak all the languages spoken by the nations that came after them. Indeed, a “single language,” such as Persian, Arabic, Greek, or Turkish, contains differences and varieties that none but Allah can enumerate; and the Arabs themselves

---

## Page 3128

have dialects peculiar to each group that others do not understand. How, then, could all these languages conceivably have been transmitted from those aboard the Ark? Not all of them left descendants; rather, the surviving descendants were Noah’s alone. All people descend from his three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. As Allah Most High said:

“And We made his descendants the sole survivors.”

Thus He left none surviving except his descendants. It is likewise reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “His sons were three.” This was related by Ahmad and others.

It is well known that these three could not possibly have spoken all these languages, nor could all these languages have been transmitted from them. Those who know one language do not know another. If there were only three original transmitters, they would have taught their children, and their children would have taught theirs. Had that been so, transmission would have remained continuous. Yet we find that, among the descendants of a single father, each tribe speaks a language unknown to the others, although their forefather is one and the same.

It cannot be argued that he taught one son one language and his other son another, for a father may have only two sons, while the languages spoken by his descendants are many times that number.
