“A man would embrace Islam at the beginning of the day out of desire for worldly gain, yet before the day ended, Islam would be dearer to him than everything upon which the sun rises.”

For this reason, faith subsequently entered the hearts of most of those who embraced Islam out of hope and fear. And His words, “But say, ‘We have submitted’”

---

## Page 3288

is a command for them to say this, whereas a hypocrite is not commanded to do anything. Then He says:

“If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.”

Yet obedience to Allah and His Messenger does not benefit a hypocrite until he first believes. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others cited this verse as evidence that one qualifies a profession of faith by saying “if Allah wills,” but not a profession of Islam, and that those guilty of major sins leave faith and enter Islam.

Al-Maymūnī said:

“I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal his opinion about saying, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’ He replied, ‘I say, “A believer, if Allah wills,” and I say, “A Muslim,” without qualification.’ I asked Ahmad, ‘Do you distinguish between Islam and faith?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ I asked him, ‘What evidence do you cite?’ He recited:

‘The Bedouins say, “We believe.” Say, “You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”’

He also mentioned other things.”

Al-Shālanjī said:

“I asked Ahmad about someone who says, ‘I regard myself as a believer in terms of legal rulings and inheritance, but I do not know my standing before Allah.’ He replied, ‘He is not a Murji’ite.’”

Abū Ayyūb Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī said:

“Making the qualification is permissible. If someone says, ‘I am truly a believer,’ without saying ‘in Allah’s sight’ and without adding the qualification, that is permissible in my view, and he is not a Murji’ite.”

Abū Khaythama and Ibn Abī Shayba held the same view. Al-Shālanjī mentioned that he asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about someone who persists in major sins and pursues them with all his effort—that is, he strives to commit sin—yet has not abandoned prayer, zakat or fasting: “Is someone in this condition considered persistent in sin?”

He replied:

“He is persistent in sin, as in his saying:

‘The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer.’

He leaves faith and enters Islam. Likewise, his saying: ‘Nor is he a believer when he drinks wine, nor

is the thief a believer when he steals.’ It is also like what Ibn ‘Abbās said concerning His words:

‘Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are indeed the disbelievers.’”

I asked him, “What kind of disbelief is this?”

He replied, “Disbelief that does not take one out of the religion. Just as faith has varying degrees, so does disbelief, until it reaches a point on which there is no disagreement.”

Ibn Abī Shayba said concerning the saying:

Ibn Abī Shayba said:

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī said:

I say: Ahmad ibn Hanbal sometimes maintained this distinction, and at other times mentioned the disagreement and withheld judgment. The latter was his later position.

Abū Bakr al-Athram said in al-Sunnah:

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said:

“If he says that faith consists of words

and deeds, and that it increases and decreases, and then qualifies his profession out of fear and caution, this is not, as they claim, an expression of doubt; the qualification relates only to deeds.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, “Allah Most High said:

That is, this is a qualification without doubt. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said concerning the inhabitants of the graves:

“And we shall, if Allah wills, join you.”

That is, he had no doubt about this, yet qualified it. He also mentioned the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

Meaning: from the grave. He also mentioned the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

I also heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked, “What do you say about Shabāba?”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, “Had you written anything down from Shabāba?”

He replied, “Yes, I wrote down a little from him long ago, before we knew that he held this view.”

He replied, “No, not a single letter.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh was told, “They claim that Sufyān held that one should qualify one’s profession of faith.”

He replied, “This is Sufyān’s well-known position: making the qualification.”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Who reports this from

## Page 3291

Sufyān?”

He replied, “Everyone who related Sufyān’s position on this reported that he made the qualification.” He added, “Wakī‘ reported from Sufyān: ‘We regard people as believers in matters of legal rulings and inheritance, but we do not know what they are in Allah’s sight.’”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Which position do you take?”

He replied, “We hold that one should make the qualification.”

He then cited Ma‘mar’s report from al-Zuhrī: “We therefore consider Islam to be the declaration of faith, and faith to be deeds.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, “‘Abd al-Razzāq narrated this to us from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhrī.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, “Do we then say that faith increases and decreases?”

He replied, “The Prophet’s hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicates this.” He then cited his words:

“Take out of the Fire anyone in whose heart there is such-and-such a weight [of faith]. Take out anyone in whose heart there is such-and-such a weight [of faith].”

“This indicates it.”

‘Īsā al-Ahmar and his position on irjā’ were mentioned in Abū ‘Abd Allāh’s presence. He said, “Yes, that is a pernicious view.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, “Mu’ammal narrated to us: Hammād ibn Zayd narrated to us: I heard Hishām say, ‘Al-Hasan and Muhammad would say, “A Muslim,” but hesitated to say, “A believer.”’”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Did anyone other than Suwayd narrate it?”

He replied, “Not to my knowledge.”

I also heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh say, “Faith consists of words and deeds.”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “What about the hadith that is narrated:

‘Free her, for she is a believer’?”

He replied, “Not everyone includes the words, ‘She is a believer.’ They say, ‘Free her.’”

He said, “Mālik, who heard it from this shaykh, Hilāl ibn ‘Alī, does not include the words, ‘For she is a believer.’”

---

## Page 3292

and some of them did say that she was a believer; when she affirms that, she has the legal status of a believing woman. That is what it means.

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Do you distinguish between faith and Islam?”

He replied, “People have differed over this. Hammād ibn Zayd, they reported, used to distinguish between faith and Islam.”

He was asked, “Who are the Murji’ah?”

He replied, “Those who say that faith consists of words without deeds.”

I say: Ahmad ibn Hanbal never meant that such a person had been stripped of all faith, leaving him with none, as the Khawārij and Mu‘tazilah maintain. Indeed, he explicitly stated in several places that those who commit major sins possess faith by virtue of which they will be brought out of the Fire. He cited as evidence the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Bring out of the Fire anyone in whose heart there is a speck’s weight of faith.”

That view is neither his position nor that of any of the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah. Rather, they all agree that sinful people who are not hypocrites possess some faith by virtue of which they will be brought out of the Fire. This is what distinguishes them from the disbelievers and hypocrites. Yet possessing some faith does not necessarily mean that a person comes within the unqualified, praiseworthy designation of “believer.” The bearer of the revealed Law denied this designation to such people, saying:

“No adulterer is a believer at the time he commits adultery.”

He also said:

“None of you believes until he loves for his brother the good that he loves for himself.”

And he said:

“He whose neighbour is not safe from his harm does not believe.”

He swore to this repeatedly. He also said:

“A believer is one whom people trust with their lives and property.”

The Mu‘tazilah, however, deny such a person the designation of faith altogether, as well as that of Islam. They say, “He possesses nothing of faith or Islam,” and, “We place him in a position between two positions.” They maintain that he will remain in the Fire forever and will not be brought out of it through intercession. This is precisely what they were reproached for.

---

## Page 3293

Otherwise, had they denied him the unqualified designation while affirming that he possessed some faith by virtue of which he would be brought out of the Fire, they would not have been innovators. All of Ahl al-Sunnah agree that he has been deprived of the obligatory fullness of faith, and has thus lost some of the faith required of him. Yet he remains subject to the threatened punishment. Only those among the Jahmiyyah and Murji’ah who say that faith is indivisible dispute this; they say that his faith is complete.

Those who deny him the unqualified designation argue that this designation entails praise and deserving reward, just as when we describe someone as God-fearing, righteous, or upon the straight path. Since these descriptions are not applied without qualification to an evildoer, neither is the designation of faith. As for his inclusion among those addressed as believers, this is because such an address encompasses everyone who possesses any faith: it conveys a command to them, and their sins do not release them from that command.

As for what Ahmad said concerning Islam, he followed al-Zuhrī, who said in connection with the hadith of Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās:

“They used to regard Islam as the declaration of faith, and faith as deeds.”

This may be understood in two ways. The declaration may be intended together with the outward deeds that follow from it. This is the Islam that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained when he said:

“Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, pay zakah, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.”

Or the declaration alone may be intended, without the performance of the outward obligations. This is not what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, defined as Islam.

It may, however, be said, “The Islam of the Bedouins was of this kind.” The response is that when the Bedouins and others embraced Islam during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they were required to perform the outward deeds: prayer, zakah, fasting, and pilgrimage. No one was left with merely uttering the declaration; rather, anyone who openly committed a sin was punished for it.

---

## Page 3294

If, in this report, Ahmad meant that Islam consists solely of the two testimonies of faith, so that whoever utters them is a Muslim, then this is one of the positions reported from him. Another report states that a person is not a Muslim until he pronounces them and prays; if he does not pray, he is a disbeliever. A third states that he is also a disbeliever if he abandons zakah. A fourth states that he becomes a disbeliever by withholding zakah if he fights the ruler over it, but not if he does not fight him. It is also reported from Ahmad that if someone says, “I pay it myself, but I will not hand it over to the ruler,” the ruler has no right to kill him. Likewise, there is a report from him that a person becomes a disbeliever by abandoning fasting and by abandoning pilgrimage if he resolves never to perform it.

Clearly, according to the view that abandoning the pillars constitutes disbelief, Islam cannot consist merely of uttering the declaration of faith. Rather, what is meant is that by uttering it, a person enters Islam. This is correct: he is acknowledged as a Muslim, but no testimony is given concerning the faith in his heart. No conditional qualification is made regarding Islam in this sense, because it is something publicly known. Islam in the sense of fulfilling the five pillars as commanded, however, does admit of conditional qualification. Thus, the Islam regarding which no conditional qualification is made consists solely of pronouncing the two testimonies of faith, for this neither increases nor decreases, and so admits of no such qualification.

People have adopted three positions concerning what the term Islam denotes. Some say that it is faith, and that the two are different names for the same thing. Others say that it is the declaration of faith. Both these positions have a basis that we shall explain. The correct starting point, however, is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained when he was asked about Islam and faith: he defined Islam in terms of outward deeds, and faith as belief in the five fundamentals. When we speak of Islam and faith together, we may not give an answer different from that given by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

When the term faith is used on its own, however, it includes Islam. When Islam is mentioned on its own, a person may, alongside his Islam, also be a believer—this is undisputed—and this

---

## Page 3295

is what is required. As for whether someone may be a Muslim without being called a believer, this has already been discussed. Likewise, does Islam necessarily entail faith? This is the dispute mentioned above, which we shall explain. The Quran’s promise of Paradise and deliverance from punishment is attached specifically to faith. As for Islam alone, the Quran does not attach admission to Paradise to it. Nevertheless, Allah has made it obligatory and declared it to be His religion, besides which He accepts no other from anyone.

Allah sent all the prophets with Islam. He, Most High, says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.”

And He says:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

Noah said:

“O my people, if my presence among you and my reminding you of Allah’s signs have become burdensome to you, then in Allah I have put my trust. So resolve upon your course of action, together with your partners, and let there be no uncertainty about your plan. Then carry it out against me and give me no respite.”

“But if you turn away, I have asked you for no reward. My reward rests only with Allah, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.”

Yet Allah has stated that none escaped punishment except the believers. He says:

“We said, ‘Load into it a pair of every kind, and your family—except those against whom the decree has already been passed—and those who believe.’ But only a few believed with him.”

And He says:

“It was revealed to Noah: ‘None of your people will believe except those who have already believed.’”

And Noah said:

“I will not drive away those who believe.”

Likewise, Allah has stated that Abraham’s religion was Islam. He, Most High, says:

“Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We certainly chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.”

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

“Abraham enjoined this upon his sons, as did Jacob: ‘O my sons, Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.’”

---

## Page 3296

And He says:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while doing good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining to the truth? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

He made felicity conditional upon these two qualities together, saying:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. There shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.”

Likewise, He made it conditional upon belief in the Last Day and righteous deeds, saying:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. There shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.”

This shows that Islam—which is sincere devotion of religion to Allah—together with doing good, namely the righteous deeds Allah has commanded, necessarily entails, and is entailed by, faith accompanied by righteous deeds. For the promise attached to both descriptions is the same: reward and freedom from punishment. The absence of fear necessarily implies the absence of what is feared. Hence He says:

“There shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.”

He did not say, “They do not fear.” Thus, there is no fear for them, even though they fear Allah. He also states that they will not grieve, because grief concerns what has passed. They will therefore not grieve under any circumstances, neither in the grave nor on the plains of the Resurrection. Fear, by contrast, may be experienced by them before they enter Paradise, although in reality there is nothing for them to fear. As He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, there shall be no fear for the allies of Allah, nor shall they grieve.”

“Those who believed and were mindful of Allah.”

As for “Islam mentioned alone, without qualification,” Allah’s Book does not make entry into Paradise conditional upon it, whereas it does make entry into Paradise conditional upon faith mentioned alone, without qualification, as in His words:

“Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of the heaven and earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah

---

## Page 3297

and His messengers.” And He says:

“Give glad tidings to those who believe that they have an honored standing with their Lord.”

He described His intimate friend, Abraham, and those who followed him as having faith, as in His words:

“So Lot believed him.”

He also described Abraham in these terms, saying:

“Which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?”

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

“That was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people.”

He described him as possessing the highest degrees of faith, and he is the best of creation after Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, prayed for provision specifically for the believers, saying:

“And provide its people with fruits—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.”

He also said:

“And make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You.”

“And Moses said, ‘O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.’”

This follows His words:

And He says:

“We revealed to Moses and his brother: ‘Establish houses for your people in Egypt, make your houses places of prayer, and establish prayer. And give glad tidings to the believers.’”

We have already mentioned the unqualified glad tidings given to Muslims in His words:

“We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and as guidance, mercy, and glad tidings for Muslims.”

Allah described the sorcerers as possessing both Islam and faith. They said:

“We believe in the Lord of all worlds,”

“the Lord of Moses and Aaron.”

They also said:

“You resent us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us.”

And they said:

“We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins because we were the first to believe.”

And they said:

“Our Lord, pour out patience upon us and cause us to die as Muslims.”

Allah described the prophets of the Children of Israel as possessing Islam in His words:

“Indeed, We sent down the Torah, containing guidance and light, by which judgment was given

---

## Page 3298

by the prophets who submitted to Allah, for the Jews.” All the prophets are believers.

He described the disciples as possessing both faith and Islam. The Most High said:

“When I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger, they said, ‘We believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

And:

“The disciples said, ‘We are Allah’s helpers. We believe in Allah, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

The essential distinction is that Islam is a religion. The word dīn (“religion”) is the verbal noun of dāna, yadīnu, dīnan, meaning to submit and humble oneself. The religion of Islam, which Allah has approved and with which He sent His messengers, is submission to Allah alone. Its foundation in the heart is submission to Allah alone through worshipping Him alone, to the exclusion of all others.

Whoever worships Him while also worshipping another god alongside Him is not a Muslim. Whoever does not worship Him, but is too proud to worship Him, is not a Muslim. Islam is surrender to Allah: submission and servitude to Him. Thus the linguists explain: aslama al-rajul means “the man surrendered himself.” Fundamentally, then, Islam concerns action—the action of the heart and the limbs.

Faith, by contrast, is founded upon affirmation, acknowledgment, and knowledge. It therefore concerns the heart’s profession, which includes the heart’s action. Affirmation is its foundation, and action follows from it. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained faith in terms of the heart’s belief and submission: belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. He explained Islam in terms of a particular form of submission: the five pillars. Likewise, throughout his other statements, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, faith is explained in terms of the former, and Islam in terms of the latter; the former is higher.

This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart.”

For people can see outward deeds, whereas

---

## Page 3299

the affirmation, knowledge, love, fear, and hope within the heart are inward. They do, however, have necessary consequences that may indicate their presence. Yet a necessary consequence is indicative only if it, in turn, necessarily entails what it indicates. Thus, some of faith’s necessary consequences are acts performed by both the believer and the hypocrite, and so are not indicative … (1)

In the hadith reported by both Abdullāh ibn Amr and Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the believer is the one whom people trust with their lives and wealth.”

He thus described the Muslim in terms of something outward—people being safe from his harm—and the believer in terms of something inward—their trusting him with their lives and wealth. The latter quality is higher than the former: people are safe from someone who is trustworthy, but not everyone from whose harm they are safe is trustworthy. Someone may refrain from harming them while they still do not trust him, fearing that he refrains out of desire for something or fear of something, rather than faith in his heart.

In the hadith narrated by Ubayd ibn Umayr from Amr ibn Abasah, a man asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“What is Islam?” He replied, “Feeding others and speaking gently.” The man asked, “Then what is faith?” He replied, “Generosity and patience.”

Feeding others is an outward deed that a person may perform for various purposes, as is speaking gently. Generosity and patience, by contrast, are two qualities within the soul. The Most High said:

“And urge one another to patience and urge one another to compassion.”

This is higher than the former: to be steadfast in patience and abundant in gratitude, generously showing mercy to others and patiently enduring hardships. This is the opposite of one who was created fretful—distressed when harm befalls him and withholding when good comes his way. Such a person shows neither generosity when blessed nor patience when afflicted.

## Page 3300

The hadith continues:

This report is reliably transmitted from Ubayd ibn Umayr, sometimes without naming a Companion and sometimes with a connected chain to the Prophet. One version reads:

His statement, “The best faith is generosity and patience,” is also narrated through another chain from Jābir, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Likewise, throughout the other hadiths, Islam is explained as submission to Allah with the heart, together with outward deeds. This is illustrated by the well-known hadith narrated by Ahmad from Bahz ibn Hakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:

He replied, “To submit your heart to Allah, turn your face towards Allah, perform the prescribed prayer, and pay the obligatory zakat. These two are brothers, each supporting the other. Allah accepts nothing from a servant who associates partners with Him after embracing Islam.”

In another version, he said:

“To say, ‘I have submitted myself to Allah and detached myself,’ to establish prayer and pay zakat. Every Muslim is inviolable to every other Muslim.”

Another wording reads:

“You say, ‘I have surrendered myself to Allah and turned my face solely towards Him.’”

Muhammad ibn Nasr also narrated a report through Khālid

## Page 3301

ibn Ma'dān, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

Allah Most High has said:

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: “This was revealed concerning the Muslims, commanding them to embrace all the ordinances of Islam.” This does not contradict the view that it was revealed concerning those among the People of the Book who had embraced Islam, or those who had not, for all these people are likewise commanded to do so. The majority explain “into al-silm” as “into Islam,” while another group explain it as obedience. Both explanations are transmitted from Ibn 'Abbās, and both are true, for Islam is obedience, as explained above: it belongs to the category of deeds.

As for His word “completely,” some have said that it means: “Enter, all of you.” Others have said that it means: “Enter into Islam in its entirety.” This is the correct interpretation, for a person is not commanded to perform someone else’s deeds, but only what lies within his own ability. His command “Enter” addresses them all. If “completely” meant “together,” it would follow that a person must refrain from embracing Islam until someone else does so. Embracing Islam would then be commanded only on condition that others join him, as with the Friday prayer. No Muslim says this. If, on the other hand, “completely” means “Enter, all of you,” then all the Quran’s commands, such as His words, “Believe in Allah and His Messenger” and “And establish prayer

and pay zakat,” all belong to this category, yet none adds “all of you.” As for His words, Most High:

they mean: fight them all, leaving no polytheist unfought. This was revealed after the treaties had been repudiated. It does not mean: fight them together, or all of you must fight them, for that is not obligatory. Rather, they are fought as circumstances and the interests at stake require, and jihad is a collective obligation. Rather, the purpose is to encompass all those to be fought.

His words:

admit two interpretations.

The point is that Allah has commanded people to enter into Islam in its entirety, as this hadith indicates. Everything belonging to Islam must therefore be embraced. If something is an individual obligation, a person must perform it. If it is a collective obligation, he must acknowledge its obligatory nature and resolve to perform it should it become incumbent upon him personally; alternatively, he may seek its merit and perform it. If it is recommended, he must acknowledge its goodness and desire to perform it.

In the hadith of Jarīr, a man said, “O Messenger of Allah, describe Islam to me.” He replied, “You testify that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, acknowledge what has come from Allah, establish prayer, pay zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.” The man said, “I acknowledge this.”

This occurs in a lengthy account which relates that he fell into rat burrows, that he was killed and had been hungry, and that two angels were placing fruit from Paradise into the side of his mouth.

His words, “They are the best of deeds,” mean after jihad, because he said, “Then there are two deeds.”

In this hadith, he thus made faith a particular category within Islam, with Islam broader in scope. Likewise, he made migration a particular category within faith, with faith broader in scope, and jihad a particular category within migration, with migration broader in scope.

Islam means worshipping Allah alone, without any partner, devoting religion sincerely to Him. This is Allah’s religion, and He accepts no other religion from anyone, whether among the earlier or later generations. Since messengers have been sent to us, worshipping Him can only be through what His messengers commanded, not through what contradicts it, for that is disobedience. Allah made Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the last of the messengers. Thus, no one is a Muslim unless he testifies that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. It is through this declaration that a person enters Islam.

Whoever says, “Islam is the declaration,” intending this meaning, has spoken the truth. There must then be a commitment to the outward deeds commanded by the Messenger, such as the five pillars. Whoever neglects any of these has his Islam diminished

## Page 3305

in proportion to what he neglects of these, as stated in the hadith:

When a person performs these deeds sincerely for Allah Most High, He rewards him for them. This can only occur when he affirms in his heart that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. He thus possesses this affirmation as a measure of faith. Yet this affirmation does not necessarily mean that he possesses certainty admitting no doubt, engages in jihad, or possesses the other qualities that distinguish a believer from a Muslim who is not a believer.

Many people who are Muslims both inwardly and outwardly possess this Islam, together with the faith it necessarily entails, but have not attained certainty and jihad. They are rewarded for their Islam and their general affirmation of the Messenger. They may not know that he brought a Book, that an angel came to him, or that he conveyed a particular teaching. If it has not reached them that the Messenger conveyed something, they are not required to affirm it in detail. Nevertheless, they must affirm that he is the Messenger of Allah and that he is truthful in everything he relates from Allah.

The faith that distinguishes the believer, however, includes detailed knowledge, reassurance, and certainty. It is thus distinct in its character and degree, both quantitatively and qualitatively. For those believers possess faith in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the details of resurrection and divine decree that these Muslims do not know. Their hearts also possess a degree of certainty, steadfastness, and abiding conviction that these Muslims lack. Those are the true believers.

Every believer must necessarily be a Muslim, for faith necessarily entails deeds. But not every Muslim is a believer with faith in this unqualified sense, because

## Page 3306

submission to Allah and acting for His sake do not depend on this particular faith. A person finds this distinction within himself and recognizes it in others. In general, when people embrace Islam after disbelief or are born into Islam, adhere to its laws, and obey Allah and His Messenger, they are Muslims and possess faith in a general sense. Yet the reality of faith enters their hearts only gradually, if Allah grants them this. Otherwise, many people never attain certainty or engage in jihad. Were doubts raised in their minds, they would doubt; were they commanded to engage in jihad, they would not do so. They are neither disbelievers nor hypocrites. Rather, their hearts lack the knowledge, understanding, and certainty needed to ward off doubt, and their love for Allah and His Messenger is not strong enough for them to give it precedence over family and wealth. If such people are spared trials and die, they will enter Paradise.

But if they are tested by someone who presents specious arguments that cause them to doubt, then unless Allah blesses them with what dispels that doubt, they become doubtful and pass into a form of hypocrisy. Likewise, if jihad becomes an individual obligation upon them and they do not undertake it, they become subject to the threatened punishment. Thus, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, arrived in Medina, most of its inhabitants embraced Islam. Then, when trials and tribulations came, some fell into hypocrisy. Had these people died before being tested, they would have died as Muslims and entered Paradise, though they would not have been among the true believers who were tested and whose sincerity became manifest.

Allah Most High says:

The interpretation some give of such verses—that they disbelieved after professing faith with their tongues, while their hearts had disbelieved from the outset—is unsound. For faith professed by the tongue while the heart disbelieves is already accompanied by disbelief. It would therefore not be said, “You have disbelieved after having believed,” since in reality they had always been disbelievers. If what is meant is, “You openly displayed disbelief after openly displaying faith,” they had not disclosed it to people, but only to their inner circle, and with their inner circle they had always been like this.

Rather, when they became hypocrites, feared that a surah would be revealed exposing the hypocrisy in their hearts, and uttered words of mockery, they became disbelievers after having believed. The wording does not indicate that they had always been hypocrites. Allah Most High also says:

having believed” and “after embracing Islam” mean the same thing. They may also have remained hypocrites all along, never having been in a state in which they possessed any faith, for they openly manifested disbelief and apostasy. This is why He called them to repent, saying:

## Page 3311

for they did not prostrate to Him in this world, but intended only to be seen by people. Recompense in the Hereafter corresponds to one’s deeds in this world. It concerns those among them who believed and then disbelieved; these are the ones who will be given a light in the Hereafter which will then be extinguished.

For this reason, He said:

to Islam inwardly. Qatādah and Muqātil said, “They will not turn back from their misguidance.” Al-Suddī said, “They will not return to Islam,” meaning inwardly, since outwardly they profess it. This parable applies only to this worldly life, and it describes some of them: those who believed and then disbelieved.

As for those who were always hypocrites, He set forth the other parable for them, saying:

This is the more correct of the two views. The commentators differed over whether both parables describe all of them, or whether this parable describes only some of them. There are two views on this, and the second is correct, because He said, “Or like a rainstorm.” The word “or” affirms only one of the two alternatives. This indicates that they are described by these two parables: none falls outside them, but some resemble the one and others resemble the other. If all of them resembled both parables, He would not have used “or,” but rather the conjunction “and.”

The claim that “or” here indicates a choice—as when one says, “Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sīrīn”—has no basis, because a choice is offered in commands and requests, not in statements. Likewise, the claim that “or” means “and,” or is intended to make those addressed uncertain

---

## Page 3312

or to leave matters obscure to them, is groundless. Allah intends His parables to clarify and impart understanding, not to cause doubt or obscurity. Their purpose is to make the believers understand the condition of these people. This is indicated by His saying in the first parable:

“Deaf, dumb and blind.”

In the second, He says:

“They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, fearing death. But Allah encompasses the disbelievers. The lightning almost snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights the way for them, they walk in it; but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah has power over all things.”

Thus, in the second parable, He makes clear that they hear and see: “Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight.” In the first, they could see, but then became enveloped “in darkness, unable to see”—“deaf, dumb and blind.” In the second, “Whenever it lights the way for them”—the lightning—“they walk in it; but when darkness covers them, they stand still.” They therefore experience two conditions: light and darkness, whereas the former remain in darkness. The first describes someone who was in light and then entered darkness. The second describes someone who settles neither in light nor in darkness; rather, his circumstances keep changing, causing him to stand still and doubt.

This is further clarified by the fact that He, glorified be He, also sets forth two parables for the disbelievers, using the conjunction “or.” He says:

“As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage on a level plain, which a thirsty person mistakes for water. But when he reaches it, he finds it to be nothing; instead, he finds Allah there, who pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.

“Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds: layers of darkness, one above another. When he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

Thus, the first

---

## Page 3313

is a parable of disbelief whose adherent thinks he follows the truth, while in fact he follows falsehood:

“What of one whose evil deeds have been made appealing to him, so that he regards them as good?”

He does not know, nor does he know that he does not know. Hence the comparison to a mirage on a level plain. The second is a parable of disbelief whose adherent holds no belief at all, but is in “layers of darkness, one above another.” So profound is his ignorance that he does not even believe himself to be following the truth; rather, he has remained ignorant and astray amid accumulated darkness.

Moreover, a hypocrite or disbeliever may sometimes exhibit one of these characteristics and sometimes the other. The distinction between the two parables thus reflects differences both between individuals and between their states. In any case, what one parable illustrates is not identical to what the other illustrates, since the two parables differ in both imagery and meaning. Hence only one parable is given for faith, because truth is one: it is likened to light. Those others, however, are likened to an illusory light, such as a mirage on a level plain, or to accumulated darkness. Likewise, the hypocrite is likened to someone who could see and then became blind, or to someone in an unsettled state who hears and sees things from which he derives no benefit.

It is thus clear that some hypocrites had believed and then inwardly fell into disbelief. Reports that certain men believed and then became hypocrites are widespread among scholars of hadith, Quranic exegesis and prophetic biography. This happened for various reasons.

One was the matter of the direction of prayer: when it was changed, a group abandoned faith because of it. It was a trial by which Allah tested the people. The Most High says:

“We appointed the direction of prayer you used to face only so that We might know who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels. It was indeed a great burden, except for those whom Allah guided.”

## Page 3314

He said:

That is, when it was changed. The meaning is that the Kaaba is the direction of prayer which We knew We would appoint for you. The Kaaba, its mosque and its sanctuary are far superior to Jerusalem. It is the Ancient House and the direction of prayer of Abraham and other prophets. Allah never commanded anyone—not Moses, Jesus or anyone else—to pray towards Jerusalem. We would therefore never have made it your permanent direction of prayer. Rather, We initially appointed it as the direction of prayer so that, by turning you away from it, We might test the people and distinguish those who follow the Messenger from those who turn back on their heels. The Most High also says:

“and so that He might know those who acted hypocritically. Allah knows best what they conceal.”

His words, “and so that He might know those who acted hypocritically,” plainly refer to those who newly engaged in hypocrisy. This includes both those who had not previously been hypocrites and those who had been hypocrites and then renewed their hypocrisy.

His words, “That day they were closer to disbelief than to faith,” show that before then they had not been closer to disbelief than to faith. Rather, they had either been equally close to both or closer to faith. And this was indeed the case, for when Ibn Ubayy

When the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought his religion, and Allah made its beauty and light manifest, people’s hearts inclined towards it. Many of them also held Ibn Ubayy in very high esteem and were loyal to him, while Ibn Ubayy had not openly shown any opposition that would necessitate a separation.

Hence, Allah Most High says:

Thus, no misgivings arose in them during trials that unsettle faith in people’s hearts. Misgivings can affect both the heart’s knowledge and its actions, whereas doubt affects knowledge alone. Hence, only someone whose heart is at peace in both knowledge and action can be described as possessing certainty. If someone knows the truth, but calamity or fear causes him profound anguish, he does not possess certainty.

People in general cannot escape these whisperings. Some yield to them and become disbelievers or hypocrites. Others have hearts so overwhelmed by desires and sins that they do not notice these whisperings until they seek to follow the religion; they then become either believers or hypocrites.

This is why people experience whisperings during prayer that they do not experience when they are not praying. Satan intensifies his attacks upon a servant when he wishes to turn to his Lord, draw near to Him, and commune with Him. Those who pray therefore experience what others do not, and those distinguished in knowledge and religious devotion experience more of this than ordinary people. Hence, seekers of knowledge and those devoted to worship experience whisperings and doubts that others do not. The latter have not followed Allah’s law and way; rather, they pursue their desires, heedless of the remembrance of their Lord. This is what Satan seeks, whereas the case of those who turn toward their Lord through knowledge and worship is different.

for he is their enemy, seeking to turn them away from Allah. The Most High says:

## Page 3321

Section

It should be understood that once the explanation and intended meaning of expressions found in the Quran and hadith are known from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, there is no need to establish their meaning by appealing to the statements of linguists or anyone else.

For this reason, the jurists have said: “Terms are of three kinds.” Some are defined by revealed law, such as prayer and obligatory alms; some are defined by language, such as the sun and the moon; and some are defined by custom, such as taking possession and the word “kindness” in His saying:

“And live with them in kindness.”

The same applies to similar expressions.

It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“The interpretation of the Quran is of four kinds: an interpretation that the Arabs understand from their language; an interpretation of which no one is excused for being ignorant; an interpretation known to scholars; and an interpretation known only to Allah. Whoever claims knowledge of the last is a liar.”

The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has explained what is meant by prayer, obligatory alms, fasting, pilgrimage, and similar terms in the words of Allah and His Messenger. The same applies to the term “intoxicants” and others: their meanings are known through that explanation. If anyone sought to interpret them differently from the Prophet’s explanation, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that interpretation would not be accepted.

As for discussing their derivation and how they convey their meanings, that belongs to rhetorical analysis. Explaining the reasons underlying rulings adds to knowledge and elucidates the wisdom of the Quran’s wording. However, understanding what these expressions mean does not depend on this. The terms faith, Islam, hypocrisy, and unbelief are of still greater importance than all these;

---

## Page 3322

for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has explained the meaning of these terms so clearly that there is no need to establish it through etymology, examples of Arab usage, or similar evidence. Thus, to determine what these terms denote, one must refer to the explanation given by Allah and His Messenger, for it is fully adequate and sufficient. Indeed, their general meanings are known to scholars and ordinary people alike.

Anyone who considers what the Khawārij and the Murjiʾah say about the meaning of faith knows with undeniable certainty that it contradicts the Messenger’s teaching. One also knows with undeniable certainty that obedience to Allah and His Messenger is part of the completeness of faith, and that the Prophet did not regard everyone who committed a sin as a disbeliever.

One also knows this: suppose a group were to say to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“We believe in our hearts, without any doubt, in what you have brought us, and we profess the two testimonies of faith with our tongues. However, we will not obey any of your commands or prohibitions. We will neither pray nor fast nor perform pilgrimage. We will not speak truthfully, fulfil trusts, keep covenants, maintain ties of kinship, or do any of the good you have commanded. We will drink intoxicants and openly commit illicit intercourse with women forbidden to us in marriage. We will kill whomever we can among your Companions and your community, and seize their wealth. Indeed, we will kill you too and fight against you alongside your enemies.”

Could any rational person imagine that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say to them:

“You are believers whose faith is complete. You are among those for whom I will intercede on the Day of Resurrection, and there is hope that none of you will enter the Fire”?

Rather, every Muslim knows with undeniable certainty that he would say to them, “You are the most extreme disbelievers in what I have brought,” and would behead them if they did not repent of that.

Likewise, every Muslim knows that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not regard a drinker of intoxicants, a fornicator, one who slanders another’s chastity, or a thief as apostates who must be put to death. Rather, the Quran and the mass-transmitted reports from him make clear that these people have punishments other than the punishment for apostasy from Islam

---

## Page 3323

as Allah mentions in the Quran the flogging of those who slander others’ chastity and those who commit fornication, and the cutting off of a thief’s hand. This is also established through mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Had they been apostates, he would have put them to death. Thus, the falsity of both positions is known with undeniable certainty from the religion of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The innovators fell into error only because they turned away from this approach and began to base the religion of Islam on premises they assumed to be sound, whether concerning what words signify or concerning rational concepts. They do not reflect on the explanations given by Allah and His Messenger. Any premises that contradict those explanations are necessarily misguidance. For this reason, Ahmad, in his well-known epistle, refuted those who cling to what they perceive as the apparent meaning of the Quran without drawing on the explanations of the Messenger, the Companions, and the Successors. He likewise discussed this in his letter to Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Jurjānī refuting the Murjiʾah. This is the approach of the other imams of the Muslims: they do not depart from the Messenger’s explanation whenever they have access to it. Whoever departs from their path falls into innovations that entail saying about Allah and His Messenger what he does not know, or what is untrue. This is something Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Allah Most High says concerning Satan:

“He only commands you to evil and immorality and to say about Allah what you do not know.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken from them that they would not say about Allah except the truth?”

This is a form of interpreting the Quran according to one’s own opinion, concerning which the hadith states:

“Whoever speaks about the Quran according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire.”

An example of this is that, when the Murjiʾah turned away from understanding the words of Allah and His Messenger, they began discussing what “faith,” “Islam,” and other terms denote through methods they had invented, such as

---

## Page 3324

saying:

“Linguistically, faith means affirmation. The Messenger addressed people only in the language of the Arabs, without changing it; therefore, what he meant by faith was affirmation.”

They then said: “Affirmation takes place only in the heart and on the tongue, or in the heart alone. Thus, deeds are not part of faith.” Their principal evidence that faith means affirmation is His statement:

“But you would not believe us.”

That is, “You would not affirm the truth of what we say.”

They may be answered as follows: The term “faith” occurs in the Quran and hadith more frequently than other terms. It is the foundation of the religion, through which people emerge from darkness into light. Through it, the blessed are distinguished from the wretched, and one knows whom to befriend and whom to oppose. The entire religion rests upon this, and every Muslim needs to understand it. Could the Messenger have neglected to explain all this and left it dependent on these two premises?

It is well known that the evidence they cite to establish that faith means affirmation comes from the Quran. Yet the meaning of faith has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through transmission far more widespread than that of the wording of this expression. The entire Muslim community needs to know what faith is, and so they transmit its meaning, unlike a particular word in a surah. Most believers had not memorized this surah. The explanation of the foundation of the religion therefore cannot be made to rest on premises such as these.

This is why disputes and confusion have proliferated among those who turned away from Allah’s straight path and followed other paths. They became among those who divided their religion and became sects, and among those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. This is a general, unrestricted argument.

It may then be said: Neither of these two premises is conceded. Who says that the word “faith” is synonymous with “affirmation”? Even granting that the meaning is sound when the latter is used in this passage, why

---

## Page 3325

do you say that this entails synonymy? If you said, “You do not submit to us,” instead of “You do not believe us,” the meaning would be sound. But why do you say that this is what the word mu’min (“one who believes”) means?

When Allah says, “Establish prayer,” someone could instead say, “Complete prayer,” “Persist in prayer,” “Commit yourselves to prayer,” or “Perform prayer,” and the meaning would be sound. Yet this does not establish the meaning of “establish.” To say that one expression is synonymous with another is to say that it conveys that very meaning.

Furthermore, it may be said that the two expressions are not synonymous, for several reasons:

(First: When one accepts a speaker’s report as true, one says saddaqahu (“he believed him”), not āmanahu or āmana bihi. Rather, one says āmana lahu (“he believed him”), as in His statement:

“So Lot believed him.”

And His statement:

“But none believed Moses except some young people from his own people.”

Pharaoh said:

“You believed him before I gave you permission!”

They said to Noah:

“Should we believe you when the lowest of people follow you?”

And Allah Most High said:

“Say: He listens for your good; he believes in Allah and believes the believers.”

They also said:

“Should we believe two men like ourselves, while their people are our slaves?”

And He said:

“If you do not believe me, then leave me alone.”

If it is objected, “But one can say, ‘You do not believe us,’ using musaddiq with lanā,” the answer is: The preposition lām can accompany an expression that normally takes a direct object when its grammatical governing force is weakened—either because it follows its object, because it is an active participle or verbal noun, or because both factors are present.

Thus one says, “So-and-so worships Allah, fears Him, and is mindful of Him.” When using the active participle, however, one says, “He is a worshipper of his Lord, mindful of his Lord, and fearful of his Lord.” Likewise, one says, “So-and-so dreads Allah,” and then, “He is one who dreads his Lord,” using lām with the active participle.

When the verb is used but placed after its object, its governing force is strengthened by lām, as in His statement:

“In their inscription were guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord.”

Yet He also said:

“So stand in awe of Me alone.”

Here He made the verb transitive

---

## Page 3326

directly, whereas in the other passage He included lām. Here, His expression fa-iyyāya (“Me alone”) is fuller than fa-lī (“for Me”). There, His expression li-rabbihim (“of their Lord”) is fuller than rabbihim (“their Lord”). The independent accusative pronoun is more complete than the genitive pronoun yā’. In the other passage, however, an explicit noun is used, so strengthening it with lām is more appropriate and complete than leaving it without that preposition.

Another example is His statement:

“If you can interpret dreams.”

Here the wording is li-l-ru’yā taʿburūn, although one says ʿabartu ru’yāhu (“I interpreted his dream”). Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, they are enraging us.”

Here the wording is lanā la-ghā’izūn, although one says ghiztuhu (“I enraged him”), not ghiztu lahu. There are many such examples. Thus, in the expression mā anta bi-musaddiqin lanā (“You do not believe us”), lām is included because musaddiq is an active participle. Otherwise, one says saddaqtuhu (“I believed him”), not saddaqtu lahu. Had they used the verb, they would have said mā saddaqtanā (“You did not believe us”).

This differs from the word īmān (“belief”), which always takes a pronominal object through lām. One never says āmantuhu; rather, one says āmantu lahu (“I believed him”), just as one says aqrartu lahu (“I acknowledged what he said”). Explaining it in terms of acknowledgment is therefore closer than explaining it in terms of accepting something as true, although there is a distinction between the two.

(Second: It is not synonymous in meaning with tasdīq (“accepting as true”). In Arabic, anyone reporting something witnessed or unseen may be told sadaqta (“You have spoken the truth”), just as he may be told kadhabta (“You have lied”). If someone says, “The sky is above us,” one may say of him, “He has spoken the truth,” just as one may say, “He has lied.”

The word īmān, however, is used only concerning a report about something unseen. There is no attested usage in which someone reporting something witnessed—for example, “The sun has risen” or “It has set”—is spoken of using āmannāhu, as he would be using saddaqnāhu (“We believed him”). Thus, concerning hadith transmitters, witnesses, and the like, one says saddaqnāhum (“We believed them”), not āmannā lahum.

Īmān is derived from amn (“security”). It is therefore used only concerning a report with which its speaker is entrusted, such as a matter unseen about which the speaker is trusted. Hence, the expression āmana lahu is never found in the Quran or elsewhere except in this kind of context. And when two people share knowledge of something,

---

## Page 3327

one says, “One has accepted the other’s statement as true,” but not “He has believed him” (āmana lahu), since it was not a matter beyond his knowledge about which he had entrusted the other. Hence Allah says:

“So Lot believed him.”

“Should we believe two human beings like ourselves?”

“You have believed him.”

“He believes in Allah and believes the believers.”

That is, he accepts as true what they tell him concerning matters beyond his knowledge, regarding them as trustworthy in that respect. Thus, alongside accepting something as true, the term conveys trust and trustworthiness, as both its usage and derivation indicate. Hence they said:

“But you will not believe us.”

That is, you will neither acknowledge our report nor trust it nor feel reassured by it, even if we are telling the truth, because he did not regard them as trustworthy in that matter. Even if they spoke the truth, he would not trust them.

(Third: In Arabic, īmān (“belief”) is not contrasted with declaring something false in the way that tasdīq (“accepting as true”) is. It is well known in Arabic that anyone reporting something may be told, “You have spoken the truth,” or “You have lied,” and one may say, “We accepted his statement as true,” or “We declared it false.” But one does not say of every person reporting something, “We believed him” (āmannā lahu), or “We declared him a liar”; nor does one say, “You believe him” (mu’min lahu), or “You declare him a liar.” Rather, the familiar opposite of īmān is kufr (“disbelief”).

One says, “He is a believer,” or “He is a disbeliever.” Disbelief is not confined to declaring something false. Indeed, if someone were to say, “I know that you are truthful, but I will not follow you. Rather, I will oppose you with hostility, hate you, and defy you rather than agree with you,” his disbelief would be even greater. Since disbelief, which is the opposite of faith, is not merely declaring something false, it follows that faith is not merely accepting something as true. Rather, if disbelief may consist either of declaring something false or of opposition, hostility, and refusal without denying its truth, then faith must consist of accepting the truth together with agreement, loyalty, and submission. Merely accepting something as true is not enough.

Islam therefore forms part of what īmān denotes, just as refusing to submit while accepting the truth forms part of what kufr denotes. Every believer must therefore be a Muslim who submits to the command—and this is action.

---

## Page 3328

If it is objected, “The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained faith by specifying what one believes in,” the reply is:

The Messenger mentioned what one believes in, not whom one believes. He himself must both be believed in and be believed. Belief in him, insofar as it affirms his reality, concerns something unseen to us of which we have been informed. Yet not everything unseen that we believe in must be obeyed. By contrast, the obligation to believe him entails obeying him. The Messenger must both be believed in and be believed; this distinction should therefore be understood. Moreover, obedience to him is obedience to Allah, and obedience to Allah is part of the completeness of faith in Him.

Fourth: Some people say that īmān (faith) derives linguistically from amn (security), which is the opposite of fear. Thus, āmana means “to enter a state of security.” They cite the following verse of poetry: … (1).

As for the “second premise,” the response is this: even assuming that faith is synonymous with accepting something as true, there are two answers to their assertion that this acceptance can occur only in the heart or through the tongue.

The first is to reject that assertion. Actions too are called tasdīq (confirmation), as established in the Sahīh, where the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The eyes commit adultery, and their adultery is looking; the ear commits adultery, and its adultery is listening; the hand commits adultery, and its adultery is grasping; the foot commits adultery, and its adultery is walking. The heart wishes for this and desires it, and the private parts confirm it or deny it.”

The linguists and various groups among the early and later generations likewise stated this. Al-Jawharī said:

“The word siddīq, formed on the same pattern as fissīq, denotes someone who constantly affirms the truth. It may also denote someone whose deeds bear out his words.”

Al-Hasan al-Basrī said:

“Faith is neither outward adornment nor wishful thinking. Rather, it is what settles firmly in the hearts and is confirmed by deeds.”

This
