Then Allah prescribed the Fire as the punishment for major sins, thereby indicating that the designation of faith no longer applies to anyone who commits a major sin.

They said:

We have not found that He guaranteed Paradise on the basis of the designation of Islam. Thus, it is established that the designation of Islam continues to apply to such a person as before, while the designation of faith no longer applies to him.

If they are asked concerning this view of theirs, “Is faith not the opposite of disbelief?” they say, “Disbelief is the opposite of the foundation of faith, for faith has a foundation and branches. A person is not deemed to have disbelieved unless the foundation of faith, which is the opposite of disbelief, is lost.”

If they are asked, “Do those from whom you maintain that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, withheld the designation of faith possess any faith?” they say:

“Yes, its foundation remains firmly established; otherwise, they would have become disbelievers. Have you not heard how Ibn Mas‘ūd disapproved of the man who testified that he was a believer, then said, ‘But we believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers’? He is telling you that he has believed in the sense of affirming the truth, yet does not deserve the designation ‘believer’ when he knows that he falls short

---

## Page 3356

because, in his view, this designation is deserved only by someone who fulfils his obligations and refrains from the forbidden acts that incur the Fire—that is, major sins.”

They said:

Since Allah has made clear that this designation is deserved by someone who deserves Paradise and for whom Allah has guaranteed it, and since we know that we have believed and affirmed the truth—for one ceases to affirm the truth only by denying it, and we neither doubt nor deny—and we know that we disobey Him and deserve punishment, which is the opposite of the reward Allah has decreed for believers on account of their designation as such, we know that we have believed, yet refrain from adopting the designation to which Allah has attached the promise of Paradise. It is a designation expressing praise and commendation from Allah. Allah has forbidden us to commend ourselves, commanded us to fear for ourselves, and prescribed punishment for our disobedience. We therefore know that we do not deserve to call ourselves believers, since Allah has attached praise, commendation, kindness, mercy, forgiveness, and Paradise to the designation of faith, while prescribing the Fire for major sins. These are two opposing judgments.

If it is said:

“How can you refrain from calling yourselves believers when you maintain that the foundation of faith remains in your hearts, namely, affirming that Allah is the Truth and that what He has said is true?”

They say:

Allah, His Messenger, and the overwhelming majority of Muslims name things according to their predominant characteristics. Thus, they call the one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse a sinner, the one who accuses another of unchastity a sinner, and the wine-drinker a sinner. They do not call any of these people God-fearing or scrupulous. Yet Muslims unanimously agree that such a person possesses the foundation of God-consciousness and scrupulousness, in that he guards against disbelief or associating anything with Allah. Likewise, out of fear of Allah, he avoids neglecting the ritual bath required for major ritual impurity or neglecting prayer, and he refrains from having intercourse with his mother. In all these respects, he is God-fearing. And there is unanimous agreement

---

## Page 3357

among Muslims—both those who agree with us and those who disagree—that they do not call him God-fearing or scrupulous when he commits wicked deeds. They unanimously agree that the foundation of God-consciousness and scrupulousness remains in him, and that he may add further branches to that foundation, as when he scrupulously avoids forbidden acts. Yet they do not call him God-fearing or scrupulous while he commits certain major sins. Rather, they call him sinful and wicked, despite knowing that he has shown some God-consciousness and scrupulousness. What prevents them from using those designations is that God-consciousness is a designation of praise and commendation, to which Allah has attached the promise of forgiveness and Paradise.

They said:

For this same reason, we do not call him a believer; we call him a sinner who commits unlawful sexual intercourse, even though the foundation of what is called faith remains in his heart. For faith is a designation by which Allah has praised and commended the believers, and to which He has attached the promise of Paradise. Hence we say, “a Muslim,” but do not say, “a believer.”

They said:

If any Muslim who affirms Allah’s oneness could rightly be considered to have neither faith nor Islam in his heart, those who have entered the Fire would be the most deserving of that description. Yet we find that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, tells us that Allah says:

“Bring out of the Fire whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart.”

Thus, it is established that even the worst Muslim has faith in his heart. Moreover, we find that the Muslim community applies to such people the rulings Allah has prescribed for Muslims, neither declaring them disbelievers nor testifying that they will enter Paradise. It is therefore established that they are Muslims, since there is unanimous agreement that the rulings applicable to Muslims are to be applied to them, but that they do not deserve to be called believers. For Islam designates the religion through which a person leaves all other religions: the designations of those religions no longer apply to him, and only the designation of Islam remains. The rulings of Islam apply to him, while the rulings of all other religions cease to apply to him.

---

## Page 3358

If someone asks them:

Why do you not say, “A disbeliever, if Allah wills,” meaning complete disbelief, just as you say, “We are believers, if Allah wills,” meaning complete faith?

They reply:

Because a disbeliever denies the truth, whereas the foundation of a believer’s faith is acknowledgment. Denial has no initial and final stages requiring one to await its full realization. Faith, however, is founded on affirmation and acknowledgment: one must await the actual fulfillment of what has been acknowledged and the realization of what has been affirmed.

This is like two men who owe something to a third man. He asks one of them for what he is owed, and the man says, “I owe you nothing.” He thus denies and repudiates the claim. Once he has denied and repudiated it, no further stage remains by which he must substantiate what he has said. The creditor then asks the other man for what he is owed, and he replies, “Yes, I owe you such and such.” Yet his acknowledgment alone does not give the creditor his due unless he pays it in full. The creditor therefore waits for him to substantiate his words through payment and confirm his acknowledgment by fulfilling his obligation. If he acknowledges the obligation but then fails to give the creditor his due, he is effectively like the one who denied it, since both have equally failed to pay. Substantiating his words therefore means giving the creditor his due. If he pays part of it, he substantiates part of what he has said and fulfills part of what he has acknowledged. With every portion he pays, he further substantiates his acknowledgment. Likewise, the believer must continue fulfilling what he has acknowledged until he dies.

That is why we say, “A believer, if Allah wills,” but do not say, “A disbeliever, if Allah wills.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

Another group among the people of hadith held a similar position, except that they called such a person a Muslim because he had left the religions of disbelief and acknowledged Allah and what He has said, but they did not call him a believer. They maintained that, although they called him a Muslim, he was a disbeliever—not a disbeliever in Allah, but a disbeliever in respect of his deeds.

They said:

This is disbelief that does not take a person outside the religion.

They also said:

It is inconceivable that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, should say:

“The one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it.”

---

## Page 3359

when disbelief is the opposite of faith. Thus, the designation of faith cannot cease to apply to him without the designation of disbelief necessarily applying to him, because disbelief is the opposite of faith. Disbelief, however, is of two kinds:

One kind consists of denying Allah and what He has said. Its opposite is acknowledging Allah and affirming Him and what He has said. The other kind consists of deeds, and is the opposite of faith that consists of deeds. Consider what is narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He whose neighbor is not safe from his harm has no faith.”

They said: If he has no faith, then he has disbelieved; no other conclusion is possible. However, his disbelief concerns his deeds, since his lack of faith concerns his deeds. He neglects his obligations and commits major sins only because his fear is slight. His fear is slight only because he has little reverence for Allah and His warning of punishment. He has thus abandoned an aspect of faith: the reverence from which fear and restraint from sin arise. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, therefore swore that a person has no faith if his neighbor is not safe from his harm.

A number of people have also narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

And that he said:

“If a Muslim says to his brother, ‘You disbeliever!’ and he is not as described, the disbelief returns upon the speaker.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus called him a disbeliever for fighting his brother, and a disbeliever for saying to him, “You disbeliever!” Yet this utterance is less grave than unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, and drinking wine.

They said:

As for the argument of those who dispute with us, claiming that if we call him a disbeliever, we must apply to him the ruling applicable to those who disbelieve in Allah, call upon him to repent, and exempt him from the prescribed punishments—because, once he disbelieves, the rulings and prescribed punishments applicable to believers no longer apply to him, which would mean exempting everyone who commits a major sin from those punishments and rulings—we have not understood the matter as they have. Rather, we say:

Faith has a foundation and a branch, and disbelief is the opposite of faith in every sense. The foundation of faith is acknowledgment and affirmation, and its branch is the full performance of deeds with the heart and body. Thus, the opposite of acknowledgment and affirmation, which

---

## Page 3360

constitute the foundation of faith, is disbelief in Allah and what He has said, and ceasing to believe in Him and affirm His truthfulness. The opposite of faith that consists of deeds, rather than acknowledgment, is a disbelief that does not amount to disbelief in Allah that takes one outside the religion. Rather, it is disbelief consisting in the neglect of deeds, just as deeds themselves constitute faith, though not the faith that consists of acknowledging Allah.

Since someone who abandons the faith that consists of acknowledging Allah is a disbeliever who must be called upon to repent, whereas someone who abandons the faith that consists of deeds—such as zakat, Hajj, and fasting—or abandons restraint from drinking wine and unlawful sexual intercourse has lost only part of his faith, we do not hold that the latter must be called upon to repent. Nor do those who disagree with us among Ahl al-Sunnah and the people of innovation who say that faith consists of affirmation and deeds, with the sole exception of the Khārijites. Likewise, our saying that he is a disbeliever with respect to his neglect of deeds does not require that he be called upon to repent, nor does it exempt him from the prescribed punishments.

Just as the loss of faith that consists of deeds does not require calling him to repent or exempting him from the prescribed punishments and legal rulings, since the foundation of his faith remains, likewise our applying the designation of disbelief to him with respect to his deeds does not require us to call him to repent or exempt him from those punishments and rulings. For he has not committed the fundamental disbelief that consists of denying Allah or what He has said.

They said:

Knowledge of Allah is faith, and ignorance of Him is disbelief. Performing the obligations is also faith, yet ignorance of them before they were revealed is not disbelief. This is because the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, acknowledged Allah when He first sent His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to them, although they did not know the obligations subsequently imposed upon them. Their ignorance of those obligations was not disbelief. Then Allah revealed the obligations to them, and their acknowledgment and observance of them constituted faith. Whoever denies them disbelieves only because he rejects what Allah has conveyed as false. Had no communication come from Allah, ignorance of them would not have made a person a disbeliever. Even after that communication had come, any Muslim whom it had not reached would not be a disbeliever because of his ignorance of them,

---

## Page 3361

whereas ignorance of Allah constitutes disbelief in all circumstances, both before and after communication from Him.

They said:

Hence we say that abandoning belief in Allah is disbelief, and that neglecting the obligations while believing that Allah has imposed them is disbelief—not disbelief in Allah, but disbelief in the sense of neglecting what is due. This is like someone saying, “You have denied me my due and been ungrateful for my favor,” meaning, “You have neglected my due and failed to give thanks for my favor.”

They said:

In this we follow the example of those Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Successors from whom such statements have been transmitted. They recognized branches of disbelief short of its fundamental form that do not take a person outside the religion of Islam, just as they affirmed branches of faith pertaining to deeds, stemming from its foundation, whose abandonment does not take a person outside the religion of Islam. An example is the statement of Ibn Abbās concerning His words:

“And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

Ibn Yahyā narrated to us: Sufyān ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, from Hishām—meaning Ibn Urwah—from Hujayr, from Tāwūs, from Ibn Abbās, concerning the verse:

“And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.”

“It is not the disbelief they take it to mean.”

Muhammad ibn Yahyā and Muhammad ibn Rāfi narrated to us: Abd al-Razzāq narrated to us: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tāwūs, from his father, who said:

Ibn Abbās was asked about His words:

“And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.”

He said, “This constitutes disbelief on his part.” Ibn Tāwūs said, “But he is not like someone who disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”

Ishāq narrated to us: Wakī informed us, from Sufyān, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tāwūs, from

---

## Page 3362

his father, from Ibn Abbās, who said:

“This constitutes disbelief on his part, but he is not like someone who disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”

Through the same chain, Wakī informed us, from Sufyān, from Maʿmar, from Ibn Tāwūs, from his father, who said: I said to Ibn Abbās:

“‘And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed’—he is a disbeliever.”

He said:

“This constitutes disbelief on his part, but he is not like someone who disbelieves in Allah, the Last Day, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”

Muhammad ibn Yahyā narrated to us: Abd al-Razzāq narrated to us, from Sufyān, from a man, from Tāwūs, from Ibn Abbās, who said: “Disbelief that does not take a person outside the religion.”

Ishāq narrated to us: Wakī informed us, from Sufyān, from Saʿīd al-Makkī, from Tāwūs, who said: “It is not disbelief that takes a person outside the religion.”

Ishāq narrated to us: Wakī informed us, from Sufyān, from Ibn Jurayj, from Atā, who said:

“Disbelief short of disbelief, wrongdoing short of wrongdoing, and wickedness short of wickedness.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

They said:

Atā spoke truly. A disbeliever may be called a wrongdoer, and a sinful Muslim may also be called a wrongdoer. Thus, there is wrongdoing that takes a person outside the religion of Islam, and wrongdoing that does not.

Allah Most High said:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing.”

And He said:

“Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.”

He then cited the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim, who said:

“When the verse ‘Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing’ was revealed, the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, found this difficult and said, ‘Which of us has not wronged himself?’

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘That is not what it means. Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: “Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong”? It refers only to associating partners with Allah.’”

---

## Page 3363

Muhammad ibn Yahyā narrated to us: al-Hajjāj ibn al-Minhāl narrated to us, from Hammād ibn Salamah, from Alī ibn Zayd, from Yūsuf ibn Mihrān, from Ibn Abbās, who reported that whenever Umar ibn al-Khattāb entered his house, he would open the Quran and read from it. One day, he entered and began reading, until he reached this verse:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing,”

to the end of the verse. He put on his sandals, took his cloak, and went to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, saying: “Abū al-Mundhir, I came across this verse earlier: ‘Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing.’ Yet we know that we do wrong and commit misdeeds.”

He replied: “Commander of the Faithful, that is not what it means. Allah says: ‘Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.’ It refers only to associating partners with Allah.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

Likewise, wickedness is of two kinds: wickedness that takes a person outside the religion, and wickedness that does not. Thus, a disbeliever is called wicked, and a sinful Muslim is also called wicked. Allah mentioned Iblīs, saying:

“He rebelled against his Lord’s command.”

That wickedness on his part constituted disbelief. Allah Most High also said:

“As for those who are wicked, their refuge is the Fire.”

He means the disbelievers, as is shown by His words:

“Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned to it, and it will be said to them, ‘Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.’”

A sinful Muslim is also called wicked, without being excluded from Islam. Allah Most High said:

“Those who accuse chaste women of adultery and then fail to produce four witnesses—flog them with eighty lashes, and never accept their testimony. It is they who are the wicked.”

And He Most High said:

“Whoever undertakes Hajj during these months must abstain from sexual relations, wickedness, and disputing during Hajj.”

The scholars explained that wickedness here means acts of disobedience.

They said:

Since wrongdoing is of two kinds and wickedness is of two kinds, disbelief likewise is of two kinds:

---

## Page 3364

(one takes a person outside the religion) and (the other does not take a person outside the religion). Likewise, associating partners with Allah is of “two kinds”: associating partners with Him in His oneness, which takes a person outside the religion, and associating partners with Him in deeds, which does not take a person outside the religion. The latter is showing off. Allah Most High said:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

What is meant here is showing off through righteous deeds. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Taking evil omens is associating partners with Allah.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

These, then, are two positions, both broadly reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal among the hadith scholars who shared his views. Ismā‘īl ibn Sa‘īd al-Shālanjī related that he asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about someone who persists in major sins, pursuing them with all his effort, yet has not abandoned prayer, zakat, or fasting: “Is someone in this condition considered persistent in sin?”

He replied: “He is persistent in sin. His case is like that described in the Prophet’s words:

‘An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer.’

“He leaves the sphere of faith and comes within the sphere of Islam. It is also like his words:

‘He does not drink wine while he is a believer, nor does he steal while he is a believer.’

“And it is like the statement of Ibn ‘Abbās concerning Allah’s words:

‘Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.’”

I said to him: “What is this disbelief?”

He replied: “Disbelief that does not take a person outside the religion. Just as faith has degrees, some lower than others, so too does disbelief, until it reaches something concerning which there is no disagreement.”

Ibn Abī Shaybah said, concerning the words, “An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer”: “He does not possess complete faith; rather, his faith is deficient.”

He said: “I also asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about ‘Islam and faith.’ He replied: ‘Faith consists of speech and deeds, while Islam is affirmation.’”

He said: “Abū Khaythamah held the same view. Ibn Abī Shaybah said: ‘There can be no Islam without faith, and no faith without Islam.’”

---

## Page 3365

I say: The inseparability of the two has already been discussed in full, although what one denotes is not identical to what the other denotes.

More than one scholar has reported the consensus of the people of the Sunnah and hadith that faith consists of speech and deeds. Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr said in al-Tamhīd:

“The scholars of jurisprudence and hadith unanimously agree that faith consists of speech and deeds, and that deeds require intention. In their view, faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience, and all acts of obedience constitute faith. The exception is what has been reported from Abū Hanīfah and his followers, who held that obedience is not called faith. They said that faith consists only of assent and affirmation; some of them also included knowledge.”

He mentioned the evidence they cited … then went on to say:

“As for the other jurists, whether adherents of reasoned opinion or transmitted reports, in the Hijaz, Iraq, Syria, and Egypt—including Mālik ibn Anas, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū ‘Ubayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Dāwūd ibn ‘Alī, al-Tabarī, and those who followed their path—they said:

“Faith consists of speech and deeds: speech of the tongue, namely affirmation; conviction in the heart; and deeds performed by the limbs, with sincerity and genuine intention.

“They said that everything through which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is obeyed, whether obligatory or voluntary, is part of faith. Faith increases through acts of obedience and decreases through sins. In their view, those who commit sins are believers whose faith is incomplete because of their sins; their faith becomes deficient through their commission of major sins. Consider the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“‘An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer.’

“And the remainder of the hadith. He meant a person whose faith is complete; he did not mean to deny all faith to someone who commits such an act. This is demonstrated by the consensus that adulterers, thieves, and wine drinkers—provided they pray facing the qiblah and profess Islam—inherit from their believing relatives who are not

---

## Page 3366

guilty of those sins.” He offered arguments in support of this, then said:

“Most of Mālik’s followers hold that faith and Islam are one and the same.”

He said:

“As for the Mu‘tazilah, they hold that faith comprises all acts of obedience, and that whoever falls short in any of them is a sinner, neither a believer nor a disbeliever. These are the true adherents of Mu‘tazilism, who advocate the intermediate position between the two positions.”

Later he said:

“Faith increases and decreases: it increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience. This is the position of the scholars of transmitted reports and the jurists who issue fatwas throughout the lands. Ibn al-Qāsim reported from Mālik that faith increases, but that he withheld judgment concerning its decrease. ‘Abd al-Razzāq, Ma‘n ibn ‘Īsā, and Ibn Nāfi‘ reported from him that it increases and decreases. This is the position of the body of hadith scholars, and praise be to Allah.”

He then cited the arguments of the Murji’ah, followed by those of the people of the Sunnah. He refuted the Khawārij’s practice of declaring sinners disbelievers by citing the prescribed punishments for adultery, theft, and similar offenses, the right of mutual inheritance, and the hadith of ‘Ubādah:

“Whoever commits any of these offenses and is punished for it in this world, that punishment is an expiation for him.”

He said:

“Faith has degrees, some higher than others. Someone whose faith is deficient is not like someone whose faith is complete. Allah Most High says:

‘The believers are only those whose hearts tremble at the mention of Allah.’

“That is, those who truly believe. Hence He says:

‘It is they who are the true believers.’

“The same applies to the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

‘A believer is one from whom people feel safe, and a Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe.’

“He means a true believer and a true Muslim. Another example is his saying:

‘The believers most complete in faith.’

“It is well known that one cannot be more complete unless another is less complete.

---

## Page 3367

And his sayings:

‘The firmest bonds of faith are loving for Allah’s sake and hating for Allah’s sake,’

and:

‘There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy,’

show that some aspects of faith are firmer and more complete than others.”

He also cited the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others: “Whoever loves for Allah’s sake and hates for Allah’s sake,” and the rest of the hadith. Likewise, Abū ‘Amr al-Talamankī reported the consensus of the people of the Sunnah that faith consists of words, deeds, intention, and conformity to the Sunnah.

Abū Tālib al-Makkī said:

“The five foundations of Islam”—meaning the two testimonies of faith, the five daily prayers, zakah, fasting the month of Ramadan, and Hajj.

He said:

“The pillars of faith are seven”—meaning the five mentioned in the hadith of Gabriel, belief in divine decree, and belief in Paradise and Hell. Both of the latter have been reported in the hadith of Gabriel, as we shall mention, if Allah Most High wills.

He said:

“Belief in the names and attributes of Allah Most High; belief in Allah’s books and prophets; and belief in angels and devils”—meaning, and Allah knows best, belief in the distinction between them, for some people regard them as a single kind, differing only in their deeds, just as righteous and wicked human beings differ—“and belief in Paradise and Hell, and that both were created before Adam; belief in resurrection after death; and belief in all that Allah ordains, good and evil, sweet and bitter: that it all comes from Allah through His decree, determination, will, and judgment; that this is justice on His part and consummate wisdom; and that He has reserved to Himself knowledge of its unseen aspects and its true meaning.”

He said:

“Some have said, ‘Faith is Islam.’ This eliminates differences in degree and spiritual stations, and comes close to the position of the Murji’ah. Others have said that

---

## Page 3368

Islam is distinct from faith. These people have introduced opposition and difference between them, and this is close to the position of the Ibādiyyah. This is a difficult question requiring explanation and elaboration. The relationship of Islam to faith resembles that between the two testimonies of faith: each is connected to the other in meaning and ruling. The testimony to the Messenger’s prophethood differs from the testimony to Allah’s oneness; they are two distinct things in themselves. Yet each is bound to the other in meaning and ruling, as though they were one thing. Likewise, faith and Islam are bound together, as though they were one thing. Whoever has no Islam has no faith, and whoever has no faith has no Islam. A Muslim necessarily possesses faith through which his Islam is valid, and a believer necessarily possesses Islam through which he gives effect to his faith. For Allah has made faith a condition of righteous deeds, and righteous deeds a condition of faith. Affirming this, He says:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer—his effort will not be denied.”

And concerning giving effect to faith through deeds, He says:

“But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds—for them will be the highest ranks.”

Someone whose outward conduct consists of the deeds of Islam, but who has no underlying firm belief in the unseen, is a hypocrite whose hypocrisy takes him outside the religion. Someone whose conviction is belief in the unseen, but who does not act according to the requirements of faith and the ordinances of Islam, is a disbeliever whose disbelief is incompatible with monotheism. Whoever believes in the unseen matters that the messengers have conveyed from Allah and acts upon Allah’s commands is both a believer and a Muslim. Were this not so, it would be possible for a believer not to be called a Muslim, and for a Muslim not to be called a believer in Allah. Those who face the qiblah have unanimously agreed that every believer is a Muslim, and every Muslim believes in Allah, His angels, and His books.”

He said:

“Faith in relation to deeds is like the heart in relation to the body: neither can be separated from the other. There can be no living body without a heart, nor anyone possessing a heart without a

---

## Page 3369

body. They are two distinct things, separate in ruling and meaning. They may also be likened to a seed with an exterior and an interior: it remains one seed. It is not called two seeds merely because the characteristics of its two parts differ. Likewise, the deeds prescribed in Islam are part of Islam and constitute the outward aspect of faith; they are deeds of the limbs. Faith is the inward aspect of Islam and consists of deeds of the heart.

It is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.’

Another wording states:

‘Faith is inward.’

Islam thus consists of the deeds of faith, while faith consists of the convictions underlying Islam. There is no faith without deeds, and no deed without inward resolve. This is like outward and inward action: deeds of the heart and deeds of the limbs are bound to one another. Similarly, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘Actions are only according to intentions.’

That is, there is no action without resolve and intent, for the word innamā (‘only’) affirms something and excludes everything else. He thereby affirmed both the deeds of the limbs in outward dealings and the deeds of the heart in intentions. Deeds stand in relation to faith as the lips do to the tongue: speech cannot function properly without both, for the lips bring the letters together and the tongue gives expression to speech. When either is absent, speech fails. Likewise, when deeds are absent, faith is lost.

Thus, when Allah enumerated His blessings upon the human being in granting speech, He mentioned the lips along with the tongue, saying:

‘Have We not given him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips?’

This means: Have We not enabled him to see and speak? He referred to speech by mentioning the tongue and lips because they are its organs. He mentioned the lips because speech—the blessing bestowed—cannot be complete without them. ‘Faith’ and ‘Islam’ may also be likened to a tent pitched on the ground, which has an exterior

---

## Page 3370

and guy ropes, with a pole inside. The tent is like Islam: its pillars consist of outward deeds and actions of the limbs, represented by the guy ropes that hold the sides of the tent in place. The pole at the centre of the tent is like faith, without which the tent cannot stand. The tent thus needs them, for it can neither stand nor remain firm without both. Likewise, Islam, consisting of deeds of the limbs, cannot stand without faith; and faith, consisting of deeds of the heart, is of no benefit without Islam, which is righteous deeds.

Furthermore, Allah has made the opposite of Islam and faith one and the same. Were they not like a single thing in ruling and meaning, they would not have the same opposite. He says:

“How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?”

And He says:

“Would he command you to disbelieve after you have become Muslims?”

Thus, He made disbelief the opposite of both.

He said:

Likewise, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described faith and Islam as belonging to the same category. In the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, he said:

“Islam is built upon five.”

In the hadith narrated by Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, they asked him about faith, and he mentioned these same characteristics. This shows that there is no inward faith without outward Islam, nor any outward, manifest Islam without inward faith, and that faith and deeds are inseparable companions: neither benefits without the other.

He said:

As for the Prophet’s distinction between faith and Islam in the hadith of Gabriel, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, this distinguishes the detailed account of the heart’s deeds and convictions—in accordance with the meanings we have described, which require these to be convictions—from the detailed account of the deeds of the limbs, which call for actions

---

## Page 3371

that are outward and which he described as openly performed—not that this establishes a difference or opposition in meaning between Islam and faith. There is no evidence here that they differ in ruling.

He said:

They come together in a single servant who is both a Muslim and a believer. The convictions of the heart that he mentioned describe that servant’s heart, while the outward actions he mentioned describe his body.

He also said:

The community is agreed that if a servant believes in all the convictions of the heart mentioned in the description of faith in the hadith of Gabriel, but does not perform the actions mentioned in the description of Islam, he is not called a believer. Likewise, if he performs everything by which Islam was described but does not hold the beliefs by which faith was described, he is not a Muslim. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has informed us that the community will not agree upon misguidance.

I say:

It appears that he meant by this the consensus of the Companions and those who followed them. Alternatively, he meant that such a person is not called a believer for the purposes of legal rulings, and that he is not a Muslim if he denies any of these pillars, or knows that the Messenger conveyed them but does not believe him. Or perhaps he did not count the dissent of those who follow their own inclinations as genuine disagreement. Otherwise, Abū Tālib was certainly familiar with their views. This—and Allah knows best—is what he intended, for he devoted “Chapter Thirty-Three” to explaining Islam and faith in detail and elucidating the convictions underlying the heart’s dealings according to the doctrine of the people of the Community.

What he has said is better than what many others have said, but two points are disputed.

The first is that a Muslim deserving of reward must possess the obligatory faith set out in detail in the hadith of Gabriel.

---

## Page 3372

The second is the claim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, uses the designation “believer” rather than “Muslim,” in statements such as “Or a Muslim,” because the person is not among the distinguished and most excellent believers. It is as though he were saying: because he is not among the foremost who are brought near to Allah, but among the righteous who follow the middle course.

Both these points are contested by the majority of scholars. They say: It was not because that man was not among the distinguished and most excellent believers—such as the foremost who are brought near to Allah—that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of him, “Or a Muslim.” If that were so, he would be denying the unqualified designation of faith to the righteous, Allah-fearing people who follow the middle course and are promised Paradise without punishment, since they belong to those on the right rather than the foremost who are brought near to Allah. But this is not the case. Rather, those on the right, together with the foremost who are brought near to Allah, are all believers promised Paradise without punishment. Everyone of this description is a believer by the agreement of Muslims, both those of the Sunnah and those of innovation.

If it were permissible to deny someone faith because another person’s faith was superior, faith would be denied to most of Allah’s pious allies, and indeed to many of the prophets. This is utterly untenable. It resembles the claim that a designation is denied because its recommended perfection is absent. We have already explained that nothing of this kind occurs in the words of Allah or His Messenger.

Rather, this hadith specifically concerns someone described as a Muslim but not a believer. He must therefore fall below the rank of the righteous who follow the middle course and are destined for Paradise. His faith must fall short of the faith of all these people, so he cannot have fulfilled all the faith that they were commanded to have. Then, if he is capable of attaining that faith but neglects what is obligatory, he deserves blame. If, however, it is supposed that he is incapable of attaining the faith that characterizes these people, then he is unable to attain faith like theirs, and this would not have been obligatory for him. Thus, even if he

---

## Page 3373

enters Paradise, he will not be like someone who, let us suppose, accepted faith in general terms and died before its details became known, before fully realizing them or acting upon any of them. Such a person enters Paradise, but is not like those others.

Yet it may be said:

The righteous, those on the right, also occupy different ranks, as stated in the authentic hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Those believers who remain behind, other than those with disabilities, are not equal…”

—to the end of the verse. Thus, the strong believer’s rank in Paradise is higher, even though each has fulfilled everything obligatory upon him. When Abū Tālib and others say, “This person is not among the distinguished believers,” they may mean precisely this: his faith is not like that of someone who has fully realized the distinctive qualities of faith, whether among the righteous or those brought near to Allah. This may be so even if he has neglected no obligation, because he was incapable of it or had not been commanded to perform it. He is therefore not blameworthy, but neither is he praised as those people are, nor does it follow that he is among those brought near to Allah.

The reply is:

This, too, does not negate his faith.

It may then be said:

He is a Muslim, not a believer, just as one may say, “He is not a scholar, a mufti, or someone qualified to exercise independent legal judgment.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not match a mudd (a small dry measure) given by one of them, nor even half of it.”

There are many such examples. Not every distinction by which a superior person excels is attainable by those below him. Likewise, some realities of faith are beyond the capacity of many people—indeed, most of them. These people enter Paradise even though they have not realized the realities of faith through which Allah has favored others over them. Nor have they neglected anything obligatory upon them, even if it is obligatory upon others. For this reason, faith includes

---

## Page 3374

things bestowed as gifts and bounty from Allah, for faith is of the nature of knowledge, whereas outward Islam is of the nature of action.

Allah Most High has said:

“But those who are guided—He increases them in guidance and grants them their righteousness.”

And He said:

“And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance.”

And He said:

“It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith along with their existing faith.”

Such tranquillity may lie beyond a person’s power to attain. Rather, Allah places it in his heart as a bounty from Him and a reward for a previous deed, as He said:

“If they had done what they were instructed to do, it would have been better for them and would have strengthened them more firmly.”

“And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.”

“And We would have guided them to a straight path.”

He also said:

“Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double share of His mercy and grant you a light by which you may walk.”

And He said:

“Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

Hence it has been said: “Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah grants him knowledge of what he did not know.” This kind of thing lies beyond people’s power, although even the outward and inward deeds within their power depend on Allah’s bounty, His assistance, and His enabling them to perform them.

Things, however, fall into two categories: those whose very nature places them within people’s power, through Allah’s assistance, such as standing and sitting; and those whose very nature places them beyond their power.

If it is said that Allah grants those who obey Him strength in their hearts and bodies, enabling them to do what others cannot, this too is true and falls within the same meaning.

Allah Most High said:

“When your Lord revealed to the angels, ‘I am with you, so strengthen those who believe.’”

He also said:

“When you encounter a force, stand firm.”

Thus He commanded them to stand firm, while revealing to the angels that they are to instill this steadfastness in the believers.

---

## Page 3375

And the point is that some aspects of faith may be commanded of certain people, who are blameworthy for neglecting them, while others who are incapable of them are not blameworthy for their absence. Allah favors the former through this faith, even though the less favored person has neglected no obligation. The response is:

The same applies to outward deeds: someone capable of an action is commanded to do what someone incapable of it is not commanded to do, and some people are commanded to do what others are commanded to do.

With outward deeds, however, a person may be granted a reward equal to that of the person who performs them if he believes in them and earnestly desires to perform them, but is physically incapable. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“There are men in Medina who have been with you whenever you have traveled a stretch of road or crossed a valley.” They asked, “Even though they are in Medina?” He replied, “Even though they are in Medina; a valid excuse has kept them back.”

Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“Not equal are those believers who remain behind—other than those with disabilities—and those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has favored those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who remain behind by a degree.”

Thus He made an exception for those with disabilities. In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward equal to the rewards of those who follow him, without their rewards being diminished in the least. Whoever calls to misguidance will bear a burden of sin equal to the burdens of those who follow him, without their burdens being diminished in the least.”

And in the hadith of Abū Kabshah al-Anmārī:

“The two are equal in reward, and the two are equal in their burden of sin.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and graded it authentic. Its wording is:

“This world is for four kinds of people: a man to whom Allah has given knowledge and wealth, who fears his Lord in his use of that wealth, maintains his ties of kinship with it, and recognizes Allah’s right over it—he occupies the highest rank; a servant whom Allah has granted knowledge but no wealth, whose intention is sincere and who says, ‘If I had wealth, I would act as so-and-so does’—he is rewarded according to his intention, so the two are equal in reward; and a servant

## Page 3376

to whom Allah has given wealth but no knowledge, who handles his wealth recklessly, without knowledge: he does not fear his Lord in its use, maintain his ties of kinship with it, or recognize Allah’s right over it—he occupies the worst rank; and a servant to whom Allah has given neither wealth nor knowledge, who says, ‘If I had wealth, I would act with it as so-and-so does’—he is judged according to his intention, so the two are equal in their burden of sin.”

Ibn Mājah’s wording is:

“This community may be compared to four men: a man to whom Allah has given wealth and knowledge, who applies his knowledge to his wealth, spending it as is right; and a man to whom Allah has given knowledge but no wealth, who says, ‘If I had what this man has, I would do as he does.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘The two are equal in reward. And a man to whom Allah has given wealth but no knowledge, who handles his wealth recklessly, spending it improperly; and a man to whom He has given neither knowledge nor wealth, who says, “If I had wealth like this man’s, I would do as he does”—the two are equal in their burden of sin.’”

Likewise, two people whose hearts are equal in faith—in knowledge, affirmation, love, strength, state, and station—may be equal even though one performs bodily deeds that the other is physically incapable of performing. As a report states:

“The believer’s strength lies in his heart, and his weakness in his body; the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body, and his weakness in his heart.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“The strong man is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling; rather, the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry.”

He also said:

---

## Page 3377

his hand, a large bucket. I have never seen a man of such prowess draw water as he did; he continued until the people had watered their camels and settled them at their resting places.”

Thus, he described Abu Bakr as weaker. Whether he meant the brevity of his tenure or his inability to match ʿUmar’s strength, there is no doubt that Abu Bakr was stronger in faith than ʿUmar, while ʿUmar was stronger in action. As Ibn Masʿūd said:

“We have enjoyed strength and honour ever since ʿUmar embraced Islam.”

Strength of faith is greater and more complete than strength in action. A person of faith may have the reward of another’s deeds recorded for him: a reward equal to that for ʿUmar’s conduct as ruler is recorded for Abu Bakr, since it was he who appointed him as his successor. In the Musnad, it is reported through two chains of transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then Abu Bakr was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then ʿUmar was weighed against the community and outweighed it.”

During the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and after his death, ʿUmar gained through Abu Bakr faith and knowledge that he had not previously possessed. Abu Bakr encouraged him to do the good he did and exerted himself to help him do it. Someone who helps bring about an action, while firmly resolved that it should be done, is like the one who performs it. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever equips a warrior has himself gone on campaign, and whoever takes good care of his family in his absence has himself gone on campaign.”

He also said:

“Whoever directs someone to a good deed will have a reward like that of the one who performs it.”

And he said:

“Whoever provides a fasting person with food to break his fast will have a reward like his.”

Al-Tirmidhī also narrated:

“Whoever consoles someone afflicted by a calamity will have a reward like his.”

These and other reports show that two people may be equal in outward deeds—or indeed, one may surpass the other—yet the one whose outward deeds are inferior may be superior before Allah because the faith in his heart is superior. But when they differ in the faith within their hearts, the one inferior in that respect can never be superior before Allah

---

## Page 3378

even if Allah has not bestowed upon the one of lesser rank the faith He has bestowed upon the superior, nor granted his heart the means of attaining that superior faith that He has granted the one of lesser rank.

For this reason, Allah has favoured some prophets over others, even if the superior has performed fewer deeds than the one of lesser rank. Thus, Allah favoured our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—whose prophethood lasted twenty-odd years—over Noah, who remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty. He also favoured the community of Muhammad, who worked from the afternoon prayer until sunset, over those who worked from the beginning of the day until the midday prayer, and over those who worked from the midday prayer until the afternoon prayer. Allah gave the community of Muhammad a double reward, while giving each of the others a single reward, because the faith in their hearts was more complete and superior. The others did more work, but these received a greater reward. This is His bounty, which He grants to whomever He wills through the means He has graciously bestowed upon them and with which He has distinguished them.

The same applies to all others whom Allah Most High favours: He favours them through the means by which they deserve a greater reward. Thus, He may endow one of two people with a capacity through which he attains knowledge, and a capacity through which he attains certainty, patience, reliance upon Allah, sincere devotion, and other qualities by which Allah grants him distinction. He favours him in reward only because of the faith with which He has favoured him.

As Allah Most High says:

“A group among the People of the Scripture said, ‘Believe in what has been revealed to the believers at the beginning of the day, then reject it at its end, so that they may turn back.’”

“‘And trust only those who follow your religion.’ Say, ‘True guidance is Allah’s guidance.’ Do you fear that anyone should be given the like of what you have been given, or that they should argue against you before your Lord? Say, ‘All bounty is in Allah’s hand.’”

He says in another verse:

“Allah knows best where to place His message.”

And He says:

“Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind.”

And He says:

“He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.”

## Page 3379

And the causes of forgiveness and punishment have already been explained elsewhere. Likewise, He provides for whomever He wills without measure, and it is known that He may favour whomever He wills with the means of provision. If there are aspects of faith beyond the capacity of many people, with which Allah favours whomever He wills, then these are among the things through which Allah grants them superiority. Others are described as lacking that faith, not by way of blame, but to indicate this distinction, for blame attaches only to neglecting something commanded or doing something forbidden.

On Abū Tālib’s account, however, it would be said that such people are Muslims, not believers, in one respect, while they are believers in another. On this view, someone may be described as lacking faith because he lacks the recommended degree of perfection—indeed, even the perfection that makes one superior to someone who lacks it, though it may lie beyond human capacity. He may even be described as lacking a perfection obligatory for someone else, although it is neither obligatory nor recommended for him. Yet such usage is not known in the Lawgiver’s speech. The only known usage there is that describing someone as lacking faith invariably entails blame; thus, only someone guilty of a sin is described in this way.

It therefore becomes clear that his words, “Or a Muslim,” express a withholding of judgment as to whether that person has fulfilled the inward and outward obligations, as the vast majority have said.

One group says that he may be a hypocrite with no faith whatsoever. These are the people who say that the Bedouins mentioned were hypocrites with no faith whatsoever. This is the view defended by a group including Muhammad ibn Nasr. Most, however, say that these people were not among the hypocrites none of whose deeds are accepted, although they had an element of hypocrisy. Rather, they possessed an assent to the truth that allowed whatever they did for Allah to be accepted from them. This is why He described them as Muslims, and why He said:

“that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful”

just as

## Page 3380

they say the same of the adulterer, the thief, and others who are described as lacking faith despite possessing assent to the truth. This is the soundest of the three views concerning them. Abū Tālib regarded those deserving blame for neglecting an obligation as being among those whose hearts were to be reconciled and who were given nothing, while regarding that man as a believer surpassed in excellence by someone else.

The majority, however, say that affirming Islam for them but not faith is like affirming it for that man: he was a Muslim, not a believer. In both cases, they are blameworthy, not merely surpassed in excellence by others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believers most perfect in faith are those best in character.”

Yet he did not deny faith to those below them. Allah Most High also said:

“Those among you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal to the others. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. Yet Allah has promised the finest reward to all.”

Thus, He affirmed faith for both the more excellent and the less excellent. This is agreed upon among Muslims. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“When a judge strives to reach a judgment and is correct, he has two rewards; if he strives and errs, he has one reward.”

He said to Saʿd ibn Muʿādh when he passed judgment concerning Banū Qurayzah:

“You have indeed judged them according to the judgment of the King from above the seven heavens.”

He would also say to someone whom he sent out with an army or a military detachment:

“If you besiege the people of a fortress and they ask you to let them surrender on the basis of Allah’s judgment, do not let them surrender on that basis, for you do not know what Allah’s judgment concerning them is. Rather, let them surrender on the basis of your judgment and that of your companions.”

These three hadiths are in al-Sahīh (the Authentic Collection). The hadith of Solomon, peace be upon him, also contains the words: “And I ask You for a judgment that accords with Your judgment.” These and other texts demonstrate what was agreed upon by the Companions and those who followed them

---

## Page 3381

in righteousness: that Allah may distinguish one of two people by enabling him to exercise independent reasoning through which he attains knowledge beyond the other’s reach. He thus receives two rewards, while the other, being unable to attain that knowledge, receives one reward and incurs no sin. The knowledge with which the former has been distinguished, and his acting upon it inwardly and outwardly, constitute an increase in his faith. This faith is obligatory for him because he is capable of it, whereas the other is incapable of it and is therefore not obliged to attain it. Thus, the former has been favoured with faith that is obligatory for him but not for someone incapable of attaining it.

This applies throughout the Muslim community in disputed matters of belief and practice. When one person is granted knowledge of the actual truth while the other strives but is unable to reach it, both are praiseworthy, rewarded believers. Yet Allah has distinguished the former with a measure of obligatory faith by which He has favoured him over the latter. The one who errs deserves neither blame nor punishment, even though the former would be blamed and punished if he did what the latter did. Similarly, Allah has distinguished our Prophet’s community with a revealed law by which He has favoured it. Were we to neglect anything He has commanded us in that law, this would be grounds for blame and punishment, whereas the prophets before us are not blamed for leaving it undone. Nevertheless, Allah has favoured Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, over the other prophets, and his community over the other communities, without this entailing any blame for any prophet or for the communities that followed them.

Furthermore, a person is obliged to fulfil only those requirements of faith of which he is capable. If he fulfils them, he deserves the Paradise Allah has promised. If such a person were called a Muslim but not a believer, it would follow that among those promised Paradise are people called Muslims but not believers—such as the Bedouins, the man concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Or a Muslim,” and all the others who are denied the designation of faith despite being Muslims, such as the adulterer and the drinker of wine

## Page 3383

will have no fear, nor will they grieve.” And He says:

There are many verses to this effect. The promise of Paradise, mercy in the Hereafter, and deliverance from punishment is linked to the designation of faith, whether mentioned without qualification or qualified by righteous deeds and the like. As explained earlier, faith mentioned without qualification includes doing what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. This promise has not been linked to the designation of Islam.

If someone who fulfils as much of faith as he is able, but cannot know its details, could be called a Muslim without being called a believer, he would be among the people of Paradise. Paradise would then be deserved by someone called a Muslim even though he was not called a believer. But this is not the case: Paradise has been linked only to the designation of faith.

This is also among the evidence cited by those who say that not every Muslim is among the believers promised Paradise. Were that the case, the promise of Paradise would have been linked to the designation of Islam, just as it has been linked to faith, to “piety” and “righteousness,” as in His words:

“Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and rivers.”

And His words:

“Indeed, the virtuous will be in bliss.”

It has also been linked to the designation of the friends of Allah, as in His words:

“Indeed, the friends of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“Those who believe and are mindful of Allah.”

“For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no changing the words of Allah. That is the supreme triumph.”

Since the designation of Islam is not used in this way, it is clear that what it denotes does not necessarily entail what faith denotes, whereas the designations of righteousness, piety, and the friends of Allah do. The designation of Islam therefore includes those subject to the threat of punishment, even though Allah rewards them for their obedience. For example, someone may have both faith and hypocrisy in his heart, with the latter making him deserving of punishment. Allah punishes such a person but does not leave him in the Fire forever, because his heart contains an atom’s weight of faith or more.

## Page 3384

The same applies to all others who commit major sins: their faith is deficient. If someone has a trait of hypocrisy in his heart, he will be punished for it unless Allah pardons him, but he will not remain in the Fire forever. Thus, calling them believers is no more warranted than calling them hypocrites, especially if they are closer to disbelief than to faith.

In the rulings of this world, they are included under the designation of faith, just as the outright hypocrite is—and with greater reason, since they possess faith by virtue of which they are included in Allah’s address:

For this commands them to do what benefits them and forbids them from doing what harms them, and they need such guidance. possess a measure of faith by virtue of which he will be gathered with the believers on the Day of Resurrection. To complete this explanation: some people may possess both a branch of faith and a branch of disbelief or hypocrisy, yet be called Muslims, as Ahmad explicitly stated. To complete this explanation: a person may possess both a branch of faith and a branch of hypocrisy. This is the position of the great majority of the early generations, and it is what Ahmad and others explicitly stated. Concerning the thief, the drinker of intoxicants, and others of whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “He is not a believer,” they held that such people are to be called Muslims, not believers. ## Page 3386

that does not take him out of Islam, but is disbelief less than outright disbelief, as Ibn ‘Abbās and his companions said concerning His words:

This is also among the evidence al-Bukhārī cited in his Sahīh. The scholars agree that the designation “Muslims” applies outwardly to the hypocrites, because they outwardly submitted and performed outward deeds: prayer, zakat, pilgrimage, and jihad in their outward forms. Thus, the Prophet applied the outward rulings of Islam to them. They also agree that whoever possesses no faith whatsoever falls under the words of Allah Most High:

The word has two readings: dark and darak. Abū al-Husayn ibn Fāris said: “Paradise has ascending ranks, and the Fire has descending depths.” Al-Dahhāk said: “Daraj refers to levels one above another, while dark refers to levels one below another.”

Thus, among those who outwardly profess Islam is one who occupies the highest rank in Paradise: the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As he said in the authentic hadith:

Resurrection.” His words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “and I hope to be,” are like his words:
