The point is that the best of the believers occupy the highest ranks of Paradise, while the hypocrites occupy the lowest depths of the Fire, even though they were outwardly Muslims in this world and subject to the outward rulings of Islam.

Thus, someone who possesses both faith and hypocrisy is called a Muslim, for he is no worse than a complete hypocrite. If his hypocrisy predominates, he does not deserve the designation of believer; rather, the designation of hypocrite is more fitting for him. Something containing both white and black, but more black than white, is more rightly called black than white. As Allah Most High says:

“That day they were nearer to disbelief than to faith.”

If, however, his faith predominates, but he also possesses hypocrisy for which he deserves the threatened punishment, he is likewise not among the believers promised Paradise. This supports what Muhammad ibn Nasr reported from Ahmad, although I myself have not found it in the statements of Ahmad that have reached me, nor was it mentioned by al-Khallāl or others like him.

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

“Others besides these reported that Ahmad said: ‘Whoever commits any of these four acts—unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking wine, and plundering that draws people’s eyes to him—or comparable or graver acts, is a Muslim, but I do not call him

---

## Page 3388

a believer. Whoever commits sins short of major sins we call a believer deficient in faith.’”

The proponent of this view argues as follows:

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, denied him faith, I deny him faith just as the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did. The Messenger denied it only to someone who committed a major sin. As for a believer who commits a minor sin, it is expiated through his good deeds and his avoidance of major sins. Nevertheless, his faith is deficient compared with that of someone who avoids minor sins. He has therefore not fulfilled the faith required of him, but has mixed it with sins that are expiated through other deeds. His rank is consequently lower than that of someone who has not committed such sins.

As for those to whom the Messenger denied faith, we deny it to them just as the Messenger did. Although they possess assent and the foundation of faith, they have abandoned enough of its requirements to deserve being denied the designation of faith. Hypocrisy and faith, or disbelief and faith, may coexist in a person. According to those who hold this view, faith without qualification is that which entitles its possessor to the promise of Paradise.

Various groups among the “followers of desires”—the Khārijites, Mu‘tazilites, Jahmiyyah, and Murji’ah, both Karrāmī and non-Karrāmī—say that faith and hypocrisy cannot coexist in a person. Some even claim consensus on this. Abū al-Hasan mentioned such a consensus in some of his books. This is where they went wrong, contradicting the Quran, the Sunnah, and the reports from the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, as well as plain reason.

Indeed, the Khārijites and Mu‘tazilites carried this false principle through consistently, saying:

A single person cannot combine an act of obedience for which he deserves reward with an act of disobedience for which he deserves punishment. Nor can the same person be praiseworthy in one respect and blameworthy in

---

## Page 3389

another, nor loved and prayed for in one respect while subject to wrath and cursed in another. In their view, it is inconceivable that the same person should enter both Paradise and Hell; rather, whoever enters one cannot enter the other. Hence they denied that anyone could leave Hell or that intercession could be made for any of its inhabitants.

It is reported that the extreme Murji’ah agreed with them on this principle, but took the opposite position, saying that those who commit major sins enter Paradise and do not enter Hell.

As for Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, and the other Muslim groups—hadith scholars, jurists, and practitioners of speculative theology, including the Murji’ah among the jurists, the Karrāmiyyah, the Kullābiyyah, the Ash‘ariyyah, and the Shī‘ah, both their Murji’ah and non-Murji’ah groups—they say:

Allah may punish a person in Hell and then admit him to Paradise, as the authentic hadiths explicitly state. Such a person has evil deeds for which he was punished and good deeds on account of which he entered Paradise. All agree that he has both disobedience and obedience to his credit. These groups did not disagree about his fate; rather, they disagreed over what to call him.

The Murji’ah, both Jahmī and non-Jahmī, said that he is a believer whose faith is complete. Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah hold that he is a believer deficient in faith; otherwise, he would not have been punished. Likewise, all Muslims agree that he is deficient in righteousness and piety. But may he be called a believer without qualification? There are two views on this, and the correct approach is to distinguish between contexts.

If the question concerns worldly rulings, such as whether freeing him would fulfil an obligation of expiation, the answer is that he is a believer. The same applies if the question is whether he is included in passages addressed to believers. But if the question concerns his standing in the Hereafter, the answer is:

A person of this kind is not among the believers

---

## Page 3390

who are promised Paradise. Rather, he possesses faith that prevents him from remaining in Hell forever and through which he will enter Paradise after being punished in Hell, unless Allah forgives his sins. Hence some have said: “He is a believer by virtue of his faith and an evildoer by virtue of his major sin,” or, “A believer deficient in faith.”

Those among Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu‘tazilah who do not call him a believer say that the designation of wickedness is incompatible with the designation of faith, because Allah says:

“How wretched is the name of wickedness after faith!”

And:

“Is one who is a believer like one who is an evildoer?”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

According to this principle, a person may possess a branch of disbelief while also possessing faith. This explains the reports in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called many sins disbelief, although the person committing them may possess more than an atom’s weight of faith and therefore will not remain in Hell forever. For example, he said:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

And:

“Do not revert after me to being disbelievers, striking one another’s necks.”

This is widely reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several chains of transmission in the Sahīh. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, orders were given for it to be proclaimed among the people. Thus, he called those who strike one another’s necks without right disbelievers, and called this act disbelief.

Nevertheless, Allah Most High said:

“If two groups of believers fight one another, make peace between them,”

up to His words:

“The believers are but brothers.”

He thus made clear that they had not departed from faith altogether, but that they possessed something constituting disbelief: this particular trait. As some of the Companions said: “A lesser form of disbelief.”

Likewise, the Prophet said:

“If someone says to his brother, ‘You disbeliever!’ one of them has incurred that charge.”

He called him his brother at the very moment those words were spoken, while stating that one of them had incurred that charge. Had either of them departed from Islam altogether, he would no longer have been his brother. Rather, he possesses an element of disbelief.

---

## Page 3391

The same applies to his statement in the authentic hadith:

“No man knowingly claims descent from someone other than his father without committing disbelief.”

And in another hadith:

“Whoever disowns his lineage, however tenuous the connection, has disbelieved in Allah.”

Among the passages of the Quran whose wording was abrogated was:

“Do not disown your fathers, for disowning your fathers is disbelief on your part.”

The rights of parents are coupled with Allah’s right in such statements as:

“Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final return.”

And:

“Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him and that you be good to your parents.”

A person’s father is the source from which he was created, and his child is among his earnings, as Allah says:

“Neither his wealth nor what he earned will avail him.”

Denying one’s parents is therefore a branch of disbelief. By denying that from which his Lord created him, he has denied his Lord’s creation of him. In the language of those before us, the Lord was called “Father,” so this involves disbelief in Allah in this respect. Yet this is not like denying the Creator altogether. We shall discuss the remaining hadiths, if Allah wills.

The purpose here is to state a “comprehensive principle” upon which an understanding of the scriptural texts can be built, and by which people’s disputes can be referred back to the Book and the Sunnah. People have disputed extensively over various aspects of what faith and Islam denote, because these two terms occur so frequently and are discussed so much. The more a term is discussed—being used without qualification in one place, with one qualification elsewhere, and with another qualification in yet another place—the more this can cause aspects of its meaning to become unclear. Then, the more widely it is heard, the greater the number of people who become confused about it.

One reason for this is that a person hears some instances of its use but not others. What he hears may be qualified in a way that confines it to a particular meaning, so he assumes that it has that same meaning wherever else it occurs. Thus, whoever pursues his study until he knows the full range of its uses and understands the source of

---

## Page 3392

confusion will give each matter its due and recognize that the best speech is Allah’s speech, that no explanation is more complete than His, and that the matters of religion which Muslims need and upon which they agree far exceed those over which they disagree.

Muslims—both those who follow the Sunnah and those who follow religious innovations—agree on the obligation to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day. They agree on the obligation of prayer, zakah, fasting, and pilgrimage. They agree that whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will enter Paradise and will not be punished, and that whoever does not believe that Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is Allah’s Messenger to him is a disbeliever. These and similar matters are the foundations of religion and the principles of faith upon which those who profess Islam and faith agree.

Their disagreement, beyond this, concerning certain rulings relating to the threat of punishment or certain meanings of particular terms is a minor matter compared with what they agree upon. Nevertheless, those who oppose the clear truth of the Book and the Sunnah are recognized by the majority of the Muslim community as adherents of religious innovation and are attested to be astray. They enjoy neither an honourable reputation nor general acceptance within the Muslim community, as is the case with the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Qadariyyah, and others like them. The disagreements among the people of knowledge and the Sunnah concern only subtle matters that elude most people. Yet whatever they dispute must be referred back to Allah and His Messenger.

Referring “the question of Islam and faith” back to Allah and His Messenger establishes that, although what each of these two terms denotes is obligatory, no one merits Paradise unless he is both a believer and a Muslim. The truth concerning this is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained in the hadith of Gabriel: he distinguished “three levels” within the religion and among its adherents. The first is Islam, the middle is faith, and the highest is excellence. Whoever reaches the highest level

---

## Page 3393

has also attained the level immediately below it. Thus, a person of excellence is a believer, and a believer is a Muslim; a Muslim, however, is not necessarily a believer. The Quran likewise divides the community into these three categories. Allah Most High says:

“Then We granted the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who, by Allah’s permission, are foremost in good deeds. That is the great bounty.”

The Muslim who has not fulfilled the obligations of faith is the one who wrongs himself. The one who follows a middle course is a believer without qualification: he fulfils his obligations and avoids what is forbidden. The one foremost in good deeds is the person of excellence, who worships Allah as though he sees Him. Allah, glorified be He, also mentions this threefold division of people in the Hereafter in Surahs al-Wāqi'ah, al-Mutaffifīn, and Hal Atā, mentioning the disbelievers as well. Here, however, He confines the division to those chosen from among His servants.

Abū Sulaymān al-Khattābī said:

“This question is among those on which people most often err. Al-Zuhrī said, ‘Islam is the declaration of faith, while faith is deeds,’ citing the verse as evidence. Others held that Islam and faith are one and the same, citing His words:

‘So We brought out whoever was there of the believers. But We found there only one household of Muslims.’”

Al-Khattābī said: “Two scholars discussed this matter, each adopting one of these two views. The later of them refuted his predecessor and wrote a book against him extending to two hundred leaves.”

Al-Khattābī said: “The correct approach is to qualify what is said on this matter rather than speak without qualification. A Muslim may be a believer in some circumstances but not in others, whereas a believer

---

## Page 3394

is a Muslim in all circumstances. Thus, every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer. If you understand the matter in this way, the verses can be interpreted coherently and explained consistently, without any contradiction between them.”

I say: Of the two men to whom al-Khattābī referred, I think the earlier was Muhammad ibn Nasr. Among the scholars of the Sunnah and hadith, he is the one I know to have discussed at length the view that Islam and faith are one and the same. I know of no one before him who treated this subject at length. As for the other, who refuted him, I think he was … (1), but I have not come across his refutation.

The view al-Khattābī preferred is that of those who distinguished between the two, such as Abū Ja'far, Hammād ibn Zayd, and 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī. It is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. I know of no early scholar who disagreed with them by holding that Islam itself is identical to faith itself. Thus, the general position of Ahl al-Sunnah was the one these scholars expressed, as al-Khattābī mentioned.

Likewise, Abū al-Qāsim al-Taymī al-Asbahānī, his son Muhammad—the commentator on Muslim—and others stated that the preferred view among Ahl al-Sunnah is that the designation “believer” should not be applied without qualification to a thief or a fornicator, as the scriptural text indicates.

In his Commentary on al-Bukhārī, al-Khattābī made statements implying that Islam and faith are inseparable despite their distinct designations. [Al-Baghawī also mentioned this in Sharh al-Sunnah, saying: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used ‘Islam’ to designate outward deeds and ‘faith’ to designate inward belief. This is not because deeds are not part of faith

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 3395

or because affirmation in the heart is not part of Islam. Rather, this distinguishes the components of a whole: they all constitute one thing, collectively called religion.”] (*)

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This is Gabriel, who came to teach you your religion.”

Both affirmation and action are encompassed by each of the terms Islam and faith. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

And His words:

“And I have approved Islam as your religion.”

And His words:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

He thus made clear that the religion He approves and accepts from His servants is Islam. Religion can receive His approval and acceptance only when affirmation accompanies action.

I say: Although the distinction made by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of Gabriel implies that excellence is the highest level, that excellence encompasses faith, and that faith encompasses Islam, it does not establish the reverse. Even supposing that it indicated their inseparability, it explicitly shows that what one term denotes is not what the other denotes. The precise explanation, however, is that their meanings differ depending on whether they occur separately or together, as we have explained. Whoever understands this will find many difficulties resolved in numerous areas where various groups have gone astray—concerning the question of faith and other matters.

His statement that religion can receive approval and acceptance only when affirmation accompanies action indicates that faith must accompany action. This establishes that faith is obligatory in all circumstances, but it does not establish that the action constituting religion is not called Islam. If faith is a condition for its acceptance, it does not follow that faith necessarily accompanies it. Even if faith necessarily accompanied it, it would not follow that faith forms part of what the term Islam denotes.

## Page 3396

Shaykh Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Salāh said:

Concerning the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah,” and the rest of the passage, and “Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers,” and the rest of the passage, he said:

This explains the foundation of faith, namely inward affirmation, and the foundation of Islam, namely outward submission and compliance. Outwardly, a person’s status as a Muslim is established by the two testimonies of faith. He mentioned the four alongside them only because they are Islam’s most manifest and principal rites. By performing them, a person completes his submission; abandoning them suggests that he is undoing the bond of his compliance, or that it is coming undone.

The term faith also encompasses the practices used to explain Islam in this hadith, as well as all other acts of obedience, because they are fruits of inward affirmation—which is the foundation of faith—and serve to sustain, complete, and preserve it. Thus, in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained faith as the two testimonies, prayer, zakat, fasting, and giving one-fifth of the spoils of war.

For this reason, the unqualified designation “believer” does not apply to someone who commits a major sin or neglects an obligatory duty. A designation denoting completeness applies to the complete instance and is not ordinarily used for a deficient one without qualification. It was therefore permissible to deny him this designation without qualification in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery.”

The term “Islam” also encompasses the “foundation of faith,” namely affirmation, and the “foundation of acts of obedience,” for all of this is submission.

He said: From what we have explained and established, it follows that Islam and faith overlap in some respects and differ in others, and that every believer is a Muslim, but not

---

## Page 3397

every Muslim is a believer. He said:

This is a thorough explanation that reconciles the various texts concerning faith and Islam, about which those discussing them have so often erred. What we have established accords with the positions of the great majority of scholars, both the scholars of hadith and others.

In response, it may be said:

What he has stated—may Allah have mercy on him—accords with the previously explained statements of the imams and with what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, making it clear that the majority hold that every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer.

His statement that the hadith mentions the foundation of faith and the foundation of Islam may be challenged as follows: the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered the questions about faith and Islam by giving what amounts to a definition of each. Thus, what he mentioned corresponds to faith and Islam themselves, not merely to their foundations. Faith, therefore, means believing in what he mentioned, both inwardly and outwardly. However, his description of faith includes Islam, just as excellence in worship includes faith.

As for the statement, “The foundation of submission is outward Islam,” Islam is submission and obedience to Allah, both outwardly and inwardly. This is the religion of Islam with which Allah is pleased, as the texts of the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Whoever submits outwardly but not inwardly is a hypocrite whose outward profession is accepted, for one has not been commanded to cut open people’s hearts.

Furthermore, if Islam encompasses the inward affirmation that constitutes the foundation of faith, it necessarily follows that every Muslim is a believer. This contradicts what has been reported from the majority. Nevertheless, Islam must involve an affirmation through which the foundation of faith is attained; otherwise, a person would not be rewarded for it. Thus, he is

---

## Page 3398

then both a Muslim and a believer. It must therefore be clarified who the Muslim who is not a believer is, and how he falls within Islam. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This was Gabriel, who came to teach you your religion.”

His statement, “Islam consists of the five pillars,” does not refer to someone who performs them without sincerity to Allah, but rather with hypocrisy. It refers instead to someone who performs them as commanded, both inwardly and outwardly. He identified these five as Islam because they are the purely devotional acts of worship owed to Allah Most High by every servant capable of performing them. Other duties are either collective obligations serving a benefit—once that benefit is secured, the obligation lapses—or concern people’s rights against one another, even though fulfilling them may also bring one nearer to Allah, and other such matters.

These other duties follow from the five pillars, as in his statements:

“A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”

“The best of Islam is to provide food and greet with peace those you know and those you do not know.”

And there are other statements to this effect. These five, then, are the pillars and foundations, just as faith has its pillars and foundations.

The statement, “Acts of obedience are the fruits of inward affirmation,” can mean two things. It can mean that they necessarily follow from it: whenever inward faith exists, they exist. This is the position of the early generations and Ahl al-Sunnah. Or it can mean that inward faith may give rise to them, yet may be complete and perfect even when they are absent. This is the position of the Murjiʾah among the Jahmiyyah and others. We have already explained that they erred in three respects:

(First): Their assumption that faith in the heart can be complete without the deeds of the heart—affirmation without such deeds of the heart as love of Allah, awe and fear of Him, reliance upon Him, and longing to meet Him.

---

## Page 3399

(Second): Their assumption that faith in the heart can be complete without outward deeds. This is the position of all the Murjiʾah.

(Third): Their claim that anyone whom the Lawgiver declares a disbeliever is declared so only because his heart lacks affirmation of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He. Many later scholars do not distinguish between the positions of the early generations and the views of the Murjiʾah and Jahmiyyah, because these are intermingled in the writings of many of them. Such a person inwardly holds the Jahmiyyah’s and Murjiʾah’s view of faith, yet venerates the early generations and the scholars of hadith. He therefore imagines that he can reconcile the two, or reconcile the statements of those like himself with those of the early generations.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī said:

“A third group—the overwhelming majority of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah and the scholars of hadith—maintained that the faith to which Allah called His servants and which He made obligatory upon them is Islam, which He established as the religion, approved for His servants, and called them to embrace. It is the opposite of disbelief, which He abhors. He said:

‘He does not approve disbelief for His servants.’

And He said:

‘I have approved Islam as your religion.’

And He said:

‘Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam.’

And He said:

‘What of one whose heart Allah has opened to Islam, so that he follows a light from his Lord?’

Thus Allah praised Islam in the same way that He praised faith, making it a designation of praise and commendation. He stated that whoever embraces Islam follows a light and guidance from his Lord, and that it is His religion, which He has approved. Whatever He has approved, He has loved and praised. Do you not see that Allah’s prophets and messengers earnestly sought it from Him and asked Him for it? Abraham and Ishmael said:

‘Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You.’

Joseph said:

‘Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.’

And He said: ‘And Abraham enjoined it

---

## Page 3400

upon his sons, as did Jacob: “O my sons, Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.”’ And He said:

‘And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, “Have you submitted yourselves?” If they submit, they are rightly guided.’

And elsewhere He said:

‘Say, “We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac,”’

up to His words:

‘So if they believe in the same as you believe in, they are rightly guided.’

Thus Allah ruled that whoever embraces Islam is rightly guided and whoever believes is rightly guided, thereby treating the two alike.”

He said:

“We have already presented the full argument that Islam is faith and that the two are neither separate nor distinct elsewhere. We therefore preferred not to repeat it here, wishing to avoid undue length and repetition. However, we shall present arguments here that we have not mentioned elsewhere and explain the error in their interpretation and in the arguments they have drawn from the Book and the transmitted reports to distinguish between Islam and faith.”

I say: Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī—may Allah have mercy on him—means that the Muslim deserving of praise is the believer deserving of praise, and that the person who is censured is deficient in both Islam and faith. He also means that every believer is a Muslim and that every Muslim must possess some faith. This is correct and agreed upon. He further means that anyone to whom the designation of Islam is applied is also given the designation of faith. There is a verbal dispute concerning this. He also means that what one term denotes is what the other denotes, but this is not known to have been held by any of the early generations.

Even if it is said, “The two are inseparable,” what one term denotes need not be identical to what the other denotes merely because the two are inseparable. It has not been transmitted from any of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the renowned imams of Islam that he said:

“The term Islam denotes the same thing as the term

---

## Page 3401

faith,” as [nasr] (1). Indeed, I know of no one among the early generations who said this. What is well known from a number of early and later scholars, however, is that the believer entitled to Allah’s promise is the Muslim entitled to Allah’s promise. Thus every Muslim is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim. The meaning of this is agreed upon by early and later scholars—indeed, by all the sects of the Muslim community. They all say that the believer promised Paradise must be a Muslim, and the Muslim promised Paradise must be a believer. Everyone, from the earliest generations to the latest, who enters Paradise without punishment is both a believer and a Muslim.

Furthermore, Ahl al-Sunnah do not say: “Those who leave the Fire and enter Paradise possess some measure of that.” The dispute concerns only the application of the designation. Reports from the early generations affirming that faith consists of speech and action have been transmitted in such numbers as to establish certainty, whereas no such statement concerning Islam has been transmitted from them. However, the overwhelming majority held that Islam encompasses the entire religion, not merely the verbal profession, contrary to the apparent meaning of what is reported from al-Zuhrī. They therefore said that prayer, zakat, fasting, Hajj, and the other commanded deeds are part of Islam just as they are part of faith. He consequently assumed that they regarded the two as one and the same, but that is not so. They agree that faith necessarily entails Islam, yet the inclusion of Islam within faith does not mean that the two are identical.

As for Islam, he has no evidence that it necessarily entails faith when the term is used without qualification. Whether it entails the faith that is obligatory or the perfection of faith is disputed, and he has no evidence that it necessarily entails faith. Nevertheless, the prophets whom Allah described as Muslims were all believers, and Allah also described them as believers. Even had He not mentioned this about them, we would still know with certainty that all the prophets are believers.

## Page 3402

Likewise, the earliest forerunners were both Muslims and believers.

Even if it were assumed that Islam necessarily entails the faith that is obligatory, the most that could be said is that the two necessarily accompany one another: every Muslim is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim. This is correct if what is meant is that every Muslim who enters Paradise possesses the faith that is obligatory. It is also agreed upon if what is meant is that every Muslim who is rewarded for his worship must possess the foundation of faith. Thus, every Muslim is a believer, even if this is not the faith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, denied to those who do not love for their brothers what they love for themselves, to those who commit major sins, and to the Bedouins and others.

If it is said that Islam and complete faith necessarily accompany one another, it does not follow that they are identical. They are like the soul and the body: among us, no soul is found except with a body, and no living body is found except with a soul, yet neither is identical to the other. Faith is like the soul, for it resides in the soul and is connected to the body, while Islam is like the body, which cannot be alive without the soul. This means that the two necessarily accompany one another, not that the two terms designate the same thing. The Islam of the hypocrites is like a dead body—a body without a soul. Every living body has a soul, but souls differ, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Souls are assembled troops: those that recognize one another unite, and those that do not recognize one another are at odds.”

Not everyone who performs prayer with his body has a heart illuminated by remembrance of Allah, humble devotion, and understanding of the Quran, even though he is rewarded for his prayer and, under the rulings applicable in this world, his obligation is discharged. Outward Islam is thus like the outward performance of prayer, while faith is like the knowledge of Allah, humble devotion, and reflection upon the Quran that reside in the heart during prayer. Thus, whoever has humble devotion in his heart

---

## Page 3403

will also manifest humble devotion in his limbs, but the converse does not hold. Hence the saying:

“Beware of hypocritical humility.”

This is when the body displays humble devotion while the heart does not. When the heart is sound, the whole body is sound; yet the body’s engagement in worship does not mean that the heart is fulfilling its inward realities.

With regard to “faith” and “Islam,” people fall into three ranks: those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those foremost in good deeds. Someone who is a Muslim outwardly and inwardly, yet wrongs himself, must possess faith, though he has not fulfilled what is obligatory. The converse does not hold, and the same applies in the other case. This will be discussed, Allah willing.

The verses cited as evidence by Muhammad ibn Nasr establish that Islam is obligatory, that it is Allah’s religion, that Allah loves it and is pleased with it, and that it is His only religion. All of this is true. Yet none of it establishes that Islam is identical to faith. Nor does it establish that Islam alone makes a person one of the people of Paradise, as he mentioned when presenting the evidence for the first position. Allah has promised the believers Paradise in numerous verses, but He has not attached this promise to the designation “Islam.” Thus, His praise of Islam, His making it obligatory, and His love for it indicate that it is included within faith and forms part of it. All the adherents of the Sunnah agree on this. They say:

Every believer is a Muslim, and everyone who fulfils the obligatory requirements of faith has fulfilled the obligatory requirements of Islam. The dispute, however, concerns the converse.

Similarly, Allah loves prayer, commands it, makes it obligatory, and praises both it and those who perform it in numerous passages. Yet this does not establish that what the term “prayer” designates is identical to what the term “faith” designates. Rather, prayer is included within faith. Thus, every believer performs prayer, but not everyone who prays while committing major sins is necessarily a believer.

---

## Page 3404

All the evidence he cited from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, distinguishes between what “faith” and “Islam” designate when they are mentioned together, as in the hadith of Gabriel and elsewhere. It also shows that when the term “faith” is used without qualification, it includes Islam.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid said in his book on the foundations of religion:

“We have already stated that faith consists of speech and deeds. As for Islam, Ahmad’s statements admit of two reported positions. The first is that it is like faith. The second is that it consists of speech without deeds. This latter position is his explicit statement as transmitted by Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd.”

He said: “The correct view is that the school has only one reported position: that Islam consists of speech and deeds. His statement that Islam consists of speech may mean that it does not require the deeds stipulated as conditions of faith. Prayer is not a condition of Islam, since his explicit statement is that a person does not become a disbeliever by abandoning prayer.”

He said: “We have established that Islam and faith are two terms designating two meanings, and we have mentioned the disagreement among the jurists.”

It had previously been stated that Islam and faith are two terms designating different meanings, and that Mālik, Sharīk, and Hammād ibn Zayd held this view, distinguishing between Islam and faith.

He said: “The followers of al-Shāfiʿī and the followers of Abū Hanīfah said that they are two terms with the same meaning.”

He said: “This implies that a person may cease to be designated a believer while remaining a Muslim. This happens when he commits the major sins mentioned in the report: he loses the designation of faith, yet remains a Muslim. If he repents of this, he returns to the faith he previously possessed. Committing minor sins does not deprive him of the designation of faith; rather, it continues to apply to him.”

He then cited the evidence for this. However, what he cited

---

## Page 3405

contains abundant evidence against those who say that Islam is merely the verbal profession. Numerous proofs show that deeds are part of Islam; indeed, all the texts indicate this. Whoever says that the prescribed outward deeds are not part of Islam holds a false view. This differs from the heart’s affirmation of truth: nothing in the texts indicates that this is part of Islam; rather, it is part of faith. Islam is religious submission, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained it: submitting one’s face and heart to Allah. Thus, devoting one’s religion sincerely to Allah is Islam. This differs from affirming the truth: the former belongs to the heart’s deeds, while the latter belongs to its knowledge.

Although Ahmad ibn Hanbal said on this occasion that Islam is the verbal profession, elsewhere he said that deeds are part of Islam. Here he followed al-Zuhrī, may Allah have mercy on him. If someone who says this means that a person enters Islam through the verbal profession without having fulfilled Islam completely, this is close to the truth. But if he means that the person has fulfilled Islam entirely even without performing any deeds, this is certainly mistaken. Indeed, following the hadith of Gabriel, Ahmad rejected this answer—the statement that the designation applies to a person even if he performs no deeds. He should therefore have quoted Ahmad’s statement in full.

Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd said:

“I asked Ahmad about Islam and faith. He replied: ‘Faith consists of speech and deeds, while Islam is acknowledgment.’”

He also said:

“I asked Ahmad about someone who made the following statement concerning Gabriel’s exchange with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he asked him about Islam—‘If I do that, am I a Muslim?’ to which he replied, ‘Yes.’ Someone then said: ‘Even if he does not do what Gabriel mentioned to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is he still a Muslim?’ Ahmad replied: ‘Such a person is contradicting the hadith.’”

---

## Page 3406

Thus, Ahmad regarded anyone who called a person a Muslim despite his failure to fulfil the five pillars as contradicting the hadith, even though Ahmad himself said that Islam is acknowledgment. This indicates that acknowledgment marks one’s initial entry into Islam, and that one has not fulfilled the obligations of Islam until one fulfils the five pillars. Applying the designation is conditional upon fulfilling them, for he censured anyone who did not follow the hadith of Gabriel.

Moreover, in most of his answers, he judged someone who abandoned prayer to be a disbeliever; indeed, he also did so for abandoning other pillars. Muslims unanimously agree that a disbeliever is not a Muslim. It is therefore clear that he did not mean that Islam consists merely of speech without deeds. Even supposing that he did mean this, it would imply that abandoning any of the four pillars does not constitute disbelief. Most reports from him, however, indicate the contrary. Those who do not judge someone who abandons these pillars to be a disbeliever—such as al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, Abū Hanīfa and others—nevertheless regard them as part of Islam. How, then, could Ahmad not regard them as part of Islam, when his position on their inclusion in Islam is stronger than that of others?

It has also been reported that he considered the hadith of Sa‘d to conflict with the hadith of ‘Umar and gave preference to the hadith of Sa‘d. Al-Hasan ibn ‘Alī said:

“I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal: ‘Which is stronger: faith or Islam?’ He replied: ‘There is this hadith of ‘Umar, but I prefer the hadith of Sa‘d.’”

It seems that he understood the hadith of ‘Umar to indicate that deeds are what the term Islam denotes, which would make what it denotes superior, whereas the hadith of Sa‘d indicates that what the term faith denotes is superior. Yet the hadith of ‘Umar mentions only outward deeds in its description of Islam. These do not constitute faith unless accompanied by the heart’s faith in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers. They then constitute part of faith, so what the term faith denotes is superior, as the hadith of Sa‘d indicates. There is therefore no contradiction between the two hadiths.

As for Ahmad’s distinction between Islam and faith, he would sometimes affirm it, and at other times report

---

## Page 3407

the disagreement without taking a firm position. When he mentioned the two together, he would sometimes say, “Islam is the declaration of faith,” and sometimes he would not. Likewise, regarding declaring someone a disbeliever for abandoning the pillars, he would sometimes do so—even becoming angry over the matter—and sometimes he would not.

Al-Maymūnī said:

“I asked, ‘Abū ‘Abd Allāh, do you distinguish between Islam and faith?’

“He replied, ‘Yes.’

“I asked, ‘What evidence do you rely on?’

“He replied, ‘The hadiths generally indicate this.’ He then quoted:

“‘An adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery, nor is a thief a believer while stealing.’

“‘And Allah Most High says:

“He said, ‘Hammād ibn Zayd also distinguishes between Islam and faith.’

“Ahmad said, ‘A man said to me, “Had nothing else reached us concerning faith but this, it would have been sufficient.”’

“I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘So you follow the apparent meaning of the Book together with the reports of the Sunnah?’
