“I asked, ‘Is this, then, the basis of our argument against them?’

“He replied, ‘Yes.’”

Thus, he reported Ahmad’s distinction without qualification, along with his appeal to the scriptural texts as evidence.

Sālih ibn Ahmad said:

“My father was asked about Islam and faith. He replied, ‘Ibn Abī Dhi’b said: “Islam is verbal profession, and faith is deeds.”’

“He was asked, ‘What do you yourself say?’

“He replied, ‘Islam is distinct from faith,’ and cited the hadith of Sa‘d and the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

---

## Page 3408

Thus, in this report, he did not adopt the view of those who say that Islam is verbal profession. Rather, he answered that Islam is distinct from faith, as indicated by the authentic hadith together with the Quran.

Hanbal said:

“Abū ‘Abd Allāh related to us the hadith of Burayda:

‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to teach them, when they went out to the graveyards, to say: “Peace be upon you, inhabitants of these dwellings, believers and Muslims. We shall, if Allah wills, join you.”’”

He then related the rest of the hadith.

He said:

“I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh say: ‘This hadith provides evidence against those who say that faith is verbal profession. Whoever says, “I am a believer,” has contradicted his words, “believers and Muslims.” He thus distinguished the believer from the Muslim and refuted those who say, “I am a believer whose faith is complete.” His words, “We shall, if Allah wills, join you,” despite his knowing that he would die, support those who say, “I am a believer, if Allah wills,” adding this qualification here.’”

Abū al-Hārith said:

“I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh about the Prophet’s words:

‘An adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery, nor is one who drinks wine a believer while drinking it.’

“He replied: ‘They have offered interpretations of this. ‘Atā’ said, “Faith withdraws from him.” Tāwūs said, “When he does that, faith departs from him.” It is reported that al-Hasan said, “If he turns back, faith returns to him.” It has also been said, “He passes from faith into Islam, but does not leave Islam.”’”

Sālih also transmitted this question and answer, for Sālih likewise transmits the questions put by Abū al-Hārith.

Sālih asked his father about this account, and he said concerning it:

“This is how it is narrated from Abū Ja‘far. He said:

‘An adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery.’

“He said: ‘He passes from faith into Islam, for faith is contained within Islam,

---

## Page 3409

so when he commits adultery, he passes from faith into Islam.’ Al-Zuhrī said—meaning, when Sa‘d’s hadith, ‘Or a Muslim,’ was narrated—‘We therefore consider Islam to be verbal profession and faith to be deeds.’ Ahmad said: ‘This is a hadith whose meaning is interpreted, and Allah knows best.’”

Thus, he mentioned the statements of the Successors without preferring any one of them. This, and Allah knows best, is because everything they said is true, and he agrees with all of it. Elsewhere, he likewise stated that a person passes from faith into Islam, and made similar statements. By “interpretation,” Ahmad and others like him among the early generations do not mean diverting an expression from its apparent meaning. Rather, interpretation, for them, is explanation and clarification of what an expression ultimately signifies. An example is the statement of ‘Ā’isha, may Allah be pleased with her:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would frequently say while bowing and prostrating, ‘Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. O Allah, forgive me,’ thereby putting the Quran into practice.”

What the Successors mentioned does not contradict the apparent meaning of the hadith; rather, it agrees with it. Ahmad’s words, “It is interpreted,” mean that its meaning is explained, even though that explanation agrees with its apparent meaning, lest an innovator suppose that it means the person has become a disbeliever with no faith whatsoever, as the Khawārij claim. The hadith does not indicate this. The very one who denied these people faith regarded them as Muslims, not as believers.

Al-Marwadhī said:

“Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, ‘Do we say, “We are the believers”?’

“He replied, ‘We say, “We are the Muslims.”’

“I said to Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Do we say, “We are believers”?’

“He replied, ‘Rather, we say, “We are Muslims.”’”

This is because one of his principles is to qualify declarations of faith by saying “if Allah wills,” since a person does not know whether he is fulfilling everything Allah has commanded him to do. Such a declaration is therefore like saying, “I am righteous,” “I am God-fearing,” or “I am a friend of Allah,” as will be discussed in

---

## Page 3410

its proper place. This does not preclude omitting the qualification “if Allah wills” when one means, “I affirm the truth,” for a person can be certain of the affirmation in his heart without being certain that he is complying with everything he has been commanded to do. Likewise, he can be certain that he loves Allah and His Messenger, hates disbelief, and possesses other such qualities that he knows are in his heart. The same applies if he means that he is outwardly a believer: he is not prevented from stating with certainty what he knows.

What is condemned is only what the scholars generally condemned in the doctrine of the Murji’ah, who say that faith is identical in all who possess it, just as every person has a head. Thus, one of them says, “I am truly a believer,” “I am a believer in Allah’s sight,” and similar statements, just as someone says, “I truly have a head,” or “In Allah’s knowledge, I truly have a head.” Whoever makes a categorical declaration on this basis has excluded inward and outward deeds from faith. The Companions, the Successors, and all the Muslims who followed them regard this as a reprehensible and false statement. People’s discussions of “the question of qualifying declarations of faith” will be addressed in their proper place.

The point here is that there are two extreme positions: the view that Islam consists solely in the verbal profession, with outward deeds falling outside the meaning of Islam; and the view that Islam and faith mean the same thing. Both are weak positions that contradict the hadith of Gabriel and the other hadiths of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Thus, when Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī defended the second position, he had no proof establishing its correctness. Instead, he relied on evidence that invalidates the first position. He cited Allah’s words concerning the Bedouins:

“Rather, it is Allah who has conferred a favor upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.”

He said: “This indicates that ‘Islam’ is faith.”

---

## Page 3411

To this it may be replied:

Rather, it indicates the opposite, for these people did not say, “We have submitted”; they said, “We believe.” Allah commanded them to say, “We have submitted.” He then mentioned their being described as having embraced Islam, saying:

“Rather, it is Allah who has conferred a favor upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful”—

that is, truthful in your statement, “We believe.” If Islam were identical to faith, there would have been no need to say, “if you are truthful,” for they would be truthful in saying, “We have submitted,” even though they did not actually say this. Rather, Allah said:

“They consider their acceptance of Islam a favor to you. Say, ‘Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, it is Allah who has conferred a favor upon you.’”

That is, they consider the Islam they have practiced a favor to you. Allah Most High thus called what they had done Islam, but nothing in this indicates that they themselves called it Islam. They merely said, “We believe.” He then explained that the favor consists in guidance to faith. As for Islam unaccompanied by faith, people would practice it out of fear of the sword, so they cannot claim to have conferred any favor by doing so. If Allah has not bestowed faith upon them, their Islam is like that of the hypocrites, and Allah does not accept it from them.

But if they are truthful in saying, “We believe,” then it is Allah who has conferred upon them the favor of this faith and the Islam it includes. He, glorified be He, initially denied that they had faith, while here He made His bestowal of it upon them conditional on their truthfulness. This indicates that they could be truthful.

It has been said that they became truthful afterward. It may also be said that making something conditional does not entail that the condition is fulfilled. Another explanation is that they possessed some degree of faith. But is this the faith He described subsequently? Rather, they possess a branch of faith.

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

Allah Most High said:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him”—and the rest of the verse.

He also said:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

Thus He called the establishment of prayer and the payment of

---

## Page 3412

zakah an upright religion, and called that religion Islam. Whoever fails to pay zakah has therefore abandoned part of the upright religion—which Allah has declared to be the religion in His sight, namely Islam.

He said:

This group, which distinguishes between Islam and faith, is also specifically reported to hold that faith consists of words and deeds, and that prayer and zakah are part of faith. Allah has called both of them religion and has stated that the religion in His sight is Islam. Thus, Allah has described Islam in the same terms as faith, and faith in the same terms as Islam. Reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, convey the same meaning. Whoever claims that Islam is merely a verbal profession and that deeds are not part of it has contradicted the Quran and Sunnah. There is no difference between him and the Murji’ah, who claim that faith is a profession without deeds.

The reply is:

His statement that Allah has made prayer and zakah part of religion, and that the religion in His sight is Islam, is sound and agrees with the hadith of Gabriel. His refutation of those who exclude deeds from Islam is likewise sound. However, his statement that Allah has described faith in the same terms as Islam, and Islam in the same terms as faith, is not correct. Allah only said:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

He never said that the religion in the sight of Allah is faith. This religion is, however, part of faith; being part of something does not make it identical to the whole. Faith is rooted in the heart’s knowledge, assent, and affirmation. Deeds follow this knowledge and assent and are inseparable from them; a servant is not a believer without both.

Islam, by contrast, is purely a matter of deeds together with a verbal profession. Knowledge and assent are not part of what the term itself denotes, although it necessarily entails some measure of assent, for there can be no action without knowledge. It does not, however, necessarily entail the faith that Allah and His Messenger have set out in detail, as Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth

---

## Page 3413

and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.” He also says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

There are also all the other texts that deny faith to those who lack the qualities He has mentioned. For many Muslims are Muslims both inwardly and outwardly and possess a general assent, yet do not possess this faith. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

And He says:

“And I have approved Islam for you as your religion.”

He did not say, “Whoever seeks knowledge, recognition, assent, and faith other than Islam”; nor did He say, “I have approved Islam for you as assent and knowledge.” Islam belongs to the category of religion, action, obedience, submission, and humility. Thus, whoever seeks a religion other than Islam will not have it accepted alongside Islam. Faith, by contrast, is tranquillity and certainty, rooted in knowledge, assent, and recognition; religion follows from it. One says, “I believe in Allah,” and “I submit to Allah.” Moses said:

“O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.”

If the two terms denoted the same thing, this would be repetition. The same applies to His words:

“Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women.”

He likewise mentions the truthful, the patient, and the humble. The believer possesses all these qualities, but these terms do not have the same general or specific scope as faith.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, to You I submit, in You I believe, in You I put my trust, to You I turn, by Your aid I contend, and to You I turn for judgment.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that he would say this when he rose to pray at night. It is also established in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere that he would say during prostration:

“O Allah, to You I prostrate, in You I believe, and to You I submit.”

And when bowing, he would say: “To You I bow, and to You

---

## Page 3414

I submit, and in You I believe.” When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained the distinctive quality of each, he said:

“A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe, and a believer is one whom people trust with their lives and property.”

It is clear that being safe from someone’s wrongdoing is different from trusting him with one’s life and property, for the latter is a higher degree. People are safe from the wrongdoing of someone they trust, but not everyone from whose wrongdoing they are safe is someone they trust.

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

“Whoever claims that Islam consists in verbal profession and that deeds are not part of it has contradicted the Quran and Sunnah.”

This is correct, for all the texts indicate that deeds are part of Islam.

He said:

“There is no difference between him and the Murji’ah, who claim that faith consists in verbal profession without deeds.”

The response is that there is indeed a difference between them. Those among Ahl al-Sunnah who made this statement, such as al-Zuhrī and those who agreed with him, say that deeds are included in faith. They regard Islam as part of faith, and faith as more complete. This accords with the Quran and Sunnah.

They also say that people differ in their degrees of faith, which accords with the Quran and Sunnah. The Murji’ah, however, say that faith is part of Islam and that Islam is superior. They say that everyone’s faith is equal, so that the faith of the Companions and that of the most wicked people are the same. They also say that no one can possess some aspects of faith without the others. This contradicts the Quran and Sunnah.

Ahmad also answered this question in one of the two reports from him by saying, as al-Zuhrī did: “Islam is the declaration.” For he sometimes agrees with those who say this, and sometimes does not agree with them,

---

## Page 3415

but instead states what the Quran and Sunnah indicate: that Islam is distinct from faith. When he answered with al-Zuhrī’s statement, al-Maymūnī related the following exchange:

“I said, ‘Abū ‘Abd Allāh, do you distinguish between Islam and faith?’
He replied, ‘Yes.’
I asked, ‘What evidence do you rely on?’
He replied, ‘The hadiths generally indicate this.’ Then he quoted:

‘An adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery, nor is a thief a believer while stealing.’

He also quoted the words of the Most High:

‘The Bedouins say, “We believe.” Say, “You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”’

I asked him, ‘So you follow the apparent meaning of the Quran together with the Sunnah reports?’
He replied, ‘Yes.’
I said, ‘What, then, if the Murji’ah say that Islam is verbal profession?’
He replied, ‘They make all this one and the same. They regard him as both a Muslim and a believer without distinction, with faith like Gabriel’s, complete in faith.’
I asked, ‘Is this, then, the basis of our argument against them?’
He replied, ‘Yes.’”

Thus, Ahmad’s answer was that they regard the openly sinful person as a believer whose faith is complete, like Gabriel’s faith. As for his statement, “They regard him as both a Muslim and a believer without distinction,” this is the position of those who say that religion and faith are one and the same. Since Islam is the religion, they make Islam and faith one and the same. Many imams, such as al-Shāfi‘ī, Abū ‘Ubayd and others, attribute this position to the Murji’ah, and it is with those holding it that they debate.

The well-known position of the Murji’ah, however, distinguishes between the terms religion and faith, and between Islam and faith. They say that Islam consists partly of faith and partly of deeds, and that deeds include both obligatory and voluntary acts. But the early generations addressed those statements of the people of innovation that became apparent to them and reached them. You find the same in their discussions of the Jahmiyyah: they sometimes report that the Jahmiyyah say Allah is everywhere. This is the position of one group among them, such as the Najjāriyyah, and it is the position of their common people

---

## Page 3416

and their devout worshippers. Most of their speculative theologians, however—among the Jahmiyyah, Muʿtazilah, Dirāriyyah and others—say only: “He is neither within the world nor outside it, nor is He above the world.”

The same applies to their statements concerning the Qadariyyah: they report that they deny foreknowledge and the prior recording of events. These are the Qadariyyah about whom Ibn ʿUmar said: “When you meet those people, tell them that I disavow them and that they disavow me.” They used to say that Allah commanded and forbade His servants without knowing who would obey Him and who would disobey Him, or who would enter Paradise and who would enter the Fire, until they acted; only after they had acted did He know it. Hence their statement, “Events arise anew”—meaning that they begin afresh. A meadow is described as unuf (“fresh, untouched”) when its growth is abundant and it has not previously been grazed. They mean that His knowledge of the blessed and the wretched arises anew: He begins to know this without any prior knowledge or written record. Thus, deeds do not follow what has already been decreed, conforming precisely to that decree; rather, they are new occurrences, beginning afresh.

When a person intends to do something, he first determines in his mind what he wishes to do, then carries it out as he mentally determined it. He may also give outward expression to his plan in a visible representation. This mental determination is called “fashioning,” as in the poet’s words:

“You carry out what you design,
While some men design, but never carry through.”

He means: when you plan something, you carry it through and accomplish it, unlike others who are incapable of carrying out what they plan. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have created all things according to a decree.”

He, glorified be He, knows everything that will happen before He creates things, and He creates by His will. Thus, He knows it and wills it, and His knowledge and will subsist in Him. He may also speak of it and announce it, as in His words: “I will surely fill

---

## Page 3417

Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.” He also says:

“Were it not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord and an appointed term, punishment would have been inevitable.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Our word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers: they will surely be given victory, and Our forces will surely prevail.”

And He, Most High, says:

“We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but differences arose concerning it. Were it not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, judgment would have been passed between them.”

He, glorified be He, has also recorded what He decrees in that in which He records it, as He says:

“Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in heaven and earth? All of that is in a Record. That is surely easy for Allah.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Allah created creation and knew what they would do. Then He said to His knowledge, ‘Become a record,’ and it became a record. He then revealed confirmation of this in His words:

‘Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in heaven and earth? All of that is in a Record. That is surely easy for Allah.’”

And He, Most High, says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves without being in a Record before We bring it into being. That is surely easy for Allah.”

And He says:

“We have already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that My righteous servants shall inherit the earth.”

And He says:

“Allah erases whatever He wills and confirms whatever He wills, and with Him is the Mother of the Book.”

And He said to the angels:

“I am placing a successor on earth.” They said, “Will You place there someone who will spread corruption and shed blood, while we glorify You with praise and sanctify You?” He said, “I know what you do not know.”

The angels thus knew of the corruption and bloodshed that the children of Adam would commit. How, then, could Allah not know it? This holds whether they knew it because Allah had informed them—as most commentators have stated, in which case He has greater knowledge of what He taught them—or whether they said it by analogy with those who came before them, as some commentators have stated, or knew it by some other means.

Allah has greater knowledge of what will happen than His creatures do, for they know only what He has taught them. Whatever He has revealed to His prophets and others concerning what will happen, He knows it better than they do, for they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.

---

## Page 3418

Moreover, He said to the angels:

“I am placing a successor on earth,”

before commanding them to prostrate to Adam, before Iblīs refused, before forbidding Adam to eat from the tree, and before Adam ate from it, thereby causing his descent to earth. Allah, glorified be He, thus knew that He would appoint Adam as a successor, even as He gave him and Iblīs commands that He knew they would disobey. Their disobedience would lead to His ordering them both down to earth and to the establishment of succession there.

This shows that He knew how they would disobey His command. Iblīs refused to prostrate to Adam and hated him, becoming his enemy. He therefore whispered to him to induce him to eat from the tree, so that Adam too would sin. Iblīs had sworn to lead them all astray and had asked for respite until the Day they are resurrected. He is therefore intent on leading Adam and his descendants astray by every means available to him. But Adam received words from his Lord, who accepted his repentance; his Lord chose him and guided him through his repentance. Thus, Adam’s descendants have a path to salvation and happiness, escaping what Satan entices them into: repentance. Allah, Most High, says:

“So that Allah may punish the hypocrites, men and women, and the polytheists, men and women, and turn in mercy to the believers, men and women.”

Allah’s decree encompassed all of this before it came to pass. Iblīs persisted in sin, invoked divine decree as an excuse, and asked for respite so that he could bring others to ruin. Adam, however, repented and turned back to Allah. He and his wife said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Allah accepted his repentance, chose him, guided him, and sent him down to earth to act there in obedience to Him. Through this, Allah would raise his rank, and his subsequent entry into Paradise would be more perfect than before. Thus, whoever among Adam’s descendants sins and follows his father Adam’s example in repentance will be blessed. And if he repents, believes, and does righteous deeds,

---

## Page 3419

Allah will replace his evil deeds with good deeds, and after repentance he will be better than he was before his sin, like Allah’s other God-fearing friends.

But whoever among them follows Iblīs, persists in sin, invokes divine decree as an excuse, and seeks to lead others astray will be among those of whom Allah said:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and those of them who follow you, all together.”

The purpose here is to discuss divine decree. It is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, 'Imrān ibn Husayn reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah existed, and nothing existed before Him. His Throne was upon the water, and everything was written in the Record. Then He created the heavens and the earth.”

In both collections, it is reported through several chains of transmission that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated:

“Allah already knew the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, and what His servants would do before they did it.”

Also in both collections, 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd reported:

“Allah sends an angel after the body has been formed and before the soul is breathed into it. The angel writes down the person’s lifespan, provision, deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.”

These hadiths will be discussed in their respective places, Allah willing. This is the divine decree denied by the Qadariyyah who appeared toward the end of the Companions’ era.

It has been reported that the first person to introduce this innovation in Iraq was a man from Basra called Sīsawayh, who was of Magian descent. Ma'bad al-Juhanī learned it from him. It is also said that it first arose in the Hijāz when the Kaaba burned, and someone said:

---

## Page 3420

“It burned by the decree of Allah Most High.”

Another said, “Allah did not decree this.” During the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, no one denied divine power. When these people introduced the innovation of denying divine decree, the surviving Companions, such as 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar, 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Abbās, and Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa', refuted them. This denial was most prevalent in Basra and Syria, with only a little of it in the Hijāz. Most of the early scholars’ condemnations of the Qadariyyah concerned these people. Thus Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāh said:

“The Qadariyyah say, ‘Matters are not determined beforehand, and Allah has not decreed the recording or the deeds.’ The Murji’ah say, ‘Verbal profession suffices in place of deeds.’ The Jahmiyyah say, ‘Knowledge suffices in place of verbal profession and deeds.’”

Wakī' said, “All of this is disbelief.” This was also narrated by Ibn . . . (1).

However, when discussion of divine decree became widespread and many speculative thinkers and devout worshippers became involved in it, the majority of the Qadariyyah came to acknowledge Allah’s prior knowledge, denying only that His will and creation encompass everything. There are two reports concerning 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd’s denial of the prior written record. Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, Ahmad, and others declared the earlier group disbelievers on account of their position. As for this later group, they are misguided innovators, but they are not on the same footing as the earlier group. Among them were many scholars and devout worshippers from whom knowledge was recorded.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim included narrations from a number of them, but they did not include narrations from those who actively propagated this belief. This is the position of the jurists among the scholars of hadith, such as Ahmad and others: anyone who propagates an innovation deserves punishment to protect people from his harm, even if his inward conviction is based on independent scholarly judgment. The least punishment he deserves is to be shunned, so that he holds no standing in religion

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 3421

—knowledge is not to be taken from him, he is not to be appointed as a judge, his testimony is not to be accepted, and so forth. Mālik’s position is close to this. This is why the compilers of the Sahīh collections did not include narrations from those who actively propagated their beliefs. Nevertheless, they and the other scholars narrated from many who privately held the views of the Qadariyyah, Murji’ah, Khawārij, and Shī‘ah.

Ahmad said:

“If we were to abandon narrating from the Qadariyyah, we would abandon most of the people of Basra.”

This is because “the question of the creation of human actions and the divine willing of all that occurs” is a difficult one. Just as the Qadariyyah, both among the Mu‘tazilah and others, erred concerning it, so too did many—or most—of those who refuted them. In refuting them, they followed the approach of Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers: they denied Allah’s wisdom in His creation and His commands, denied His mercy towards His servants, and denied the causes He had established in creation and in His commands. They rejected realities present in His creatures and His revealed laws, to such an extent that most rational people who understood their doctrine became averse to what they supposed to be the Sunnah. For they claimed that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah on divine decree was the doctrine innovated by Jahm. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is simply that, when refuting the Murji’ah, Jahmiyyah, Qadariyyah, and others, the “early scholars” refuted the statements reported to them from these groups and those they had heard from some of their members. Such a statement might represent the position of only one faction among them, or it might have been altered in transmission. Thus, they refuted those Murji’ah who regarded religion and faith as one and the same, and said that it consists in verbal profession.

Moreover, in their time there had not yet appeared among the Murji’ah anyone who said:

“Faith is mere verbal profession, without assent or knowledge

---

## Page 3422

in the heart.” This was introduced only by Ibn Karrām, and it was his sole distinctive teaching. Everything else he said had already been said before him. Thus, neither al-Ash‘arī nor the other writers who recorded people’s doctrines attributed any distinctive teaching to him except this one. They attributed his other views to people who preceded him, without mentioning him. Ibn Karrām had not yet emerged in the time of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the other imams. Hence, they reported a consensus against this view, as did Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Thawr, and others.

Before him, the Murji’ah held that faith consists of verbal profession and assent in the heart, while Jahm held that it consists of assent in the heart. When Ibn Karrām said that it consists merely of verbal profession, the Murji’ah’s positions became three. Ahmad, however, was more knowledgeable about people’s doctrines than others and knew the Jahmiyyah’s position on faith. Abū Thawr, by contrast, did not know it; he knew only the Murji’ah among the jurists. This is why a consensus was reported against the positions of the Jahmiyyah and the Karrāmiyyah.

Abū Thawr said in his refutation of the Murji’ah, as transmitted by Abū al-Qāsim al-Tabarī al-Lālakā’ī and others, on the authority of Idrīs ibn ‘Abd al-Karīm, who said:

A man from Khurasan asked Abū Thawr about faith: what is it, and does it increase and decrease? Does it consist of profession, profession and action, or assent and action?

Abū Thawr answered him as follows:

“You asked—may Allah have mercy on you and pardon us and you—what faith is, whether it increases and decreases, and whether it consists of profession, profession and action, or assent and action. I shall therefore tell you the positions of the various groups and their disagreements.

---

## Page 3423

Know—may Allah have mercy on us and on you—that faith consists of assent in the heart, profession by the tongue, and action by the limbs. The scholars do not disagree that if a man were to say, ‘I testify that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is One, and that what the messengers brought is true,’ and acknowledge all the prescribed laws, but then say, ‘My heart holds none of this as true, and I do not believe it,’ he would not be a Muslim. Likewise, if he were to say, ‘The Messiah is Allah,’ and repudiate Islam, then say, ‘My heart holds none of that as true,’ he would be a disbeliever by openly declaring this, and not a believer.

Thus, neither profession without assent nor assent without profession makes a person a believer: he must assent in his heart and profess with his tongue. When there is assent in the heart and profession by the tongue, they regard him as a believer. Some of them, however, hold that he is not a believer unless action accompanies assent; he becomes a believer when these things are combined.

Since they denied that faith consists of one thing alone, and said that it consists of two things according to some, and three according to others, a person could only be a believer through all three things, concerning which they agreed. For when he fulfils all three, they all testify that he is a believer. We therefore adopted what they agreed upon: assent in the heart, profession by the tongue, and action by the limbs.

As for the group that held that action is not part of faith, they are asked: What did Allah want from His servants when He said to them, ‘Establish prayer and give zakah’: acknowledgment of this, or acknowledgment and action?

If they say, ‘Allah wanted acknowledgment but did not want action,’ then, according to the scholars, they have disbelieved (like someone who says, ‘Allah did not want His servants to pray or give zakah’?

If they say, ‘He wanted acknowledgment from them,’ they are told: ‘If, then, He wanted both things from them,

---

## Page 3424

why do you claim that he can be a believer through one without the other, when He wanted both?’

They are asked: “Suppose a man says, ‘I carry out everything Allah has commanded, but I do not acknowledge it.’ Would he be a believer?”

If they say, “No,” they are asked: “Then suppose he says, ‘I acknowledge everything Allah has commanded, but I do not act upon it.’ Would he be a believer?”

If they say, “Yes,” they are asked: “What is the difference? You have maintained that Allah wanted both things. If someone can be a believer through one while abandoning the other, then he can likewise be a believer through the other—by acting without acknowledging. There is no difference between the two.”

If someone objects, saying, “Suppose a man embraces Islam and acknowledges everything the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. Is he a believer by virtue of this acknowledgment before the time for any action comes?” he is told: “He is given this designation only because he affirms that action is obligatory upon him and declares that he will perform it when its appointed time comes. At this point, he is not required to acknowledge everything through which he becomes a believer. But if he were to say, ‘I acknowledge it, but I will not act,’ he would not be given the designation of faith.”

I say: Imām Abū Thawr—may Allah have mercy on him—means that a person is not a believer unless, alongside acknowledgment, he commits himself to acting. If he acknowledges but does not commit himself to acting, he is not a believer.

This argument presented by Abū Thawr establishes the obligation of both acknowledgment and action. It demonstrates that each is part of the religion, and that a person is neither obedient to Allah, nor deserving of reward, nor praiseworthy before Allah and His Messenger except through both together. It is an argument against those who exclude actions from both religion and faith.

As for someone who says that actions are part of the religion, yet maintains that a sinful person is a believer because he has embraced part of the religion—which, in their view, is faith—while abandoning another part, a different argument must be brought against him. However, Abū Thawr and other scholars of the Sunnah generally direct their arguments against this group. Ahmad had a broader knowledge of the various positions and arguments than

---

## Page 3425

Abū Thawr. For this reason, the consensus he reported was only against the position of the Karrāmiyyah. Then, exercising his customary caution in his wording, he did not categorically deny that any disagreement existed, but said: “I do not think anyone says this.”

This appears in his letter to Abū ʿAbd al-Rahīm al-Jūzajānī, which al-Khallāl recorded in his Book of the Sunnah—the most comprehensive compilation of Ahmad’s statements on the foundations of religion, although he made additional statements not included in it. Likewise, al-Khallāl’s book on knowledge is the most comprehensive compilation of Ahmad’s statements on the principles of jurisprudence.

Al-Marwadhī said: “I saw Abū ʿAbd al-Rahīm al-Jūzajānī with Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Abū ʿAbd Allāh had previously mentioned him, saying, ‘His father was a Murjiʾī,’ or he said, ‘an adherent of juristic opinion.’ As for Abū ʿAbd al-Rahīm himself, he praised him. He had written to Abū ʿAbd Allāh from Khurāsān, asking him about faith.”

He recorded the letter through two chains of transmission from Abū ʿAbd al-Rahīm, together with Ahmad’s reply:

“In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

“May Allah be gracious to us and to you in all matters, and, through His mercy, keep us and you safe from every evil. Your letter has reached me, mentioning the arguments advanced by some of the Murjiʾah.

“Know—may Allah have mercy on you—that disputation in religion is not the way of the people of the Sunnah, and that the interpretation offered by anyone who interprets the Quran without a Sunnah indicating the meaning Allah intended by it, or a report from the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the intended meaning is known through what has come from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or from his Companions. They saw the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and witnessed the Quran’s revelation, what Allah related to him in the Quran, what was meant by it, and what He intended by it: whether it is specific or

---

## Page 3426

general? As for anyone who interprets it according to its apparent meaning without any indication from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or any of the Companions, this is the interpretation of the people of innovation. A verse may be particular while its ruling is general, or its apparent wording may be general while something specific is intended. Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the one who explains Allah’s Book and His intended meaning. His Companions knew this better than we do, because they witnessed the circumstances and knew what was intended. Thus, a verse may be particular—that is, in its meaning—as in His saying, Exalted is He:

“Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, a share equal to that of two females.”

Its apparent wording is general: anyone to whom the designation ‘child’ applies is entitled to what Allah has prescribed. Yet the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established that a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever. It has also been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—though the report is not firmly established—that a killer does not inherit; it is, however, reported from his Companions that they did not allow a killer to inherit. Thus, Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained the Book, making clear that the verse was intended for the Muslim, not the disbeliever. Anyone who takes it according to its apparent meaning would have to allow anyone designated a child to inherit, whether a disbeliever or a killer. The same applies to the rulings concerning either parent as an heir, and other cases, along with many verses whose discussion would make this letter lengthy. The Muslim community has followed the Sunnah transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and from his Companions, except for those who rejected it among the people of innovation, the Khawārij, and their like. You have seen where they ended up.”

I say:

The terms mujmal (undetailed), mutlaq (unrestricted), and ‘āmm (general) were synonymous in the terminology of the leading scholars, such as al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, Abū ‘Ubayd, Ishāq, and others. By mujmal they did not mean something whose meaning cannot be understood, as some later scholars mistakenly explained it. Rather, the mujmal is that which, on its own, does not suffice for

---

## Page 3427

acting upon it, even though its apparent meaning is true, as in His saying, Exalted is He:

“Take charity from their wealth to purify and cleanse them thereby.”

The apparent sense and meaning of this verse are intelligible; it is not a passage whose intended meaning cannot be understood. Rather, what it conveys does not, on its own, suffice for acting upon it. What is commanded is charity that purifies and cleanses them, and this can only be known through the explanation of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Hence Ahmad said: “Anyone discussing jurisprudence should beware of these two ‘principles’: undetailed texts and analogical reasoning.”

He also said: “Most of people’s errors arise from interpretation and analogical reasoning.” By this he meant that one should not rule according to what general and unrestricted wording indicates before examining what specifies its scope and restricts it, nor act upon analogical reasoning before examining whether the implications of the texts invalidate it. Most of people’s errors arise from their adherence to what they suppose the wording and analogical reasoning indicate. Matters resting on probability must not be acted upon until a search for contrary evidence has been conducted thoroughly enough to reassure the heart. Otherwise, anyone who fails to do so will err. This is what happens to those who adhere to apparent meanings and analogies. Hence, invoking apparent meanings as evidence while disregarding the explanation of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions was deemed the way of the people of innovation. He has a substantial work on this subject.

Likewise, adhering to analogies while disregarding the texts and transmitted reports is the way of the people of innovation. Thus, every position these people originated was unsound; the only sound positions among their statements are those in which they agreed with the early generations—the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness.

He called His saying, Exalted is He,

“Allah instructs you concerning your children,”

general, whereas it is unrestricted with respect to circumstances, encompassing them as alternative possibilities, just as His saying,

“then the freeing of a slave,”

encompasses all slaves. It does not encompass them in the way that the term ‘child’ encompasses

---

## Page 3428

children. Whoever adopts this view is not following what the apparent wording of the Quran indicates, but rather what appears to him concerning something about which the Quran is silent. Its apparentness thus arises from the Quran’s silence about it, not from the Quran indicating it as its apparent meaning. They are therefore holding to an apparent inference from the wording, not to the apparent meaning of the wording itself. Their mainstay is their lack of knowledge of the texts that explain the relevant restrictions. Otherwise, everything the Quran clarifies and makes manifest is true. This is unlike something that appears to a person for a reason other than the Quran itself, yet is called the Quran’s apparent meaning—as in the arguments of the people of innovation among the Murjiʾah, Jahmiyyah, Khawārij, and Shīʿah.

Ahmad said:

“As for someone who claims that faith is verbal profession, what does he say about knowledge? Is knowledge needed alongside verbal profession? Must one also assent to what one knows? If he claims that knowledge is needed alongside verbal profession, then he has claimed that faith consists of two things. If he claims that one must both profess and assent to what one knows, then it consists of three things.

“If, however, he denies this and says that knowledge and assent are not needed, he has made a grave statement. I do not think anyone would reject knowledge and assent, or deeds alongside these things.”

I say: Ahmad, Abū Thawr, and other imams understood the fundamental premise of the Murjiʾah’s position: that part of faith cannot disappear while another part remains. Accordingly, it can only be a single thing, not something consisting of two or three elements. For if it consisted of several elements, some could disappear while others remained. Rather, it must be only a single thing. Hence the Jahmiyyah said that it is a single thing in the heart, while the Karrāmiyyah said that it is a single thing on the tongue. All this was to avoid

---

## Page 3429

faith being divisible and consisting of multiple elements. Thus, the imams argued against them with evidence showing that faith is not a single thing, as they claimed. Abū Thawr appealed to what “the jurist Murji’ah” agreed upon: that faith consists of assent and deeds. Either the position of their theologians and the Jahmiyyah among them had not reached him, or he did not regard their dissent as carrying any weight.

Ahmad explained that knowledge and assent are indispensable alongside verbal profession. He said that anyone who denies the need for knowledge and assent has made a grave statement, for the falsity of this position is known from the religion of Islam. Hence, no one adopted it before the Karrāmiyyah. Yet the Karrāmiyyah do not deny that knowledge and assent are obligatory; rather, they say that these do not fall within the meaning of faith, lest faith be divisible and consist of multiple elements. They held that some of it could not disappear while the rest remained, since this would entail faith and arrogance coexisting in the heart. They believed there was a consensus ruling this out, as al-Ash‘arī and others reported.

This specious argument is what led them astray, despite the learning, devotion, and sound Islam and faith of many of them. Thus, a number of people whom the Muslim community recognizes as learned and religious adopted “the jurists’ doctrine of irjā’.” For this reason, none of the early generations declared any of “the jurist Murji’ah” to be unbelievers. Rather, they regarded this as an innovation in statements and deeds, not an innovation in beliefs, since much of the dispute over it concerns wording.

Nevertheless, the wording that accords with the Quran and Sunnah is what is correct. No one may speak contrary to the words of Allah and His Messenger, particularly since this became a means leading to the innovations of the speculative theologians among the Murji’ah and others, and to the spread of sinful conduct. That slight error in wording thus became a cause of grave error in beliefs and deeds. This is why irjā’ was condemned so severely, to the point that Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī said:

“The trial they pose—meaning the Murji’ah—is more to be feared for this community than the trial posed by

---

## Page 3430

the Azāriqah.”

Al-Zuhrī said:
“No innovation introduced into Islam has been more harmful to its people than irjā’.”

Al-Awzā‘ī said:
“Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr and Qatādah used to say that no deviant doctrine, in their view, posed a greater threat to the community than irjā’.”

Sharīk the judge, mentioning the Murji’ah, said:
“They are the most wicked people. The Rāfidah are wicked enough, but the Murji’ah tell lies about Allah.”

Sufyān al-Thawrī said:
“The Murji’ah have left Islam thinner than Sābirī cloth.”

Qatādah said: “Irjā’ only arose after the turmoil involving Ibn al-Ash‘ath’s faction.”

Maymūn ibn Mihrān was asked about the doctrine of the Murji’ah and replied: “I am older than that.” Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr said to Dharr al-Hamdānī: “Are you not ashamed of holding a view younger than yourself?” Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: “I am older than the religion of the Murji’ah. The first person to speak of irjā’ was a man from Medina, of Banū Hāshim, called al-Hasan.”

Zādhān said:
“We went to al-Hasan ibn Muhammad and asked, ‘What is this treatise you have written?’ He was the one who had published the Murji’ah’s treatise. He said to me, ‘Abū ‘Umar, I wish I had died before publishing this treatise—or writing this treatise.’”

An error concerning the designation of faith is not like an error in the name of a hadith transmitter, or in other names, since the rulings of this world and the Hereafter hinge upon the designations of faith, Islam, disbelief, and hypocrisy.

Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—distinguished between knowledge in the heart and assent in the heart, for assent expressed by the tongue is verbal profession. He mentioned three things, and this admits two interpretations. He may be distinguishing between the heart’s assent and its knowledge, and this is the view of

---

## Page 3431

Ibn Kullāb and al-Qalānisī. Al-Ash‘arī and his followers distinguish between the heart’s knowledge and its assent, for the heart’s assent is its affirmation. In their view, the heart’s affirmation is not knowledge but something of another kind.

For this reason, Ahmad said:
“Is knowledge needed alongside profession? Must one also assent to what one knows? If he claims that knowledge is needed alongside profession, he has claimed that faith consists of two things. If he claims that one must profess and assent to what one knows, then it consists of three things. But if he denies this and says, ‘Knowledge and assent are not needed,’ he has made a grave assertion. I do not think anyone would reject knowledge and assent.”

As for those who say, “Faith is profession,” profession by the tongue includes verbal assent. The Murji’ah have not disagreed that profession by the tongue includes assent. Thus, it is clear that he meant the heart’s assent and knowledge, together with profession by the tongue—unless it is argued that he meant assent by both heart and tongue, together with knowledge and profession, and that by profession he meant commitment, not assent, as Allah Most High says:

“And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: ‘Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom, should a messenger then come to you confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him.’ He said, ‘Have you acknowledged this and accepted My binding covenant?’ They said, ‘We have acknowledged it.’ He said, ‘Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.’”

The covenant taken from them was that they would believe in him and support him; they had been commanded to do so. This acknowledgment is not assent to a statement, for Allah Most High had not conveyed a statement to them to be believed. Rather, He had obliged them to believe in that messenger and support him if he came to them. They affirmed this acknowledgment and committed themselves to it: this was their acknowledgment.

A person may acknowledge the Messenger in the sense of committing himself to what he commands, without knowing or assenting to the fact that he is Allah’s Messenger. Yet none of the Murji’ah has said that this acknowledgment constitutes faith.

---

## Page 3432

Rather, in their view, a declarative acknowledgment is essential: one must acknowledge that he is Allah’s Messenger, just as a person acknowledges the rights he admits to owing. The term “acknowledgment” encompasses both commitment and assent, and both are indispensable. Yet acknowledgment may also mean assent alone, without a commitment to obedience.

The Murji’ah sometimes identify this alone as faith, and sometimes define faith as assent and commitment together. The latter is the acknowledgment that the jurists among the Murji’ah call faith. Otherwise, if someone said, “I obey him, but I do not assent to his being Allah’s Messenger,” or, “I assent to him, but I do not commit myself to obeying him,” he would be neither a Muslim nor a believer in their view.

Ahmad said:
“Alongside this acknowledgment, one must assent, possess knowledge, and assent to what one knows.”

In another report, the wording is:
“Assent to what one acknowledges.”

This entails that inward assent is indispensable. It is possible that, in his usage, the term “assent” encompasses both affirmation and action, as we have already cited examples of the expression, “He affirmed it in word and deed.” In that case, the heart’s assent, in his usage, would mean that, alongside knowing in his heart that he is Allah’s Messenger, a person has humbled himself before him and submitted to him. Thus, he has assented to him through both his heart’s affirmation and its action, in love and reverence. Otherwise, merely knowing in one’s heart that he is Allah’s Messenger, while turning away from submission to him and to what he brought—whether out of envy, arrogance, attachment to one’s own religion that opposes his, or some other reason—does not constitute faith.

Faith necessarily includes both the heart’s knowledge and its action. Thus, by assent Ahmad meant that, alongside knowing him, the heart has come to assent to him, follow him, love him, and revere him. This is indispensable. Whoever denies that this is part of faith is like someone who denies that knowledge is part of faith. This is the more plausible way to

---

## Page 3433

interpret Ahmad’s words, for the necessity of the heart’s submission alongside its knowledge is evident and established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslim community. Indeed, it is known by necessity to be part of Islam. Any Jahmī who disputes that the heart’s submission is part of faith is like a Karrāmī who disputes that the heart’s knowledge is part of faith. Understanding Ahmad’s words in this way is therefore appropriate to his discussion here.

Furthermore, the distinction between the heart’s knowledge and its mere assent devoid of submission—which is regarded as the heart’s affirmation—is subtle, and most rational thinkers deny it. Even assuming that this distinction is valid, not everyone is required to stipulate two things when they cannot conceive of any difference between them. Most people cannot conceive of a distinction between the heart’s knowledge and its assent. They say:

“The distinction proposed by Ibn Kullāb and al-Ashʿarī is an invalid claim with no reality.”

Many of his followers have acknowledged that there is no distinction. Their principal argument rests solely on the assertion made by a liar. They say:

“In his heart there is an assertion contrary to what he knows, which demonstrates the distinction.”

Others replied:

“That consists in supposing an assertion and knowledge; it is neither actual knowledge nor an actual assertion. As for what they posit as an affirmation of the heart distinct from knowledge and will, it amounts only to supposing instances of knowledge and will, not some other kind of thing distinct from them.”

For this reason, they maintained that a person cannot have within his heart an assertion contrary to what he knows. He can only utter such a statement with his tongue. As for an assertion contrary to what he knows existing within his heart, that is impossible. This is among the arguments they used to establish that, with regard to the Lord Most High, it is inconceivable for falsehood to subsist

---

## Page 3434

in His essence, because He knows all things, and no attribute contrary to knowledge can subsist in the essence of one who knows. A false inward assertion is contrary to knowledge.

They may therefore be told:

If an inward assertion were distinct from knowledge, knowledge could coexist with the contrary of that assertion, just as they themselves argue in many other cases. This is among the strongest arguments employed by al-Qādī Abū Bakr and those who agree with him concerning the intellect and other questions, including al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Abū Muhammad ibn al-Labbān, Abū ʿAlī ibn Shādhān, Abū al-Tayyib, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Abū al-Khattāb, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others.

They say:

“The intellect is a kind of knowledge, since it is not contrary to knowledge. If it were not a kind of knowledge, it would be distinct from it; and if it were distinct, knowledge could coexist with the contrary of intellect.”

Although this argument is weak—as the majority have judged it, with Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī among those who have criticized it—anything that entails something else cannot be contrary to it, since the two coexist. Nor is it a kind of that other thing; rather, it is distinct from it, according to their terminology, which classifies any two things as alike, distinct, or contrary.

Thus, an attribute that entails another—as will entails knowledge, or knowledge entails life—is neither contrary to nor like the attribute it entails; rather, it is distinct from it. Nevertheless, it cannot coexist with the contrary of its necessary condition, because the contrary of that condition excludes it, and the existence of what entails something without what it entails is impossible—as with the existence of will without knowledge, or knowledge without life. Each such pair consists, in their terminology, of two distinct things, yet one cannot coexist with the contrary of the other.

Likewise, knowledge entails intellect: everyone who possesses knowledge possesses intellect, and intellect is a condition of knowledge. It is neither like knowledge, nor contrary to it, nor a kind of it. Nevertheless, knowledge cannot coexist with the contrary of intellect.

---

## Page 3435

But this argument can be turned against them concerning knowledge and inward speech that takes the form of an assertion. Such speech is neither contrary to knowledge nor like it, but distinct from it. Knowledge can therefore coexist with the contrary of a true assertion—namely, a false one. Thus, their argument that inward falsehood is impossible for someone who possesses knowledge is invalid. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere. The point here is that, upon examining himself, a person finds it difficult to distinguish between his knowledge that the Messenger is truthful and his heart’s affirmation that he is truthful, considered apart from submission and the other acts of the heart.

Imam Ahmad then advanced numerous proofs that deeds are part of faith. He said:

“The delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about faith. He replied: ‘Testifying that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakah, fasting Ramadan, and giving a fifth of the spoils of war.’”

Thus, he counted all of these as part of faith.

He said:

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Modesty is a branch of faith.”

He also said:

“The believers most complete in faith are those best in character.”

And he said:

“Simplicity in appearance is part of faith.”

And he said:

“Faith has sixty-odd branches. The lowest is removing harmful things from the road, and the highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah.’”

There are many other reports, including:

“Bring out of the Fire anyone who has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart.”

There is also what is narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the description of a hypocrite:

“There are three traits: whoever possesses them is a hypocrite.”

These are accompanied by many other proofs. There are also the reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning one who abandons prayer, and those from his Companions after him; then there is what Allah Most High has described in His Book

---

## Page 3436

concerning the increase of faith in several passages, as in His words:

“He is the One who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith along with their existing faith.”

And He said:

“So that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith.”

And He said:

“When His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith.”

And He, Most High, said:

And He, Most High, said:

And He said:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him, inclining away from falsehood, and to establish prayer and give zakah. That is the upright religion.”

[Ahmad said: His position requires him to say that a person is a believer by virtue of his acknowledgment. These are among the most repugnant implications of their position] (*).

I say: What Imam Ahmad has mentioned is among the best arguments people have advanced against them. He brought together a number of arguments, only some of which others have stated. They have no way of escaping this implication. Thus, when their speculative theologians, such as Jahm and those who agreed with him, recognized that it necessarily followed from their position, they accepted it and said:

“If he were to do

## Page 3437

any outward deeds whatsoever, he would not thereby become a disbeliever inwardly; rather, this would constitute evidence of disbelief for the purposes of worldly rulings.” When they are confronted with scriptural texts indicating that he will be a disbeliever in the Hereafter, they say:

“These texts indicate that inwardly he possesses no knowledge of Allah whatsoever.”

For they regard such knowledge as a single entity. Thus they contradict both clear reason and explicit revelation. Besides being invalid both rationally and scripturally, this view, upon examination, does not affirm any real faith: they have made faith a single entity devoid of reality. The Jahmiyyah and those who agree with them have said something similar concerning the Lord’s oneness: that He is an essence without attributes. They have also said that the Quran is created and that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter. Similar, too, are Ibn Kullāb’s statements concerning the oneness of speech and the other attributes. Their positions concerning the Lord, His attributes, His speech, and faith in Him thus amount to sheer negation.

Many later groups have fallen into this, despite their affiliation with the Sunnah, jurisprudence, and hadith, and their adherence to the four imams, while being partisan supporters of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah—indeed, of the Murji’ah as well. Because they do not understand the underlying realities from which these innovations arose, they combine contradictory positions.

Yet it is part of Allah’s mercy toward His Muslim servants that the imams who enjoy an honorable reputation within the Muslim community—the four imams and others, such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā’ī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Ishāq, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Hanīfah, Abū Yūsuf, and Muhammad—used to denounce the Jahmī speculative theologians for their positions concerning the Quran, faith, and the Lord’s attributes. They agreed upon the position of the early generations: that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter, and that

---

## Page 3438

the Quran is the uncreated speech of Allah, and that faith necessarily entails affirmation by both the heart and the tongue. Thus, according to all of them, anyone who insults Allah and His Messenger is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly. Those who agree with Jahm’s position on faith because Abū al-Hasan championed it alternate between adopting the position of the early generations and the imams and adopting that of the speculative theologians who agree with Jahm.

Even on the question of insulting Allah and His Messenger, I have seen some Hanbalīs, Shāfiʿīs, and Mālikīs say, when speaking in the terms of the imams:

“This constitutes disbelief both inwardly and outwardly.”

Yet when speaking in the terms of those theologians, they say:

“This constitutes outward disbelief, but inwardly the person may be a believer whose faith is complete.”

For, in their view, faith is indivisible. When al-Qādī ʿIyād learned that some members of his own school held this position, he rejected it and defended the position of Mālik and Ahl al-Sunnah, and he did well in doing so. I have discussed some matters relating to this in my book, “The Unsheathed Sword against the One Who Insults the Messenger.”

Likewise, on questions of faith, you find them citing the positions of the imams and the early generations while pursuing lines of argument consistent with the Jahmiyyah’s position. This is because they took their arguments from the books of speculative theologians who championed Jahm’s position on questions of faith. When al-Rāzī wrote “The Merits of al-Shāfiʿī,” he cited al-Shāfiʿī’s position on faith. Al-Shāfiʿī’s position is that of the Companions and the Successors; indeed, al-Shāfiʿī stated that it was the consensus of the Companions, the Successors, and those whom he had met.

Al-Rāzī found al-Shāfiʿī’s position exceedingly difficult to accept because the specious argument concerning faith advanced by the people of innovation had already taken firm hold in his mind: the Khawārij, the Muʿtazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and the Karrāmiyyah

---

## Page 3439

and the rest of the Murji’ah: that when a composite thing loses some of its parts, it must cease to exist altogether. Yet he mentioned only the apparent form of their specious argument. What they have stated is easily answered: one may concede to him that the composite whole no longer remains intact as it was, but the loss of some of its parts does not entail the loss of all the remaining parts.

Al-Shāfiʿī, together with the Companions, the Successors, and the rest of the early generations, maintains that sin detracts from the completeness of faith. This is why the Lawgiver denied faith to such people. Thus, the whole that constitutes faith no longer remains intact in the presence of sins. Nevertheless, they maintain that some of it remains—whether its foundation, most of it, or some other portion. The point, then, is that some of it disappears while some remains.

For this reason, the Murji’ah were far more averse to the term “decrease” than to the term “increase.” For, in their view, if faith decreases, it must disappear altogether—if it is divisible and consists of multiple parts, as held by those who maintain this, namely the Khawārij and the Muʿtazilah. As for the Jahmiyyah, they regard it as a single entity admitting no multiplicity. They thus affirm a single entity that has no reality, just as they made similar claims concerning the oneness of the Lord and, among those of them who affirm His attributes, the oneness of His attributes.

What is remarkable is that the premise that led them into this was their belief that some faith and some disbelief—or something constituting faith and something constituting disbelief—cannot coexist in a person. They believed that Muslims agreed on this, as Abū al-Hasan and others mentioned. Because they believed in this consensus, they fell into a position that contradicts the actual consensus—the consensus of

---

## Page 3440

the early generations, which a number of imams have reported. Indeed, several of them explicitly declared that whoever adopted Jahm’s position on faith was a disbeliever. There are many comparable cases: someone advances a position that actually contradicts revelation and the consensus of the early generations, while believing that he is adhering to revelation and consensus. If this represents the limit of his knowledge and scholarly striving, Allah rewards him for the obedience embodied in that striving and forgives his failure to discern the underlying truth that lay beyond his ability to discover.

When they mistakenly supposed that the faith required of all people was a single kind, some of them came to think that this kind, considered in itself, admitted no differences in degree.

One of them once said to me:

“Faith, considered simply as faith, admits neither increase nor decrease.”

I replied:

“Your phrase ‘considered in itself’ is like saying that a human being considered simply as a human being, an animal considered simply as an animal, existence considered simply as existence, blackness considered simply as blackness, and the like, admit neither increase nor decrease nor attributes. You thus ascribe to the things designated by these terms an absolute existence, stripped of every qualification and attribute. Yet this has no reality outside the mind. It is merely something a person conceives in his mind, just as he conceives a being that is neither eternal nor originated, neither self-subsisting nor subsisting in another; or conceives a human being who is neither existent nor nonexistent, and says: ‘Essence as such is described neither by existence nor by nonexistence.’

“Essence as such is something the mind conceives, and it exists in the mind, not outside it. As for positing something that exists neither in the mind nor outside it, that is impossible. This conception itself can exist only in the mind, like all other conceptions of impossible things—for example, conceiving of the world as originating from multiple makers, and similar notions. These things are conceived in the mind.

---

## Page 3441

The same applies, then, to positing a faith that characterizes no believer, but is stripped of every qualification, or a human being who is neither existent nor nonexistent. In reality, faith exists only in believers, and human nature exists only as an attribute of human beings. Every human being has a human nature particular to him, and every believer has a faith particular to him. Zayd’s human nature resembles Umar’s, but is not identical to it. When they belong to the same human species, this means that the two resemble one another as they exist outside the mind, and share an unqualified universal concept that exists in the mind.

Likewise, when it is said, ‘Zayd’s faith is like Amr’s faith,’ each has his own particular faith. Even supposing faith to be alike in everyone, each believer would still have a faith particular to him. That faith is specific and determinate; it is not faith considered simply as faith, but a particular instance of faith, and that faith admits increase.

Those who deny differences of degree in these matters conceive in their minds an unqualified faith, an unqualified human being, or an unqualified existence, stripped of all the attributes that give it particular determination. They then suppose that this is the faith that exists in people. Yet that conception admits neither differences of degree nor multiplicity in itself, for it is a particular conception present in the mind of the one conceiving it. This is why many of them suppose that things sharing a single feature are one and the same individual entity.

Some of their learned and devout scholars went so far as to treat existence in this same way. They conceived of existing things as sharing in what is denoted by ‘existence.’ Having conceived this in their minds, they supposed that it existed outside the mind just as it did within it. They then supposed it to be Allah, thus identifying the Lord with this existence, which never exists anywhere except in the mind of the one conceiving it, and has no existence outside the mind.

---

## Page 3442

Likewise, many philosophers have conceived of abstract numbers and abstract realities, which they call Platonic Forms, as well as time abstracted from motion and moving things, and extension abstracted from bodies and their attributes. They then supposed that these existed outside the mind. All these people have confused what exists in the mind with what exists in external reality.

They may turn one thing into two and two things into one. At times, they take things that are multiple and differ in degree in external reality and treat them as one or as identical in kind and degree. At other times, they take living beings, space, and time as they exist outside the mind and turn one thing into two. The adherents of philosophy and the Jahmiyyah have fallen into both errors. They took the Lord’s attributes—His being knowing and powerful—and made one attribute identical to the other, and the attribute identical to the One described by it.

Likewise, those who say that faith is one thing and that it is the same in all human beings have erred both in considering it one and in considering it uniform, just as they have erred in comparable questions concerning “divine oneness,” “the attributes,” “the Quran,” and similar matters. Thus, the error of Jahm and his followers concerning faith was like their error concerning the attributes of the Lord in whom believers believe, and concerning His speech and His attributes. Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say.

Blackness and whiteness likewise admit greater and lesser intensity. Indeed, attributes generally admit differences of degree in those who possess them. Hence intellect admits differences of degree, as do obligation and prohibition: one obligation may be stronger than another, and one prohibition stronger than another. Likewise, the knowledge present in hearts admits differences of degree

---

## Page 3443

, according to the correct view among Ahl al-Sunnah. All these matters are disputed. Some who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah deny differences of degree in all of them; this is the position preferred by al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others. Two positions have been reported from Ahmad concerning differences of degree in knowledge.

Denying differences of degree in these attributes is akin to the fundamental position of the Murjiʾah, yet it is also maintained by people who oppose them. These people say: “Differences of degree concern deeds alone; faith in the heart does not vary in degree.” Matters are not as they claim. Rather, all of these vary in degree. They may also say: “The deeds of the heart vary in degree, unlike its knowledge.” This too is incorrect. Rather, faith in people’s hearts varies according to what is obligatory upon one person and what is obligatory upon another: their obligations are not identical.

Although faith became obligatory upon the entire community of Muhammad once the revealed law was fully established, the obligation to believe in a particular matter depends, if it is a report, on its reaching the person; if it is a command, on his needing to act upon it; and if it is a matter of knowledge, on his knowing it. Otherwise, it is not obligatory for every Muslim to know every report and every command in the Quran and Sunnah, understand its meaning, and have knowledge of it, for no one is capable of this. Thus, what is obligatory varies according to people’s differing circumstances. They also differ in the extent to which they fulfill their obligations.

Knowledge itself also varies: it may be general or detailed, strong or weak, continually present in the mind or accompanied by heedlessness. For it is not the case that detailed knowledge, consciously present and firmly established, whose possessor Allah makes steadfast through the word

---

## Page 3444

that is firm, in this worldly life and in the Hereafter, is like general knowledge of which one is heedless, recalling it to mind when something causes him to doubt it, then turning to Allah to dispel that doubt. Moreover, people differ in the states and deeds of their hearts—such as love for Allah and His Messenger, fear of Allah, reliance upon Him, patience with His decree, gratitude to Him, turning to Him in repentance, and devotion to Him alone in their deeds—to an extent known only to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever denies these differences is either ignorant and has not grasped the matter, or is obstinately denying it.

Imam Ahmad said:

“If they claim that they do not accept that faith increases because they do not know what its increase is and because it has no defined limit, what do they say about Allah’s prophets, scriptures, and messengers? Do they acknowledge them in general and maintain that this is part of faith?

“If they say, ‘Yes,’ they should be asked: ‘Can you enumerate them and do you know their number? Do they not simply acknowledge them in general and then refrain from specifying their number? The same applies to the increase of faith.’”

Ahmad explained that their not knowing the ultimate extent of faith’s increase does not prevent them from acknowledging it in general, just as they believe in the prophets and scriptures without knowing the number of scriptures and messengers. What Ahmad, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and others mentioned makes clear that they did not know the number of scriptures and messengers, and that they did not regard the hadith of Abū Dharr on this subject as established.

As for those who equate Islam with faith and say, “Allah has applied the term faith to what He has called Islam, and the term Islam to what He has called faith,” this is not so, for Allah

---

## Page 3445

and His Messenger have explained faith as belief in Allah, His angels, His scriptures, His messengers, and the Last Day, and have also made clear that carrying out what He has commanded is included in faith. Allah has not called belief in His angels, His scriptures, His messengers, and resurrection after death Islam. Rather, what He has called Islam is submitting to Him in one’s heart and intention, devoting one’s religion sincerely to Him, and carrying out His commands, such as prayer and zakah, seeking His Face alone. This is what Allah has called Islam and appointed as the religion. He says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

He did not include within it what He assigned specifically to faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His scriptures, and His messengers. Nor did He include such deeds of the heart as love for Allah and His Messenger and the like, for He made these part of faith. A Muslim who is a believer possesses these qualities, but his possessing them does not necessarily mean that they are part of Islam; rather, they are part of faith. Islam is obligatory, and faith is obligatory, and Islam is included within faith.

Whoever fulfils the faith he has been commanded to have must therefore have fulfilled Islam, which encompasses all obligatory deeds. But whoever fulfils what is called Islam has not necessarily fulfilled faith, unless separate evidence establishes this. Thus, we know that all those whom Allah praised for their Islam, from the prophets and their followers down to the disciples, were believers as well as Muslims. As the disciples said:

“We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims.”

And He says:

“And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My messenger, they said, ‘We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims.’”
