## Page 3483

Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning qualification in faith, because faith consists of words and deeds, and deeds mean action. We have made the verbal profession, but we fear that we may have fallen short in our deeds. I therefore prefer that one qualify one’s profession of faith by saying, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’”

He said: I also heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked about the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And we shall, if Allah wills, join you.”

“What does the qualification refer to here?”

He replied, “To the places of burial. He does not know whether he will be buried in the place whose occupants he greeted or elsewhere.”

[It is also related from al-Maymūnī that he asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh about his position and opinion concerning the statement, “A believer, if Allah wills.” He replied, “I say, ‘A believer, if Allah wills,’ and, ‘A believer, I hope,’ because one does not know whether one’s deeds have discharged one’s obligations as required.”] (*)

Statements like these occur frequently in the words of Ahmad and others like him. This accords with what has already been explained: a believer in the unqualified sense is someone who fulfils his obligations and deserves Paradise if he dies in that state. Someone who falls short by neglecting what is commanded or doing what is forbidden is not called a believer without qualification. A believer in the unqualified sense is a righteous, Allah-fearing person, a close friend of Allah. Thus, saying, “I am certainly a believer,” is like saying, “I am certainly righteous, Allah-fearing, and a close friend of Allah.”

Nevertheless, Ahmad and other early scholars disliked a man asking another, “Are you a believer?” They also disliked answering this question, because it was an innovation introduced by the Murji’ah to support their position. A man knows that he is not a disbeliever; indeed, he finds that his heart affirms what the Messenger brought, so he says, “I am a believer.” This is then used to establish that faith is assent: you are certain that you are a believer, yet you are not certain that you have done everything you were commanded to do. Thus, when the early scholars learned

## Page 3484

their purpose, they became reluctant to answer, or answered with a distinction. This is because the term “faith” may be used either without qualification or in a qualified sense. They would therefore affirm faith in a qualified sense that did not entail testifying to their own perfection. Thus, the correct view is that one may say, “I am a believer,” without adding “if Allah wills,” if this is the sense intended. However, one should accompany this statement with something clarifying that one does not mean complete faith in its unqualified sense. This is why Ahmad disliked giving an unqualified answer without first adding that qualification.

Al-Marwadhī said:

“Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, ‘Should we say, “We are the believers”?’ He replied, ‘We say, “We are Muslims.”’”

He also said:

“I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Should we say, “We are believers”?’ He replied, ‘Rather, we say, “We are Muslims.”’”

Nevertheless, he did not condemn someone who omitted the qualification if that person did not intend what the Murji’ah intended—that faith consists merely of words. Rather, he dislikes omitting it because he knows that there is faith in his heart, even though he is not certain that his faith is complete.

Al-Khallāl said:

“Ahmad ibn Asram al-Muzanī informed me that Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, ‘What if a man asks me, “Are you a believer?”’ He replied, ‘Your asking me this is an innovation.’ He does not doubt his faith—or he said, ‘We do not doubt our faith.’”

Al-Muzanī said:

“What I remember is that Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, ‘I say as Tāwūs said: “I believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His Messengers.”’”

---

## Page 3485

Al-Khallāl said:

“Harb ibn Ismāʿīl and Abū Dāwūd informed me. Abū Dāwūd said: ‘I heard Ahmad say: I heard Sufyān—meaning Ibn ʿUyaynah—say that when he was asked, “Are you a believer?” he would not answer the question, but would say, “Your asking me this is an innovation, and I do not doubt my faith.” He also said, “If one says, ‘if Allah wills,’ this is not objectionable, nor does doubt enter into it.”’”

Thus, it is reported from Ahmad that he said, “We do not doubt our faith,” and that the questioner does not doubt the faith of the person questioned. This is an even stronger statement. Yet he is certain only that he acknowledges and accepts as true what the Messenger brought; he is not certain that he is fulfilling his obligations. It is therefore clear that Ahmad and others among the early generations were certain, without doubt, of the faith present in the heart in this situation. They understood the qualification “if Allah wills” to refer to faith in its unqualified sense, which includes doing what is commanded.

They also argued that this qualification is permissible concerning matters about which one has no doubt. This is a “second rationale”: even though we do not doubt the faith within our hearts, the Sunnah has established the use of this qualification concerning things known to exist, because of the wisdom it contains.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Hārūn reported:

“I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about adding ‘if Allah wills’ when affirming one’s faith. He replied: ‘Yes, this qualification is used not out of doubt, but out of fear and caution concerning one’s deeds. Ibn Masʿūd and others used it, and this is the position of al-Thawrī. Allah Most High says:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions:

“Indeed, I hope to be the most mindful of Allah among you.”

And he said concerning the deceased:

“And upon it you will be resurrected, if Allah wills.”’”

Ahmad thus explained that he adds this qualification out of fear and caution concerning his deeds: he fears that he may not have fully accomplished what he was commanded to do, so he takes the precaution of adding “if Allah wills.” He said, “Not out of doubt,” meaning, without

---

## Page 3486

doubt concerning what a person knows of himself. He does, however, doubt whether he has fully performed the deeds he fears he may have left incomplete. Thus, he fears their deficiency without doubting their foundation.

Al-Khallāl said:

Muhammad ibn Abī Hārūn also informed me that Hubaysh ibn Sindī related to them concerning this question. Abū ʿAbd Allāh said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said when he stood by the graves: ‘We shall indeed join you, if Allah wills.’ Yet he had already been informed of his impending death and knew that he would die. Likewise, in the account of the person in the grave: ‘Upon it you lived, upon it you died, and upon it you will be resurrected, if Allah wills.’ There are also the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘I have reserved my supplication, and, if Allah wills, it will reach whoever associates nothing with Allah.’

“A man also asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘If one of us wakes up in a state of major ritual impurity, may he fast?’ He replied, ‘I do that, and then I fast.’ The man said, ‘You are not like us: Allah has forgiven your past and future sins.’ He replied, ‘By Allah, I do indeed hope to be the most fearful of Allah among you.’

“There are many such examples, all involving certainty.”

He said:

An elderly man came to him and asked him about faith. He told him, “It consists of words and deeds; it increases and decreases.”

The man asked, “Should I say, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills’?”

He replied, “Yes.”

The man said, “They tell me that I am in doubt.”

He replied, “What an evil thing they have said!”

Then the man left, and he said, “Bring him back.” He asked him, “Do they not say that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases?”

He replied, “Yes.”

He said, “These people themselves make this qualification.”

The man asked, “How so, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?”

He replied, “Tell them: ‘You maintain that faith consists of words and deeds. You have uttered the words, but you have not fulfilled the deeds. This qualification therefore concerns those deeds.’”

He was asked:

---

## Page 3487

“Should one make this qualification when professing faith?”

He replied:

“Yes. I say, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’ I make this qualification with certainty, not doubt.”

He then said:

“Allah says, ‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety.’ Allah Most High has thus declared that they will enter the Sacred Mosque.”

Ahmad thus made clear in his statement that he makes this qualification while remaining certain of the faith he presently possesses: he affirms it with his tongue, and his heart has no doubt about it. He makes the qualification because deeds are part of faith, and he is not certain that he has performed them fully; rather, he doubts this. Thus, he denied doubt and affirmed certainty regarding what he knows with certainty about himself, while affirming doubt regarding what he does not know to be present. He explained that this qualification is recommended concerning the latter—what a person does not know whether he has fulfilled or not—and is also permissible concerning what he knows with certainty.

Thus, even if he made the qualification concerning the very faith present in his heart, it would be permissible, as in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“By Allah, I do indeed hope to be the most fearful of Allah among you.”

This concerns something present, not future: his being the most fearful of Allah among us. He does not hope to become the most fearful of Allah among us; rather, he hopes that, at the time of making this statement, he is the most fearful of Allah among us. Similarly, when a believer performs a deed, he hopes that Allah has accepted it from him and fears that He has not accepted it from him.

As Allah Most High says:

“And those who give what they give while their hearts tremble, knowing that they will return to their Lord.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is the man who prays, fasts, and gives charity, yet fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

Acceptance is a present or past matter, yet he entertains both hope and fear concerning it. This is because, when something has a future outcome, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy, and a person considers it possible that it has or has not occurred, he may be said to hope for it or to fear it. Hope and fear thus relate to the present and the past because the desired or dreaded outcome lies in the future. He hopes that Allah has accepted his deed, so that He will reward him for it and show him mercy in the future. And he fears that He may not have

---

## Page 3488

accepted it, in which case he will be deprived of its reward. Likewise, he fears that Allah may have become displeased with him for his disobedience and may therefore punish him for it.

When someone is pursuing a desired end—as with a merchant or a courier whom he has sent to attend to some business at a particular time—once that time has passed, he says, “I hope that so-and-so has taken care of that matter.” Its completion lies in the past, but the joy, happiness, and other desired benefits it brings him lie in the future.

At the time when pilgrims customarily enter Mecca, someone may say, “I hope they have entered.” Concerning a military detachment dispatched against the disbelievers, one may say, “We hope that Allah has granted the believers victory and spoils.” At the time when the Nile in Egypt rises, one may say, “We hope that the Nile has risen,” just as someone present in Egypt at such a time says, “We hope that the Nile will rise high this year.” When rain falls in some areas, someone who owns land and wishes for rain on it may be told, “I hope the rain has been widespread, and I hope that such-and-such a tract of land has received rain.” This is because what one hopes for is something whose occurrence brings joy and delight, whereas what one dreads is something whose occurrence causes pain.

This is connected to knowing what has happened, and that knowledge lies in the future. When someone learns that the Muslims have been victorious, that the pilgrims have entered, or that rain has fallen, he rejoices, and other objectives of his are thereby fulfilled. If matters turn out otherwise, that desired and welcome outcome is not attained. Thus, he says, “I hope” and “I fear,” because what brings joy or distress is connected to learning what has happened, and this lies in the future.

Likewise, the happiness and salvation sought through faith lie in the future. Thus, the qualification “if Allah wills” is made concerning present faith on this account, because the goal sought through it lies in the future. Moreover, every future outcome one seeks is contingent upon Allah’s will

---

## Page 3489

even if one is certain that it will occur, since nothing in the future can occur except by Allah’s will.

Thus, our statement, “This will happen, if Allah wills,” is true, for it will happen only if Allah wills. The wording merely makes its occurrence conditional; making something conditional does not necessarily imply doubt. Rather, that depends on the speaker’s knowledge: sometimes he is doubtful, and sometimes he is not. Since doubt frequently accompanies this expression because people do not know how things will turn out, some have supposed that doubt forms part of its meaning. That is not so.

In His words,

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills,”

no doubt on Allah’s part is conceivable, nor indeed on the part of His Messenger, who was being addressed, or the believers. Hence Thaʿlab said: “This is a qualification made by Allah concerning something He knows, whereas created beings make such qualifications concerning what they do not know.”

Abū ʿUbaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said that in (“if”) here means idh (“when”), that is, “when Allah willed.” The point of this is to express the certainty of the action through in, just as it is expressed through idh. Strictly speaking, however, idh is an adverb specifying time, whereas in is a conditional particle.

If it is objected that the Arabs say, “When the unripe dates turn red, come to me,” but do not say, “If the unripe dates turn red,” the answer is: The purpose here is to specify the time of coming as the time when the dates turn red. They therefore use the temporal adverb that conveys certainty. The word in does not specify a time; it merely expresses a condition, linking the second action to the first. The parallel to the matter under discussion would be their saying, “The unripe dates will turn red and become sweet, if Allah wills.” This is true, and it is analogous to the expression in question.

If it is objected: Some people sought to avoid this meaning and took the qualification to refer to something uncertain. Thus al-Zajjāj said concerning “You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque”: that is, He commanded you

---

## Page 3490

to do so. It has also been said that the qualification concerns security and fear: that is, “You will surely enter it in safety”; as for entering itself, there is no doubt about that. Another view is: “You will surely enter, all or some of you,” because He knew that some of them would die. The qualification thus concerns the fact that not all of them would enter.

The answer is that the proponents of all these views have fallen into the very difficulty they sought to escape, while also departing from the meaning conveyed by the Quran. They have thus distorted its meaning without gaining anything thereby. As for the interpretation, “Allah commanded you to do so,” He, glorified be He, already knew whether He would command them or not. His knowledge that He would command them to enter it is just like His knowledge that they would enter. They have therefore attached the qualification to something the wording does not indicate, although Allah’s knowledge encompasses both what is explicitly stated and what is implicit.

The same applies to their security and fear: He knows whether they will enter in safety or in fear. He stated that they would enter in safety, knowing that they would indeed enter in safety. Neither matter, then, involved any doubt on Allah’s part, nor indeed on the part of His Messenger.

As for the view, “All or some of them,” the answer is that what is made conditional upon His will is the entry of those intended by the wording. If He intended all of them, then all of them must enter it. If the majority were intended, then it is their entry that is made conditional upon His will. What He did not intend cannot be made conditional by in (“if”); rather, what is made conditional by in is what will occur. This was a promise whose fulfilment was certain. Thus, when ʿUmar said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah:

“Did you not tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it?”

He replied, “Yes. But did I tell you that you would come to it this year?”

He said, “No.”

He replied, “You will certainly come to it and circumambulate it.”

If it is asked, “Why did He not make the other promises in the Quran conditional in this way?” the answer is: Because this verse was revealed after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions had returned

---

## Page 3491

from al-Hudaybiyyah. They had gone to perform the lesser pilgrimage that year and had striven to enter, but the polytheists prevented them. They returned in anguish whose extent Allah alone knew. They had expected this promise to be fulfilled that year, since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had given them a promise without specifying a time. It is also reported:

“He saw in a dream someone saying, ‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.’ The next morning, he told the people about his dream and instructed them to set out for the lesser pilgrimage. They were unable to perform it that year, so this verse was revealed.”

The verse promised them what the Messenger had promised them—the very thing they had thought would happen that year.

His words, “If Allah wills,” here served to affirm that the entry would take place and that Allah would bring it about for them. Similarly, someone firmly resolved to do something says, “By Allah, I shall certainly do such-and-such, if Allah wills.” He does not say this because he doubts his own intention or resolve, but to secure its fulfilment. He fears that, if he does not say, “If Allah wills,” Allah may overturn his resolve and what he seeks may not come about. Thus, the two Sahīh collections relate:

“Solomon, peace be upon him, said, ‘By Allah, tonight I shall go to a hundred women, each of whom will bear a horseman who will fight in Allah’s cause.’ His companion told him, ‘Say: “If Allah wills.”’ But he did not say it, and none of them conceived except one woman, who gave birth to half a human being.

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘By Him in Whose hand is my soul, had he said, “If Allah wills,” they would all have fought as horsemen in Allah’s cause.’”

Thus, when someone says, “If Allah wills,” it is not because he doubts his own desire and intention, but so that Allah may bring it about for him, since nothing happens except by Allah’s will. If a servant swears presumptuously concerning Him without making his oath conditional upon His will, his purpose will not be fulfilled. For Allah proves wrong whoever swears presumptuously concerning Him. Hence the reported saying: “I shall not bring a planner’s purpose to completion.”

---

## Page 3492

One of them was asked, “How did you come to know your Lord?”

He replied, “Through the undoing of resolutions and the frustration of aspirations.” Allah Most High has said:

“Never say of anything, ‘I will do that tomorrow,’ without adding, ‘If Allah wills.’”

When someone says, “I shall certainly do it,” his words express both an intention and an assertion. His intention is firm, but whether what he seeks actually happens depends upon Allah’s will. In seeking to perform the deed, he must turn to Allah, relying on His might and power. In expressing what he seeks, he must ask Allah; in making an assertion, he must state only what Allah has made known to him. If he asserts it categorically without making it conditional upon Allah’s will, this resembles swearing presumptuously concerning Allah, and Allah will prove him wrong.

Thus, when a Muslim is firmly resolved upon something, desires it, and seeks it without hesitation, he says, “If Allah wills,” to secure what he seeks and bring about what he has sworn to do, since it can happen only by Allah’s will—not because he is uncertain of his own intention. The Lord Most High, however, firmly wills to fulfil what He has promised them, without reservation, and He does whatever He wills. For whatever He—glory be to Him—wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He is not like the servant, who desires things that do not happen, while things he does not desire happen.

Thus His words—glory be to Him—“If Allah wills” affirm: “What I have promised you will assuredly come to pass through My will and volition, for whatever I will comes to pass, and whatever I do not will does not come to pass.” Here, then, the qualification was intended to affirm fulfilment, because they had not obtained that year what they sought and had been promised. This was not the case with the other things they had been promised.

For this reason, the jurists disagreed about someone who, by qualifying his oath with Allah’s will, intends this meaning—affirming its fulfilment rather than making it conditional: does this count as a valid qualification of his oath, or must he offer expiation if he breaks it? This differs from someone whose intention is uncertain: his qualification is valid without dispute. The correct view is that he

---

## Page 3493

has validly qualified his oath in every case, because Allah’s will encompasses all things. Moreover, although a man may firmly intend what he has sworn to do, he has made it conditional upon Allah’s will. He is certain of his intention, but not certain that what he intends will come to pass. Nor does he will it on the assumption that it will not occur, for that is a distinction, not an act of will. He has undertaken it only if Allah wills; if Allah does not will it, he is neither bound to it by his oath nor has he sworn that it will happen. Although his intention is firm, not everything a person intends is something he binds himself by oath to do. Thus, no expiation is due from him.

What we have explained makes clear that a person may say, “If Allah wills,” while fully intending to attain what he seeks. He says it to bring about what he seeks by asking Allah’s help, not because he is uncertain of his intention. This concerns what he swears to do and intends, as in the words of the Most High:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque.”

This is a statement about something Allah willed to happen, knowing that it would happen, yet He qualified it with His words:

“If Allah wills.”

The same applies to what a person says about his own future affairs when he is certain both of his intention and that the event will occur. He says, “If Allah wills,” to secure its occurrence, not out of doubt about either his intention or his knowledge that it will occur. Thus, he adds this qualification when his longing for the matter he has made conditional is at its height and his desire for it is strong. Yet fearful thoughts continue to contend with his hope, so he says, “If Allah wills,” to secure the fulfilment of his hope, despite knowing that it will happen. Likewise, he asks Allah and supplicates to Him concerning something he already knows will happen, just as:

“On the day of Badr, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had told them where the polytheists would fall. Yet after this, he entered the shelter, seeking his Lord’s help and saying, ‘O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me.’”

For knowing what Allah decrees does not preclude His having decreed it through certain means, and supplication is among the greatest

---

## Page 3494

means of bringing it about. Likewise, hoping for Allah’s mercy and fearing His punishment are among the greatest means of escaping His punishment and attaining His mercy.

Qualifying a statement with “if Allah wills” applies both to purely declarative statements and to statements that also convey a directive.

The first is when someone swears to a declarative statement, intending neither to urge an action nor to prevent it, but merely to affirm or deny something, as when he says: “By Allah, such-and-such will surely happen, if Allah wills,” or, “Such-and-such will not happen.” The person adding this qualification may know that the event will or will not occur, as in His words:

“You will surely enter.”

Here, the clause answering the oath is not omitted.

The second is a statement that conveys a directive, as when someone says: “By Allah, I will certainly do such-and-such—or will not do it—if Allah wills.” Its form is declarative, but he has invested it with the force of a directive. He has not said, “By Allah, I desire this,” nor that he is resolved upon it. Rather, he has said: “By Allah, it will surely happen.” If it does not happen, he has broken his oath, because events have turned out contrary to what he swore would happen; his oath is thus broken. But when he says, “If Allah wills,” he has sworn to it only on the condition that Allah wills it, not unconditionally.

For this reason, many jurists hold that whenever what a person swore would happen fails to happen, he has broken his oath; likewise, whenever he does what he swore not to do, he has broken his oath—whether he acted forgetfully, mistakenly, or in ignorance. They regard this as having the force of a declaration: if events turn out contrary to what he stated, he has broken his oath.

Others, however, say that its purpose is to urge or restrain, like a command or prohibition. When someone is forbidden to do something but does it forgetfully or mistakenly, he has not disobeyed; the same applies here.

---

## Page 3495

The proponents of the first view reply:

An oath may serve to affirm or deny something, as when someone says, “By Allah, it will certainly rain,” or, “It will not rain.” This is a purely declarative statement, containing neither encouragement nor restraint. Even if he swears according to his belief, he has broken his oath if matters turn out contrary to what he swore. This makes clear the distinction between swearing about the past and swearing about the future. An oath concerning the past does not become binding, so if he is mistaken, no expiation is required, just as none is required for a deliberately false oath. An oath concerning the future is different. Nor is he required to add “if Allah wills” concerning the future if he has done it.

Allah Most High says:

“Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that is easy for Allah.’”

Thus, He commanded him to swear about what would happen in the future. Likewise, He says:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘The Hour will not come to us.’ Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you.’”

He also commanded him to swear about a present reality, saying:

“They ask you, ‘Is it true?’ Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, the son of Mary will surely descend among you as a just judge and an equitable leader.”

He also said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, this world will not pass away until a day comes upon people when neither the killer knows why he killed nor the slain why he was killed.”

And he said:

“When Chosroes perishes—or, Chosroes will surely perish—there will then be no Chosroes after him. When Caesar perishes, there will be no Caesar after him. By Him in whose hand is my soul, their treasures will surely be spent in Allah’s cause.”

Both reports are in al-Sahīh (The Authentic Collection). Thus, on many occasions, he—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—swore about the future without adding “if Allah wills.”

Allah—glorified and exalted is He—knows best. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

---

## Page 3496

And the learned shaykh, who put his knowledge into practice, the scrupulous and devout worshipper, Shaykh al-Islām, a surviving exemplar of the noble early generations, Abū al-ʿAbbās Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Halīm ibn ʿAbd al-Salām al-Shāmī—may Allah have mercy upon him—said:

Section

The hadith recounts the questions put to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning Islam, faith, and excellence, his answers to them, and his statement at the end:

“This was Gabriel, who came to teach you your religion.”

He thus included all of this within religion. People have said a great deal about Islam and faith, sometimes disagreeing and at other times agreeing, so that there is a need to ascertain the truth concerning them. This is done by clarifying the established principles on which there is agreement, and then using these to arrive at the truth of the matter in dispute.

We therefore say: What is known from the Quran, the Sunnah, and consensus, and has been transmitted through numerous independent channels

---

## Page 3497

from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—indeed, what is necessarily known to belong to Islam, the religion of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is that people in Medina during his lifetime fell into “three categories”: believers; disbelievers who openly professed their disbelief; and hypocrites who outwardly professed Islam but inwardly were disbelievers. In accordance with this division, Allah mentioned these three categories at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah, revealing four verses describing the believers, two describing the disbelievers, and ten-odd verses describing the hypocrites.

Thus His words, exalted is He:

“Guidance for the righteous,”

“Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them,”

“And who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and are certain of the Hereafter,”

“Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is they who are successful,”

describe the believers.

His words:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve—it is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe,”

and the following verse describe the disbelievers who die in disbelief.

His words:

“And among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers,”

and the ensuing verses describe the hypocrites, continuing until He sets forth two parables for them: one involving fire and the other water. Likewise, He uses these two to set forth a parable for the believers in His words, exalted is He:

“He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure,”

and the remainder of the verse.

---

## Page 3498

Before the Hijrah, however, people were either believers or disbelievers; there were no hypocrites. The Muslims were weak and oppressed, so whoever believed did so both inwardly and outwardly, while whoever did not believe was a disbeliever.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, migrated to Medina, the believers gained strength and supporters there, and most of its inhabitants embraced Islam willingly and of their own choice. Among their relatives and others, however, were some who outwardly professed Islam to conform, whether out of fear or hope of gain, while inwardly remaining disbelievers. Their leader was ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, concerning whom, and other hypocrites like him, verses were revealed. The Quran mentions the believers and the hypocrites in numerous places, including the surahs al-Baqarah, Āl ʿImrān, al-Nisāʾ, al-Māʾidah, al-ʿAnkabūt, and al-Ahzāb.

These hypocrites were found among both the inhabitants of Medina and the desert dwellers, as Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Among the Bedouins around you are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those entrenched in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them.”

Some of the hypocrites had originally been polytheists, while others had originally belonged to the People of the Book. They are also mentioned in the surahs al-Fath, al-Qitāl, al-Hadīd, al-Mujādalah, al-Hashr, and al-Munāfiqūn. Indeed, He mentions the hypocrites in most of the Medinan surahs.

Allah, exalted is He, says in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān:

“O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers when they travelled through the land or went out to fight, ‘Had they been with us, they would not have died or been killed.’”

The passage continues to His words:

## Page 3506

the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it.” Zayd ibn Arqam informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of this, but some people accused him of lying, until Allah revealed Quranic verses confirming his truthfulness.

The point is that people actually fall into three categories: a “believer”; a “hypocrite,” who is inwardly a disbeliever while outwardly a Muslim; and someone who is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly.

When non-Arabs became numerous among the Muslims, they began using the term “zindīq,” which became widespread in the language of the jurists. People debated whether a zindīq’s repentance would be accepted in outward legal judgment. If he is identified as a zindīq and brought before the ruler before repenting, the position of Mālik, Ahmad—in the better-known of the two reports from him—and a group of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers is that his repentance is not accepted. This is also one of the two positions within Abū Hanīfah’s school.

The well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī’s school is that it is accepted, as stated in the other report from Ahmad and the other position within Abū Hanīfah’s school. Some scholars distinguished between different cases.

The point here is that, in these jurists’ usage, a “zindīq” is the same as the hypocrite who existed during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: someone who outwardly professes Islam while inwardly holding something else. This applies whether he secretly follows another religion, such as Judaism, Christianity, or some other religion, or is an atheist who denies the Creator, the Resurrection, and righteous deeds.

Some people say that a “zindīq” is a denier and atheist. Such a person is called

---

## Page 3507

a zindīq in the terminology of many speculative theologians, ordinary people, and those who record people’s doctrines. However, the zindīq whose legal status the jurists discussed is the first type, because their concern is to distinguish between disbelievers and others, apostates and others, and those who disclose such beliefs and those who conceal them.

This ruling applies equally to all kinds of disbelievers and apostates, although their degrees of disbelief and apostasy differ. Allah has spoken of an increase in disbelief, just as He has spoken of an increase in faith, saying:

“Postponing the sacred months is only an increase in disbelief.”

And one who abandons prayer or any of the other pillars, or those who commit major sins; just as He has stated that some disbelievers will receive greater punishment than others in the Hereafter, saying:

“Those who disbelieve and bar others from Allah’s path—We shall add punishment upon punishment for them.”

This is a “principle” that should be understood, for it is important in this subject. Many who have discussed “questions of faith and disbelief”—in connection with declaring adherents of deviant doctrines to be disbelievers—have overlooked this matter and failed to distinguish between outward judgment and inward reality. Yet the distinction between the two is established by scriptural texts transmitted through numerous independent channels and by well-established consensus. Indeed, it is necessarily known as part of the religion of Islam.

Anyone who reflects on this will understand that many adherents of deviant doctrines and religious innovations may be believers who are mistaken, ignorant, and astray concerning some of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. They may also be hypocritical zindīqs who outwardly profess the opposite of what they conceal.

There is “another principle” here: the Quran and Sunnah describe certain people as having Islam but not faith. The Most High says:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed

---

## Page 3508

, but say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts. If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”

The Most High also says concerning the people of Lot:

“So We brought out those believers who were there.”

“But We found there only one household of Muslims.”

Some people have supposed that this verse implies that faith and Islam denote the same thing, and have regarded the two passages as contradictory. This is not so. Rather, this verse agrees with the first, for Allah states that He brought out those who were believers there, and that He found only one household of Muslims. Lot’s wife was among the members of the household who were there, but she was not among those brought out and saved. Rather, she was among those who remained behind to suffer the punishment. Outwardly, she sided with her husband and followed his religion, but inwardly she sided with her people and followed theirs, betraying her husband by alerting her people to his guests.

As Allah Most High says concerning her:

“Allah sets forth an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were married to two righteous servants of Ours, but betrayed them.”

Their betrayal of their husbands concerned religion, not marital fidelity, for no prophet’s wife has ever committed adultery. “Marriage to a disbelieving woman” may be permissible under some revealed laws, and our own law permits marriage to certain categories of such women, namely women of the People of the Book. As for “marriage to an unchaste woman,” this amounts to tolerating sexual immorality in one’s wife. Allah has safeguarded prophets from tolerating such conduct.

Thus, the correct view is that of those jurists who hold that marriage to an unchaste woman is forbidden until she repents.

---

## Page 3509

The point is that Lot’s wife was not a believer, nor was she among those brought out and saved. Thus, she was not included in His words:

“So We brought out those believers who were there.”

She was, however, a member of the Muslim household and among those found there. Hence the Most High says:

“But We found there only one household of Muslims.”

This reveals the wisdom of the Quran in mentioning faith when speaking of bringing them out, and Islam when speaking of finding them there.

The Most High also says:

“Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women…”

He thus distinguishes between the two. These, then, are three passages in the Quran.

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave to some men but did not give to another man. I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you gave to so-and-so but left out so-and-so, although he is a believer.’ He said, ‘Or a Muslim?’ Then my feelings overcame me, and I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you gave to so-and-so and so-and-so but left out so-and-so, although he is a believer.’ He said, ‘Or a Muslim?’”

This occurred twice or three times. The remainder of the hadith mentions that he gives to some men while leaving out others whom he loves more, for fear that Allah might cast the former headlong into the Fire.

Al-Zuhrī said: “They used to consider Islam to be the declaration of faith, and faith to be action.”

Thus, the Prophet answered Sa‘d in two ways. First: The man whose faith you have attested to may be a Muslim without being a believer.

Second: Even if he is a believer and better than those others, I may give to someone whose faith is weaker, lest being deprived lead him to apostasy and Allah cast him into

---

## Page 3510

the Fire headlong. This is an instance of giving to those whose hearts are to be reconciled.

Now, are those whom the Quran and Sunnah describe as having Islam, but not faith, hypocrites who are inwardly unbelievers? Or do they also include people who possess some faith? Scholars of various persuasions have disagreed over this.

A group of hadith scholars, speculative theologians, and others said: Rather, they are hypocrites who have outwardly submitted and complied, while no faith has entered their hearts. Those who hold this view may say that the Islam that is accepted is faith. These people, however, submitted outwardly, not inwardly; thus, they were neither inwardly Muslims nor believers.

They said: Allah, glorified is He, says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

Their explanation is that every Muslim is a believer: whatever is not part of Islam is not accepted, which requires that faith be part of it.

They maintain that every believer is a Muslim, and every Muslim is a believer, provided that he is inwardly a Muslim. As for someone who is inwardly an unbeliever and a hypocrite, the Muslims unanimously agree that he is excluded from the believers who deserve reward. None of the early generations of the Muslim community or its leading scholars, nor any of the Muslim groups, call such people believers—with the exception of one group among the Murji’ah: the Karrāmiyyah, who said that faith consists merely of outward assent.

Accordingly, once someone gives such assent, he is a believer, even if he inwardly denies it. They nevertheless acknowledged that he would be punished eternally in the Hereafter. Thus, they disputed his designation, not

---

## Page 3511

his fate. Some people report that they regarded such people as inhabitants of Paradise, but this misrepresents their position.

Nevertheless, their calling such a person a believer is an innovation they introduced in opposition to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. This heinous innovation, unlike their other doctrines, was peculiar to the Karrāmiyyah.

The majority of the early and later scholars said: Rather, those described as having Islam but not faith are not necessarily inwardly unbelievers; they possess some measure of Islam that is accepted.

They say that Islam is broader than faith: every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer. Regarding the Prophet’s saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“No one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is a believer while doing so; no thief is a believer while stealing; and no one who drinks wine is a believer while drinking it,”

they say that such a person passes out of faith into Islam. They drew a circle representing Islam, with a smaller circle representing faith inside it, and said: When someone commits unlawful sexual intercourse, he passes out of faith into Islam, but this does not take him out of Islam into unbelief.

The evidence for this is that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, says:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed. Rather, say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts. If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.’ Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah

---

## Page 3512

—it is they who are truthful.”

“Say, ‘Would you inform Allah of your religion?’ Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah has knowledge of all things.”

“They regard their acceptance of Islam as a favour to you. Say, ‘Do not regard your Islam as a favour to me. Rather, Allah has bestowed a favour upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.’”

Allah Most High said:

“You have not believed. Rather, say, ‘We have submitted,’ for faith has not yet entered your hearts.”

This particle—*lammā* (“not yet”)—negates something whose occurrence is near and anticipated, but which has not yet happened. Thus, one says to someone awaiting an absent person, “Not yet.” One says, “He has come”; “He has not come yet.”

When they said, “We believe,” they were told, “You have not believed”—not yet; rather, faith was still hoped for and expected of them.

Then He said:

“If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish for you…”

That is, He will not diminish the reward of your recorded deeds “in the least”—meaning, in this present condition. For if they meant obedience to Allah and His Messenger after faith had entered their hearts, this would convey nothing of benefit to them or anyone else. It was already known that believers are rewarded for obeying Allah and His Messenger, and they themselves acknowledged this.

If they were told, “The one obeyed is rewarded,” and what was meant was the believer who knows that he is a believer, this would convey no new information.

Furthermore, these very people were being addressed. He had stated that faith had not yet entered their hearts, and they were told:

“If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.”

If they were not rewarded for obeying Allah and His Messenger while in this condition, that would contradict what these words signify. This is further clarified by His description of the believers, from whose ranks He excluded these people. Allah Most High said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives

---

## Page 3513

in the cause of Allah—it is they who are truthful.”

This describes someone who has attained full faith, not someone who possesses merely an atom’s weight of faith. Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

“Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them.”

“It is they who are truly believers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and who, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger.”

The Prophet’s saying (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) is another example:

“An adulterer is not a believer at the time he commits adultery.”

There are other similar statements.

This explanation shows that the faith denied to these Bedouins is the same faith denied to sinful members of the Muslim community who will not remain in the Fire forever. Indeed, one of them may possess an atom’s weight of faith. Denying this faith does not entail affirming the disbelief that condemns a person to remain in the Fire forever.

Properly understanding “this point” removes the confusion here and makes it clear that there is a category of Muslims who are neither outright hypocrites in the lowest depth of the Fire nor among the believers of whom it is said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah—it is they who are truthful.”

Nor are they among those of whom it is said:

“It is they who are truly believers.”

Thus, they are neither hypocrites nor are they

---

## Page 3514

among these truthful, genuine believers, nor among those who enter Paradise without punishment. Rather, such a person has acts of obedience and disobedience, good deeds and evil deeds. He possesses enough faith to keep him from remaining in the Fire forever, yet has committed major sins that warrant entering it.

Some people call a person in this category “a sinful person who remains within the Muslim community.” People have disputed both his designation and his religious status. This was the first dispute to arise in Islam concerning “the fundamentals of religion.”

We therefore say: After the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, was killed, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib went to Iraq, and the well-known strife and division arose within the Muslim community at the Battle of the Camel and then at Siffīn. The renegade Khārijites rebelled against both sides. The Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) had foretold their emergence and explained the ruling concerning them. Imam Ahmad said, “The hadith concerning the Khārijites has been authentically transmitted through ten routes.” Muslim included these ten routes in his Sahīh, in keeping with Ahmad’s statement. Al-Bukhārī also related several of these routes, while the compilers of the Sunan and Musnad collections transmitted reports concerning them through other routes.

Among the most authentic reports concerning them are those narrated by ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī. In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib is reported to have said:

“When I relate a hadith to you from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), then, by Allah, I would rather fall from heaven to earth than tell a lie about him. But when I speak to you about matters between us, war is deception. I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) say: ‘At the end of time, a people will emerge

---

## Page 3515

young in age and foolish in judgment, uttering some of the finest words spoken by mankind. Their faith will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.’”

The two Sahīh collections also relate that Abū Sa‘īd said:

“‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib sent the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) a small quantity of gold from Yemen, wrapped in a cut piece of leather, with its earth not yet separated from it. He divided it among four men. One of his Companions said, ‘We were more entitled to this than these men.’ This reached the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), who said, ‘Will you not trust me, when I am trusted by the One above the heavens, and news from heaven comes to me morning and evening?’

“A man then stood up. He had deep-set eyes, prominent cheekbones, a protruding forehead, a thick beard, a shaved head, and his waist-wrapper tucked up. He said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, fear Allah!’ He replied, ‘Woe to you! Am I not the person on earth who should fear Allah most?’ The man then turned away, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, shall I strike off his head?’ He replied, ‘No; perhaps he prays.’ Khālid said, ‘How many people pray yet say with their tongues what is not in their hearts!’ The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said, ‘I have not been commanded to probe people’s hearts or split open their bellies.’

“Then he looked at the man as he walked away and said, ‘From this man’s stock there will emerge people who recite the Book of Allah smoothly, yet it will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry.’”

The narrator said, “I think he said, ‘If I live to encounter them, I will kill them as ‘Ād were killed.’”

This is Muslim’s wording.

---

## Page 3516

Muslim also relates through some of his chains of transmission from Abū Sa‘īd:

“The Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) mentioned people who would arise within his community at a time of division among the people, their distinguishing mark being shaved heads. He then said, ‘They are the worst of creation—or among the worst of creation. They will be killed by whichever of the two factions is closer to the truth.’”

Abū Sa‘īd said, “You were the ones who killed them, people of Iraq.” In another wording recorded by Muslim:

“Whichever of the two factions is nearer to the truth will kill them.”

Alongside this hadith is the report established in the Sahīh collection from Abū Bakrah that the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said concerning al-Hasan ibn ‘Alī:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great factions of believers.”

He thus made clear that both factions were believers, and that their reconciliation, as brought about by al-Hasan, was more beloved to Allah, Glorified is He, and His Messenger (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) than their fighting one another. He also made clear that, although their fighting had not been commanded, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and his companions were closer to the truth than Mu‘āwiyah and his companions, and that fighting the Khawārij was something he (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) had commanded. For this reason, the Companions and the imams agreed on fighting them.

These Khawārij have several names. They are called the “Harūriyyah” because they rebelled at a place called Harūrā’. They are also called the people of Nahrawān because ‘Alī fought them there. Their branches include the “Ibādiyyah,” the followers of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ibād; the “Azāriqah,” the followers of Nāfi‘ ibn al-Azraq; and the “Najadāt,” the followers of Najdah al-Harūrī.

They were the first to declare those who face the qiblah in prayer unbelievers on account of sins—indeed, on account of what they themselves regarded as sins. On that basis, they deemed it lawful to shed their blood. Thus they were just as the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) described them:

---

## Page 3517

“They kill Muslims and leave the idolaters alone.”

They declared ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, and those loyal to them unbelievers. They killed ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, believing it lawful to do so. His killer, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muljam al-Murādī, was one of them. He and other Khawārij were diligent in worship, but they were ignorant and had departed from the Sunnah and the Muslim community.

They said: “People are either believers or unbelievers. A believer is someone who fulfils every obligation and abstains from everything forbidden. Whoever does not do so is an unbeliever who will remain in the Fire forever.”

They then applied this judgment to everyone who disagreed with them, saying: “‘Uthmān, ‘Alī, and others like them ruled by something other than what Allah revealed and committed injustice, thereby becoming unbelievers.”

Their doctrine is false, as shown by abundant evidence from the Quran and Sunnah. Allah, Glorified is He, commanded that the thief’s hand be cut off, not that he be killed. Had he been an unbeliever who had apostatized, he would have had to be put to death, for the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said:

“Whoever changes his religion, put him to death.”

He also said:

“It is not lawful to shed a Muslim’s blood except in one of three cases: disbelief after embracing Islam, unlawful sexual intercourse after marriage, or taking a life for which he is put to death.”

Allah, Glorified is He, commanded that the man and woman guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse each receive one hundred lashes. Had they been unbelievers, He would have commanded that they be put to death. He likewise commanded that anyone who accuses a chaste woman of unlawful sexual intercourse receive eighty lashes. Had such a person been an unbeliever, He would have commanded that he be put to death.

The Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) used to flog the wine-drinker, not put him to death. Indeed, it is established from him in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere:

“A man named ‘Abd Allāh Himār used to drink wine and would make the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) laugh. Whenever he was brought before the Prophet, he would flog him. On one occasion, when he was brought before him, a man cursed him. The Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said:

---

## Page 3518

‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

He thus forbade cursing this particular man and testified that he loved Allah and His Messenger, even though he had cursed wine-drinkers in general. This is among the strongest arguments that the command to put the wine-drinker to death on the “third” and “fourth” occasions was abrogated, since this man was brought before him three times. The greatest imams have struggled to answer this hadith.

However, abrogating the obligation does not rule out permissibility. It may therefore be argued that he may be put to death if the ruler considers that doing so serves the public interest. For lashes beyond forty, up to eighty, do not constitute a fixed prescribed punishment according to the sounder of the two scholarly views. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him. Rather, increasing the number beyond forty, up to eighty, is left to the ruler’s judgment: he does so when it serves the public interest, as with other forms of discretionary punishment. The same applies to the manner of beating: a wine-drinker may be flogged with palm stalks, sandals, and the ends of garments, unlike someone guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse or of making an unsubstantiated accusation of it. It may therefore be argued that putting him to death on the fourth occasion falls into this category.

Furthermore, Allah, Glorified is He, said:

“If two groups of believers fight one another, make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, fight the transgressing group until it returns to Allah’s command. If it returns, make peace between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably. The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers.”

He thus described them as believers and brothers, and commanded us to make peace between them. When the matter of the Khawārij became widely known throughout the Muslim community, the Companions spoke about them and narrated from

---

## Page 3519

the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) hadiths concerning them and explained the Quran’s refutation of them. Their innovation became widespread among the people.

After them came the Mu‘tazilah—those who withdrew from the Muslim community after the death of al-Hasan al-Basrī: ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd, Wāsil ibn ‘Atā’ al-Ghazāl, and their followers. They said: “Those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever,” as the Khawārij maintained. “We call them neither believers nor disbelievers; rather, they are grave sinners whom we place in an intermediate position between the two.” They denied the Prophet’s intercession (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) for those of his community who committed major sins, and denied that they would leave the Fire after entering it. They said: “People are of only two kinds: the blessed, who will not be punished, and the wretched, who will experience no bliss. The wretched are of two kinds: disbelievers and grave sinners.” They did not agree with the Khawārij in calling them disbelievers. These people may be refuted with the same arguments they themselves used against the Khawārij.

They may be told: Just as the Khawārij divided people into believers with no sins and disbelievers with no good deeds, you have divided people into believers with no sins, and disbelievers and grave sinners with no good deeds. If all the good deeds of such a sinner were nullified and he were to remain in the Fire forever, he would deserve unqualified hostility, through killing and enslavement, just as an apostate does; for, unlike the hypocrite, he has openly declared his religion.

Allah Most High has said in His Book:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

He thus made forgiveness of anything less than associating partners with Him subject to His will. This cannot be understood as referring to someone who repents, for in the case of someone who repents, there is no distinction between

---

## Page 3520

associating partners with Allah and other sins. As He, glorified be He, says in another verse:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

Here He made forgiveness comprehensive and unconditional, because the passage concerns those who repent; in the earlier verse, He restricted it and made it conditional.

Allah Most High also says:

“Then We caused those whom We chose from among Our servants to inherit the Book. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s permission. That is the great bounty.”

“Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be silk.”

“And they will say, ‘Praise be to Allah, who has removed sorrow from us. Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Appreciative.’”

“‘He who, out of His bounty, has settled us in the everlasting abode, where neither toil nor weariness touches us.’”

Thus, He, glorified be He, divided the community whom He chose and caused to inherit the Book into “three categories”: those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds. These three correspond to the three levels mentioned in the hadith of Gabriel: “Islam,” “faith,” and “excellence,” as we shall explain, “if Allah wills.”

It is clear that if “those who wrong themselves” were intended to mean those who avoid major sins and those who repent of all sins, such people would belong either to those who follow a middle course or to those who are foremost. For no descendant of Adam is free from sin, but whoever repents belongs to one of these latter two categories. Likewise, whoever avoids major sins has his lesser sins expiated, as Allah Most High says:

“If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will expiate your lesser sins.”

There must therefore be someone who wrongs himself yet is promised Paradise, even if only after punishment that purifies him of his sins. For the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) explained that the afflictions which befall a believer in this world serve to discharge his liability and expiate his sins, as related in the two Sahīh collections

---

## Page 3521

from him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), that he said:

“No illness, fatigue, worry, sorrow, distress, or harm befalls a believer—even the prick of a thorn—without Allah expiating some of his sins thereby.”

The Musnad and other collections also relate:

“When this verse was revealed, ‘Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it,’ Abū Bakr said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, this is a back-breaking blow! Which of us has not done evil?’ He replied, ‘O Abū Bakr, do you not grow weary? Do you not grieve? Does hardship not befall you? These are among the things through which you receive your recompense.’”

Furthermore, mass-transmitted hadiths from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) establish that some people will emerge from the Fire after entering it, and that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) will intercede for people who have entered the Fire.

These hadiths constitute evidence against both groups: the “Wa‘īdiyyah,” who say that any person who affirms Allah’s oneness and enters the Fire will never emerge from it; and the “Murji’ah who withhold judgment,” who say, “We do not know whether anyone who affirms Allah’s oneness will enter the Fire at all.” This latter view is held by groups among the Shī‘ah and the Ash‘arīs, such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and others.

As for the view attributed to the “extreme Murji’ah,” that no one who affirms Allah’s oneness will ever enter the Fire, we know of no prominent figure regarded as a scholar to whom this view is attributed.

Furthermore, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) testified that the man who had repeatedly been flogged for drinking wine loved Allah and His Messenger, and he forbade cursing him. It is well known that whoever loves Allah and His Messenger is loved by Allah and His Messenger in proportion to that love. Furthermore, those who slandered ‘Ā’ishah, the Mother of

---

## Page 3522

the Believers, included Mistah ibn Uthāthah, who had taken part in Badr. When Abū Bakr swore that he would no longer support him, Allah revealed concerning him:

“Let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to their relatives, the needy, and those who emigrated in the cause of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love for Allah to forgive you?”

Even if it is said that Mistah and others like him repented, Allah did not make repentance a condition when commanding that they be pardoned, their wrongdoing overlooked, and kindness shown to them. Likewise:

“Hātib ibn Abī Balta‘ah wrote to the polytheists with news of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). When ‘Umar wanted to kill him, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said, ‘He took part in Badr. How do you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said, “Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.”’”

It is likewise established in al-Sahīh that he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“No one who pledged allegiance beneath the tree will enter the Fire.”

These texts indicate that sins are forgiven by virtue of those good deeds, without repentance being stipulated as an additional condition. Otherwise, those people would have no special distinction in this regard. The hadith indicates that forgiveness comes through that deed.

If it is said that this is because none of those people had committed anything but minor sins, that would not distinguish them from others either. This also entails acknowledging the possibility that those who have been forgiven may commit a major sin.

Furthermore, the texts of the Quran and Sunnah indicate that punishment for sins is averted from a servant through approximately ten means.

The first is repentance. This is a matter of agreement among Muslims. Allah Most High says:

---

## Page 3523

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do they not know that Allah accepts repentance from His servants and receives their charities, and that Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Most Merciful?”

And He says:

“He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons their misdeeds.”

There are other such verses.

The second means is seeking forgiveness, as related in the two Sahīh collections from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who said:

“When a servant commits a sin and says, ‘My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me,’ He says, ‘My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sins and punishes for them. I have forgiven My servant.’ Then he commits another sin and says, ‘My Lord, I have committed another sin, so forgive me for it.’ His Lord says, ‘My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sins and punishes for them. I have forgiven My servant, so let him do whatever he wishes.’ He said this on the third or fourth occasion.”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is related that he said:

“If you did not sin, Allah would do away with you and bring a people who would sin, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them.”

It may be said that seeking forgiveness, understood in this way, is accompanied by repentance, as stated in the hadith:

“One who seeks forgiveness is not persisting in sin, even if he returns to it a hundred times a day.”

It may, however, be said that seeking forgiveness without repentance is both possible and does occur. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere. For if this seeking of forgiveness is accompanied by repentance, the ruling applies to everyone who repents. If it is not accompanied by repentance, it applies to some of those who seek forgiveness: those who, while seeking forgiveness, may experience such fear of Allah and such a turning back to Him that their sins are erased. This is like what is related in the hadith of the card, in which the words “There is no deity

---

## Page 3524

but Allah” outweighed those sins, because he uttered them with a degree of truthfulness and sincerity that erases sins. Likewise, Allah forgave the prostitute for giving a dog water because of the faith that arose in her heart at that moment. There are many similar examples.

The third means: good deeds that erase sins. Allah Most High says:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“The five daily prayers, one Friday prayer to the next, and one Ramadan to the next expiate the sins committed between them, provided major sins are avoided.”

He also said:

“Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking Allah’s reward will have his past sins forgiven.”

He said:

“Whoever spends the Night of Decree in prayer out of faith and seeking Allah’s reward will have his past sins forgiven.”

He said:

“Whoever performs pilgrimage to this House, neither engaging in sexual indecency nor committing sin, will return free of sins as on the day his mother bore him.”

He said:

“The trials a man faces concerning his family, wealth, and children are expiated by prayer, fasting, charity, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong.”

He said:

“Whoever frees a believing slave, Allah will free every part of his body from the Fire in return for the corresponding part of the slave’s body—even his private parts in return for the slave’s private parts.”

These hadiths and others like them are found in the authentic collections.

He also said:

“Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, and envy consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood.”

Their objection to this line of reasoning is to say that good deeds expiate only minor sins, whereas major sins are forgiven only through repentance, as stated in some hadiths:

“So long as major sins are avoided.”

This objection may be answered in several ways.

---

## Page 3525

First: this condition is stated concerning obligatory acts, such as the five daily prayers, Friday prayer, and fasting the month of Ramadan. Allah Most High says:

“If you avoid the major sins you have been forbidden to commit, We will expiate your misdeeds.”

Thus, performing the obligatory acts while avoiding major sins brings about the expiation of misdeeds. Additional voluntary acts must therefore have a further reward, for Allah, glorified is He, says:

“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

(Second): many hadiths explicitly state that forgiveness may occur even when major sins have been committed, as in the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“He will be forgiven, even if he has fled the battlefield.”

The Sunan collections also relate:

“We came to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) concerning a companion of ours who had committed a sin deserving of the Fire. He said: ‘Free a slave on his behalf; for every part of the slave’s body, Allah will free a corresponding part of his body from the Fire.’”

And in the two authentic collections, the hadith of Abū Dharr states:

“Even if he has committed adultery, and even if he has stolen.”

(Third): if the statement addressed to those who fought at Badr and others like them—“Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you”—were understood to concern only minor sins, or forgiveness accompanied by repentance, there would be no distinction between them and anyone else. Just as this hadith cannot be understood to include disbelief, since disbelief is known to be forgiven only through repentance, it cannot be restricted to minor sins that are expiated by avoiding major sins.

(Fourth): it is related in more than one hadith:

“The first thing for which a servant will be called to account among

---

## Page 3526

his deeds on the Day of Resurrection will be prayer. If he has performed it in full, all is well; otherwise it will be said: ‘See whether he has any voluntary prayers.’ If he has, his obligatory prayer will be completed with them. Then the rest of his deeds will be treated in the same manner.”

It is evident that the shortfall thus made good cannot consist in omitting something recommended, since omitting a recommended act requires no compensation. Moreover, there would then be no difference between the recommended act omitted and the one performed. Thus, it is clear that deficiencies in obligatory acts are made good through voluntary acts.

This does not contradict the statement that Allah does not accept voluntary worship until the obligatory duty has been discharged. Even if this statement contradicted the first report, the first would have to be given precedence, since it is more firmly established and better known. The latter report is singular in its attribution to the Prophet; what is well known is that it occurs in Abū Bakr’s counsel to ʿUmar. Ahmad mentioned it in his Treatise on Prayer.

The explanation is that acceptance of voluntary worship here means receiving its reward. It is evident that one is not rewarded for voluntary worship until the obligatory duty has been discharged: if someone performs a voluntary act while the obligatory act remains deficient, it makes good and completes that deficiency. It therefore carries no reward as a voluntary act. For this reason, one of the early Muslims said:

“Worship is truly additional only for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because Allah has forgiven his past and future sins, whereas others need forgiveness.”

He understood Allah’s words in this sense:

“And during part of the night, rise in prayer with it as an additional prayer for you.”

Yet it does not follow that, whenever someone performs a voluntary act while neglecting an obligation, the voluntary act replaces the obligatory one without qualification. Rather, the punishment for neglecting the obligation may be greater than the reward for the voluntary act.

If it is said: “When a servant sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, he must perform it when he remembers, according to the explicit text and scholarly consensus. If voluntary prayers could replace it, making it up would not be obligatory.”

The answer is: “This is mistaken. If this argument is advanced, it can be applied to all the means by which punishment is averted. Thus, one might say: ‘If a servant

---

## Page 3527

can avert punishment through repentance, he would not be forbidden to commit the act.’ Yet it is well known that a servant must do what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden, because failing to do so is grounds for blame and punishment—even though that punishment may be averted through these means despite his failure. Likewise, he must protect himself against deadly poisons, even though, after taking them, he might counteract their harm with medicines.

Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise, Most Merciful. He commands them to do what benefits them and forbids them from doing what corrupts them. Then, if they expose themselves to causes of destruction, He does not leave them to despair of His mercy. Rather, He provides means by which they can avert the harm. Hence the saying:

‘The truly discerning scholar is one who neither makes people despair of Allah’s mercy nor emboldens them to disobey Him.’

For this reason, the servant is commanded to repent whenever he sins. Someone once said to his shaykh, ‘I commit sins.’
He replied, ‘Repent.’
‘Then I return to them.’
‘Repent.’
‘Then I return to them.’
‘Repent.’
‘For how long?’
‘Until you grieve Satan.’

In the Musnad, ʿAlī reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘Allah loves the servant who is often tempted and repeatedly repents.’

Furthermore, when someone sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, performing it upon waking or remembering serves as its expiation. This discharges his obligation, removes blame and punishment, and earns him praise and reward. As for the voluntary acts he performs, we do not know how much would be needed for their reward to take the place of that prayer. Even if this were known, he might be unable to perform them alongside all his other obligations. Moreover, if we suppose that he were commanded to perform something that would take its place, that act would become obligatory and would therefore no longer be voluntary.

Voluntary acts of worship were prescribed to draw one still nearer to Allah, as Allah Most High says in the authentic hadith:

‘My servant draws near to Me through nothing like fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him.’

The hadith continues.

---

## Page 3528

Thus, if the servant has not fulfilled the obligatory duties as commanded, he will not attain the intended benefit of voluntary acts of worship. Yet Allah does not wrong him, for Allah does not wrong anyone even by an atom’s weight. Rather, He counts those voluntary acts towards their corresponding obligatory duties. This is like someone who owes debts to people and wishes to give them voluntary gifts:

If he repays them and also gives them gifts, he is both just and benevolent. If he repays them without giving them gifts, he is just. But if he gives them something that discharges his debt and regards it as a voluntary gift, he is mistaken in doing so. Rather, it counts towards the obligation that is their due.

It is astonishing that the Muʿtazilah pride themselves on being the people of “divine oneness” and “justice,” yet, in their conception of divine oneness, they deny Allah’s attributes in a manner that entails stripping Him of His attributes and associating partners with Him. As for “the justice with which Allah has described Himself,” it means that He does not wrong anyone even by an atom’s weight, and that:

“Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

Yet they hold that all a servant’s good deeds and faith are nullified by a single major sin. This is among the injustices from which Allah has declared Himself free. It is therefore more fitting to describe the Lord, glorified be He, with the justice with which He has described Himself than to make justice consist in denying Allah’s decree.
