Another version reads, “faith in Me and affirmation of My messengers”; and another, “motivated solely by striving in Allah’s cause and affirmation of His words.” In all these versions, the wording of affirmation pertains to words and messengers. Likewise, the hadith in the Sahīh collection states:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—mentioned lofty stations in Paradise. He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, those are stations that none but the prophets can attain.’ He replied, ‘On the contrary! By Him in whose hand is my soul, men who have faith in Allah and affirm the messengers can attain them.’”

One does not now find among the familiar usages in the speech of the early generations such expressions as “I have affirmed Allah,” “So-and-so affirms Allah,” “He affirmed Allah,” and the like, as one finds “So-and-so has faith,” “He has faith in Allah,” “with faith in Allah,” “We have faith in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers,” “We have faith in Allah alone,” and similar expressions. The Quran, hadith, and the speech of both the learned and ordinary people abound in such expressions as “faith in Allah,” “He has faith in Allah,” “We have faith in Allah,” and “O you who have faith.” Yet I know of no instance of “affirmation of Allah,” “They affirmed Allah,” “O you who have affirmed Allah,” or the like—unless there is something that does not come to mind at this moment, though I do not think there is.

The word “faith” is also used in relation to a report, as in:

“Each has faith in Allah,”

meaning that each acknowledges Him. The Messenger is believed insofar as he conveys a report, and one has faith in him insofar as his messengership is among the things he has reported, just as one has faith in Allah, His angels, and His Books. Thus “faith” entails acknowledgment of what he has reported

---

## Page 3569

; disbelief, in turn, is sometimes considered in terms of failing to believe the Messenger and have faith in him. In this respect, everything he has reported stands on the same footing. At other times, it is considered in terms of failing to acknowledge what he has reported. Fundamental to this is what he has reported about Allah and His names. Thus, denying matters in this category is graver than denying other matters, even though the Messenger has reported both.

Merely believing his report and knowing that what he has reported is true does not constitute faith if it is accompanied by neither inward nor outward obedience to his command, nor love or reverence for Allah. The disbelief of Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, and others like them did not originate in a lack of belief or knowledge. No one conveyed a report to Iblīs; rather, Allah commanded him to prostrate before Adam, but he refused, acted arrogantly, and became one of the disbelievers. His disbelief consisted in refusal, arrogance, and what followed from them—not in disbelieving a report.

Likewise, Pharaoh and his people rejected the signs out of injustice and arrogance, though inwardly they were certain of them. Moses said to him:

“You know well that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these signs.”

Here, one of two things may be said. The first is that arrogance, refusal, envy, and similar things that constitute disbelief necessarily entail the absence of the knowledge and affirmation that constitute faith. For anyone whose knowledge and affirmation were complete would necessarily submit and obey, with an example to follow, just as a firm resolve necessarily brings about the intended act when the ability is present. Thus, if the intended act does not occur despite the ability to perform it, this indicates that there is no determination or will in the heart. Likewise, if the love and submission of the heart that necessarily follow from affirmation and knowledge are absent, this indicates that what the heart possesses is neither affirmation nor knowledge; rather, there is a misgiving

---

## Page 3570

and doubt, as various groups maintain. This is the basis of the position of Jahm, al-Sālihī, al-Ashʿarī—according to the view widely attributed to him—and most of his followers, such as Judge Abū Bakr and those who follow him. They regard inward and outward deeds as necessary consequences of faith, rather than constituents of faith itself, and regard whatever is indispensable to faith as an inseparable consequence of affirmation. On this view, inward affirmation cannot coexist with disbelief under any circumstances.

Alternatively, it may be said that the heart can possess knowledge and affirmation of the truth, while the envy, arrogance, and similar traits within it prevent its surrender, submission, and love. This is not comparable to the relationship between will and action, for will, when coupled with ability, necessarily brings about what is intended. Knowledge and affirmation of the truth, however, even when accompanied by the ability to act, do not necessarily produce that action. There must also be a desire for the truth and love for it.

Thus, if someone says, “Complete ability, without firm resolve, necessarily brings about the intended outcome that lies within one’s power and ensures its occurrence,” he is mistaken. Will is also indispensable.

This makes clear the error of those philosophers who say that Allah’s knowledge of created things alone necessarily brings them into existence. Likewise, people judge mistaken anyone who says that merely willing possible things, without the power to bring them about, necessarily brings them into existence. They likewise judge mistaken anyone who says that power alone suffices. Rather, knowledge, power, and will are all indispensable for bringing into existence what is within one’s power and intended. Will necessarily entails conceiving of what is intended and knowing it.

As for knowledge, will, power, and similar attributes, although it may be said that they necessarily accompany one another in a living being, or that life necessarily entails these attributes, or that some attributes depend upon others, there is no doubt that not everything known is willed

---

## Page 3571

or loved or within one’s power, nor is everything within one’s power willed or loved. Since this is so, something’s being known and affirmed does not necessarily mean that it is loved and worshipped. Rather, knowledge is indispensable, as is something else whereby one becomes the lover and the other the beloved.

Thus, the claim that mere knowledge and affirmation within a person constitute faith and necessarily produce deeds of the heart—so that their absence indicates the absence of knowledge—is comparable to saying that Allah’s mere knowledge of the order of the world necessarily brings it into existence, without any will on His part. It also resembles the philosophers’ claim that the soul’s happiness consists merely in knowing realities, without coupling this with love for Allah Most High and worship of Him, without which happiness cannot be complete. It is likewise comparable to saying that the perfection of the body or soul consists in love without any accompanying voluntary movement, or that pleasure consists merely in perception and awareness.

All rational people agree that this is mistaken. Rather, one must perceive something agreeable; and this agreeableness requires love on the part of the perceiver for what is perceived. That love, harmony, and agreeableness are not identical with perceiving the object and being aware of it.

Many philosophers, physicians, and their followers have said that “pleasure” is the perception of what is agreeable. Yet their account falls short. Rather, pleasure is a state that follows the perception of what is agreeable. Consider someone who loves and craves something sweet, then perceives it through tasting and eating. Pleasure is not merely the tasting itself, but something he experiences within himself that accompanies the tasting.

Thus, two things are required “initially,” and two “subsequently.” “Initially,” there must be awareness of the beloved object and love for it. What one has no awareness of cannot conceivably be desired; and what one is aware of, but has no love for within oneself, is not desired. Then, when

---

## Page 3572

he perceives the beloved object itself, pleasure and joy follow, accompanying that perception.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the transmitted supplication:

“O Allah, I ask You for the pleasure of looking upon Your Face and the longing to meet You, without harmful affliction or a trial that leads astray.”

And in the authentic hadith:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will announce, ‘O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise that He wishes to fulfil for you.’ They will say, ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and protected us from the Fire?’ He said: ‘Then He will lift the veil, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him.’”

Narrated by Muslim and others. Pleasure thus accompanies looking upon Him. Nothing is dearer to them than looking upon Him because of the pleasure that accompanies it—not because looking itself is pleasure.

In sum, faith in the heart must include believing in Allah and His Messenger and loving Allah and His Messenger. Mere belief accompanied by hatred of Allah and His Messenger and hostility towards Allah and His Messenger is not faith, by the consensus of the Muslims. Mere belief and knowledge do not necessarily entail love unless the heart is free of obstacles such as envy and pride, for the soul is naturally disposed to love the truth, which accords with its nature. Nothing is dearer to sound hearts than Allah. This is pure monotheism, the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, whom Allah took as an intimate friend.

Allah Most High said:

“On the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit, except to one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

Thus, mere

---

## Page 3573

knowledge does not necessarily produce love for its object unless the soul possesses another faculty attuned to that object—and this faculty does exist in the soul. Each of these two faculties strengthens the other: knowledge strengthens action, and action strengthens knowledge. Whoever knows Allah and has a sound heart loves Him. The more he knows Him, the more he loves Him; and the more he loves Him, the more he remembers Him and knows His names and attributes. Strong love leads to frequent remembrance of the beloved, just as hatred leads one to avoid mentioning the one one hates. Whoever is hostile to Allah and His Messenger and sets himself against Allah and His Messenger is thereby led to refrain from speaking well of Allah and His Messenger and from mentioning what inspires love. His knowledge of Him consequently weakens, until he may even forget Him.

As Allah Most High said:

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

And Allah Most High said:

“And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desires, and whose conduct is beyond all bounds.”

Belief and knowledge may nevertheless coexist with hatred and hostility, but they are weak belief and weak knowledge. Were it not for that hatred and hostility, however, this would produce enough love for Allah and His Messenger to make the person a believer. Thus, complete knowledge is a condition of faith. Hence, the correct view is that ignorance of some of Allah’s names and attributes does not make a person a disbeliever, provided that he acknowledges what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, and nothing has reached him that would require him to know what he is ignorant of in such a way that his failure to know it would constitute disbelief. An example is the hadith of the man who instructed his family to burn him and then scatter his ashes. Indeed, those who know Allah differ in their knowledge of Him. This is why someone who does not act upon his knowledge is described as ignorant and lacking knowledge.

Allah Most High said:

“Allah only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterwards.”

Abū al-ʿĀliyah said:

---

## Page 3574

“I asked the Companions of Muhammad about this verse, and they told me: ‘Everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant, and everyone who repents before death has repented soon afterwards.’”

Another example is the statement of Ibn Masʿūd: “To fear Allah is knowledge enough, and to be deluded about Allah is ignorance enough.” Al-Shaʿbī was once addressed as “O scholar!” He replied: “The scholar is one who fears Allah.” Allah Most High has said:

“Of all His servants, only those with knowledge fear Allah.”

Abū Hayyān al-Taymī said: “Scholars are of three kinds: one who knows Allah and His commands; one who knows Allah but does not know His commands; and one who knows His commands but does not know Allah. The one who knows Allah is he who fears Him, and the one who knows Allah’s commands is he who knows His limits and prescribed duties.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Of all His servants, only those with knowledge fear Allah.”

This indicates that everyone who fears Allah possesses knowledge, which is true. It does not indicate that everyone who possesses knowledge fears Him. However, since knowledge of Him necessarily produces fear when nothing counteracts it, the absence of that fear indicates weakness in the underlying knowledge: were that knowledge strong, it would overcome whatever counteracts it.

Likewise, the word “intellect” may refer to the innate faculty through which one acquires knowledge, to various kinds of knowledge, or to acting as that knowledge requires. Similarly, the word “ignorance” may express either the absence of knowledge or the failure to act as knowledge requires. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you is fasting, let him neither speak obscenely nor behave foolishly. If someone insults him or fights him, let him say: ‘I am a man who is fasting.’”

Here, ignorance means wrongful speech, akin to compound ignorance. Another example is the poet’s saying:

Let no one act foolishly toward us—
Or we shall outdo the foolish in their folly.

---

## Page 3575

It is in this sense that jāhiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) received its name: it involves either a lack of knowledge or a failure to act upon it. Another example is the Prophet’s saying to Abū Dharr, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he exchanged insults with a man and taunted him about his mother: “You are a man who still has a trait of pre-Islamic ignorance.” Allah Most High has also said:

“When those who disbelieved harboured pride in their hearts—the pride of the Age of Ignorance.”

Anger and pride drive a person to do what harms him and abandon what benefits him. This is ignorance in the sense of acting contrary to knowledge: a person may go so far as to do what he knows will harm him and abandon what he knows will benefit him, because of the hatred and hostility he harbours towards certain people and actions. In this state, he is not entirely devoid of knowledge and assent to the truth. Rather, because of the hatred and envy within him, their demands overpower the dictates of knowledge. The absence of the effects and conduct that knowledge should produce thus indicates its weakness.

Yet this effect and outcome do not arise from knowledge alone, but from knowledge together with the soul’s love of what benefits it and hatred of what harms it. If the soul contracts a disease that corrupts it, it comes to love what harms it and hate what benefits it. It then becomes like a sick person who consumes something harmful because he craves it, despite knowing that it harms him.

I say: This is the meaning of the report attributed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah loves penetrating insight when doubts arise, and He loves sound reason when desires assail.”

Al-Bayhaqī related it as a mursal report (one attributed directly to the Prophet by a Successor). Allah Most High has said:

“And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men of strength and insight.”

He thus described them as possessing strength in action and insight in knowledge. The foundation of strength is strength of heart, which gives rise to love of good and hatred of evil. The believer’s strength lies in his heart and his weakness in his body, whereas the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body and his weakness in his heart. Thus, faith must

---

## Page 3576

contain these two foundations: affirmation of the truth and love for it. The former is the foundation of speech, and the latter the foundation of action. Perfect love, when accompanied by ability, necessarily entails bodily activity in the form of outward speech and action, as explained above. Whoever regards knowledge and affirmation alone as necessarily producing everything encompassed by the term faith, and everything called faith, is mistaken. Rather, both knowledge and love are essential.

Knowledge is a prerequisite for loving the beloved, just as life is a prerequisite for knowledge. Yet knowing something and affirming its existence do not necessarily entail loving it, unless there is something within the lover that draws him to what he knows and gives him reason to love it. Thus, a person affirms the existence of many things and knows them while hating them. For example, he affirms the existence of devils and disbelievers while hating them. Merely affirming something’s existence does not entail loving it.

Allah, glorified is He, however, deserves in Himself to be loved and worshipped, and His Messenger deserves to be loved for His sake. Hearts possess an innate disposition that calls for loving and obeying Him, just as they possess a disposition that calls for knowing Him and affirming belief in Him. Whoever affirms belief in Him and His Messenger but does not love Him and His Messenger is not a believer until, alongside that affirmation, he also possesses love for Him and His Messenger.

When affirmation of belief in Him and love for Him are established in the heart, the body must necessarily respond with the outward words and deeds that they entail. The words and deeds manifested by the body are the necessary consequence of what is in the heart, its evidence and its effect. Likewise, the body’s words and deeds also influence what is in the heart. Each thus influences the other, but the heart is the root, and the body its branch. The branch draws sustenance from its root, while the root is strengthened and made firm by its branch. This is like the tree used as a parable for the declaration of faith. He says:

---

## Page 3577

exalted is He:

“Allah sets forth a parable: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly established and whose branches reach into the sky. It yields its fruit at all times by its Lord’s permission.”

This is the declaration of Allah’s oneness. The stronger, more deeply rooted, and better watered a tree’s root becomes, the stronger its branches become. Likewise, when its branches are nourished by rain and wind, this affects its root. The same applies to “faith” in the heart and “Islam” as outwardly manifested. Since outward words and deeds both necessarily follow from and necessarily imply inward words and deeds, the former serve as evidence of the latter, as in His saying, exalted is He:

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsfolk. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

He thus states that those who believe in Allah and the Last Day will not be found showing affection for the enemies of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, faith itself is incompatible with affection for them. If such affection arises, it indicates a deficiency in faith. Likewise, He says:

“You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies. Evil indeed is what their souls have sent ahead for them: Allah is angry with them, and they will abide in the punishment forever.”

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

Likewise, He says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He, exalted is He, thus states that these are the ones who are truthful when they say, “We believe.” This indicates that, among those who say, “We believe,” some are truthful and others are lying. The one who lies has hypocrisy in proportion to his lying.

Allah, exalted is He, says concerning the hypocrites:

---

## Page 3578

“Among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ yet they are not believers.”

—through to His saying—

“They will have a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

There are two well-known readings of yakdhibūn (“they lie”). A hadith states:

“The foundation upon which hypocrisy is built is lying.”

Allah, exalted is He, says:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

He, exalted is He, also says:

“Among them are those who pledged to Allah, ‘If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous.’ But when He gave them of His bounty, they became miserly with it and turned away in aversion. So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they broke their promise to Allah and because they used to lie.”

He also says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the charitable alms.”

There are many similar passages.

In short, no one who reflects on what he is saying can doubt that a man does not become a believer merely through assent in his heart while hating Allah and His Messenger, arrogantly refusing to worship Him, and showing hostility towards Him and His Messenger. For this reason, the great majority of the Murji’ah held that the actions of the heart are included in faith, as reported by writers on sectarian doctrines. Among them is al-Ash‘arī, who said in his book, Maqālāt (Doctrinal Views):

“The Murji’ah disagreed over what faith is, dividing into twelve groups. The first group claims that faith in Allah consists solely of knowing Allah, His Messenger, and everything that has come from Allah. Anything other than this knowledge—verbal profession, submission of the heart, love for Allah and His Messenger, reverence for them both, fear, and bodily deeds—is not faith. They claimed that disbelief in Allah consists of ignorance of Him. This is a view attributed to al-Jahm

---

## Page 3579

ibn Safwān.” He said:

“The Jahmiyyah claimed that if a person attains knowledge and then denies it verbally, he does not become a disbeliever through that denial; that faith is indivisible and those who possess it do not differ in their degree of faith; and that faith and disbelief exist only in the heart, not in the bodily limbs.”

He said:

“The second group of the Murji’ah claim that faith consists solely of knowing Allah, and disbelief consists solely of ignorance of Him. Thus, faith in Allah is nothing but knowledge of Him, and disbelief in Allah is nothing but ignorance of Him. They maintain that saying, ‘Allah is the third of three,’ is not itself disbelief, but that such a statement can come only from a disbeliever. This is because Allah has declared whoever says it a disbeliever, and the Muslims unanimously agree that only a disbeliever would say it. They claimed that knowing Allah is loving Him and submitting to Him.

“Those who hold this view do not claim that faith in Allah is itself faith in the Messenger. Yet they say that no one believes in Allah unless he believes in the Messenger—not because believing in Allah without believing in the Messenger is impossible, but because the Messenger said:

‘Whoever does not believe in me does not believe in Allah.’

“They also claimed that prayer is not worship of Allah, and that the only worship is faith in Him, which consists of knowing Him. According to them, faith neither increases nor decreases, but is a single quality; the same applies to disbelief. The proponent of this view is Abū al-Husayn al-Sālihī.”

Al-Ash‘arī mentioned this view of al-Sālihī, along with other views, in his book al-Mūjaz (The Compendium), then said:

“With regard to names, I adopt al-Sālihī’s view. As for general and specific application, I do not determine conclusively from the apparent wording of a report that it is general or specific when the language allows either possibility. I suspend judgment on this and do not affirm either general or specific application without revealed guidance or consensus.”

He then said in al-Maqālāt:

“The third group of the Murji’ah claim that faith consists of knowing Allah

---

## Page 3580

, submitting to Him—which means refraining from arrogance toward Him—and loving Allah. Whoever possesses all these qualities is a believer. They claimed that Iblīs knew Allah but became a disbeliever through his arrogance toward Allah. This is the view of some followers of Yūnus al-Samarī.

“The fourth group, the followers of Abū Shimr and Yūnus, claim that faith consists of knowing Allah, loving Him, submitting to Him in one’s heart, and affirming that He is One and that nothing is like Him, so long as the proof brought by the prophets has not been established against a person. If the proof brought by the prophets has been established against him, faith entails acknowledging them and affirming their truthfulness; knowing what they have conveyed from Allah is included in faith.

“They do not call any individual quality among these either faith or part of faith until all these qualities come together. Once they come together, they call them faith because they are combined. They liken this to whiteness in an animal: they do not call it piebald unless black is also present. They regard the abandonment of any one of these qualities as disbelief, and do not regard faith as divisible or capable of increasing or decreasing.”

He reported that the fifth group, the followers of Abū Thawbān, hold that faith consists of acknowledging Allah and His messengers, as well as whatever reason holds it necessary to do.

He reported that the sixth group hold that faith consists of knowing Allah, His messengers, and the obligations He has prescribed upon which there is consensus; submitting to Him in all of this; and verbal affirmation. They claimed that each of the qualities of faith is an act of obedience, but that any one of them, if performed without the others, is not an act of obedience—as with knowledge without affirmation. They also held that abandoning any one of these qualities is an act of disobedience, and that a person does not become a disbeliever

---

## Page 3581

by abandoning any single quality; that people differ in their faith, some having greater knowledge and stronger affirmation of Him than others; and that faith increases but does not decrease. This is the view of al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Najjār and his followers.

The seventh group, the Ghaylāniyyah, the followers of Ghaylān, claim that faith consists of the second knowledge of Allah, love, submission, and acknowledgment of what the Messenger brought and what came from Allah. This is because, according to him, the initial knowledge arises necessarily, so he did not count it as part of faith. All those whose views we have related—the Shimriyyah, Jahmiyyah, Ghaylāniyyah, and Najjāriyyah—deny that disbelievers possess faith or that they may be said to possess some faith, since, in their view, faith is indivisible.

He said: “The eighth group among the Murjiʾah, the followers of Muhammad ibn Shabīb, claim that faith consists of acknowledging Allah and knowing that He is One and that nothing is like Him; acknowledging and knowing His prophets and messengers and everything they brought from Allah that Muslims have expressly affirmed and transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as prayer, fasting, and similar matters over which they have no disagreement; and submitting to Allah, which means refraining from arrogance toward Him.

“They claimed that Iblīs knew Allah and acknowledged Him, and that he was a disbeliever only because he was arrogant; were it not for his arrogance, he would not have been a disbeliever. They also held that faith is divisible and that its adherents differ in degree; that a particular quality of faith may be an act of obedience and constitute part of faith, while the person possessing it is a disbeliever because he has abandoned another part of faith; and that a person is not a believer unless he possesses all of it. Every man who knows that Allah is One and has no equal

---

## Page 3582

but denies the prophets is a disbeliever because of his denial of the prophets, yet possesses one quality of faith: his knowledge of Allah, glorified be He.

The ninth group of the Murjiʾah consists of those who affiliate themselves with Abū Hanīfah and his followers. They claim that faith consists of knowing Allah and the Messenger, and acknowledging what has come from Allah in general, without detailed specification.

The tenth group of the Murjiʾah consists of the followers of Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī. They claim that faith consists of avoiding the gravest major sins. It is a designation for qualities whose abandonment, whether altogether or individually, renders a person a disbeliever. Thus, any quality whose abandonment constitutes disbelief is faith. As for any act of obedience whose omission is not unanimously held by Muslims to constitute disbelief, it is one of the ordinances of faith. If that act is obligatory, the person who abandons it is described as committing sinful conduct: one says that he acts sinfully, but does not label him a sinner. Major sins do not exclude a person from faith, provided they do not constitute disbelief.

Whoever abandons obligations such as prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage out of denial, rejection, or contempt for them is a disbeliever in Allah. His disbelief is due to that contempt, rejection, and denial. But if he abandons them without considering their abandonment lawful, being distracted and procrastinating, saying, “I will pray shortly, when I have finished my amusement and my work,” he is not a disbeliever, even if he prays on a given day and at one of the prayer times. Nevertheless, we deem him guilty of sinful conduct.

Abū Muʿādh used to say: “Whoever kills or slaps a prophet becomes a disbeliever. His disbelief is not because of the slap itself, but because of his contempt, hostility, and hatred toward him.”

---

## Page 3583

The eleventh group of the Murjiʾah consists of the followers of Bishr al-Marīsī. They say that faith is assent, because faith in the linguistic sense means assent, and whatever is not assent is not faith. Bishr claims that assent involves both the heart and the tongue. Ibn al-Rāwandī also held this view. Ibn al-Rāwandī claimed that disbelief consists of denial, rejection, concealment, and covering; nothing can constitute disbelief unless it is disbelief in the linguistic sense, and nothing can constitute faith unless it is faith in the linguistic sense. He claimed that prostrating to the sun is not disbelief, nor is prostrating to anything other than Allah disbelief. Rather, it is a sign of disbelief, because Allah has made clear that only a disbeliever prostrates to the sun.

He said: “The twelfth group of the Murjiʾah is the Karrāmiyyah, the followers of Muhammad ibn Karrām. They claim that faith consists of acknowledgement and assent with the tongue, without the heart. They deny that knowledge in the heart, or anything other than verbal assent, constitutes faith.”

Most of these views that al-Ashʿarī reported from the Murjiʾah imply that, according to them, faith necessarily includes some actions of the heart. Only a small minority disputed this, such as Jahm and al-Sālihī.

In al-Maqālāt, he also presented a summary of the position of the adherents of hadith and the people of the Sunnah. He said:

“In summary, the adherents of hadith and the people of the Sunnah affirm Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, what has come from Allah, and what trustworthy narrators have transmitted from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They reject none of this. They affirm that Allah is one God, unique, the Self-Sufficient, who has taken no consort

nor a child, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger; that Paradise is real and Hell is real; that the Hour is coming, beyond any doubt; that Allah will resurrect those in the graves; and that Allah is above His Throne, as He said:

They affirm that He has two hands, without specifying how, as He said:

And as He said:

## Page 3585

of their views, we affirm the same and adhere to it.”

This is his position in this book, in which he agreed with Ahl al-Sunnah and the adherents of hadith, contrary to the position he defended in al-Mūjaz. The point here is that most groups within the Muslim community include acts of the heart within faith. Even most groups among the Murjiʾah affirm this. As for the Muʿtazilah, the Khawārij, Ahl al-Sunnah, and the adherents of hadith, their position on this is well known. Only those Murjiʾah who followed Jahm ibn Safwān disputed it. This position is anomalous, just as the position of the Karrāmiyyah, who say that faith consists merely of verbal profession, is also anomalous.

This, too, deserves careful attention. Many who discuss “the question of faith”—whether deeds are included in it and whether it consists of speech and action—suppose that the disagreement concerns only bodily deeds, and that “speech” means verbal profession. This is mistaken. By Muslim consensus, mere verbal profession without inward belief does not constitute faith. Nor, according to Muslims generally, does inward assent alone constitute faith, apart from certain outliers among the followers of Jahm and al-Sālihī. Their position involves greater intellectual sophistry and more serious conflict with religious rulings than Ibn Karrām’s position does, except in the case of certain outliers among Ibn Karrām’s followers.

Likewise, the heart’s assent, when unaccompanied by love or reverence for Allah, but instead accompanied by hatred and hostility towards Allah and His messengers, is not faith by Muslim consensus.

Ibn Karrām’s position differs in designation, not in judgment. Although he calls the hypocrites believers, he says that they will remain in the Fire eternally. Thus, he differs from the Muslim community in designation, not in judgment, whereas the followers of Jahm differ in both designation and judgment.

---

## Page 3586

Section

Once it is understood that faith is rooted in the heart, the term “faith” sometimes refers to the heart’s inward affirmations and acts, such as assent, love, reverence, and the like. Outward words and deeds are then its necessary consequences, effects, and signs. At other times, it refers to what is in both the heart and the body, thus including what faith entails and requires within the meaning of the term. This makes clear that outward deeds are called Islam, and that they sometimes fall within the meaning of faith and sometimes do not.

This is because the meaning of a single term varies according to whether it is used alone or alongside another term. Used alone, it may encompass two meanings; when paired with another term, it may denote only one of them. For example, when either “the poor” or “the needy” is used alone, it includes the other; when the two are mentioned together, each denotes a distinct category. Likewise, when “what is right” and “what is wrong” are used without qualification, as in the words of the Most High:

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong,”

this includes immorality and transgression. But when “what is wrong” is mentioned alongside either one of these, as in His words:

“Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing,”

or alongside both, as in the words of the Most High:

“And He forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and transgression,”

then, according to one view, “wrongdoing” is restricted to what falls outside those other categories; according to another, it encompasses them all—depending on

---

## Page 3587

whether conjoining a specific term to a general term prevents the general term from encompassing it, or whether it is thereby mentioned twice—a disputed question. Outward words and deeds are the result and necessary consequence of inward acts.

When the term “faith” is used alone, it may encompass both, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

In this case, Islam falls within the meaning of faith and forms part of it. Thus, “faith” is said to encompass all inward and outward acts of obedience. Another example is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, to the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? To testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakah, to fast Ramadan, and to pay one-fifth of the spoils.”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. Here he explained faith in the same terms with which he explained Islam, because by the two testimonies he meant bearing witness to them both inwardly and outwardly. He was addressing the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays, who were among the best of people. They were the first to hold Friday prayer in their own locality after the people of Medina, as Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The first Friday prayer held in Islam after the Friday prayer in Medina was at Jawāthā, a village in Bahrain.”

They said:

“O Messenger of Allah, between us and you lies this tribe of the unbelievers of Mudar, and we can reach you only during a sacred month. So give us clear, decisive instructions that we may follow and call those we have left behind to follow.”

By this they meant the people of Najd—Tamīm, Asad, Ghatafān, and others—who were unbelievers. These people were sincere and eager to learn the religion, so when the Prophet commanded them

---

## Page 3588

—peace and blessings be upon him—to utter words and perform deeds outwardly, they did so both inwardly and outwardly, and were believers by virtue of them.

When, however, faith is mentioned alongside Islam, faith is in the heart, while Islam is outward, as reported in al-Musnad from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart. Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

Whenever a person attains this faith, it necessarily follows that he also attains Islam: the two testimonies of faith, prayer, zakah, fasting, and Hajj. His belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers entails surrender and submission to Allah. It is impossible for acknowledgment, love, and submission to exist inwardly without being expressed outwardly when one is able to do so, just as firm resolve, coupled with the ability to act, cannot exist without the intended act taking place.

From this, you can understand that someone whose heart has firm faith cannot fail to utter the two testimonies when able to do so. Failure to utter them despite having the ability necessarily entails the absence of complete faith in the heart. This reveals the error of Jahm and his followers in claiming that mere faith, without outward faith, benefits a person in the Hereafter. This is impossible, for complete faith cannot exist in the heart without its necessary consequences appearing outwardly, according to one’s ability. It is impossible for someone to love another with firm love, be able to maintain ties with him, and yet make no outward move toward doing so.

Abū Tālib’s love for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was only because of his kinship with him, not for Allah’s sake; he only

---

## Page 3589

supported and defended him out of loyalty to lineage and kinship. This is why Allah did not accept that from him. Had it stemmed from faith in his heart, he would necessarily have uttered the two testimonies. The very motive that led him to support the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him—family loyalty—also led him to refuse to utter the two testimonies, unlike Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and others like him. Allah Most High says:

“But the most righteous will be kept away from it—the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay anyone for a favor, but only seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be pleased.”

Errors in these matters arise in several ways:

(First) The belief that knowledge and assent necessarily entail everything that faith requires.

(Second) The assumption that people do not differ in what is within their hearts.

(Third) The assumption that acceptable faith can exist in the heart without outward speech and outward action.

(Fourth) The assumption that there is nothing in the heart but assent, and nothing outward but the actions of the limbs. The correct understanding is that the heart has actions alongside assent, while what is outward comprises both speech and action; both necessarily entail what is inward.

The Murjiʾah excluded outward action from faith. Those among them who also intended to exclude the actions of the heart, treating them as nothing more than assent, are plainly astray. As for those who intended to exclude outward action, they are told: outward action necessarily accompanies inward action and cannot be separated from it; the absence of what is outward is evidence of the absence of what is inward.

---

## Page 3590

Thus, the remaining dispute concerns whether outward action is part of what the term “faith” denotes, conveyed by inclusion within its meaning, or a necessary concomitant of what it denotes.

The precise answer is that outward action is sometimes included within the term and sometimes necessarily accompanies what it denotes, depending on whether the term is used alone or alongside another term. When faith is mentioned alongside Islam, what “Islam” denotes falls outside the meaning of “faith,” as in the hadith of Gabriel, although it necessarily accompanies it. Likewise, when faith is mentioned alongside deeds, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,”

one may say that deeds are not included within the term “faith,” although they necessarily accompany it. Alternatively, one may say that they are included, and that their separate mention joins the particular to the general. In either case, deeds give practical expression to what faith denotes and confirm it. For this reason, a group of scholars—including Shaykh Abū Ismā'īl al-Ansārī? and others—said: Faith consists entirely of affirmation: the heart affirms what the messengers brought, the tongue confirms what is in the heart, and deeds confirm speech, as when one says, “His deeds confirmed his words.” Another example is the Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“The eyes commit fornication, and their fornication is looking; the ears commit fornication, and their fornication is listening; the hand commits fornication, and its fornication is grasping; the foot commits fornication, and its fornication is walking. The heart wishes and desires, and the private parts confirm this or belie it.”

Affirmation applies both to reports and to intent. Thus, one says, “So-and-so is sincere in his resolve,” “sincere in his love,” and “They launched a resolute charge.”

The early generations strongly condemned the Murji'ah when they excluded deeds from faith and said that people are alike in faith. There is no doubt that their claim that people’s faith is equal

---

## Page 3591

is among the gravest errors. People are not equal in affirmation, love, reverent fear, or knowledge; rather, they differ in degree in many respects.

Moreover, their exclusion of deeds suggests that they have also excluded deeds of the heart, and this is unquestionably false. Someone who affirms the Messenger’s truthfulness yet hates him and opposes him in heart and deed is unquestionably a disbeliever, as is self-evident. If, however, they include deeds of the heart within faith, they are still mistaken, since faith cannot exist in the heart without any bodily action.

The purpose here is not to enumerate every particular act. Rather, consider someone who believes in Allah and His Messenger in his heart: if he sees the Messenger and his enemies fighting him, and can watch them and urge others to support the Messenger without suffering harm, can it ordinarily be conceived that he would make no move whatsoever to support the Messenger? It is well known that this is impossible. Thus, jihad that is incumbent upon a person, according to his ability, is part of faith, and its absence is evidence that the reality of faith is absent. Indeed, it is authentically reported from him:

“Whoever dies without having fought or contemplated fighting dies with a trait of hypocrisy.”

This hadith indicates that a person may possess some traits of hypocrisy alongside the faith he has. Also relevant are the words of Allah Most High:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

Furthermore, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

---

## Page 3592

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then with his heart. That is the weakest level of faith.” In another narration: “Beyond that there is not a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

This makes clear that if the heart has no hatred for the evils that Allah hates, it is devoid of faith. Hatred and love are deeds of the heart. It is well known that Iblīs and those like him know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden these things, yet they do not hate them. Rather, they call others to what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Furthermore, those who follow the view of Jahm and al-Sālihī have explicitly stated that reviling Allah and His Messenger, professing the Trinity, and uttering any words of disbelief do not constitute inward disbelief, but are merely outward evidence of disbelief. They hold that someone who reviles and insults in this way may nevertheless inwardly know Allah, affirm His oneness, and believe in Him. When they are confronted with proof from a scriptural text or scholarly consensus that such a person is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly, they say: “This implies that such conduct necessarily entails inward denial, and that faith necessarily excludes it.”

They should be told: We have two established facts. (The first) is necessarily known from the religion, and (the second) is necessarily known from reflection on our own selves. As for the first, we know that anyone who willingly reviles Allah and His Messenger without compulsion—indeed, anyone who willingly utters words of disbelief without being compelled, or mocks Allah, His verses, and His Messenger—is

---

## Page 3593

a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly, and that anyone who says, “Such a person may inwardly be a believer in Allah and be a disbeliever only outwardly,” has made a claim whose falsity is necessarily known from the religion.

Allah has mentioned the disbelievers’ statements in the Quran and, on account of them, declared them disbelievers deserving of the threatened punishment. If their statements of disbelief were merely like witnesses’ testimony against them, or like an admission in which the person making it is mistaken, Allah would not have deemed them deserving of the threatened punishment on the basis of testimony that might be true or false. Rather, He would have punished them only on condition that the testimony was true. Examples include His words, Most High:

“Those who say, ‘Allah is the third of three,’ have certainly disbelieved.”

“Those who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,’ have certainly disbelieved.”

And there are other such passages.

As for the second established fact: if a person believes in his heart that the Messenger is truthful and that he is Allah’s Messenger, and loves and reveres him, it is impossible for him, while in that state, to curse and revile him. Such conduct is inconceivable without some measure of disregard for him and his sanctity. It is therefore clear that merely believing him to be truthful does not constitute faith unless accompanied by love and reverence for him in the heart.

Furthermore, Allah, glorified is He, says:

“Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in jibt and tāghūt?”

And He says:

“Whoever rejects tāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the firmest handhold.”

This makes clear that tāghūt can be believed in or rejected. It is well known that believers and disbelievers alike may affirm its existence and the attributes it possesses. Both believers and disbelievers know the nature of idols, Satan, and magic.

Allah, Most High, has said concerning magic:

“Until they both say, ‘We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.’ Yet they learn

---

## Page 3594

from them that by which they cause division between a man and his wife,” up to His words:

“And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter.”

Those who followed what the devils recited during Solomon’s reign and cast Allah’s Book behind their backs as though they did not know, know that they will have no share in the Hereafter; yet they disbelieve nonetheless.

Likewise, if someone who believes in jibt and tāghūt knows how magic causes division between a man and his wife and other such effects of jibt, and knows the nature of Satan and the idols and the trials they bring about, that knowledge does not constitute his belief in them. It is well known that no one believed that they create things, do whatever they will, or possess other attributes exclusive to lordship. Rather, people believed that worshipping them would secure some of the things they sought. Thus, devils would speak to them from within the idols and inform them of certain matters. Similar things occur in these times with the idols worshipped by the people of India and China, the Turks, and others.

Their disbelief on account of these idols consisted in submitting to them, supplicating to them, worshipping them, taking them as intermediaries, and the like—not simply acknowledging the effects that occur in connection with such practices. A knowledgeable believer knows of these effects and acknowledges their existence, but he also knows the harm that follows in this world and the Hereafter, and therefore hates such practices. A disbeliever may also know that this harm exists, but his love of the present life drives him to disbelief.

This is made clear by His words:

“Those who disbelieve in Allah after having believed—not those who are compelled while their hearts remain firm in faith, but those who open their hearts to disbelief—will incur Allah’s wrath and have a tremendous punishment.”

---

## Page 3595

“That is because they preferred the life of this world to the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.”

“Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing, and sight Allah has sealed, and it is they who are heedless.”

“Without doubt, they will be the losers in the Hereafter.”

Allah Most High mentions those who disbelieve in Him after having believed and the punishment He threatens them with in the Hereafter. He then says:

“That is because they preferred the life of this world to the Hereafter.”

He thus makes clear that this is why they deserved the threatened punishment. It is well known that affirmation and denial, knowledge and ignorance, belong to a different category from love and hatred. These people say that they deserved the threatened punishment only because affirmation and faith had departed from their hearts, even if this departure may have resulted from preferring the present life to the Hereafter. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, identifies this preference for the present life over the Hereafter as the fundamental cause of their loss. Such a preference may coexist with knowing and affirming that disbelief brings harm in the Hereafter and that one will have no share therein.

Furthermore, He, glorified is He, exempted those compelled from being counted among the disbelievers. If disbelief could only consist in the heart’s denial and ignorance, He would not have made an exception for those compelled, since it is impossible to compel the heart to deny or be ignorant. It is therefore clear that uttering words of disbelief constitutes disbelief, except under compulsion.

As for His words, Most High:

“But those who open their hearts to disbelief”—

that is, because they prefer the present life to the Hereafter. The Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also illustrate this:

“A man will be a believer in the morning and a disbeliever by evening, and a believer in the evening and a disbeliever by morning, selling his religion for some worldly gain.”

The verse was revealed concerning ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, Bilāl ibn Rabāh, and others like them among the believers

---

## Page 3596

who were oppressed, when the polytheists compelled them to revile the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and utter similar words of disbelief. Some complied verbally, like ‘Ammār, while others endured the ordeal, like Bilāl. None of them was compelled to change his inner convictions; rather, they were compelled to speak. Whoever uttered such words without coercion did so only with his heart open to them.

Furthermore, “A group of Jews came to the Prophet and said, ‘We testify that you are indeed a messenger.’ They did not thereby become Muslims, because they said this merely to report what they held within themselves—that is, ‘We know and are certain that you are the Messenger of Allah.’ He said, ‘Why, then, do you not follow me?’ They replied, ‘We fear the Jews.’”

Thus, mere knowledge and reporting that knowledge do not constitute faith. One must profess faith as a declaration entailing commitment and submission, while also expressing one’s inner conviction. The hypocrites made a false assertion and were therefore disbelievers inwardly. These people uttered it without commitment or submission and were therefore disbelievers both outwardly and inwardly.

Likewise, it is widely reported that Abū Tālib knew that Muhammad was a prophet. The following verse is attributed to him:

“I know indeed that Muhammad’s religion
Is among the finest religions of mankind.”

Yet he refused to acknowledge Allah’s oneness and Muhammad’s prophethood out of love for his forefathers’ religion and aversion to being reproached by his people. His inward knowledge was not accompanied by the love and submission that exclude their opposites—love of falsehood and aversion to the truth—and so he was not a believer.

---

## Page 3597

As for Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, and others like them, the disbelief, desire for supremacy, and envy within them prevented them from loving Allah and worshipping Him in their hearts, without which faith cannot be complete. Their hearts harboured such aversion to Allah’s pleasure and pursuit of what angered Him as constituted disbelief, against which knowledge was of no avail.

Section

Faith varies in degree, increasing and decreasing, in several respects:

(The first)

Outward deeds: people differ in these, and their deeds increase and decrease. There is agreement that these admit of increase and decrease; the disagreement concerns whether they fall within the meaning of faith. Those who deny their inclusion say that they are the fruits of faith and what it entails, and are therefore included in it figuratively on that account. This is what they mean by faith increasing and decreasing: its fruits increase and decrease.

The response is that, as explained above, these deeds are necessary consequences of faith and are entailed by it. It is impossible for complete faith to exist in the heart without any outward speech or action. As for whether deeds are a necessary consequence of faith or a part of it, this varies according to whether the term “faith” is used on its own or alongside the terms “Islam” and “deeds,” as explained above. As for their claim that the increase concerns outward deeds, not what gives rise to and entails them, this is mistaken,

---

## Page 3598

for if the effects and consequences of things differ in degree, this entails that the things themselves differ in degree. Otherwise, identical determining causes would necessarily produce identical effects and consequences. Thus, differences in people’s outward deeds entail differences in what gives rise to and necessitates those deeds. This makes clear:

(The second)

The second respect in which faith increases and decreases is the increase and decrease of the deeds of the heart. Every believer knows from direct experience that people differ in their love for Allah and His Messenger, their fear of Allah, their turning to Him, their reliance upon Him, and their sincerity towards Him. They also differ in how free their hearts are from showing off, arrogance, self-admiration, and similar traits, and in their compassion for others, their sincere concern for them, and other qualities of faith.

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for Allah’s sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has saved him from it as much as he hates to be cast into the Fire.”

Allah Most High says:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your clan”

up to His words:

“are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Allah, I fear Allah more than any of you and know His prescribed limits best.”

He also said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father, and all people.”

“ʿUmar said to him, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than everything except myself.’ He replied, ‘No, ʿUmar—not until I am dearer to you than your own self.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Then you are indeed dearer to me than my own self.’ He replied, ‘Now, ʿUmar.’”

## Page 3599

These hadiths and others like them are found in the authentic collections, and they show that love and reverent fear vary in degree. Allah Most High says:

“Those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

This is something a person experiences within himself: he may love the same thing more at one time than at another, and fear it more at one time than at another. Hence, people of knowledge are among those who most emphatically affirm that faith increases and decreases, because they experience this within themselves. Another example is His saying, Most High:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but it increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

What increased in them was tranquility and calm. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believers most complete in faith are those with the best character.”

(The third respect)

The assent and knowledge within the heart vary in degree according to whether they are general or detailed. The assent of someone who believes the Messenger in general, without knowing the details of what he conveyed, is not like that of someone who knows what he conveyed about Allah, His names and attributes, Paradise, Hell, and the nations, and believes him concerning all of this. Nor is someone who commits himself to obeying him in general, but dies before learning the details of what he commanded, like someone who lives long enough to learn those details and obey him in them.

(The fourth respect)

Knowledge and assent themselves vary in degree, just as the other attributes of a living being—ability, will, hearing, sight, and speech—vary in degree. Indeed, so do all accidental properties, such as motion, blackness, whiteness, and the like. If the ability to do something varies in degree, then reporting about it likewise varies in degree. And if someone says, “Knowledge of a thing

---

## Page 3600

does not vary in degree,” this is tantamount to saying, “The ability to do one and the same thing does not vary in degree,” or, “Seeing one and the same thing does not vary in degree.” Yet it is well known that people differ in how clearly they see the same crescent moon. Likewise, they differ in their perception of the same sound. Two people may utter the same word yet differ in how they pronounce it. They may likewise differ in their perception of the smell or taste of the same thing.

There is no attribute of a living being, no form of its perception or movement—indeed, no attribute even of things other than living beings—that does not admit differences of degree beyond human reckoning. Thus, it may be said: no created being knows anything in every respect as Allah knows it. Rather, Allah’s knowledge of a thing is more perfect than anyone else’s knowledge of it, however the matter is conceived. The difference between these two kinds of knowledge is not merely that one has a beginning while the other is eternal; they differ in other respects as well.

A person experiences within himself varying degrees of knowledge of the same object, just as he experiences varying degrees in hearing the same sound, seeing the same object, exercising his ability to do the same thing, loving what he loves, hating what he hates, being pleased with what pleases him, being displeased with what displeases him, willing what he wills, and disliking what he dislikes. Whoever denies differences of degree in these realities is a sophist.

(The fifth respect)

These matters vary in degree because of the causes that give rise to them. Someone whose assent and love rest on evidence that produces certainty and exposes the falsity of an intervening doubt is not on the same footing as someone whose assent rests on lesser grounds. Indeed, someone granted immediate knowledge that he cannot dismiss from his mind is not on the same footing as someone who is confronted by

---

## Page 3601

doubts and seeks to dispel them through reflection and inquiry. No reasonable person doubts that knowledge attained through numerous strong proofs, recognition of the falsity of opposing doubts, and demonstration of the invalidity of the arguments advanced in their support is unlike knowledge obtained from a single proof without awareness of the doubts raised against it. For the stronger and more numerous a thing’s causes become, and the more its obstacles are removed and disappear, the more this ensures its perfection, strength, and completeness.

(The sixth respect)

These matters differ in degree according to their persistence and stability, and according to how consistently they are remembered and kept in mind, just as hatred arises through heedlessness of something and turning away from it. Knowledge, assent, love, reverence, and other such things within the heart are attributes, accidents, and states that endure and arise as their causes endure and arise. Although knowledge resides in the heart, heedlessness prevents it from being actively present. Someone who knows something but is heedless of it is at a lower level than someone who keeps it in mind.

ʿUmayr ibn Habīb al-Khatmī, one of the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Faith increases and decreases.” They asked, “How does it increase and decrease?” He replied, “When we praise Allah, remember Him, and glorify Him, that is its increase. When we become heedless, forget, and neglect our duties, that is its decrease.”

(The seventh respect)

It may be said that nothing within a human being admits greater differences and disparities of degree than faith. Whatever attributes or actions are affirmed despite their differences of degree, faith admits even greater differences. For example, a person knows from his own experience that the love within his heart varies in degree, whether it is love for his child or his wife

---

## Page 3602

or his position of authority, his homeland, his friend, a physical form, his horses, his garden, his gold, his silver, or any of his other possessions. Love begins with attachment, because the heart becomes attached to the beloved; then comes yearning, as the heart pours itself out toward the beloved; then consuming passion, which clings to the heart as a creditor clings to his debtor. It then becomes ardent love, until it reaches enslavement—meaning servitude; Taym Allāh means “servant of Allah.” The heart thus becomes a slave to the beloved, obedient and unable to depart from the beloved’s command. Many who are infatuated with physical forms have reached conditions well known to people: some have been driven to kill themselves and their beloved, or to disbelief and apostasy from Islam. Others have been driven to madness and the loss of reason, to abandoning such greatly cherished things as family, wealth, and authority, or to disease in their bodies and teeth.

Whoever says that love neither increases nor decreases has therefore made one of the most manifestly false claims. It is well known that people differ in their love for Allah more greatly than they differ in their love for anything else. He, glorified is He, took Abraham as an intimate friend, and He also took Muhammad as an intimate friend, as is widely reported from him that he said:

“Were I to take an intimate friend from among the people of the earth, I would take Abū Bakr as an intimate friend. But your companion is Allah’s intimate friend.”

He meant himself, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He also said:

“Allah has taken me as an intimate friend just as He took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

Intimate friendship is more specific than love in general. The prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers love Allah, and Allah loves them, as He said:

“Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him,”

to the end of the verse. He, the Exalted, also said:

“But those who believe love Allah more intensely.”

Allah has stated that He loves those who are mindful of Him, loves those who act justly, loves those who continually repent, loves those who purify themselves, and loves
