## Page 3603

those who fight in His cause in ranks as though they were a firmly joined structure. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, expressed his love for several people, as recorded from him in the Sahīh concerning al-Hasan and Usāmah:

“O Allah, I love them both, so love them both, and love whoever loves them.”

‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās asked him, “Whom do you love most?”

He replied, “‘Ā’ishah.”

He asked, “And among men?”

He replied, “Her father.”

He also said:

“By Allah, I love you.”

People vary in their love for Allah, ranging from the best of creation, Muhammad and Abraham, to those of the lowest rank, such as someone whose heart contains an atom’s weight of faith. Only the Lord of the earth and the heavens can enumerate the degrees between these two extremes. No other kind of created beings differs in excellence as greatly as the descendants of Adam. A single horse, for example, cannot equal a million horses.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections, in a hadith narrated by Abū Dharr, that he was sitting with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when a man of high social standing passed by. The Prophet asked, “Abū Dharr, do you know this man?”

I replied, “Yes, Messenger of Allah. This is a man whose marriage proposal would likely be accepted, whose words would be heeded, and whose absence would prompt people to ask after him.”

Then a man of low standing among the Muslims passed by, and he asked, “Abū Dharr, do you know this man?”

I replied, “Yes, Messenger of Allah. This is a man of low standing. His marriage proposal would likely be rejected, his words would go unheeded, and his absence would not prompt anyone to ask after him.”

He said, “Abū Dharr, this man is better than an earth full of men like the other.”

Thus the truthful one, who never exaggerates in what he says, has told us that a single descendant of Adam

---

## Page 3604

can be better than an earth full of other human beings. If one of them is superior to the angels while another is worse than beasts, then the differences in excellence among them are greater than those among the angels. Their differing degrees of excellence are fundamentally determined by their knowledge and love of Allah. Thus, only Allah can encompass the extent of their differences in this regard. Whatever differences are known among them in their love for the things they cherish, their differences in love for Allah are greater.

The same applies to their differing degrees of fear of what they fear, and of humility and submission before whatever they humble themselves and submit to. They likewise differ in their knowledge of things, their belief in them, and their acknowledgment of them. If they differ in their knowledge of the angels and their attributes, and in their belief in them, then their differences in knowledge of Allah and His attributes, and in belief in Him, are greater.

Likewise, if they differ in their knowledge of the human soul and its attributes, and in their belief in it; or in their knowledge of the jinn and their attributes, and in their belief in them; or in their knowledge of the bliss and torment of the Hereafter—as reported, including food, drink, clothing, spouses, and dwellings—then their differences in knowledge of Allah and His attributes, and in belief in Him, are greater than their differences in knowledge of the “spirit,” which is the rational soul, and in knowledge of the bliss and torment of the Hereafter.

Indeed, if they differ in their knowledge of their own bodies, their attributes, their health and illness, and all that follows from this, then their differences in knowledge of Allah are greater still, far greater. For everything that is known and spoken of falls within the scope of knowing Allah, since everything that exists is His creation. All the attributes, names, measures, and actions found in created beings bear witness to and provide evidence for

---

## Page 3605

the Most Beautiful Names and sublime attributes of Allah, glory be to Him. For every perfection in created beings is an effect of His perfection; every perfection established for a created being is more fittingly attributed to the Creator; and every imperfection from which a created being is free is even more fittingly denied of the Creator. This holds according to the approach and terminology of every school.

Thus, one says, “The perfection of an effect derives from the perfection of its cause,” while another says, “The perfection of what is made and created derives from the perfection of its Maker and Creator.”

In the hadith narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad and by Ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No servant is afflicted by worry or sorrow and says, ‘O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant. My forelock is in Your hand. Your judgment concerning me takes effect, and Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You by every name belonging to You with which You have named Yourself, or which You have revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept exclusively with Yourself in Your knowledge of the unseen, to make the Quran the springtime of my heart, the light of my breast, the dispeller of my sorrow, and the remover of my worry and distress,’ without Allah removing his worry and sorrow and replacing them with joy. They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should we not learn these words?’ He replied, ‘Yes indeed. Whoever hears them should learn them.’”

In this hadith, he states that Allah has names which He has kept exclusively with Himself in His knowledge of the unseen. Allah’s names encompass His attributes; they are not mere proper names. Rather, His names—such as the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Most Merciful, the All-Wise, and others—each indicate meanings of His attributes that the other names do not indicate, while all share in denoting His Essence. And if there are names of His whose knowledge He has reserved for Himself, and names He has made known exclusively to

---

## Page 3606

whomever He wills among His servants, it follows that people differ more greatly in their knowledge of Him than in their knowledge of anything else they know.

This makes clear to you that those speculative theologians and rational thinkers who claim to have known Allah fully—such that none of His attributes remains unknown to them, and that whatever they do not know and have no evidence to establish is therefore nonexistent in reality—are mistaken, in error, innovators, and astray. Their argument is untenable. For the absence of conclusive or presumptive evidence for something is evidence of its nonexistence, unless it is known that its existence necessarily entails that evidence.

An example is something which, had it existed, people would have had ample interest and motivation to report. Such reporting would then be a necessary consequence of its existence, so the absence of that necessary consequence would establish the absence of what entails it. Thus, we know that if there were a great city like Baghdad or Cairo between Syria and the Hijaz, people would report its existence. If only one, two, or three people reported it, we would know that they were lying.

Likewise, we know that if anyone had claimed prophethood during the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as Musaylima, al-ʿAnsī, Tulayha, and Sajāh did, people would have reported his claim just as they reported theirs. Had anyone attempted to rival the Quran and produced something people thought comparable to it, that too would have been transmitted, just as the ‘Quran’ of Musaylima the Liar was transmitted, as were al-Fusūl wa-l-Ghāyāt by Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī and other compositions by those who attempted to rival it—even when these were absurdities that no rational person would consider comparable to it.

Accordingly, ordinary human habits and inclinations would provide an even stronger impetus and greater eagerness to transmit something displaying an apparent resemblance and equivalence to it, whether people loved it or hated it. This is something inherent in human nature.

---

## Page 3607

Likewise, it is known that if ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib had sought the caliphate during the reigns of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān and fought for it, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted what happened after them. Similarly, had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed ʿAlī to lead the people in prayer, they would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted his instruction to Abū Bakr and Abū Bakr’s leading the people in prayer. Had he designated ʿAlī as his successor to the caliphate, they would have transmitted that, just as they transmitted matters of lesser importance.

Indeed, it is likewise known that he and his Companions did not gather to listen to frame drums or handclapping, nor for dancing and pipe-playing. Likewise, he and they did not gather after the prayers to supplicate, raise their hands, and so forth; had he done so, they would have transmitted it. Similarly, it is known that he did not perform the noon, afternoon, and night prayers as four units while travelling. Had he sometimes prayed four units while travelling, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted his combining two prayers on some occasions.

Likewise, it is known that he did not perform the obligatory prayers alone, but rather performed them in congregation. Similarly, he and his Companions did not carry earth with them while travelling for dry ablution, offer funeral prayers every night for Muslims who died, or intend a devotional retreat whenever they entered a mosque to pray. Likewise, it is known that he did not offer a funeral prayer in absentia for anyone other than al-Najāshī.

Similarly, it is known that had he regularly recited an audible, prescribed qunūt supplication in the dawn prayer or any other prayer, people would have transmitted this—just as they transmitted his occasional qunūt, in which he supplicated for some people and against others. They would have had even stronger reason to transmit such a regular practice.

Likewise, when he shortened and combined the prayers at ʿArafah and Muzdalifah, had he instructed anyone praying behind him to complete his prayer in full or not to combine the prayers with him, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted matters of lesser importance.

---

## Page 3608

Likewise, it is known that he did not command women in his time who were menstruating for the first time to perform a ritual bath after one day and one night had elapsed; that he did not command his Companions to wash off semen that came into contact with their bodies or clothes; and that he did not prescribe any particular wording for marriage, sale, lease, or any other contract. When he performed the Farewell Pilgrimage, he did not perform an ʿumrah immediately afterward. When he departed from Minā for Mecca on the Day of Sacrifice, he did not first perform circumambulation and saʿy, then circumambulate a second time. There are many other such examples, too numerous to mention. Anyone who carefully examines the two Sahīh collections and other similarly authoritative works, and acquaints himself with the statements of the Companions, the Successors, and the esteemed imams who followed their path—in earlier and later times—will recognize the soundness of what we have presented in this discussion.

And (the point here) is that if the existence of what is indicated necessarily entails the existence of evidence for it, then the absence of that evidence is evidence of its nonexistence. But if it can exist while we remain unaware of the evidence establishing it, then our lack of knowledge of evidence for its existence is not evidence of its nonexistence. Thus, if we have no evidence indicating some of Allah’s names and attributes, this does not necessarily entail their nonexistence. Neither revelation nor reason indicates that we must know every name and attribute that belongs to Him, exalted is He. Indeed, the best of creation and the most knowledgeable of them about Allah said in an authentic hadith:

“I cannot enumerate Your praises; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

And in the authentic hadith concerning intercession:

“I shall fall down in prostration and praise my Lord with praises He will inspire me to utter, which I cannot now enumerate.”

If the best of creation cannot enumerate His praises, and does not now know the praises with which he will praise Him when prostrating to intercede, how could anyone else know all the praises of Allah

---

## Page 3609

and the praise offered to Him? All His most beautiful names form part of His praise and of what is said in praise of Him. Since this is so, the more thoroughly a person knows His names and attributes, the more thoroughly he knows Allah.

Indeed, the more a person knows the names and attributes of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the more he knows the Prophet. Someone who knows that he is a prophet is not like someone who knows that he is a messenger; someone who knows that he is a messenger is not like someone who knows that he is the last of the messengers; and someone who knows that he is the last of the messengers is not like someone who knows that he is the foremost of Adam’s descendants. Nor is someone who knows this like someone who knows the distinctions Allah has granted him: intercession, the Pool, the Praiseworthy Station, the religion, and his other virtues, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Not everyone who is unaware of one of his distinctive qualities is thereby a disbeliever. Indeed, many believers have never heard of many of his virtues and distinctive qualities. Likewise, not everyone who is unaware of some of Allah’s names and attributes is thereby a disbeliever, for many believers have never heard much of what His Messenger said in describing Him and reporting about Him.

These considerations and others like them demonstrate the varying degrees of faith within the heart. As for the differences between people in their outward words and deeds, these are plain to everyone. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 3610

Section

Once this is clear, and it is understood that faith in the heart—affirmation, love, and other such qualities—necessarily entails outward words and deeds, just as complete resolve, together with the ability to act, necessarily brings about what is intended, and that the faith required in the heart cannot exist without its necessary consequences becoming manifest, the “intellectual doubts” concerning this issue are dispelled. All that remains is a “verbal dispute”: are the necessary consequences of inward faith part of faith itself, included within its meaning, so that the term “faith” encompasses them through inclusion and its general scope? Or do they necessarily follow from faith as its effect and fruit, so that the term “faith” signifies them by necessary implication?

The “truth of the matter” is that the term “faith” is sometimes used in one sense and sometimes in the other, as explained previously. When faith is mentioned together with Islam or deeds, it denotes only what is inward. When mentioned on its own, however, it may encompass both the inward and the outward. In this way, the scriptural texts are reconciled.

Thus, in the statement:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is none worthy of worship but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

The term “faith” is mentioned on its own, so it includes both the inward and the outward. As for his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of Gabriel:

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.”

He mentioned this alongside his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Islam is to testify that there is none worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of

---

## Page 3611

Allah, establish prayer, pay zakah, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.” Thus, when he mentioned it separately from the term “Islam,” he described what the term encompasses in that hadith, where it stands alone without being paired with another term. In this hadith, however, it is paired with the term “Islam.” In the statement of the Most High:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him,”

Islam includes what is inward. If someone performed the outward deeds without the inward reality, he would not have embraced the religion that, in Allah’s sight, is Islam. But when Islam is mentioned alongside faith, as in the statement of the Most High:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,”’”

and His statements:

“So We brought out whoever was there of the believers.”

“But We found there only one household of Muslims.”

And the statement of the Most High:

“Indeed, Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women,”

Islam may denote outward deeds, as in the hadith of Anas in al-Musnad, reporting that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.”

Whoever understands that a term’s meaning varies according to whether it stands alone or is paired with another—as with the terms “poor,” “needy,” “right,” “wrong,” “transgression,” and other terms, and as is also the case in the languages of all peoples, Arab and non-Arab—will have his doubts concerning this subject dispelled. And Allah knows best.

If someone says, “The term ‘faith’ encompasses deeds only figuratively,” the response is:

First, this claim is no better founded than the claim that deeds are excluded from it only figuratively. Indeed, the latter claim is stronger, because deeds are excluded from its meaning only when it is mentioned alongside the terms “Islam” and “deeds.” Deeds are included in its meaning when it stands alone, as in the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Faith has seventy-odd branches

---

## Page 3612

, the highest of which is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road; and modesty is a branch of faith.” What a term denotes when paired with another is more properly called figurative than what it denotes when used alone and without qualification.

Second, he should be told: There is no disagreement that outward deeds are an offshoot of the inward state, necessitate it, and are entailed by it. But are they included in what the term denotes and constitute part of it, or are they a necessary accompaniment to it, like an extrinsic condition or a consequent effect?

It is well known that religious and legal terms, such as “prayer,” “zakah,” “pilgrimage,” and the like, denote—by agreement of the jurists—the entirety of prayer and pilgrimage as prescribed by Islamic law. Some maintain that such a term denotes only what it ordinarily denotes in the language, and that whatever the Lawgiver has added is merely an additional legal requirement and a condition, rather than part of what the term denotes. This was the position of al-Qādī Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, and those who agreed with them: Islamic law introduced additional legal requirements, making them conditions relating to intention, deeds, and supplication, without including them in what the terms “pilgrimage,” “fasting,” and “prayer” denote. Their view is regarded as the weaker one by the jurists and the great majority of those associated with religious learning. Hence, the majority of the followers of the four imams oppose this view.

Thus, if someone says that the term “faith” denotes nothing more than assent, while its being assent to Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers, and its necessarily entailing love for Allah and His Messenger and the like, are conditions of the legal ruling rather than part of what the term denotes—then this view, if not weaker than the preceding one, is no less weak. The same applies to someone who says, “Outward deeds

---

## Page 3613

are necessary accompaniments of the inward state and are not included in what the term denotes when used without qualification”—his view resembles theirs. When the Lawgiver couples deeds with faith, this is like coupling pilgrimage with acts that complete it, as when one says, “Whoever performs pilgrimage to the House, circumambulates it, walks between Safā and Marwah, stands at ʿArafah, and stones the pillars”; or, “Whoever prays, reciting, bowing, and prostrating.” Likewise, he said, “Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and in hope of reward.” It is well known that this would not be fasting as prescribed by Islamic law unless it were done out of faith and in hope of reward.

He also said:

“Whoever performs pilgrimage to this House, neither engaging in sexual intercourse nor committing sins, returns free of sins as on the day his mother gave birth to him.”

It is well known that sexual intercourse invalidates the pilgrimage, while sin diminishes its reward. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever offers our prayer, faces our direction of prayer, and eats what we slaughter.”

A person is not considered to be praying unless he faces our direction of prayer during it. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed five prayers for His servant each day and night. Whoever observes them diligently has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise. Whoever does not observe them diligently has no covenant with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will forgive him.”

He thus mentioned the person who observes them diligently. It is well known that a person does not perform them in the manner commanded unless he observes them diligently. Yet he explained that the warning of punishment is subject to this condition. Thus, failure to observe them diligently does not necessarily mean that he does not perform them after their appointed time, though he would not thereby be observing them diligently.

For observing them diligently necessarily entails performing them, as Allah said:

“Guard strictly the prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

This was revealed when the afternoon prayer was delayed in the year of the Battle of the Trench. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah fill their bellies and their graves with fire, just as they kept us from the middle prayer until the sun had set.”

---

## Page 3614

And this makes it clear that citing this as evidence that one who abandons prayer does not become a disbeliever is a weak argument. Rather, it indicates that one who fails to observe the prayers diligently does not become a disbeliever. Thus, if he performs a prayer after its prescribed time, he does not become a disbeliever. Hence the report concerning rulers who delay the prayer beyond its prescribed time:

“It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should we not fight them?’ He replied, ‘No, so long as they pray.’”

Likewise, when Ibn Masʿūd was asked about Allah’s words, “They neglected prayer,” he said, “This means delaying it beyond its prescribed time.” He was told, “We thought it meant abandoning it.” He replied, “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.”

The point is that an “unqualified term” may encompass many things, even though they may also be mentioned separately.

To someone who says, “Outward deeds are included in the term ‘faith’ only figuratively,” the response is: “Your disagreement is merely verbal. For if you concede that these deeds are necessary accompaniments and consequences of the obligatory faith within the heart, then the absence of a necessary accompaniment entails the absence of that which necessitates it. Thus, the absence of these outward deeds necessarily entails the absence of inward faith. If you acknowledge this, the disagreement is merely verbal.”

But if you assert what Jahm and his followers actually maintain—that the full measure of obligatory faith can remain firmly established in the heart while a person outwardly manifests disbelief and abandons all outward obligations—you are told: “This contradicts your statement that outward deeds necessarily accompany inward faith and are entailed by it.” Indeed, you are told: “What your position really amounts to is that outward deeds sometimes accompany inward faith and are sometimes absent from it. They are therefore neither its necessary accompaniment nor something it entails or causes. Rather, they are an indicator: when present, they indicate the presence of inward faith, but when absent, their absence does not indicate its absence. This is what your position really amounts to.”

---

## Page 3615

And this is as unsound rationally as it is according to revealed law. Such outward conduct is not conclusive evidence, since it also appears in a hypocrite. It serves as evidence only in certain matters pertaining to worldly life, just as words indicate meanings. This is what your position really amounts to. You are therefore told:

It would follow that outward deeds are neither a fruit of inward faith nor a necessary consequence of it or something it entails. For if inward faith itself were what necessitates this outward conduct, its existence would not depend on anything else. An effect that necessarily results from something does not depend on anything else; rather, the existence of the cause necessarily entails the existence of its effect. Thus, if outward conduct were a necessary consequence of inward faith, it would not depend on anything else: whenever the necessitating cause existed, its necessary consequence would exist.

But if outward conduct sometimes accompanies inward faith and is sometimes absent, it could result from that other factor, or it could depend on both together. That other factor would either operate independently of faith or jointly with it. At best, outward conduct would depend on both together: that other factor and faith.

Indeed, outward conduct is known to exist without faith, as in the deeds of a hypocrite. In that case, outward deeds neither necessarily imply faith nor necessarily accompany it. Rather, they sometimes coexist with faith and sometimes with its opposite. Faith would therefore be neither their cause nor what necessitates or entails them. This would invalidate their being evidence of faith, because evidence must necessarily imply what it indicates. And this is indeed true: merely uttering the two testimonies of faith does not necessarily imply the faith that benefits a person before Allah.

Thus, when Sa'd said, “He is a believer,” the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, “Or

## Page 3616

a Muslim?” And Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah knows best their faith. If you find them to be believers, do not send them back to the disbelievers.”

This shows that merely displaying Islam is not evidence of inward faith. Were it otherwise, the emigrant women who came as Muslims would not have needed to be examined. It also shows that examination and testing reveal a person’s inward state, so that it becomes known whether he is a believer or not. Thus, in the hadith traced back to the Prophet:

“If you see a man regularly attending the mosque, testify to his faith, for Allah says: ‘The mosques of Allah are maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah’—to the end of the verse.”

If it is said: “Outward deeds sometimes result from faith and sometimes from something else. Uttering the two testimonies of faith, for example, sometimes results from faith in the heart and sometimes amounts to dissimulation, as with the faith professed by the hypocrites. Allah Most High says: ‘Among the people are those who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not believers.’ When we call these deeds a fruit of faith, we mean when they proceed from faith in the heart, not from hypocrisy.”

The response is: If they proceed from faith, then either faith itself necessitates them, or they depend on something else. If faith itself necessitates them, this establishes that they necessarily accompany faith in the heart as an effect inseparable from it. This is precisely the point to be established. If, however, they depend on something else, faith would be part of the cause; this would make them a fruit and effect of the other part, since in reality they are an effect and fruit of both together. It thus becomes clear that righteous outward deeds cannot be a fruit of inward faith and an effect

---

## Page 3617

of it unless faith necessitates and entails them. In that case, the consequence necessarily accompanies what necessitates it, and the effect necessarily accompanies its cause. Any deficiency in obligatory outward deeds is therefore due to a deficiency in the faith within the heart. It is inconceivable that the required faith within the heart should be complete while obligatory outward deeds are absent. Rather, completeness in the former necessarily entails completeness in the latter, just as deficiency in the latter entails deficiency in the former. To suppose complete faith within the heart without outward words and deeds is like supposing a fully realized consequence without what necessitates it, or a complete cause without its effect. This is impossible.

This and other considerations demonstrate the falsity of the position of Jahm, al-Sālihī, and those who followed them concerning “faith,” such as al-Ashʿarī in the better-known of his two positions, most of his followers, and a group of later followers of Abū Hanīfah, such as al-Māturīdī and others like him. They regarded faith as mere assent within the heart, in which all people are equal: it is either absent or present and admits of no division. They held that faith can exist in its entirety within the heart even while a person willingly, without coercion, utters words of disbelief and reviles Allah and His Messenger; and that whenever outward statements establish that their speaker is a disbeliever, this is because those statements necessarily imply the absence of that assent within the heart—in deeds … (1) They also held that righteous outward deeds do not necessarily accompany inward faith within the heart; rather, faith within the heart can be complete without them.

This position is erroneous in several respects:

First: They excluded the love of Allah, fear of Him, and similar things that reside within the heart

## Page 3618

from faith itself.

Second: They held that those known to be disbelievers—such as Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, Abū Tālib, and others—were disbelievers only because their conduct necessarily implied a lack of inward assent. This flies in the face of reason and direct observation. Likewise, they held that hating and envying the Messenger out of aversion to his religion necessarily implies not knowing that he is truthful, and made other similar claims.

(Third): They held that uttering words of disbelief—such as reviling Allah and His Messenger, professing the Trinity, and the like—may coexist with the reality of faith within the heart, and that someone who does this may truly be a believer in Allah’s sight, destined for bliss in the Hereafter. The falsity of this is necessarily known from the religion of Islam.

(Fourth): They held that someone who never professes faith, despite being able to do so, and never performs any outward act of obedience to Allah, despite being obliged and able to do so, may nevertheless be a believer in Allah whose faith is complete, destined for bliss in the Hereafter. These outrageous positions are peculiar to the Jahmiyyah, as distinct from the Murji’ah among the jurists and others.

(Fifth): This objection applies both to them and to the Murji’ah: they said that a person may be a believer whose faith is complete, equal to the faith of the prophets and the utterly truthful, even if he does no good—neither praying, maintaining ties of kinship, nor speaking truthfully—and commits every major sin without exception. It follows that

---

## Page 3619

in their view, a man who lies whenever he speaks, breaks his promises, and betrays whatever is entrusted to him—persistently lying, betraying trusts, and breaking covenants, never prostrating once to Allah, never doing anyone a single kindness, never fulfilling a trust, and committing every lie, injustice, and indecency within his power—is nevertheless a believer whose faith is complete, equal to the faith of the prophets.

This consequence follows for everyone who does not hold that outward deeds are necessary consequences of inward faith. Once someone affirms that they are its necessary consequences, and that inward faith necessarily entails outward righteous deeds, whether those deeds are necessary consequences of what is denoted by faith or are part of it becomes (a merely verbal dispute, as explained earlier).

(Sixth): Their position entails that someone who willingly prostrates to the cross and idols, deliberately throws a copy of the Quran into a latrine, kills a person unjustly, kills everyone he sees praying, sheds the blood of everyone he sees performing pilgrimage to the House, and does to the Muslims what the Qarmatians did, may nevertheless be a believer and an ally of Allah, with faith equal to that of the prophets and the utterly truthful. For inward faith is either incompatible with these acts or it is not. If it is not incompatible with them, they can coexist with it; thus, they can occur only in the absence of inward faith. If, however, these acts are incompatible with inward faith, refraining from them is something faith necessarily entails, requires, and brings about. Thus, only someone who refrains from these acts can possess the required inward faith. Whoever does not refrain from them thereby demonstrates the corruption of his inward faith. And if deeds and acts of abstention

---

## Page 3620

in outward conduct are necessary consequences of inward faith, then they are entailed and required by it. It is evident that they grow stronger as it grows stronger, increase as it increases, and decrease as it decreases. For an effect increases only when that which necessitates and produces it increases, and decreases only when that decreases. Thus, if outward action is held to be entailed and required by inward faith, its increase must result from an increase in inward faith and therefore indicate that increase. Likewise, its decrease must result from a decrease in inward faith and therefore indicate that decrease. This is precisely the point to be established.

When the believer reflects rationally on all these matters, it becomes clear to him that the position of the early generations is the true position, from which there can be no departure. Whoever opposes them is committed to untenable consequences whose invalidity is evident from plain reason and sound transmitted evidence, just as with all other positions that contradict those of the early generations and the leading scholars. And Allah knows best.

The assertion of Jahm and those who agree with him—that faith is merely knowledge and assent, and that through this alone a person deserves reward and felicity—resembles the assertion of certain Peripatetic philosophers and their followers that human felicity consists merely in knowing existence as it truly is. Just as the positions of the Jahmiyyah and these philosophers closely resemble one another on “questions of the divine names and attributes” and “questions of compulsion and divine decree,” so too do their positions on “questions of faith.”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained some of its flaws. For example, knowledge is only one of the soul’s two faculties. The soul has “two faculties”: the faculty of knowledge and assent, and the faculty of will and action, just as an animal has “two faculties”: the faculty of sensation and the faculty of voluntary movement.

---

## Page 3621

A person does not become upright merely by knowing the truth without loving it, desiring it, and following it. Likewise, his felicity does not consist in knowing Allah and acknowledging what He deserves without loving, worshipping, and obeying Him. Rather, the person most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection will be a scholar whose knowledge Allah did not make beneficial to him. When a person knows the truth but hates it and opposes it, he deserves a measure of Allah’s wrath and punishment that someone unlike him does not deserve. Similarly, someone who intends and seeks the truth—but is ignorant of what he seeks and the path to it—is affected by misguidance and deserves a measure of the curse—which means being far removed from Allah’s mercy—that someone unlike him does not deserve.

For this reason, Allah has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who have gone astray.”

“Those who have incurred wrath” knew the truth but neither loved nor followed it. “Those who have gone astray” sought the truth, but were ignorant and misguided concerning both the truth and the path to it. The former resembles a wicked scholar, and the latter an ignorant worshipper. The former is the condition of the Jews, who have incurred wrath; the latter is the condition of the Christians, who have gone astray. As is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he said:

“The Jews have incurred wrath, and the Christians have gone astray.”

The “philosophers” are in a worse condition than the Jews and Christians, for they combine the ignorance and misguidance of the latter with the wickedness and wrongdoing of the former. Thus, they possess a degree of ignorance and wrongdoing found in neither the Jews nor the Christians. They locate felicity merely in knowing realities, so that a person becomes an intelligible world corresponding to the existing world. Yet they acquired no knowledge of Allah

---

## Page 3622

and His names, attributes, angels, books, messengers, creation, and command, except for a scant amount. Their ignorance thus exceeded their knowledge, and their misguidance outweighed their guidance. They vacillated between simple and compound ignorance.

Their discussions of natural philosophy and mathematics do not bring the soul to perfection and soundness. This is attained only through knowledge of divine matters, yet their discourse on these matters is like:

“The flesh of a lean camel atop a rugged mountain: neither is the mountain easy to climb, nor is the flesh fat enough to be worth carrying away.”

Their discourse on the “Necessary Existent” contains a little truth amid much falsehood and error. The same applies to their discourse on the “intellects” and “souls,” which their followers among religious communities claim are the angels described by the messengers. This is not so. Rather, their claim that these are the angels is akin to their claim that the “Necessary Existent” is absolute existence subject to the condition of absoluteness, despite their acknowledgment that what is absolute under this condition exists only in the mind. Likewise, upon examination, their discourse on intellects and souls reduces to entities posited in the mind that have no reality in the external world.

Moreover, their discourse contains notions—associating partners with Allah; affirming a lord who originates the entire universe apart from itself, though it is itself an effect of Him; and affirming a lord who originates everything beneath the lunar sphere and is an effect of the lord above it, that lord in turn being an effect of a lord above it—that are far, far more abhorrent than the Christians’ claim that the Messiah is the son of Allah, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Their early authorities had nothing whatsoever to say about prophethood. Their later thinkers are bewildered concerning it. Some deny it, as did Ibn Zakariyyā al-Rāzī and others like him, despite maintaining that the world came into existence.

---

## Page 3623

They affirmed five eternal principles and adopted some of the worst and most corrupt doctrines. Others affirm prophethood while maintaining that the world is eternal, such as Ibn Sīnā and those like him. Yet they place the prophet on the level of a just king, treating prophethood in its entirety as the same kind of unveiling, influence, and imaginative experience that some righteous people attain. They identify “three things” as the prophet’s distinctive qualities: the faculty of sound intuition, which they call the sacred faculty; the faculty of exerting influence upon the world; and the sensory faculty through which he hears and sees intelligible realities represented within his own imagination. Thus, according to them, Allah’s speech consists of the sounds within his soul, and His angels are the forms and lights within their souls. These qualities are attained by most people who practise spiritual discipline and purification; hence, in their view, prophethood can be acquired.

Consequently, all who followed their path—such as al-Suhrawardī, who was put to death, Ibn Sabʿīn al-Maghribī, and others like them—sought prophethood and hoped to be told, “Arise and warn.” One says, “I shall not die until I am told: ‘Arise and warn.’” The other takes up residence in Mecca and makes his way to the Cave of Hirāʾ, seeking revelation to descend upon him there just as it descended upon the one who, like himself, was wrapped and cloaked. Each of these two, and others like them, pursues his aim through various forms of sīmiyā, which is a kind of magic, imagining that the prophets’ miracles were a form of sīmiyā magic.

Those unable to seek or claim prophethood—because they knew the saying of the truthful and trustworthy Prophet:

“There is no prophet after me,”

or for some other reason—such as Ibn ʿArabī and those like him, sought what they considered higher than prophethood. They maintained that the Seal of the Friends of Allah is greater than the Seal of the Prophets, and that a friend of Allah receives directly from Allah without an intermediary

---

## Page 3624

whereas the prophet receives through the intermediary of an angel. This was founded on a principle held by the philosophers he followed. According to them, angels are the luminous, imaginary forms that take shape within the soul of a prophet or a friend of Allah. Thus, “angels,” in their view, are what he imagines within himself. The “prophet,” according to them, receives through this act of imagining, whereas the “friend of Allah” receives intellectual knowledge without it. There is no doubt that someone who receives knowledge without imagining is more perfect than someone who receives it through imagining.

Having adopted these would-be philosophers’ conception of prophethood, they began to say that friendship with Allah is greater than prophethood, just as many philosophers say that the philosopher is greater than the prophet. This is the position of al-Fārābī, Mubashshir ibn Fātik, and others. They say that prophethood is the highest attainment in the eyes of the masses, but not in those of the elite. They also say that the prophet’s distinctive quality is his skill in evoking images and forming them in his own imagination.

Then came those who cast philosophy in the mould of friendship with Allah, calling the practitioner of philosophy a friend of Allah. They took the philosophers’ ideas and presented them as spiritual unveiling and being addressed by Allah. They said that the friend of Allah is greater than the prophet because he receives abstract meanings from Allah without the intermediary of imagining anything within himself, whereas the prophet receives them through the forms and sounds he imagines within himself.

This falsehood did not satisfy them: they went so far as to claim that all the prophets and messengers draw their knowledge of Allah from the lamp-niche of the Seal of these friends of Allah—someone who is among the most ignorant of all creation concerning Allah and among those furthest removed from His religion. In their view, knowledge of Allah consists in knowing Him as “absolute existence” pervading all beings, so that the existence of every being is identical with the existence of the Necessary Existent. In reality, this doctrine is that of the naturalist eternalists, who deny that the world has

---

## Page 3625

an Originator who brought it into being and is the Necessary Existent in Himself; rather, they say: “The world itself is the Necessary Existent in itself.” In reality, these people’s doctrine is worse than that of the theistic eternalists and, upon examination, amounts to the doctrine of the naturalist eternalists.

We have been told that Ibn ʿArabī and Shaykh Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī disagreed over whether, when the Real manifests Himself to a servant, He can address him or not. Shaykh Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī said: “Yes, that is possible.” Ibn ʿArabī said: “That is not possible.” I think each spoke in the other’s absence. Ibn ʿArabī was then told: “Al-Suhrawardī says such-and-such.” He replied: “Poor fellow! We were speaking of witnessing the Essence, while he is speaking of witnessing the attributes.”

Many followers of Sufism and spiritual discipline, and seekers of the path of spiritual realization and knowledge—despite believing that they follow the messengers and avoid innovations contrary to their teaching—repeat and revere these words, and esteem Ibn ʿArabī for saying such things. They do not know that he based these words on his corrupt foundation of heresy, which combines the negation of the divine attributes with the identification of Allah with creation. For, in his view, the Lord’s reality is abstract existence, having neither name nor attribute. He cannot be seen in this world or in the Hereafter, nor does He possess speech, knowledge, or any other attribute subsisting in Him. Rather, He is seen appearing in created beings and manifesting Himself in things that have been made. In his view, this is other than the existence of existing beings. He also likened it, at times, to a universal manifesting itself in its particulars, as a genus manifests itself in its species, and a species in the particular—just as animality appears in every animal and humanity in every human being.

He based this on the error of his predecessors, the “Greek logicians,” who supposed that

---

## Page 3626

concrete entities are accompanied by intelligible substances corresponding to the universals predicated of them. Thus, they suppose that within a particular human being there is an intelligible human, an intelligible animal, an intelligible rational being, an intelligible sentient being, and an intelligible body. This is the essence to which existence accrues, and that essence is shared by all particular individuals. Such discourse impresses those who have neither understood it nor reflected upon it. Once someone understands its true nature, however, it becomes clear to him that it resembles the speech of madmen more than that of rational people, for it contradicts both sense perception and reason.

Their error arose from conceiving “absolute universals” in their minds and then supposing that these existed in external reality. Their error here is the reverse of their error concerning the prophets: the prophets witnessed things outside themselves, yet these heretics claimed that those things were within their minds. These heretics, meanwhile, perceived “absolute universals” within their own minds and supposed that they existed externally, although they existed only in their minds. Thus, they placed what was in their minds in external reality, where it did not exist, and placed what the prophets reported within the prophets’ minds, although it existed externally. Hence, they denied the unseen realities reported by the prophets.

They then held that the existence of the Lord—the Creator of the worlds, distinct from all His creatures—is of the same kind as the existence of humanity in human beings and animality in animals, or something similar, such as existence inhering in subsistence—according to those who say that the nonexistent is a thing. They wanted to make Him something existing within created beings while remaining other than them. Accordingly, they drew analogies for Him, sometimes with universals, sometimes with matter and form, and sometimes with existence as distinct from subsistence. When they likened Him to perceptible things, they likened Him to light in glass or air in a tuft of wool.

---

## Page 3627

and thus they drew analogies for the Lord of the worlds, went astray, and could find no way forward.

They are misguided in these analogies in several respects:

First: Upon examination, everything they use in these analogies—matter together with form, universals together with particulars, and existence together with subsistence—amounts to one thing, not two. They have made one thing into two, just as they make two things into one in matters such as Allah’s attributes: they identify knowledge with the knower, knowledge with the known, knowledge with power, and knowledge with will. When a rational person reflects upon such claims, it becomes clear to him that these people are among the most ignorant concerning divine matters and among the greatest proponents of falsehood. Yet they and their followers entertain extravagant, sweeping claims about themselves, just as their brethren, the esotericist Qarmatians, claim to be infallible imams like the prophets, although they are among the most ignorant, misguided, and unbelieving of people.

(Second): On every one of these assumptions, they make His existence conditional upon the existence of something else that He did not originate. The existence of universals in external reality is conditional upon particulars; the existence of matter is conditional upon form, and vice versa; and the existence of concrete entities is conditional upon their subsistence, fixed in nonexistence. On every assumption, therefore, their position entails that the Necessary Existent is dependent upon something He did not originate. Whatever depends for its existence upon something else that it did not create cannot be necessarily existent in itself. This is clear.

---

## Page 3628

Third: Upon examination, this argument amounts to identifying the Creator’s existence with the very existence of created beings. They state this explicitly, yet claim a distinction between existence and subsistence, or between existence and essence, and between the whole and the part—which is the distinction between the absolute and the particular. Hence their doctrine of indwelling: sometimes they make the Creator dwell within created beings, and sometimes they make Him that within which created beings dwell. When the matter is rigorously examined and it is established against them that there is no distinction, their position amounts to saying that the Creator is the very same as created beings. There is then neither Creator nor creation; rather, the world is necessarily existent in itself.

Fourth: They profess what they claim to be “divine oneness,” declaring Him free of multiplicity in His necessary attributes and His names, of temporal events inhering in Him, and of being a body or a substance. Yet, upon examination, they identify Him with the very repulsive bodies that come into being and pass away, and ascribe every deficiency to Him. They have explicitly stated this, saying:

“Do you not see that the Real manifests Himself with the attributes of originated things? He has spoken of Himself in these terms, and with attributes of deficiency and blame.”

They also say:

“He who is Most High in Himself is the one whose perfection encompasses all existential realities and privative relations, whether praiseworthy according to custom, reason, and revealed law, or blameworthy according to custom, reason, and revealed law. This belongs exclusively to the One named Allah.”

Thus, according to them, He possesses every blameworthy attribute just as He possesses every praiseworthy attribute. These people have been discussed at length elsewhere, for their case is too extensive to expound here. The purpose, however, is to draw attention to the resemblance between the leaders of misguidance, so that, when the believer understands

---

## Page 3629

the teaching of one of them, this helps him understand that of another, guard himself against them, and expose their misguidance, given the many errors they have spread in the world.

For Ibn ‘Arabī, according to his claim, the self-disclosure of the Essence is nothing more than an absolute witnessing, which is the existence of existing things, abstracted and unqualified, without name or attribute. It is well known that anyone who conceives of this cannot be addressed by it. Hence his claim that no address occurs when the Essence discloses itself.

Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī, however, was more knowledgeable about the Sunnah, more faithful to it, and better than him. He had encountered the hadiths stating that Allah reveals Himself to His servants and addresses them when He reveals Himself to them, and he believed this. Yet Ibn ‘Arabī was more renowned for his philosophy than al-Suhrawardī was for his adherence to the Sunnah. Thus, the followers of both held Ibn ‘Arabī in greater esteem, despite acknowledging that al-Suhrawardī followed the Sunnah more closely.

This was related to me by a visiting shaykh known as Husām al-Dīn, who followed the path of Ibn Hamawayh, whom his followers called “Sultan of the Spiritual Poles.” He held Ibn ‘Arabī and Ibn Hamawayh in immense reverence and went to great extremes in exalting them. I explained to him much of the corruption, heresy, and hadiths falsely attributed to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, contained in their writings. Lengthy discussions ensued on this subject because of his reverence for them, despite his failure to understand the true nature of their statements and the errors they contained.

He was also among those who related to me, from his shaykh al-Tāwūsī, who was in Hamadan, on the authority of Sa‘d al-Dīn

---

## Page 3630

ibn Hamawayh that he said:

“Muhyī al-Dīn Ibn ‘Arabī is an ocean that buckets cannot muddy. Yet the light of following the Prophet upon the face of Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī is another matter.”

I said to him: “This is like saying: ‘These men were granted immense dominion of the kind possessed by unbelievers. Yet the light of Islam upon Shihāb Ghāzī, the ruler of Mayyāfāriqīn, is another matter.’”

They held Ibn ‘Arabī in such esteem because Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn was not as accomplished in knowing and following the Sunnah, and ascertaining the truth brought by the messengers, as Ibn ‘Arabī was in the path he pursued, in which he combined philosophy and Sufism.

These people can only be cut off at the root by affirming the distinction between the Creator and creation, and affirming His distinct identity, separate from creation: hands are raised to Him in supplication, and to Him the Seal of the Prophets ascended. Al-Suhrawardī stated in his well-known creed:

“Without pointing to Him or identifying Him distinctly.”

This was precisely what these people used to gain the upper hand over him. For once pointing to Him and identifying Him distinctly are denied, nothing remains but sheer nonexistence and negation of the divine, or heresy, the oneness of all existence, and divine indwelling.

Ibn Sab‘īn and other heretics like him say:

“No pointing, no distinct identification;
The very thing you see is an essence unseen,
And an essence unseen is the very thing you see.”

In their formulas of remembrance, they say, “There is nothing but Allah,” instead of the Muslims’ declaration, “There is no god but Allah,” because they believe that He is the existence of everything that exists, and thus nothing exists but Him.

Muslims, however, know that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything; that He is neither created things, nor a part of them, nor an attribute of them, but is separate from them. They affirm that He is the God who deserves worship to the exclusion of all other

---

## Page 3631

beings; there is no god but Him. As the Most High says:

And as the Most High says:

These “Jahmiyyah” among the speculative theologians and Sufis, who say that faith is merely knowledge and assent, say that the object of this knowledge is the existent described through negation and denial. Thus they say: “He is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither separate from the world nor occupying the same place as it”; then

---

## Page 3632

they turn around and make Him indwell created beings, or make Him a locus for them, or identify Him with them; or else they negate Him altogether.

In this they resemble the Peripatetic philosophers, who locate human perfection in knowledge. For them, the “highest science” and “first philosophy” consist in studying being and its concomitants. They make the Necessary Existent absolute existence, subject to the condition of absoluteness. Section

The hadith begins with his question about “Islam.” He answered him:

“Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform the pilgrimage to the House.”

These are the five mentioned in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Islam is built upon five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and performing the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to make the journey.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said this after Allah had made the pilgrimage obligatory; hence he mentioned all five. Most hadiths do not mention the pilgrimage. In the hadith concerning the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, he said:

“I command you to believe in Allah alone. Do you know what believing in Allah alone means? Testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and giving one-fifth of the spoils.”

---

## Page 3633

The hadith concerning the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays is among the best-known and most authentic hadiths. Some versions in al-Bukhārī do not mention fasting, but it is mentioned in many of his versions and in Muslim’s collection. It is also mentioned in the hadith of Abū Saʿīd recounting the visit of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, which Muslim narrated from him in his Sahīh. Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, which states that he commanded them to give one-fifth of the spoils. The obligation to pay this fifth was not instituted until the Battle of Badr, whereas fasting Ramadan had been made obligatory before that.

The delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays was among the finest delegations to visit the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Their visit took place before the pilgrimage became obligatory. It has been said that they came in the Year of Delegations, the ninth year, but the correct view is that they came earlier. They said, “Between us and you is this group of unbelievers from Mudar”—meaning the people of Najd—“and we can only reach you during a sacred month.” By the ninth year, however, the Arabs had been subdued and had abandoned warfare. They were either Muslims or apprehensive parties to treaties, after Allah had granted the conquest of Mecca and the Muslims had defeated Hawāzin at Hunayn. They had merely been waiting for the conquest of Mecca before embracing Islam.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the pilgrimage in the ninth year. He then sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, after him to give effect to the treaties between the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Arabs. However, he granted them a respite of four months from the time of Abū Bakr’s pilgrimage, which took place in Dhū al-Qaʿdah.

Allah Most High said:

“Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists”—to the end of the verse.

These four months for which they granted a respite are the four sacred months.

---

## Page 3634

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, campaigned against the Christians in Byzantine territory during the expedition to Tabūk in the ninth year, before sending Abū Bakr to lead the pilgrimage. He was only able to campaign against the Christians once he was secure against the Arab polytheists and knew that they posed no threat to Islam. Hence, he permitted no one fit for combat to remain behind. Only hypocrites, the three whose repentance was accepted, and those with a valid excuse stayed behind. Thus:

“When he appointed Alī to take charge of Medina during the expedition to Tabūk, the hypocrites disparaged him because this appointment carried little weight. Previously, he had appointed others to take charge of Medina while men fit for combat remained there. The reason was that, by the time of Tabūk, there was no one in Arabia—whether in Mecca, Najd, or similar regions—who would fight or intimidate the inhabitants of the lands of Islam: Mecca, Medina, and elsewhere.

Then, upon returning from Tabūk, he confirmed Abū Bakr’s appointment to lead the pilgrimage, conducting its rites and leading the prayers, and proclaiming that after that year no polytheist was to perform the pilgrimage and no one was to circumambulate the House naked. He sent Alī after him to annul the treaties, since the Arabs customarily accepted such a declaration only from a chief whose authority they recognized or from a man of his household.

(The point is that this demonstrates that the delegation of Abd al-Qays arrived before then. As for the “hadith of Dimām,” Muslim narrated it in his Sahīh on the authority of Anas ibn Mālik:

This hadith of al-Nuʿmān dates from an early period, for al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal was killed before the conquest of Mecca by a member of Banū Saʿd ibn al-ʿĀs, as established in the Sahīh. The two compilers also included it in their Sahīh collections on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, and Muslim narrated it from Jābir, with the wording:

“I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah. If they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except as required by that testimony.”

Abū Bakr said: “By Allah, I shall fight those who distinguish between prayer and zakah, for zakah is a right due on wealth.”

It was part of Abū Bakr’s understanding of the religion that he understood from this abridged hadith that fighting to enforce zakah was fighting to enforce a right due on wealth. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, clarified what he meant in the fuller wording narrated by Ibn ʿUmar.

The Quran explicitly accords with the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, as Allah Most High says:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then let them go their way.”

## Page 3639

And in the hadith concerning Muʿādh, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent him to Yemen, he mentioned only prayer and zakah. The fact that some hadiths mention certain pillars but not others has puzzled some people. Some have explained this by saying that certain narrators abridged the hadiths they transmitted. But this is not so, for such an explanation impugns the narrators and accuses them of lying. What this explanation describes applies only to different accounts of the same hadith: for example, the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, in which some narrators mentioned fasting while others did not; the hadith of Dimām, in which some mentioned all five while others did not; and the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal, in which some mentioned fasting while others did not. In such cases, we know that one of the two narrators either omitted part of the report or mistakenly added something.

With two separate hadiths, however, the matter is different, especially since the reports establishing that the answers differed have been transmitted through so many channels as to yield certainty. They also contain conclusive evidence that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said one thing on one occasion and another on another occasion. The Quran confirms this, for in some verses Allah made brotherhood in faith conditional only upon prayer and zakah, as in His words, Most High:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then they are your brothers in religion.”

Likewise, He made the cessation of fighting conditional upon this in His words, Most High:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then let them go their way.”

The hadith of Ibn ʿUmar in the two Sahīh collections, which agrees with this verse, has already been cited.

Furthermore, in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, he mentioned the fifth of the spoils because they were a community capable of defending itself and engaged in fighting.

## Page 3640

and such a matter would not be mentioned in answer to someone asking about his personal obligations. There are, however, two answers to this:

The first is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered according to the obligations that had been revealed. The first thing Allah made obligatory was the two testimonies of faith, followed by prayer. He commanded prayer at the very beginning of revelation. Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh collection that the first revelation he received was:

“Recite in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging substance,”

down to His words:

“Taught man that which he knew not.”

Then, after that, it was revealed to him:

“O you wrapped in your cloak, arise and warn.”

This address commissioned him as a messenger to humankind, and that commissioning followed his receiving revelation, for the earlier address contained no such commission. The end of Surah Iqraʾ reads:

“Prostrate and draw near.”

Thus, the beginning of the surah commands recitation, while its end commands prostration. Prayer consists of words and actions: its finest words are Quranic recitation, and its finest action is prostration. Recitation is the first of its utterances intended in their own right, and what follows is subordinate to it.

It has been reported that when prayer was first made obligatory, it consisted of two units in the morning and two in the evening. Then the five daily prayers were made obligatory on the night of the Ascension, each consisting of two units. When he emigrated, the prayer offered while travelling was left unchanged, while additional units were added to the prayer offered while resident.

Prayer was brought to completion gradually. At first, they would speak during prayer, and it contained no tashahhud (the testimony of faith recited while seated). They were then commanded to recite the tashahhud and forbidden to speak. Likewise, they had no call to prayer in Mecca; it was instituted only in Medina after the migration. The Friday prayer, the Eid prayer, the eclipse prayer, the prayer for rain, the night prayers of Ramadan, and other such prayers were likewise instituted only in Medina after the migration.

---

## Page 3641

They were also commanded in Mecca to give zakat and to do good, but the prescribed dues and minimum thresholds of zakat were instituted only in Medina. As for “fasting the month of Ramadan,” it was made obligatory only in the second year after the Hijrah, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, lived through nine Ramadans.

As for “Hajj,” people differed over when it became obligatory. One group said that it was made obligatory in the sixth year after the Hijrah—the year in which, by common agreement, al-Hudaybiyah took place. They said: “This verse indicates that both Hajj and umrah are obligatory, because the command to complete an act entails the command both to begin it and to complete it.”

The majority, however, said that Hajj became obligatory only later. Some said in the ninth year, others in the tenth; this is the correct view. For the verse establishing its obligation is His saying, Most High:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people.”

This verse occurs in Surah Āl ‘Imrān, in the course of His address to the People of the Book. The opening of Āl ‘Imrān, together with its passages addressing the People of the Book, was revealed when the Christian delegation from Najrān came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and debated with him concerning the Messiah.

They were the first of the People of the Book to pay the jizyah. This was after the revelation of Surah Barā’ah, in which Allah instituted the jizyah and commanded fighting the People of the Book until they pay it with their own hands while humbled. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, undertook the expedition to Tabūk, in which he went out to fight the Christians, when Allah commanded this in His saying:

“Fight those among the People of the Book who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not follow the religion of truth, until they pay

---

## Page 3642

the jizyah with their own hands while humbled.” For this reason, he did not mention the obligation of Hajj in most hadiths; it appears only in the later hadiths.

The delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. According to the correct view, their arrival preceded the conquest of Mecca, as we have explained. They said: “O Messenger of Allah, between us and you lies this tribe of unbelievers from Mudar.” They meant the people of Najd—Tamīm, Asad, and Ghatafān—because they lay between al-Bahrayn and Medina. ‘Abd al-Qays belong to Rabī‘ah, not Mudar. Once Mecca was conquered, this fear disappeared. When the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to him, he commanded them to observe prayer, pay zakat, fast Ramadan, and pay one-fifth of the spoils of war; he did not command them to perform Hajj.

As for the hadith of Dimām, we have already noted that al-Bukhārī did not mention Hajj in it, just as he did not mention it in the hadiths of Talhah, Abū Hurayrah, and others, despite their assertion: “These hadiths relate to the account of Dimām.” This is possible, although the date of this Dimām’s arrival is not certain.

As for His saying:

“And complete Hajj and umrah for Allah.”

This verse contains only the command to complete them, which makes their completion obligatory upon anyone who has begun them. This command was revealed when they entered the state of consecration for umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah and were then prevented from proceeding. They were commanded to complete it, and He explained to them the ruling concerning being prevented from completing the rites. At that time, neither umrah nor Hajj had yet become obligatory upon them.

(The second answer: In each situation, he would mention what was appropriate to it. Sometimes he would mention the outward obligations for whose abandonment a group that refuses to comply is fought, such as prayer and zakat

## Page 3643

and at other times he would mention what was obligatory upon the questioner. Those whom he answered by mentioning prayer and fasting had no zakat to pay. As for those whom he answered by mentioning prayer, zakat, and fasting, either this occurred before Hajj became obligatory—which must be the case with reports such as that of ‘Abd al-Qays—or the questioner was someone for whom Hajj was not obligatory.

Prayer and zakat have a standing unlike that of the other obligations. For this reason, Allah Most High mentioned in His Book fighting over them, because they are both acts of worship. Fasting, by contrast, is an inward matter entrusted to people’s honesty. In this respect, it is like ablution, ritual bathing following sexual defilement, and similar matters entrusted to the servant. A person can refrain from intending to fast and can eat secretly, just as he can conceal his state of minor or major ritual impurity. Prayer and zakat, however, are outward matters from which a person cannot refrain while living among the believers.

When speaking of Islam, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would mention the outward deeds for whose neglect people are fought and by performing which they become Muslims. He therefore made this conditional upon prayer and zakat, rather than fasting, even though fasting is obligatory. This is the case in the two verses of Surah Barā’ah, which, by universal agreement, was revealed after fasting became obligatory.

Likewise, “when he sent Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal to Yemen, he said to him: ‘You are going to a people from among the People of the Book. If they respond to you in this, inform them that Allah has enjoined upon them five prayers each day and night.
