## Page 3644

take care not to take the choicest of their wealth, and beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah.’” Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this in their Sahīh collections.

He sent Mu‘ādh to Yemen toward the end of his mission, after fasting had been made obligatory—indeed, after the conquest of Mecca, after Tabūk, and after Hajj and jizyah had been made obligatory. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died while Mu‘ādh was in Yemen, and Mu‘ādh returned to Medina only after his death. He did not mention fasting in this hadith because it is subsidiary and inward. Nor did he mention Hajj, because its obligation applies to particular people rather than everyone, and it is obligatory only once in a lifetime.

For this reason, the scholars differed over declaring someone a disbeliever for abandoning any of these “four obligations” while acknowledging that they are obligatory. As for the “two testimonies of faith,” anyone who does not pronounce them despite being able to do so is a disbeliever by the agreement of the Muslims. According to the early generations of this community, its imams, and the great majority of its scholars, he is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly.

A group among the Murji’ah—the Jahmī Murji’ah, such as Jahm, al-Sālihī, and their followers—held that if he assents in his heart, he is a disbeliever outwardly but not inwardly. The basis of this view has already been pointed out. It is an innovated view in Islam that none of the imams held. It has already been explained that inward faith necessarily entails outward profession—and indeed, more than that—and that inward faith, consisting of assent, love, and submission, cannot exist without outward profession.

As for the “four obligations,” if someone denies that any of them is obligatory after the proof has reached him,

---

## Page 3645

he is a disbeliever. The same applies to anyone who denies the prohibition of any manifestly forbidden thing whose prohibition is established through mass transmission, such as acts of gross indecency, injustice, lying, intoxicating drink, and the like.

As for those against whom the proof has not been established—for example, someone who has only recently embraced Islam, or who grew up in a remote desert region where the laws of Islam had not reached him, or someone in similar circumstances—or those who mistakenly believe that people who believe and do righteous deeds are exempt from the prohibition of intoxicating drink, as did those whom ‘Umar called upon to repent: such people are called upon to repent, and the proof is established against them. If they persist, they then become disbelievers; they are not judged to be disbelievers before that. Likewise, the Companions did not judge Qudāmah ibn Maz‘ūn and his companions to be disbelievers when they fell into their mistaken interpretation.

As for someone who abandons any of these four pillars while acknowledging its obligation, the scholars hold several views on declaring him a disbeliever, all of which are reported from Ahmad:

The first is that he becomes a disbeliever by abandoning any one of the four, even Hajj. Although the scholars differ over whether Hajj may be deferred, whenever he resolves to abandon it altogether, he becomes a disbeliever. This is the view of a group among the early generations and one of the positions reported from Ahmad, which Abū Bakr adopted.

The second is that he does not become a disbeliever by abandoning any of these duties so long as he acknowledges its obligation. This is the well-known position among many jurists belonging to the schools of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and al-Shāfi‘ī. It is also one of the positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by Ibn Battah and others.

---

## Page 3646

The third is that he becomes a disbeliever only by abandoning prayer. This is the third position reported from Ahmad, and the view of many of the early generations, a group of Mālik’s and al-Shāfi‘ī’s followers, and a group of Ahmad’s followers.

The fourth is that only abandoning prayer or zakat renders him a disbeliever.

The fifth is that abandoning prayer renders him a disbeliever, as does withholding zakat if he fights the ruler over it, but not abandoning fasting or Hajj.

This issue has two aspects: the first concerns establishing outward disbelief, and the second concerns establishing inward disbelief.

As for the second aspect, it rests upon the question of faith consisting of speech and action, as discussed above. It is impossible for a man to have firmly established faith in his heart that Allah has obligated him to pray, pay zakat, fast, and perform Hajj, yet live his entire life without making a single prostration to Allah, fasting any part of Ramadan, paying any zakat for Allah’s sake, or performing Hajj to His House. This is impossible. Such conduct can only arise from hypocrisy and heresy in the heart, not from genuine faith.

For this reason, it is only the disbelievers whom He, glorified be He, describes as refusing to prostrate, as in His words:

“On the Day when the Shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostrate, but will be unable to do so.”

“Their eyes downcast, humiliation will overwhelm them, although they used to be called to prostrate while they were sound.”

---

## Page 3647

It is established in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere, in the lengthy hadith about Allah’s manifestation narrated by Abū Hurayrah, Abū Sa‘īd, and others:

“When He, Most High, manifests Himself to His servants on the Day of Resurrection, the believers will prostrate before Him. But anyone who used to prostrate in this world for show and reputation will be left with a back as rigid as a slab, unable to prostrate.”

If this is the condition of someone who prostrated for show, what, then, of someone who never prostrated at all? It is also established in the Sahīh:

“The Fire consumes every part of the son of Adam except the places of prostration, for Allah has forbidden the Fire to consume them.”

Thus, it is known that the Fire will consume the entirety of anyone who did not prostrate to Allah. Likewise, it is established in the Sahīh:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will recognize his community on the Day of Resurrection by their radiant faces, hands, and feet, bearing the traces of ablution.”

This indicates that anyone without this radiance will not be recognized by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and so will not belong to his community.

And His words, Most High:

“Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while; indeed, you are criminals. Woe that Day to those who deny the truth! And when they are told, ‘Bow down,’ they do not bow down. Woe that Day to those who deny the truth!”

And His words, Most High:

“What is the matter with them that they do not believe, and when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate? Rather, those who disbelieve deny the truth. And Allah knows best what they keep hidden.”

Likewise, His words, Most High:

“He neither affirmed the truth nor prayed, but denied and turned away.”

Likewise, His words, Most High:

“‘What brought you into Saqar?’ They will say, ‘We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor. We used to indulge in vain discourse with those who did so, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until death came to us.’”

Thus, He describes him as abandoning prayer just as He describes him as failing to affirm the truth. He also describes him as denying and turning away. The one who “turns away” is the disobedient person who refuses to obey, as He says,

Most High:

“You will be called to face a people of great military might, whom you will fight unless they submit. If you obey, Allah will grant you a good reward; but if you turn away as you did before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.”

Furthermore, in the Quran, He makes brotherhood in religion conditional upon actually establishing prayer and giving zakah, just as He makes it conditional upon repentance from disbelief. When these conditions are absent, brotherhood is absent.

Moreover, prayer is the distinguishing mark of the Muslims. Hence they are referred to by it: people say, “Those who pray have differed,” and, “Those who face the direction of prayer have differed.” Writers on Muslim doctrines speak of “The Doctrines of the Muslims and the Disagreements among Those Who Pray.” And in the Sahīh:

“Whoever prays as we pray, faces our direction of prayer, and eats the animals we slaughter is a Muslim, entitled to the same rights as us and bound by the same duties.”

There are many similar texts in the Quran and Sunnah. As for those who do not regard abandoning prayer and similar duties as disbelief, they have no argument that is not

applicable to one who denies its obligation just as it is to one who abandons it. Whatever answer they give concerning the former also serves as an answer to them concerning the latter. Moreover, the texts connect disbelief with turning away, as explained above. This resembles their appeal to the general statements invoked by the Murji’ah, such as his saying:

“Whoever testifies that there is no god but Allah, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that Jesus is Allah’s servant and Messenger, His word which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him … Allah will admit him to Paradise.”

They invoke other similar texts as well. The strongest evidence they rely upon is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has prescribed five prayers for His servants each day and night. Whoever observes them faithfully has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise. Whoever does not observe them faithfully has no covenant with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will admit him to Paradise.”

They say: “He thus leaves the one who does not observe them faithfully subject to Allah’s will, whereas a disbeliever is not subject to His will.”

Yet this provides no evidence for their position. The promise is conditional upon observing the prayers faithfully, which means performing them at their appointed times as commanded. As the Most High says:

“Observe the prayers faithfully, especially the middle prayer.”

Failure to observe them faithfully can occur even when they are performed, if they are performed after their appointed time. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, delayed the afternoon prayer on the Day of the Trench, whereupon Allah revealed the verse commanding faithful observance of that prayer and the other prayers.

The Most High also says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will meet with doom.”

Ibn Mas‘ūd and others were asked, “What does neglecting prayer mean?” He replied, “Delaying it beyond its appointed time.” They said, “We thought it meant nothing other than abandoning it.” He replied, “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.”

Likewise, His words:

“So woe to those who pray, yet are heedless of their prayer.”

---

## Page 3650

He censured them despite their praying, because they neglected its obligatory requirements: performing it at its appointed time and completing its obligatory acts. As established in Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! He watches the sun until, when it is between Satan’s two horns, he rises and pecks out four rak‘ahs, remembering Allah only a little during them.”

He described this as the hypocrites’ prayer because the person delayed it beyond its appointed time and pecked through it. It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned rulers who would come after him and commit objectionable deeds. They asked, “Messenger of Allah, should we not fight them?” He replied, “No, so long as they pray.”

It is also established that he said:

“There will be rulers who delay prayer beyond its appointed time. Perform the prayer at its appointed time, then let your prayer with them be voluntary.”

Thus, he forbade fighting them so long as they prayed, indicating that if they did not pray, they were to be fought. He also explained that they would delay prayer beyond its appointed time. This constitutes a failure to observe it faithfully, not its abandonment.

Once the distinction between these two matters is understood, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, placed only those who failed to observe the prayers faithfully under Allah’s will, not those who abandoned them. The very reference to faithful observance implies that they prayed but failed to observe the prayers faithfully; it does not include those who failed to observe them faithfully. For if it did include such a case, they would undoubtedly be put to death as disbelievers and apostates.

It is inconceivable in ordinary circumstances that a man who believes in his heart, acknowledges that Allah has made prayer obligatory upon him, and is committed to the law of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and what he brought, would refuse the ruler’s command to pray until he is put to death, yet still be a believer inwardly. Such a man can only be a disbeliever. Even if he were to say, “I acknowledge that it is obligatory, but I do not perform it,”

---

## Page 3651

such a statement, given his conduct, would be a lie on his part. It would be like someone throwing a copy of the Quran into a latrine while saying, “I testify that its contents are Allah’s words,” or setting about killing a prophet while saying, “I testify that he is Allah’s Messenger,” or committing similar acts incompatible with faith in the heart. If someone acting in this way says, “I am a believer in my heart,” his outward declaration is a lie.

This point deserves careful reflection. Whoever understands the connection between the outward and the inward will have his doubts concerning this matter dispelled. He will recognize that any jurist who says that someone who acknowledges the obligation of prayer but refuses to perform it should not be put to death—or should be put to death while remaining a Muslim—has been affected by the same misconception that affected the Murji’ah and the Jahmiyyah, and those who hold that firm resolve, together with full ability, may produce no action at all. Thus, those jurists who opposed putting such a person to death based their position on their view concerning “the question of faith”: that deeds are not part of faith.

It has already been explained that deeds, as a category, necessarily accompany faith in the heart, and that complete faith in the heart without any outward deeds is impossible, whether outward deeds are regarded as a necessary consequence of faith or as part of faith, as explained earlier. Accordingly, when a servant performs some of what he has been commanded to do and leaves some undone, he possesses faith in proportion to what he has done. Faith increases and decreases, and faith and hypocrisy may coexist in a servant.

As is established from him in the Sahīh, he said:

“Four traits, whoever possesses them all is a pure hypocrite; whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted with something, he betrays the trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he transgresses all bounds.”

---

## Page 3652

This dispels the confusion concerning this matter. Many people—indeed, most people in many towns—neither regularly observe the five daily prayers nor abandon them altogether. Rather, they sometimes pray and sometimes neglect prayer. Such people possess both faith and hypocrisy, and the outward legal rulings of Islam apply to them regarding inheritance and similar matters. If these rulings apply to an outright hypocrite—such as Ibn Ubayy and other hypocrites like him—then they apply to these people with still greater reason.

Clarifying “this point” helps dispel the confusion. Many jurists suppose that anyone described as an unbeliever must be subject to the rulings governing someone who has openly apostatized: he may neither inherit nor be inherited from, nor enter into marriage with Muslims. They have even applied these rulings to adherents of innovation whom they declared unbelievers on the basis of interpretation. Yet this is not the case. It is established that people fell into “three categories”: a believer; an unbeliever who openly professed unbelief; and a hypocrite who outwardly professed Islam while concealing unbelief.

Among the hypocrites were some whom people recognized through signs and indications—indeed, some whose hypocrisy they did not doubt, and whose hypocrisy the Quran had revealed, such as Ibn Ubayy and others like him. Nevertheless, when these people died, their Muslim heirs inherited from them; and when a relative of theirs died, they were given their share of the inheritance. Their lives remained protected unless one of them became liable to punishment under the revealed law.

When the Harūriyyah rose against ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and separated themselves from the Muslim community, he told them:

“You have the right that we neither bar you from the mosques nor withhold your share of the public revenues (fay’).”

But when they deemed it lawful to kill Muslims and seize their property, he fought them at the command of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace;

---

## Page 3653

for he said:

“One of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Thus, fighting the Harūriyyah was established by the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the agreement of his Companions. Fighting them was not a battle of civil strife like the fighting that occurred between two great groups of Muslims. Rather, it is established in an authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his son al-Hasan:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great groups of Muslims.”

He also said in an authentic hadith:

“A renegade faction will break away at a time of division among the Muslims, and the nearer of the two groups to the truth will kill them.”

This indicates that al-Hasan’s decision to refrain from fighting was either obligatory or recommended, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have praised him for abandoning something obligatory or recommended. The other hadith indicates that those who fought the Khawārij—namely, ‘Alī and his companions—were nearer to the truth than Mu‘āwiyah and his companions. It also indicates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded fighting the Khawārij. Fighting them was not like the fighting at the Battle of the Camel and at Siffīn, for which there was no command from the Prophet.

The point is that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others among his companions did not declare them unbelievers, nor did they fight them until the Khawārij initiated hostilities against them. Scholars have differed over declaring the adherents of religious innovations and deviant inclinations unbelievers and over their remaining eternally in the Fire. “Two views” on this matter have been reported from every one of the imams

---

## Page 3654

such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others. Some of their followers came to present this disagreement as applying to all adherents of religious innovation and to their remaining eternally in the Fire, even going so far as to maintain that every particular individual they considered an innovator would remain there forever. This involves countless errors. At the opposite extreme, others came to think that no adherent of deviant inclinations could be declared an unbeliever, even if they espoused heresy and the doctrines of those who deny the divine attributes and those who teach union between Creator and creation.

The correct understanding of this matter is as follows:

A statement may constitute unbelief—as with the doctrines of the Jahmiyyah, who said that Allah does not speak and will not be seen in the Hereafter—yet some people may not realize that it constitutes unbelief. A general declaration is made that whoever utters it is an unbeliever, as the early generations said:

“Whoever says, ‘The Quran is created,’ is an unbeliever, and whoever says, ‘Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter,’ is an unbeliever.”

Yet a particular individual is not judged an unbeliever until the proof has been established against him, as explained earlier. This is like someone who, on the basis of an interpretation, denies the obligation of prayer and zakat or considers wine and illicit sexual intercourse lawful. These rulings are far more widely known among Muslims than the doctrinal matters just mentioned. If someone whose interpretation of those rulings is mistaken is not judged an unbeliever until the matter has been explained to him and he has been called upon to repent—as the Companions did with the group who considered wine lawful—then this applies all the more to other matters.

This is also the basis for understanding the authentic hadith about the man who said:

“When I die, burn me, then grind me to powder in the sea. By Allah, if Allah has power over me, He will punish me as He has punished no one in all creation.”

Allah forgave this man despite his doubt about Allah’s power and His restoring him to life if they burned him. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 3655

If it is asked:

“Allah has commanded striving against the unbelievers and the hypocrites in two verses of the Quran. If the hypocrite is outwardly subject to the rulings of Islam, how can one strive against him?”

The answer is that whatever faith or hypocrisy becomes firmly established in the heart must manifest its effects in speech and action. As one of the early generations said:

“No one conceals anything within himself without Allah revealing it in his facial expressions and slips of the tongue.”

Allah Most High says concerning the hypocrites:

“If We willed, We could show them to you, and you would recognize them by their marks; but you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech.”

Thus, if a hypocrite openly neglects obligations or commits prohibited acts in a manner that warrants punishment, he is punished for his outward conduct. He is not punished for what is known of his inward state without outward evidence. Hence, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knew those hypocrites whom Allah had identified to him. They would swear oaths to him while lying, yet he accepted their outward professions and entrusted their inner secrets to Allah.

The very foundation upon which hypocrisy rests is that the hypocrite’s private and public selves, his outward and inward states, necessarily differ. This is why Allah describes them in His Book as liars, just as He describes the believers as truthful. Allah Most High says:

“They will suffer a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

And He says:

“Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars.”

There are many similar passages. Allah Most High also says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truly sincere.”

And He says:

“Righteousness is not that you turn your faces towards the east or the west”—up to His words—“It is they who have been truthful, and it is they who are mindful of Allah.”

In brief, the fundamental principle underlying these issues is to understand that unbelief is of two kinds: overt unbelief

---

## Page 3656

and the unbelief of hypocrisy. In rulings pertaining to the Hereafter, the hypocrite has the same status as the unbelievers. In worldly rulings, however, the rulings applicable to Muslims may apply to the hypocrite.

It has become clear that religion necessarily involves both speech and action. It is impossible for someone to believe in Allah and His Messenger in his heart, or in both his heart and his speech, while performing no outward obligation whatsoever—neither prayer, nor zakat, nor fasting, nor any other obligatory duty. Performing such duties, but not because Allah has made them obligatory—for example, returning a trust, speaking truthfully, or acting justly in one’s allocations and judgments, without faith in Allah and His Messenger—does not bring a person out of unbelief. For the polytheists and the People of the Book also regard these things as obligatory. Thus, a person cannot be a believer in Allah and His Messenger while performing none of the duties uniquely enjoined by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Anyone who maintains that the faith which is obligatory can be attained without performing any obligatory deeds is plainly mistaken, whether he regards performing those duties as a necessary consequence of faith or as part of it—this distinction is merely verbal. This is the innovation of irjāʾ, whose adherents the early generations and the imams denounced so vehemently, making the well-known stern pronouncements concerning it. Prayer is the greatest, most universal, foremost, and most exalted of these duties.

## Page 3657

As for ihsān (excellence), it is explained in his words:

## Page 3658

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

Among the principles discussed earlier, I explained that “Islam”—the religion of Allah with which He revealed His Books and sent His messengers—means that the servant submits to Allah, Lord of all worlds. He surrenders to Allah alone, without partner, and devotes himself exclusively to Him, worshipping Him and no other. This is made clear by the finest of words and the foundation of Islam: the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah.

Islam has two opposites: arrogance and associating partners with Allah. Thus, it is reported that “Noah, peace be upon him, enjoined his sons to declare, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’ and ‘Glory be to Allah,’ and forbade them arrogance and associating partners with Allah,” in a hadith I have cited elsewhere. Whoever is too arrogant to worship Allah does not worship Him and therefore does not surrender to Him. Whoever worships Him and also worships another associates a partner with Him and therefore is not exclusively devoted to Him; rather, his devotion is divided.

The word “Islam” encompasses submission and purity of devotion, which is sincerity. It is known that all the messengers were sent with Islam in its general sense, which encompasses these meanings. As Allah Most High says:

“The prophets who submitted to Allah judged by it.”

Moses said:

“If you believe in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you have submitted to Him.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with

his Lord.”

Joseph said:

“Cause me to die as a Muslim.”

There are many similar passages.

It is known that Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, is the leader of the upright Muslim monotheists who came after him. “The Jews have incurred Allah’s anger, and the Christians have gone astray.”

Each of these two communities departed from Islam and became predominantly characterized by one of its two opposites. Arrogance predominates among the Jews, while associating partners with Allah is less common among them. Among the Christians, associating partners with Allah predominates, while arrogance is less common.

Allah has explained this in His Book, saying concerning the Jews:

“And when We took the covenant from the Children of Israel: ‘Worship none but Allah.’”

This is the foundation of Islam. The passage continues up to His words:

“And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear signs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?”

This interrogative wording expresses condemnation of their conduct and blame for it. They are blamed only for what they actually did. Thus, it is clear that whenever a messenger came to them with something contrary to the desires of

## Page 3660

their souls, they grew arrogant, killing some prophets and rejecting others. Such is the condition of an arrogant person who refuses to accept whatever does not accord with his desires. In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained arrogance as rejecting the truth and looking down on people. In Sahīh Muslim, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No one with an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire, and no one with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.”

He replied, “No. Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Rather, arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.”

Rejecting the truth means denying and repudiating it; looking down on people means despising and belittling them. Allah likewise mentions “arrogance” in the passage beginning with His words:

and continuing to His words:

“I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right. Even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. If they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as their way; but if they see the way of error, they will take it as their way.”

Such is the condition of someone who does not act upon his knowledge but instead follows his desires: he is one who goes astray. As Allah says:

“Relate to them the account of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but who cast them off. Satan then pursued him, and he became one of those who went astray. Had We willed, We would have elevated him through them, but he clung to earthly life and followed his desires.”

And so the verse continues. This is the likeness of corrupt scholars. Concerning Moses’s return to them, Allah said:

“When Moses’s anger subsided, he took up the Tablets, and in their inscription were guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord.”

Those who stand in awe of their Lord are the opposite of those who follow their desires. As Allah Most High says:

## Page 3661

Thus, those arrogant people who follow their desires are turned away from Allah’s signs: they neither know nor understand. “I am your supreme lord.”

“So Allah seized him in exemplary punishment for the last and the first.”

That is, punishment for the first statement and punishment for the last. Inwardly, Pharaoh knew that the Creator existed; he merely acted arrogantly, like Iblīs, and denied His existence. Hence Moses said to him:

“You certainly know that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these signs as clear proofs.”

When he denied the Creator, he continued worshipping the deities he already worshipped. Allah Most High did not describe him as associating partners with Him, but rather as denying the Creator and worshipping other deities. Those among them who deny the Creator are arrogant: they often worship deities, yet never worship Allah.

Such a person says, “This world is necessarily existent in itself, and some of its parts exert an influence upon others.” He also says that he has benefited only through worshipping heavenly bodies, idols, and the like. Thus, the underlying meaning of the doctrine of these advocates of union who claim affiliation with Islam is the doctrine of Pharaoh.

---

## Page 3667

I used to explain that this was their doctrine and that it was the true substance of Pharaoh’s doctrine, until a trustworthy man reported to me that one of their leaders in falsehood had said, “We follow Pharaoh’s doctrine.” Hence the immense veneration they show Pharaoh in their books.

They do not acknowledge a Maker who created the world, nor do they affirm a Lord who governs created beings. Rather, they make nature itself the Maker. Thus they permit the worship of anything, saying that whoever worships it has worshipped Allah. In their view, worshipping anything other than Allah is inconceivable: whatever is worshipped is Allah. These existing things, they believe, are His parts or attributes, like a human being’s parts or attributes. When these people worship existing things, therefore, they do not worship them to bring them nearer to Allah, but because, in their view, they are Allah, a locus of His manifestation, one of His parts, one of His attributes, or one of His particular determinations.

These people worship what Pharaoh and other polytheists worship. But Pharaoh does not say, “They are Allah,” nor, “They bring us nearer to Allah.” The polytheists say, “They are our intercessors and bring us nearer to Allah,” whereas these people say, “They are Allah,” as explained above. Those others are greater in unbelief insofar as they acknowledged that they worshipped something other than Allah or denied Him. These people, however, are more far-reaching in their error insofar as they permit the worship of anything, claiming that it is Allah and that the worshipper is the one worshipped—even if they intended only to worship Allah.

Given that those others were polytheists, as they have been described, whereas the Pharaoh of Moses’s time was the one who denied the Maker and worshipped other deities, without Allah describing him as a polytheist, it is clear that polytheists may love their deities as they love Allah, or may love them more than they love Allah. Hence they revile Allah when their deities are reviled, as the Most High says:

“Do not insult

---

## Page 3668

those whom they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in hostility without knowledge.”

Pharaoh’s people may have turned away from Allah altogether after previously associating partners with Him, accepting Pharaoh’s declarations:

“I am your lord, the Most High,”

and:

“I know of no god for you other than myself.”

Thus, when the believer addressed them, he mentioned both matters, saying:

“You call me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge.”

He mentioned disbelief in Him, which may include denying His existence, and also mentioned associating partners with Him. His words thus encompassed both positions and both states.

It has therefore become clear that one way an arrogant person becomes a polytheist is by worshipping other deities while arrogantly refusing to worship Allah. Calling this polytheism, however, is analogous to doing so in the case of someone who arrogantly refuses to devote his worship exclusively to Allah. As the Most High says:

“Indeed, whenever it was said to them, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ they would grow arrogant and say, ‘Are we really to abandon our gods for a mad poet?’”

These people are both arrogant and polytheists; their arrogance consists in refusing to devote their worship exclusively to Allah. An arrogant person who does not outwardly acknowledge Allah, such as Pharaoh, is therefore greater in unbelief than they are. Iblīs, who commands and loves all of this and arrogantly refuses to worship and obey his Lord, is greater in unbelief than these people, even though he knows that Allah exists and knows His greatness—just as Pharaoh, too, knew that Allah exists.

Since religious innovations and sins constitute a branch of unbelief and derive from its branches, just as acts of obedience are all a branch of faith and derive from it, and since it is known that someone who knows the truth but does not follow it is wayward and resembles the Jews, whereas someone who worships Allah without knowledge or revealed law is misguided and resembles the Christians—as some of the early generations used to say:

“Whoever among the scholars becomes corrupt

---

## Page 3669

bears a resemblance to the Jews; and whoever among the worshippers becomes corrupt bears a resemblance to the Christians.”

A Muslim must therefore guard against these two blameworthy resemblances: resembling people whose arrogance and hardness of heart turn them away from worship and devotion, despite having been given a share of the Scripture and a measure of knowledge; or resembling people who engage in worship and devotion while associating partners with Allah and straying from His path, revelation, and law. He has placed compassion and mercy in their hearts, and they have invented monasticism. This is common and widespread among people, though the resemblance is sometimes slight and sometimes strong.

As for the arrogant who devote themselves to others besides Allah, who do not worship Allah but worship others solely to derive benefit from them, these resemble Pharaoh.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—also said:

Section

The term “Islam” is used in two ways: transitively, as in His words:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while doing good?”

And His words:

“Say, ‘I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me.’ And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, ‘Have you submitted yourselves?’”

And the rest of the verse. Likewise, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said in his supplication before sleep:

“I have submitted myself to You.”

It is also used intransitively, as in His words:

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

And His words:

“To Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth.”

And His words concerning Bilqīs:

“I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds.”

It encompasses two meanings: first, obedience and submission; second, directing that submission sincerely and exclusively to Allah, as in His words:

“Allah presents an example: a man shared by quarrelling partners, and a man belonging exclusively to one man.”

Its defining declaration is, “There is no god but Allah.” It has two senses.

---

## Page 3671

The first is the religion common to all the prophets: worshipping Allah alone, without partner. All the prophets were sent with this religion, as the texts of the Quran and Sunnah establish that their religion was one.

The second is the religion, law, and way specific to Muhammad—the revealed law, the path, and the reality. This has two levels:

The first consists of outward words and deeds: the five pillars. The second is that these outward expressions accord with the inward state. The two verses in Allah’s Book and the two hadiths from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—use the first interpretation. In this sense, Islam is broader than faith: every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer.

The second interpretation is intended in His words:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

And His words:

“And that is the upright religion.”

It is also intended in the Prophet’s words, “I command you to have faith in Allah,” which he explained through the practices of Islam. According to this interpretation, complete faith, religion, and Islam are equivalent. This is the only meaning understood by the Muʿtazilah.

A third meaning may also be intended: the perfection of Islam. This is expressed in his words:

“A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe.”

He has thus made others safe—that is, safe from himself.

As for the term “faith,” it is said that its original meaning is assent—though it is not synonymous with assent. Rather, it must be assent concerning something unseen; assenting to a report about something directly witnessed is not faith. This is because the word derives from security, meaning reassurance. This applies only to the one conveying a report, about whom doubt may arise, whereas things directly witnessed admit no doubt, except on this basis—then it is either assent by the heart alone, as maintained by

---

## Page 3672

the Jahmiyyah and those of the Ash‘ariyyah who follow them; or assent of both heart and tongue, as the Murji’ah maintain; or of the tongue alone, as the Karrāmiyyah maintain; or assent through the heart, speech, and deeds—for all of these fall within the meaning of assent according to the scholars of hadith, as Shaykh al-Islām and others explained (*).

It has also been said that faith is, rather, acknowledgment: assent applies only to a report, whereas acknowledgment applies to both a report and a command, as in His words:

“Do you acknowledge this and accept My covenant on that basis?” They said, “We acknowledge it.”

Moreover, qarra and āmana are close in meaning. Faith means entering into security, while acknowledgment means entering into acknowledgment. Accordingly, the spoken declaration is an acknowledgment, and acting upon it is also an acknowledgment.

In the Quran, faith is used in two senses, involving a foundation and an obligatory branch. The foundation is what lies in the heart, distinct from deeds. Hence the distinction between them in His words:

“Those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

The sense encompassing both occurs in His words:

“The believers are only…”

“Those who believe do not ask your permission.”

It also occurs in the hadith of “al-hayyā” and that of “the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays.”

Faith comprises an indispensable foundation; an obligatory element whose absence diminishes it in a manner that makes a person deserving of punishment; and a recommended element whose absence deprives a person of a higher rank. Thus, with respect to faith, people include those who wrong themselves, those who take a middle course, and those who are foremost. The same applies to Hajj, the body, a mosque, and other entities, deeds, and attributes.

Among its various components are those whose loss leaves it short of the highest perfection; those whose loss leaves it short of the required completeness, through neglecting obligations or committing prohibited acts; and those whose loss removes an essential pillar—namely, abandoning belief and speech, which the Murji’ah and Jahmiyyah claim alone constitute what is meant by faith. This resolves the misconceptions of the various sects.

Faith is rooted in the heart and perfected through outward deeds. Islam is the reverse: its foundation is outward, and its perfection lies in the heart.

It is well known that the foundation of “faith” is faith in Allah and His Messenger. This is also the foundation of knowledge of Allah, as I explained at the beginning of this volume (*).

As for “faith in Allah,” humanity at large has generally acknowledged it, apart from fringe sects such as the Dahrī philosophers, the Ismā‘īliyyah, and others like them, or those who hypocritically profess it while outwardly claiming adherence to the religions. ## Page 3674

in what he reports and submitting to him in what he commands—just as acknowledging Allah entails recognizing Him and worshipping Him. Hypocrisy frequently concerns one’s relationship with the Messenger, and this is the predominant form of hypocrisy that Allah mentions in the Quran concerning the hypocrites during his lifetime. Disbelief is the absence of faith, whether accompanied by denial, arrogance, refusal, or aversion. Whoever lacks affirmation and submission in his heart is therefore a disbeliever.

There are, then, “two kinds of hypocrisy”: hypocrisy among people of learning and speculative theology, and hypocrisy among people of religious practice and worship.

As for outright hypocrisy, whose perpetrator is unquestionably a disbeliever, it consists in not considering it obligatory to believe what the Messenger reports or to obey what he commands, even while believing that the Messenger possesses great knowledge and excellence in practice, and that believing and obeying him is permissible. Such a person nevertheless says that differences between religions do not matter so long as the One worshipped is the same. He holds that salvation and happiness can be attained both by following the Messenger and without following him—through philosophy and Sabianism, or through Judaism and Christianity. This is the position of the Sabian philosophers on this question and on others. For even if they believe and obey him, they do not consider this obligatory for everyone on earth, such that whoever fails to believe and obey him will be punished. Rather, they regard it as comparable to adhering to an imam’s school, following a shaykh’s path, or obeying a king. This is the religion of the Tatars and those who join them.

As for the lesser degree of hypocrisy, it consists in seeking knowledge of Allah independently of what the Messenger reports, or seeking to act for Allah independently of what he commands. Many speculative theologians are afflicted with the former, and many Sufis with the latter. They believe that he must be believed or that he must be obeyed, yet in their pursuit of knowledge

and practice, they do not follow this path, but take another: through analogical reasoning and rational inquiry, through spiritual experience and inward feeling, or through imitation. As for what has come from the Messenger, they either disregard it or subordinate it to the approach they have adopted.

Consider, then, the hypocrisy of these two groups, despite their inward and outward acknowledgment that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the most perfect and excellent of all creation, that he is a Messenger, and that he is the most knowledgeable of people. Yet if they do not regard following him as obligatory and consider it permissible not to follow him, they fall into disbelief. This is exceedingly common, but a detailed discussion of the ruling concerning such people belongs elsewhere.

## Page 3676

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Is there any spiritual station or state above faith in Allah and His Messenger? Does faith encompass every station and state commended by Allah and His Messenger? Is faith to be described as a light that Allah places in a servant’s heart, enabling him, when it enters his heart, to distinguish truth from falsehood?

Is there some means by which faith is first attained—such as seeing righteous people, sitting with them and keeping their company, learning to perform a particular act, or something else? If its initial attainment has a cause, what is that cause? And what are the means—in their proper order—by which faith is strengthened until it reaches perfection?

Should one begin with renunciation until one practices it soundly? Or with knowledge until one becomes firmly grounded in it? Or with worship until one has fully exerted oneself? Or should one combine these according to one’s ability? How, then, does one attain the reality of the faith praised by Allah and His Messenger?

Explain to us the means by which the reality of faith is attained, detailing their various kinds, and describe the person who possesses it—may Allah be pleased with you.

---

## Page 3677

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The term “faith” is used both without qualification and with qualification. When used without qualification, it encompasses everything Allah and His Messenger love of a servant’s inward and outward words and deeds. This is the understanding generally held by the early generations and leading scholars among the Companions, the Followers, and their followers, who hold that faith consists of words and deeds, increases through obedience, and decreases through disobedience. They include within its meaning all acts of obedience, both obligatory and voluntary. This is the position of the vast majority of scholars of hadith, Sufism, speculative theology, and jurisprudence among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

This includes what may be called spiritual stations and states, such as patience, gratitude, fear, hope, reliance upon Allah, contentment, reverent fear, turning to Allah, sincerity, affirming Allah’s oneness, and other such qualities.

Among the evidence for this is the hadith recorded in the two Sahīh collections, in which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Faith has sixty-odd—or seventy-odd—branches. The highest is the declaration that none is worthy of worship but Allah; the lowest is removing something harmful from the road; and modesty is a branch of faith.”

He thus mentioned the highest branch of faith: the declaration that none is worthy of worship but Allah. Nothing is better than this declaration, as reported in al-Muwattaʾ and elsewhere from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“The best supplication is the supplication on the Day of

---

## Page 3678

ʿArafah, and the best that I and the prophets before me have said is: ‘None is worthy of worship but Allah alone, with no partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

In al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, he is reported to have said:

“Whoever dies knowing that none is worthy of worship but Allah will enter Paradise.”

In the Sahīh, it is reported that he said to his uncle as death approached:

“My uncle, say, ‘None is worthy of worship but Allah’—a declaration with which I may plead your case before Allah.”

The evidence is abundant and mutually reinforcing that the greatest good deed is affirming Allah’s oneness, just as the worst evil deed is associating partners with Him. This is the sin that Allah does not forgive, as He, the Exalted, says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

Affirming His oneness is the good deed that necessarily brings bliss to the one who possesses it. This is established in the authentic hadith concerning the two determining causes: that which entails bliss and that which entails misery. Whoever dies testifying that none is worthy of worship but Allah will enter Paradise, whereas whoever dies associating anything with Allah will enter the Fire. In the hadith, he also described this declaration as the highest branch of faith.

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? It is to testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakat, and to pay one-fifth of the spoils.”

He thus included these deeds within faith, while also including them within Islam in the authentic hadith of Gabriel. When Gabriel came to him in the form of a Bedouin and asked him about faith, he replied:

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

He then asked him about Islam, and he replied:

“It is to testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah

---

## Page 3679

and to establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.” In a hadith in al-Musnad, he said:

“Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.”

The foundation of faith lies in the heart and consists of the heart’s affirmation and action—its acknowledgment through assent, love, and submission. Whatever is in the heart must manifest its necessary effects and implications in the limbs. If a person does not act accordingly, this indicates its absence or weakness. Thus, outward deeds are among the necessary effects and implications of the heart’s faith. They confirm, indicate, and bear witness to what is in the heart. They are a branch and a constituent part of faith considered in its entirety. Yet what is in the heart is the foundation of what the limbs do. As Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“The heart is a king, and the limbs are its soldiers. If the king is good, its soldiers are good; if the king is corrupt, its soldiers are corrupt.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“Indeed, there is a piece of flesh in the body: when it is sound, the rest of the body is sound because of it; and when it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt because of it. Indeed, it is the heart.”

For this reason, some groups thought that faith resides exclusively in the heart, and that the deeds of the limbs do not fall within its meaning, but are merely its fruits and consequences, which indicate its presence. Their extremists—such as Jahm and his followers—went so far as to say that a person may believe in his heart while uttering nothing but words of disbelief, despite being capable of making an outward profession, and that what is in his heart would nevertheless constitute faith that benefits him in the Hereafter. They also said that whenever the Lawgiver judges someone to be a disbeliever on account of a deed or statement, it is because that deed or statement indicates the absence of what is in the heart.

Their position is contradictory. If that is evidence necessarily entailing the absence of faith from the heart, then it is impossible for faith to be present in

---

## Page 3680

the heart alongside evidence that necessarily entails its absence. If, however, it is not evidence, it cannot be used to establish inward disbelief. Allah, glorified is He, explains in several places that faith is realized and confirmed through outward and inward deeds. For example, He says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

“Those who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them.”

“It is they who are truly believers.”

He also says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning their disputes, then find within themselves no unease over what you have decided and submit completely.”

If someone says, “This indicates that faith is absent when these things are absent; it does not indicate that they are part of faith,” the reply is: This is an acknowledgment that inward faith is absent when outward matters such as these are absent. Thus, one cannot claim that the heart can contain faith incompatible with disbelief without any outward manifestation, whether in speech or action. This is the point to be established—and that acknowledgment confirms it.

This is because, when what is in the heart is firmly established, it necessarily affects what is outward; the two cannot be separated. A firm resolve to act, together with full ability, necessarily brings about the action within one’s power. Thus, if love for Allah and His Messenger is firmly established in the heart, it necessarily entails loyalty to His allies

---

## Page 3681

and enmity toward His enemies.

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred.”

“Had they believed in Allah and the Prophet and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

This necessary connection is inescapable. Some have erred by supposing that no such connection exists, just as others have erred in considering it possible for a firm resolve to coexist with full ability without action. They have even disputed whether a person is punished for an intention without acting upon it.

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that an intention unaccompanied by whatever action the person is capable of performing is not a firm resolve. A firm resolve must be accompanied by whatever action lies within the person’s ability. Pardon applies to someone who contemplated an evil deed but has not committed it—not to someone who intended it, did what was within his power, but was unable to achieve his aim. An example is someone who intended to kill his companion and fought him until one of them was killed. Such a person is punished because he intended the deed and carried out whatever part of it was within his power. Whoever understands the necessary connections between inward and outward matters will be freed of many doubts concerning issues such as these, over which people have differed greatly.

One question remains: Does the term “faith” designate only the foundation, or both the foundation and its branches?

The precise answer is that the unqualified term encompasses both. When used in conjunction with another term, the name alone may be singled out for that designation; it may also encompass only the foundation when that alone is specified. The designation “tree,” for example, encompasses the root and branches when present. If the branches were cut off, the designation “tree” would encompass the root alone. Likewise, the designation “Hajj” encompasses everything prescribed within it, including essential pillars and obligatory acts

---

## Page 3682

and recommended acts. It remains a complete Hajj without the recommended acts, but is deficient when obligatory acts whose omission is compensated for by a sacrifice are left out.

The Lawgiver (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) does not deny a person’s faith for omitting something recommended, but for omitting something obligatory: the person has neglected what is required for faith’s perfection and completeness, not merely something recommended. The terms “perfection” and “completeness” may refer to either obligatory or recommended perfection. Thus, some jurists distinguish between a complete ritual bath and one that fulfills the minimum requirements. Accordingly, when the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) says:

“There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy,”

and:

“A person who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it,”

or makes similar statements, this is because something obligatory within faith is absent, not because its recommended perfection is absent.

Faith has constituent parts, and people differ in their degree of faith, just as they do in Hajj and prayer. Hence, he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Those with a speck’s weight of faith in their hearts, and those with a barley grain’s weight of faith, will be brought out of the Fire.”

When, however, the term “faith” is used with a qualification—as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,”

and His words:

“Those who believed and were mindful of Allah,”

and the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death,”

and similar expressions—it may be said that faith encompasses these matters, and that conjoining them to it is an instance of conjoining the particular to the general, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“and His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael,”

and His words:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

---

## Page 3683

Or it may be said that the meaning of a term varies according to whether it is used alone or alongside another term. This is the case with “the poor” and “the needy”: when either is used alone, it includes the other, but when they occur together, they denote two distinct categories, as in the verse on zakat. Undoubtedly, the branches of faith stand in relation to its foundations as two terms joined by a conjunction, while their relation to faith in its entirety is that of a part to the whole. This is where dispute and confusion have arisen over whether deeds are included in faith, since they are mentioned alongside it using a conjunction.

Similarly, some of faith’s higher branches or loftier forms, such as certainty and knowledge, may be mentioned alongside faith using a conjunction, suggesting a distinction between them. Thus, one may say, “This is the highest form of faith”—meaning that certainty and knowledge are higher than faith unaccompanied by such certainty and knowledge. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.”

It is well known that people differ in faith and affirmation themselves: in their strength and weakness, their breadth and specificity, their persistence and continuity, what they entail and what contradicts them, and other aspects. One of the two forms is therefore distinguished by a name indicating its superiority over the other, while in such usage the term “faith” continues to denote the other category. The same occurs in comparable cases, as when one says, “Human beings are better than animals,” or “Human beings are better than other living creatures,” even though human beings are included among the living creatures mentioned in His words:

“Indeed, the worst of living creatures in Allah’s sight are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.”

Once this is understood, wherever an acceptable statement describes something as superior to faith, it merely gives precedence to a particular form over faith in general, or to some of its higher branches over the rest,

---

## Page 3684

and the term “faith” may encompass both categories or be restricted to one of them, as explained above. As has been said, “Most disagreement among rational people arises from the terms they use.”

Section

As for the question, “Is the quality of faith a light that Allah casts into a servant’s heart, so that when it enters his heart, the servant recognizes truth and falsehood?” the answer is:

Allah Most High has said:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp.”

Ubayy ibn Ka‘b and others said, “The likeness of His light in the believer’s heart.” The passage continues up to His words:

“And whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

He Most High also says:

“Is one who was dead, then We gave him life and granted him a light by which to walk among people, like one who is in darkness?”

Thus, Allah called the faith He bestows upon His servant a light. The revelation sent down from heaven, through which faith is attained, is likewise called:

“A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

He Most High also says:

“So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him.”

There are other passages of this kind. Undoubtedly, the believer distinguishes truth from falsehood; indeed, he discerns the greatest truths. Yet it cannot be said that everyone who possesses faith can, merely through the faith he has been given, distinguish every truth from every falsehood.

---

## Page 3685

Section

As for his question, “Is there a cause for faith’s initial emergence?” undoubtedly, it arises through a cause: listening to the Quran; observing believers and reflecting on their lives; learning about the Prophet’s life and miracles—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and reflecting on them; contemplating the signs of Allah Most High; reflecting on one’s own circumstances; or experiencing the pressing needs that Allah brings upon a servant, compelling him to humble himself before Allah, surrender to Him, and seek refuge in Him.

One cause may bring about one aspect of faith, while another brings about another. Indeed, everything that occurs in the world must have a cause. The causes of faith and its branches sometimes come from the servant himself and sometimes from someone else. For example, Allah may provide someone with a person who calls him to faith, enjoins good upon him, forbids him from evil, and explains to him the signs, arguments, and proofs of the religion. There are also events that befall him, upon which he reflects and from which he takes admonition, along with other causes.

## Page 3686

Section

As for his question, “What are the means by which faith grows stronger until it reaches perfection, and in what order should they be pursued? Should one begin with renunciation, knowledge, or worship, or combine them according to one’s ability?”

The answer is: One must have the obligatory measure of faith, worship, and renunciation. Beyond that, people differ in their levels of faith just as they differ in its branches. Each person should pursue what is within his reach and give priority to the more excellent deeds he is capable of undertaking.

People differ in this regard. Some find acquiring knowledge easier than renunciation; others find renunciation easier; and still others find worship easier than either. What is prescribed for each person is to do whatever good he can, as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

When the branches of faith compete for his attention, he should give priority to what is more pleasing to Allah and what he is better able to perform. He may be more capable of performing a less excellent deed than a more excellent one, and may gain more from the former than from the latter. It is therefore better for him to pursue what benefits him more, since that is better in his particular case. He should not pursue what is better in absolute terms if it is beyond his ability or so difficult that it causes him to miss what is better and more beneficial for him.

An example is someone who recites the Quran at night, reflects upon it, and benefits from his recitation, whereas prayer is burdensome for him and he derives no benefit from performing it; or someone who benefits more from remembering Allah than from reciting the Quran.

---

## Page 3687

Thus, whatever deed is more beneficial to him and more obedient to Allah is better for him than forcing himself to undertake a deed that he performs inadequately rather than properly, thereby missing what would benefit him more.

It is well known that prayer is more emphatically enjoined than reciting the Quran, and that reciting the Quran is better than remembrance of Allah and supplication. It is also well known that remembrance of Allah in the particular acts to which it belongs—such as bowing and prostration—is better than reciting the Quran in those positions, and that remembrance, recitation, and supplication at sunrise and sunset are better than prayer.

Renunciation is the opposite of desire, just as hatred is opposed to love and aversion to willing. Both willing and aversion have various forms, whether considered in themselves or in relation to their objects. Renunciation, likewise, may be considered from two perspectives: what is renounced and renunciation itself.

As for the former, renunciation … (1)

As for renunciation itself, which is the opposite of desire and consists in aversion and hatred, its prescribed form consists in the servant’s aversion, hatred, and love being governed by Allah’s love, hatred, pleasure, and displeasure. He therefore loves what Allah loves, hates what Allah hates, is pleased with what Allah is pleased with, and is displeased with what Allah is displeased with. In this way, he follows not his own desires but his Master’s command.

Many who renounce worldly life have turned away from its excesses without turning toward what Allah and His Messenger love. Such renunciation is not what Allah and His Messenger command. Thus, there have been ascetics among the polytheists, among the People of the Book, and among the followers of religious innovation.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 3688

Some people renounce worldly life to find relief from its toil. Others do so to seek handouts from worldly people and escape their harm. Still others renounce wealth in pursuit of ease. These and similar forms of renunciation are not commanded by Allah or His Messenger. Rather, Allah and His Messenger command a person to renounce what they do not love and desire what they love. His renunciation thus consists in turning away from whatever Allah and His Messenger have not enjoined, whether as an obligation or a recommendation—whether it is forbidden, disliked, or permissible such that doing it and leaving it are equally preferable for that servant. At the same time, he must devote himself to what Allah and His Messenger have commanded.

Merely abandoning what is disliked without doing what is loved is not what is sought. The primary aim is to do what Allah and His Messenger love. Abandoning what is disliked is likewise necessary; through this the soul is purified. For good deeds flourish when evil deeds are removed from them. Through purification, the soul is cleansed of impurities and grows in obedience, just as crops, when cleared of weeds, flourish, rise, and grow.

Section

As for the way to attain this, it lies in striving to do what is commanded, abandoning what is forbidden, and seeking Allah’s help in doing so. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done this, such-and-such would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He has done what He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the way to the work of

---

## Page 3689

Satan.”

The Sunan collections relate:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled against a man, who then said, ‘Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Allah reproaches a person for helplessness, but you must act prudently. Then, if a matter overcomes you, say: “Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.”’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus commanded the servant to strive for what benefits him and to seek Allah’s help in doing so. Striving for what benefits him means exerting himself in goodness, which is worship. For the servant is commanded to seek everything that benefits him. He is only forbidden to seek what harms him—even if he believes it benefits him—as when he seeks forbidden things, which harm him, or pursues an inferior course that does not benefit him.

Allah Most High has permitted believers wholesome things, which benefit them, and forbidden them unwholesome things, which harm them. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

## Page 3690

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah bless his resting place—said:

Section

As for faith: is it created or uncreated?

The answer is that disagreement over this issue arose when the Jahmiyyah’s inquisition began over whether the Quran was created or uncreated. This was the ordeal suffered by Imam Ahmad and other Muslim scholars. Much occurred during it that would take too long to describe here.

However, when the position that the Quran is Allah’s uncreated speech prevailed, and Allah extinguished the fire of the Jahmiyyah, who deny His attributes, a group began saying that the speech Allah had sent down was created. They expressed this in terms of “utterance,” saying, “Our utterances of the Quran are created,” or, “Our recitation,” or, “Our reading is created.” They did not mean merely their own speech and movements; rather, they included in their statement the very speech of Allah, which we recite with our voices and movements.

Another group opposed them, saying, “Our utterances of the Quran are uncreated.” Imam Ahmad refuted both groups, saying: “Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ is a Jahmī; and whoever says, ‘It is uncreated,’ is an innovator.”

---

## Page 3691

People then began discussing faith. One group said, “Faith is created,” including in this what Allah had spoken concerning faith, such as the statement, “There is no god but Allah.” Their position thus implied that this very statement was created and that Allah had not spoken it. Imam Ahmad declared these people innovators and said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Faith has sixty-odd branches, the highest of which is saying, “There is no god but Allah.”’ Can the statement ‘There is no god but Allah’ then be created?”

His meaning was that whoever declared this statement created without qualification thereby implied that Allah had not spoken it. Likewise, whoever said, “Our utterances, recitation, and reading of the Quran are created,” thereby implied that Allah had not spoken the Quran He sent down; that the revealed Quran was not Allah’s speech; that Gabriel had brought down something created, not Allah’s speech; and that Muslims were reading a created Quran that was not Allah’s speech.

Yet it is necessarily known as part of the religion of Islam that the Quran Muslims read is the speech of Allah Most High, even when it is heard from someone conveying it on His behalf. For speech may be heard from the one who speaks it, as Moses heard it without an intermediary. This is hearing in an unqualified sense, just as one may see something in an unqualified sense. Or it may be heard from someone conveying it on the speaker’s behalf, in which case it is heard in a qualified sense—just as something is seen in water or a mirror in a qualified, rather than unqualified, sense. Or, as the Most High said:

“And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah.”

Everyone addressed by the Quran understood that he would hear it in a qualified sense from the person conveying it; what was meant was not that he would hear it from Allah.

Some of these people said that one hears the reciter’s voice from Allah. Among these, in turn, are those who

---

## Page 3692

say that the Lord’s voice has come to dwell within the servant. Others say that it has become manifest in him without dwelling within him. Others say, “I say neither that it has become manifest nor that it has come to dwell within him.” Others say that the voice heard is uncreated, or eternal. Still others say that two voices are heard from him: one created and one uncreated.

Among those who say that it is heard from Allah are those who maintain that one hears the eternal meaning subsisting in the Lord’s essence while also hearing the newly produced voice. These say that one hears both the eternal and the newly produced, just as the others say that one hears two voices, one eternal and one newly produced.

Another group said, “People have not heard Allah’s speech, either from Allah or from anyone else.” They argued that speech can be heard only from its speaker. Some of these said that a reproduction of it is heard; others said that an expression of it is heard, not a reproduction. Among those who say that it is created are those who said, “Two things are heard: the created speech; the one who created it; and the servant’s voice.”

All these positions are invented innovations. The early generations held none of them, and all are false according to both revelation and reason. Yet those who held them were driven to them by ambiguity in words and confusion over meanings.

When someone says, “I heard Zayd’s speech,” or, “This is Zayd’s speech,” this refers to the speech he uttered, in both its wording and its meaning, whether it is heard from him or from someone conveying it on his behalf. The distinction between the two situations is nevertheless understood: when it is heard from him, it is heard in his voice; when it is heard from someone else, it is heard in the voice of the person conveying it, not in the original speaker’s voice, even though the wording is that of the original speaker.

With an accompanying indication, one may also say, “This is so-and-so’s speech,” even when it has been translated into different wording. Thus Allah recounts in Arabic the speech of people from the various nations whose words He relates, even though they originally spoke in Hebrew or Syriac

---

## Page 3693

or Coptic or another language. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that disagreement arose among the people of Sunnah and hadith over “the two issues of the Quran and faith” because of ambiguous expressions and meanings liable to confusion. A group of scholars who adhered to the Sunnah, including al-Bukhārī, the compiler of al-Sahīh, Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī, and others, said, “Faith is created.” They did not mean any of Allah’s attributes by this. Rather, they meant the actions of His servants. The imams of the Muslims agreed that the actions of Allah’s servants are created. Yahyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qattān said, “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The actions of Allah’s servants are created.’”

Some people came to think that al-Bukhārī and these scholars had opposed Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah. Al-Bukhārī suffered an ordeal because of this, and some liars even claimed that, when al-Bukhārī died, Ahmad ibn Hanbal ordered that no funeral prayer be offered for him. This is an obvious lie, for Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Bukhārī—may Allah have mercy on him—died about fifteen years after Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with him—died in 241 AH, whereas al-Bukhārī died in 256 AH. Ahmad ibn Hanbal loved al-Bukhārī and held him in great esteem and respect. As for the esteem in which al-Bukhārī and others like him held Imam Ahmad, this is well known.

When al-Bukhārī composed his book on the creation of the actions of Allah’s servants and included chapters on this subject at its end, he mentioned that both groups—those who say that our utterance of the Quran is created and those who say that it is uncreated—are affiliated with Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal

Yet another group—including Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm and others who likewise say that they follow Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the other imams of the Sunnah—together with still others who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah and the school of hadith, claim to hold the creed of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other such adherents of the Sunnah.
