Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other leading scholars. Al-Khallāl also recorded this in his book al-Sunnah (The Sunnah), and Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Battah recorded some of it in al-Ibānah (The Elucidation). Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mandah likewise recorded much of it in his writings on “the question of utterance.”

Abū Muhammad ibn Qutaybah al-Dīnawarī said: “The people of hadith did not differ over any aspect of their creed except the question of utterance.” Ibn Qutaybah then explained that lafz (“utterance”) can denote the act of uttering, as the verbal noun of “to utter”; it can also denote speech itself, which is the servant’s act and voice and is created. As for Allah’s own speech, which His servants utter, it is not created.

Likewise, regarding “the question of faith,” Ahmad ibn Hanbal never said that faith is uncreated. Nor did Ahmad or any other member of the early generations say that the Quran is eternal. Rather, they said: “The Quran is Allah’s speech, revealed and uncreated.” Neither Ahmad ibn Hanbal nor anyone among the early generations said that any of the servant’s attributes or actions are uncreated—not his voice when reciting the Quran, his utterance of the Quran, his faith, his prayer, or anything of that kind.

Later scholars, however, split into many groups over this matter. Among those who said, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” some also stated without qualification that faith is uncreated. Others described both utterance and faith as eternal. Some distinguished between verbal expressions of faith and deeds, saying that the verbal expressions are uncreated and eternal, whereas the deeds of faith are created.

Concerning deeds pertaining to faith, some say that those which are forbidden are created. As for acts of obedience, such as prayer and the like, some say that they are uncreated, while others withhold judgment and do not say that they are

---

## Page 3696

created or uncreated. Some withhold judgment concerning forbidden deeds. Others say: “Rather, all the deeds of Allah’s servants are uncreated, or eternal.” Such a person says: “By deeds I do not mean bodily movements; rather, I mean the reward that will come on the Day of Resurrection.” He argues that divine decree is uncreated and divine legislation is uncreated, identifying the servants’ deeds with divine decree and legislation. He does not distinguish between the decree and what is decreed, or between legislation and what is prescribed. Divine legislation, meaning Allah’s commands and prohibitions, is uncreated; the deeds commanded or forbidden, however, are undoubtedly created. Likewise, divine decree, meaning His knowledge, will and speech, is uncreated; but the things decreed—lifespans, provisions and deeds—are all created. These views and their proponents have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that Imam Ahmad, the imams of the Sunnah who preceded him, and those who followed him are all free of these innovated doctrines that contradict revealed law and reason. None of them said that the Quran is eternal—whether as a meaning subsisting in the Divine Essence, or that He uttered it in pre-eternity with letters and sound, or that He uttered it in pre-eternity with eternal letters. None of them said any of these things. What they agreed upon is that Allah’s speech is revealed and uncreated, that Allah, exalted is He, has always spoken whenever He wills, and that His speech has no end. As Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted.’”

It is eternal in the sense that Allah has always spoken by His will, not in the sense that any particular sound is eternal. Elsewhere I have discussed at length the differing views of the people of the earth concerning the speech of Allah, exalted is He. Some regard it as an emanation from the Active Intellect upon

---

## Page 3697

souls, as held by a group of Sabians and philosophers. This is the most unsound of these views. Others say that it is created, and that He created it separate from Himself, as held by the Jahmiyyah, Najjāriyyah and Mu‘tazilah. Others say that it is an eternal meaning subsisting in the Divine Essence, as held by Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash‘arī. Others say that it consists of letters and sounds, as held by Ibn Sālim and a group of others. Still others say that He began to speak after not having spoken, as held by Ibn Karrām and a group of others.

The correct view among these is that of the early generations and the imams, whose statements I have presented at length elsewhere.

When the Inquisition arose, Ahl al-Sunnah maintained that Allah’s speech is uncreated, whereas the “Jahmiyyah,” including the Mu‘tazilah and others, maintained that it is created. Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb al-Qattān was a man of merit and learning. He used his knowledge to refute the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah who denied the divine attributes, and explained that Allah Himself is above the Throne, discussing this at length. Yet he did not entirely free himself from the specious argument of the Jahmiyyah. Rather, he supposed that the Lord cannot be characterized by acts of choice dependent on His power and will. Thus, He does not speak by His will and power, nor does He come to love a servant and be pleased with him after his faith and obedience, or become angry and displeased with him after his disbelief and disobedience. Rather, He loves and is pleased with those whom He knows will die as believers, or is angry and displeased with those whom He knows will die as unbelievers. Nor does He utter one statement after another.

Yet Allah, exalted is He, has said:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus in the sight of Allah is that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“So when they provoked Our anger, We exacted retribution from them.”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked what pleased Him, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

---

## Page 3698

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne.”

This is a fundamental matter that has been discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is merely to draw attention to the grounds for disagreement among Muslims over “issues such as these.” Once this is understood, we must affirm what the Quran and Sunnah affirm and deny what the Quran and Sunnah deny.

An ambiguous expression that does not occur in the Quran and Sunnah must not be applied affirmatively or negatively until its intended meaning is clarified. Thus, if someone says, “The Lord occupies space,” or “does not occupy space,” or “He is in a direction,” or “is not in a direction,” the response is: These expressions are ambiguous. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah uses them, whether affirmatively or negatively, nor did any of the Companions or those who followed them in righteousness affirm or deny them.

If by your statement you mean that something created encompasses Him, that it is not He who upholds the Throne and its bearers by His power, and that He is not the Most High, the Most Exalted, the Most Great, the Magnificent—whom no vision can encompass, while He encompasses all vision, and who, glorified is He, is greater than all things—then He does not occupy space in this sense. But if you mean that He is distinct from His creatures, exalted above them, above His heavens and over His Throne, then He, glorified is He, is indeed distinct from His creation. This was stated by the imams of the Sunnah, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and other leading figures of Islam. It is also established by authentic transmitted evidence and clear reason, as explained at length elsewhere.

The same applies to the expression “direction”: if by direction one means an existing entity that encompasses the Creator, or

---

## Page 3699

on which He depends, then everything that exists other than Allah is created. Allah is the Creator of all things; everything besides Him is dependent upon Him, while He has no need of anything besides Himself. But if he means that Allah, glorified is He, is above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation, then this is correct, whether expressed using the word “direction” or otherwise.

The same applies to the expression “compulsion.” If someone asks, “Is the servant compelled or not?” the response is: If by compulsion he means that the servant has no will, no power, or no action of his own, then this is false. The servant performs his voluntary actions through his own power and will. But if by compulsion he means that He is the Creator of the servant’s will, power, and action, then Allah, exalted is He, is indeed the Creator of all these.

If someone asks, “Is faith created or uncreated?” he should be asked: What do you mean by “faith”? Do you mean something belonging to Allah’s attributes and speech, such as His saying, “There is no god but Allah,” and His “īmān” (affirmation of truth), indicated by His name al-Mu’min (the Affirmer of Truth)? If so, it is uncreated. Or do you mean something belonging to the servants’ actions and attributes? The servants are all created, and all their actions and attributes are created. A servant who was brought into existence and created cannot possess an eternal, uncreated attribute. No one who understands what he is saying would claim this.

Once clarification is sought and the distinctions are made, guidance becomes evident and the way becomes clear. It has been said: Most disagreements among rational people arise from words having more than one meaning. In these and similar matters over which people frequently dispute, affirming or denying them, a precise explanation distinguishes error from what is correct. People are obliged to affirm whatever the Book and the Sunnah affirm, and whatever is negated by the Book

---

## Page 3700

and the Sunnah, they must negate. Regarding anything that the Book and the Sunnah neither affirm nor deny, they must ask the speaker to clarify what he means. Whoever affirms what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed is correct, and whoever denies what Allah and His Messenger have denied is correct. But whoever affirms what Allah has denied, or denies what Allah has affirmed, has mixed the religion of truth with falsehood. He must therefore distinguish the truth in his words from the falsehood, follow the truth, and abandon the falsehood.

Whatever contradicts the Book and the Sunnah also contradicts sound reason, for sound reason does not contradict authentic revelation, just as the teachings transmitted from the prophets, peace be upon them, do not contradict one another. Yet many people imagine that these contradict one another. Such people are among those who differ over the Scripture:

“Indeed, those who differ over the Scripture are in deep discord.”

We ask Allah to guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favor—the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

## Page 3701

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

“Qualifying one’s profession of faith is Sunnah.”

This is the position of our scholars and most of Ahl al-Sunnah. The Murji’ah and the Mu‘tazilah, however, say that such qualification is impermissible, since it constitutes doubt.

Qualification means saying: “I am a believer, if Allah wills”; “I am a believer, I hope”; “I believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers”; or: “If by faith you mean that which renders my blood inviolable, then yes. But if you mean:

‘The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned,’

then Allah knows best.”

There are three views here. The first is that qualification is obligatory, so an unqualified assertion is impermissible. This view is stated by al-Qādī in ‘Uyūn al-Masā’il, among other sources. The second is that qualification is recommended, while an unqualified assertion is permissible from another standpoint. The third is that both are permissible, each from a particular standpoint. The statement that qualification is Sunnah means only that it is permissible, in refutation of those who prohibit it.

If we say that it is obligatory, al-Qādī’s reasoning is that, if we could categorically assert that we are believers, this would amount to categorically asserting that we are destined for Paradise, since Allah has promised Paradise to the believers. Yet we cannot categorically assert that the promise of Paradise applies to us, because this is conditional upon dying in faith, and only Allah knows that,

---

## Page 3702

and likewise, faith is only realized by remaining faithful until death, and this cannot be known.

For this reason, Ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Why did he not entrust the former to Allah, just as he entrusted the latter?” This refers to the report cited as evidence: a man said in his presence, “I am a believer.” Ibn Mas‘ūd was told, “This man claims that he is a believer.” He replied, “Then ask him whether he is in Paradise or in the Fire.” They asked him, and he said, “Allah knows best.” ‘Abd Allāh then said, “Why did you not entrust the first matter to Allah, just as you entrusted the second?”

I say: Further evidence for the obligation to qualify one’s profession of faith may be drawn from ‘Umar’s statement: “Whoever says that he is a believer is an unbeliever; whoever claims that he is in Paradise is in the Fire; and whoever claims that he is learned is ignorant.” When the opponent argued that qualification is needed only for a future event whose occurrence is uncertain, he replied: “The answer is that there is indeed a future event here whose occurrence is uncertain: dying in faith. The parts of faith are interconnected, so it is like a single act of worship.”

I say: In essence, this position holds that faith denotes an act of worship extending from the moment one enters it until one dies upon it. If it is invalidated, its beginning is shown to have been invalid—as when one loses ritual purity at the end of prayer, has intercourse at the end of Hajj, or eats at the end of a day of fasting. The unqualified designation “believer” implies fulfilling faith in its entirety, just as do the designations “one who prays,” “one who fasts,” and “one who performs Hajj.” This, then, is the basis of al-Qādī’s reasoning.

After this discussion in al-Mu‘tamad, he addresses the related “question of one’s state at death”: in the case of a believer whom Allah knows will die an unbeliever—and vice versa—do Allah’s pleasure and anger, love and hatred, relate to the person’s present state or to the state in which he dies? This question is connected to whether His pleasure and anger are eternal or arise anew.

---

## Page 3703

The second basis is that the designation, when used without qualification, implies completeness, which the speaker cannot know he possesses. Thus,

[Abū al-‘Āliyah said: “I met thirty of Muhammad’s Companions, all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves. Not one would say, ‘My faith is like Gabriel’s faith.’”] (1)

For a man to declare that his faith is complete is to make a claim about something he does not know. This is the meaning of Ibn al-Munazzil’s statement: “The Murji’ah say that their good deeds are accepted, whereas I do not testify to that.” This reasoning can support making qualification obligatory. It is also al-Qādī’s second basis: his opponent argued that, since qualifying one’s profession of Islam is impermissible, the same must apply to faith.

He replied: “The answer is that Islam consists simply of the two testimonies of faith, which he has pronounced, whereas faith comprises words and deeds, as indicated by the saying, ‘Faith has seventy-odd aspects.’ He cannot be certain that he has fulfilled them all.”

The third basis is that such a claim amounts to praising oneself, whereas Allah has said:

“So do not claim purity for yourselves.”

This can support recommending qualification; otherwise, a person may lawfully describe himself as he actually is, even if this entails praise. It may also support making qualification obligatory.

Al-Athram said in al-Sunnah: “Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated to us: ‘I heard Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd say: “Everyone among our companions whom I met or heard about qualified his profession of faith.”’” Al-Athram said: “I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked about qualifying one’s profession of faith: ‘What is your view of it?’ He replied: ‘As for me, I do not disapprove of it… (2) I qualify it out of fear and caution, not out of doubt, as they claim. Qualification concerns only deeds.’”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said: “Allah has said:

‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.’”

That is, this qualification does not express doubt. The Prophet also said

---

## Page 3704

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“And indeed, if Allah wills, we shall join you.”

That is, he had no doubt about this, yet he qualified his statement. He also mentioned the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“We shall be raised from the grave, if Allah wills.”

He also mentioned the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“Indeed, by Allah, I hope to be the one among you who fears Allah most.”

He said: “All of this supports qualifying one’s profession of faith.”

I said to Abū ‘Abd Allāh: “So it seems that you see no harm in omitting the qualification?” He replied: “If the person holds that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases, then I find this less objectionable.” Then Abū ‘Abd Allāh said: “Some people’s hearts are too weak to make this qualification.” He expressed amazement at them and spoke at length; I have omitted those remarks.

Ahmad’s words thus indicate that the qualification concerns deeds—this is the “second basis”—and that it does not arise from doubt about the foundation of faith. This resembles the “third basis” and implies that omitting the qualification is permissible.

As for saying without qualification, “I am a believer,” this is valid if one means the foundation of faith rather than its completeness, and having entered into it rather than having attained its fullness. Likewise, someone who has begun Hajj or fasting may say, “I am a pilgrim,” or “I am fasting.” The same applies to the unqualified statement, “I believe in Allah and His messengers,” and to the statement, “If you mean such-and-such…” The point is that permission to describe oneself using a verb entails permission to use the corresponding noun when the context makes the intended meaning clear.

On this basis, one may understand what is reported from a companion of Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, as well as the report of al-Hārith, who said, “I am truly a believer,” and the report of the delegation who said, “We are the believers”—although both chains of transmission are open to question.

---

## Page 3705

He was asked:

What is the meaning of the Prophet’s hadith—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“When a person commits unlawful sexual intercourse, faith leaves him and remains above his head like a canopy. When he ceases that act, faith returns to him.”

It was narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd. Is someone a believer while committing unlawful sexual intercourse, or not? Have any of the imams understood this hadith according to its apparent meaning, or have they unanimously agreed to interpret it otherwise?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Regarding a sinful Muslim—such as someone who commits unlawful sexual intercourse, steals, drinks alcohol, or the like—people fall into “three groups”: two extremes and a middle position.

One extreme holds that such a person is not a believer in any respect and is not included within the general scope of the rulings attached to the designation of faith. Some who hold this view say that he is a disbeliever, like a Jew or a Christian. This is the position of the Khawārij. Others say: “We assign him a position between the two positions: the position of a sinner, who is neither a believer nor a disbeliever.” These are the Muʿtazilah.

These groups maintain that those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever and that none of them will ever emerge from it. This is among the “doctrines of the people of innovation” contradicted by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. Allah Most High says:

“If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them.”

Then, further on, He says:

“The believers are but brothers, so make peace

---

## Page 3706

between your brothers.” Thus, He called them believers and designated them as brothers despite their fighting and the aggression of some against others. Allah Most High also says:

“Then a believing slave must be freed.”

If someone frees a sinful slave, that emancipation fulfills the requirement by scholarly consensus.

For this reason, the scholars of the early generations state in their formulations of creed: “We do not declare anyone among those who face the qiblah a disbeliever on account of a sin, nor do we exclude him from Islam on account of a deed.” Unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, and drinking alcohol were established against certain people during the Prophet’s lifetime—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—yet he did not treat them as disbelievers or sever the bonds of allegiance between them and the Muslims. Rather, he flogged one and cut off another’s hand, while seeking forgiveness for them and saying: “Do not help Satan against your brother.” All the rulings of Islam rest upon this principle.

The second extreme is the view of those who say: “Their faith remains just as it was, without diminishing.” This rests on the premise that faith is nothing more than assent and firm conviction, which have not changed; only their observance of Islam’s prescriptions has diminished. This is the position of the Murji’ah, the Jahmiyyah, and those who follow their path. It too contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the earliest Muslims and those who followed them in righteousness. Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He also says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned”—through to His words—“It is they who are truly believers.”

He also says:

“And it increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us.’”

And He says:

“So that they might increase in faith beyond the faith they already had.”

And He says:

“It has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.”

---

## Page 3707

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

He also said to the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? To testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and to pay one-fifth of whatever spoils you acquire.”

The early generations unanimously agreed that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases. This means the affirmation and actions of the heart, followed by the speech of the tongue and the deeds of the limbs. The heart’s affirmation is firm assent to Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, and the Last Day. This includes believing in everything the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought.

People differ in this respect. Some affirm it as a whole without knowing its details, while others affirm it both as a whole and in detail. Some remain constantly mindful of this affirmation and keep it present in their hearts, while others become heedless of it and lose awareness of it. Some gain clear insight into it through the light and faith Allah casts into their hearts. Others are firmly convinced on the basis of evidence against which a doubt might arise, or through firm reliance on the authority of others.

This affirmation is followed by the actions of the heart: loving Allah and His Messenger; venerating Allah and His Messenger; supporting and honoring the Messenger; fearing Allah; turning to Him in repentance; being sincere to Him; relying upon Him; and other such states. All these actions of the heart are part of faith. Affirmation and conviction necessarily give rise to them, just as a cause necessarily produces its effect. Conviction is followed by the speech of the tongue, and the heart’s actions are followed by bodily deeds, such as prayer, zakah, fasting, Hajj, and the like.

---

## Page 3708

In light of this, the balanced position—that of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah—is neither to deny the designation “believer” without qualification nor to confer it without qualification.

Thus we say: “He is a believer whose faith is deficient,” “a sinful believer,” or “a believer by virtue of his faith and an evildoer by virtue of his major sin.” It may also be said: “He is not a true believer,” or “His faith is not genuine.” Every statement made in the Quran and Sunnah must be accompanied by something that clarifies its intended meaning. Some rulings depend only on the foundation of faith, such as the validity of manumission as expiation, bonds of allegiance, mutual inheritance, and similar matters. Others depend on both its foundation and its branches, such as deserving praise and reward, forgiveness of sins, and similar matters.

With “this principle” understood, the report in the Sahīh records the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—as saying:

“A fornicator is not a believer at the time he commits fornication; a thief is not a believer at the time he steals; a person is not a believer at the time he drinks wine; and a person is not a believer at the time he seizes valuable plunder as people raise their eyes to him.”

The additional wording narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī is authentic and explains the well-known narration.

The questioner’s words, “Did any of the imams understand the hadith according to its apparent meaning?” can mean different things. If he means that its apparent meaning is that the fornicator becomes a disbeliever and is entirely stripped of faith, then none of the imams understood the hadith in this way. Nor is this its apparent meaning, because the words,

“Faith leaves him and is like a canopy above his head,”

are evidence that faith

---

## Page 3709

does not leave him entirely, for a canopy shades the person beneath it and remains attached and connected to him in some way. But if by its apparent meaning he means what is actually understood from it, as we shall explain, Allah willing, then yes.

The scholars of the early generations generally affirm these hadiths and let them stand as transmitted. They disapprove of interpretations that divert them from the intent of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Disapproval of interpreting the hadiths containing threats of punishment has been reported from Sufyān and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with them—and a great many other scholars. Ahmad explicitly stated that a hadith of this kind must not be interpreted in a way that diverts it from its intended apparent meaning.

Al-Khattābī and others have offered strained interpretations, such as their statement: “Its wording is declarative, but its meaning is prohibitive”—that is, a believer ought not to do such a thing. They also say: “Its purpose is to threaten and deter, not actually to negate faith.” They justify such wording by the resemblance and closeness between his condition and that of someone devoid of faith. They also say: “What is absent is only the perfection and completeness of faith, or its prescribed practices and fruits,” and so forth. The shortcomings of all these interpretations are plain to anyone who examines them closely.

The truth, then, is this: he has not lost the assent that distinguishes him from a disbeliever. Yet had this assent remained unchanged, he would affirm that Allah has forbidden this major sin, that He has threatened severe punishment for it, and that He sees and observes the person committing it. He—glorified and exalted is He—in His greatness, majesty, loftiness and grandeur, detests the person committing this act. If the person truly grasped all this, he could not commit the act. Whenever he commits this sin, therefore, one of “three things” must be present.

---

## Page 3710

Either his belief is unsound: he believes that the apparent meaning of the threat does not reflect its actual meaning and that its purpose is merely deterrence, as the Murji’ah maintain; or that this is forbidden only to ordinary people, not to the spiritual elite, as the Ibāhiyyah (antinomians) maintain; or he holds some similar belief that takes a person outside the fold of Islam.

Or he is heedless and oblivious to the prohibition, the greatness of the Lord, and the severity of His punishment.

Or his desire is so excessive that it overpowers what faith demands and prevents faith from producing its proper effect. His belief thus becomes submerged and overpowered, like reason in someone asleep or intoxicated, or the soul in someone asleep. Clearly, “faith”—faith in its true sense—does not remain as it was, for it is no longer firmly established and manifest in the heart. The unqualified designation “believer” applies only to someone whose faith remains intact and produces its effects.

In some respects, it resembles the soul of someone asleep, for He—glorified is He—“takes souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep.” A sleeping person is therefore dead in one respect and alive in another. Likewise, someone intoxicated or unconscious possesses reason in one respect but lacks it in another. If someone says, “An intoxicated person is not rational; when he sobers up, his reason returns to him,” he speaks truthfully, even though we know that such a person is not like an animal: his reason is concealed, whereas the animal has none. Indeed, anger may drive a person to a state in which his reason and judgment desert him. A report states:

“When Allah wills to carry out His decree and ordainment, He deprives those endowed with reason of their reason. Once He has carried out His decree and ordainment, He restores their reason so that they may take heed.”

The reason upon which religious accountability depends has not been taken away. What has been taken away is the reason by which one manages one’s affairs rightly in this world and the Hereafter.

---

## Page 3711

Likewise, the adulterer, the thief, the drinker of intoxicants, and the looter have not lost the faith by virtue of which they are entitled not to remain eternally in the Fire, for which intercession and forgiveness may be hoped for them, and by virtue of which they retain the rights of marriage and mutual inheritance. But they lack the faith that entitles them to deliverance from punishment, the expiation of sins, the acceptance of acts of obedience, and Allah’s honour and reward—the faith by virtue of which they deserve praise and approval.

This makes clear that the hadith is to be understood according to its apparent meaning, in a manner befitting it. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 3712

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

What is the meaning of the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise”?

Does this hadith apply specifically to believers or to disbelievers? If we say it applies specifically to believers, our claim is untenable, because believers enter Paradise by virtue of their faith. If we say it applies specifically to disbelievers, what purpose does the hadith serve?

He replied:

The wording of the hadith in al-Sahīh is:

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise, and no one who has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire.”

A person whose arrogance is incompatible with faith will not enter Paradise, as Allah says:

“Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation.”

This includes the arrogance of Iblīs, Pharaoh, and others whose arrogance was incompatible with faith. Likewise, the arrogance of the Jews and those of whom Allah says:

“Whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, did you grow arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?”

All arrogance is incompatible with the faith one is required to have. Whoever has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart fails to do what Allah has required of him and to refrain from what He has forbidden him. Rather, his arrogance leads him to deny the truth and hold others in contempt. This is the “arrogance” that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) explained when he was asked in

---

## Page 3713

the remainder of the hadith.

He was asked: “O Messenger of Allah, a man likes his clothes and shoes to look fine. Is that arrogance?”

He replied: “No. Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.”

Rejecting the truth means denying and repudiating it; looking down on people means belittling and despising them. Anyone with an atom’s weight of this in his heart is thereby led to deny the truth he is obliged to acknowledge and to hold people in contempt, thus wronging them and transgressing against them. Whoever neglects the truth he is obliged to uphold and wrongs others is not among the people of Paradise and does not deserve it; rather, he is among those subject to the threat of punishment.

Thus, his statement, “will not enter Paradise,” implies that such a person is not among its people and does not deserve it. But if he repents, has good deeds that erase his sin, is afflicted by Allah with calamities through which He expiates his sins, or experiences something similar, then the consequence of this arrogance that bars him from Paradise is removed, and he enters it. Or Allah may, out of His bountiful mercy, forgive him for that arrogance within him. He will not enter Paradise while retaining any arrogance.

This is why some have said concerning this and other hadiths that what is ruled out is unqualified entry, involving no punishment, rather than qualified entry, which occurs when someone enters the Fire and then enters Paradise. For when a hadith states without qualification that someone is in Paradise or is among the people of Paradise, the understood meaning is that he enters Paradise without entering the Fire.

Once this is clear, the meaning is that anyone with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart is not among the people of Paradise and will not enter it without punishment. Rather, he deserves punishment for his arrogance, just as others who commit major sins deserve punishment. Yet he may be punished in the Fire for as long as Allah wills, for

---

## Page 3714

no one who affirms Allah’s oneness will remain in the Fire forever. This is like his saying:

“No one who severs ties of kinship will enter Paradise.”

And his saying:

“You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I tell you something which, if you do it, will make you love one another? Spread greetings of peace among yourselves.”

There are other similar hadiths containing threats of punishment. Accordingly, the hadith applies generally to both disbelievers and Muslims.

If someone says, “Muslims enter Paradise by virtue of their Islam,” the reply is: Not all Muslims enter Paradise without punishment. Rather, those subject to the threat of punishment enter the Fire and remain there for as long as Allah wills, despite not being disbelievers. A man who possesses some faith but has committed major sins may enter the Fire and then leave it, whether through the intercession of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or otherwise. As he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“My intercession is for those of my community who commit major sins.”

And as related in an authentic hadith, he said:

“Whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will be brought out of the Fire.”

The same applies to the threats of punishment concerning murderers, those who commit unlawful sexual intercourse, those who drink wine, those who devour orphans’ wealth, those who bear false witness, and others who commit major sins. Although they are not disbelievers, they are not among those who deserve Paradise and have been promised entry into it without punishment.

The position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah is that sinful Muslims will not remain in the Fire forever, contrary to what the Khawārij and Muʿtazilah maintain. Nor are they perfect in religion, faith, and obedience. Rather, they have both good deeds and evil deeds, deserving punishment for the latter and reward for the former. This is discussed at length in its proper place. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 3715

Shaykh al-Islām was asked about the innovation of the Marāziqah.

He replied:

Furthermore, there are groups who affiliate themselves with Shaykh ʿUthmān ibn Marzūq yet say things contrary to his teachings. He belonged to the school of Ahmad and was among the companions of Shaykh ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Abī al-Faraj al-Shīrāzī. These people affiliate themselves with the school of al-Shāfiʿī, yet express views contrary to the teachings of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—indeed, to those of all the imams. Their shaykh was a man of learning and religion and should be treated like others of his standing. If he expressed a view known to contradict that of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, their view must take precedence over his, with the Quran and Sunnah also supporting the imams’ position. How much more so when the view contradicts his teachings, those of the imams, and the Quran and Sunnah!

An example is their saying:

“We do not say ‘definitely.’ We say, ‘We testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,’ but we do not affirm this with certainty. We say, ‘The sky is above us,’ but we do not affirm this with certainty.”

They relate a report from ʿAlī—some of them attributing it to the Prophet—that he said, “Do not say ‘definitely.’” This is a fabricated lie, by agreement of the scholars. Their shaykh did not say this; rather, it is an innovation introduced by some of his companions after his death. If one of them is asked, “Will you not affirm this with certainty?” he replies, “Allah is able to change this

---

## Page 3716

horse.” He imagines that saying “definitely” denies Allah’s power to change it. This is ignorance: this horse is definitely a horse in its present state, and Allah is able to change it.

The source of “these people’s misconception” was that the early generations would qualify their affirmation of faith, saying, “I am a believer—if Allah wills.” Muhammad ibn Yūsuf al-Firyābī, al-Bukhārī’s teacher and a companion of al-Thawrī, had settled in the frontier towns of Syria, such as Ashkelon. He was stern towards the Murji’ah and, like his teacher al-Thawrī and others among the early generations, upheld “qualifying one’s affirmation of faith.”

People hold “three views” concerning this qualification. Some prohibit it, as do a group of Hanafis, who say that anyone who uses it is a doubter. Others require it, as do a group of hadith scholars. Still others permit it—or consider it recommended. This is the most balanced view, for the qualification has a valid basis.

Someone who says, “I am a believer, if Allah wills,” believing that faith consists in fulfilling all obligations and fearing that he may not be fulfilling them, has done well. This is why the Companions feared hypocrisy for themselves. Ibn Abī Mulaykah said, “I met thirty of Muhammad’s Companions—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and every one of them feared hypocrisy for himself.”

Likewise, someone who believes that a believer in the unqualified sense is one who deserves Paradise, and therefore adds this qualification out of fear of a bad end, is correct. This is the meaning of the report related from Ibn Mas‘ūd, who was told of a man being asked, “Are you a believer?”

---

## Page 3717

and he replied, “Yes.” He was then asked, “Are you among the people of Paradise?” He replied, “I hope so.” Ibn Mas‘ūd said, “Why did he not entrust the first matter to Allah as he did the second?”

Whoever adds this qualification out of fear of declaring himself pure or praising himself, or to make matters conditional upon Allah’s will, has done well. Whoever states with certainty what he knows of the belief within himself is also correct.

The point is that these people’s misconception originated in “qualifying one’s affirmation of faith,” as practised by the people of the frontier town of Ashkelon and its vicinity. Most of these people live near Ashkelon. Many of them then began qualifying their statements about righteous deeds, saying, “I prayed, if Allah wills,” fearing that they might not have performed the prayer as commanded. The people of the frontier wrote a treatise on this. Their shaykh, Ibn Marzūq, did no more than follow these people. Neither he nor any scholar before him refrained from saying of something known to exist, “This definitely exists.”

Some shaykhs have reported that he used this qualification in everything. It seems, however—and Allah knows best—that he used it when speaking about future matters, in accordance with His words [the Exalted] (1):

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills,”

and the Prophet’s words [may Allah bless him and grant him peace] (2):

“And we, if Allah wills, shall join you?”

What is obligatory is to remain in accord with the Muslim community. Saying, “That is definitely so,” is like saying, “I testify to that,” “I am certain of that,” or “I know that.” If someone says, “I testify, but I cannot say definitely,” he is ignorant. An ignorant person must retract his error, not persist in his ignorance or oppose what the Muslim scholars uphold; otherwise, he becomes an ignorant, misguided innovator.

## Page 3718

Likewise, their ignorance is shown by their claim that Allah does not accept a Rāfidī’s repentance. They attribute the following saying to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Reviling my Companions is an unforgivable sin.”

They also say that reviling the Companions infringes a human right, which is therefore not extinguished by repentance. This is false for two reasons.

First, the hadith is a fabrication, by the unanimous agreement of hadith scholars, and contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah and scholarly consensus. Allah says in two verses of His Book:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

The people of the Sunnah cite this against the people of innovation who claim that those who commit major sins will not be forgiven unless they repent. For Allah says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

This applies to those who repent: Allah accepts the repentance of everyone who repents, even if their sin is the gravest of sins. He also says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

This concerns those who have not repented.

Second, even if the hadith were genuine, it would mean that this sin is not forgiven for someone who does not repent of it. No sin is greater than associating partners with Allah, yet Muslims unanimously agree that Allah forgives this sin when the person who committed it repents. As the Exalted says:

“But if they repent, establish prayer and give zakah, then let them go their way.”

And in the other verse:

“Then they are your brothers in faith.”

It is well known, by scholarly consensus, that if a belligerent unbeliever reviles the prophets and then repents, Allah accepts his repentance, for he had regarded that conduct as lawful. Likewise, a Rāfidī regards reviling the Companions as lawful. If it becomes clear to him that it is forbidden, and he seeks forgiveness for them in place of his former conduct, Allah will replace his evil deeds with good deeds. The human right involved would then be subordinate to Allah’s right, because he regards it as lawful

---

## Page 3719

to engage in such conduct. Even supposing that this were a matter of a human right, his case would be like that of someone who repents of slander and backbiting. According to the stronger of the two scholarly opinions, his repentance does not require him to seek pardon from the person he wronged. Rather, it is enough to do good to that person in his absence, so that the good offsets the wrong.

Among the reprehensible innovations is one Muslim group declaring other Muslim groups unbelievers and deeming it lawful to shed their blood and seize their property, saying, for example, “This is the innovator’s crop,” and similar things. This is a grave matter for two reasons.

First, the other group’s innovation may be no greater than that of the group declaring it unbelieving. Indeed, the innovation of the group making that declaration may be graver, comparable, or less serious. This is the situation of most adherents of innovation who declare one another unbelievers. If it is supposed that an innovator becomes an unbeliever, then both groups would be declared unbelievers; if it is supposed that he does not, then neither group would be unbelievers. For one group to declare the other unbelieving without declaring its own group unbelieving is therefore an act of ignorance and injustice. Such people are among those of whom Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who have divided their religion and become sects—you have nothing to do with them.”

Second, even supposing that innovation were confined to one of the two groups, the people of the Sunnah would not be entitled to declare everyone who makes an erroneous statement an unbeliever. For Allah, glorified is He, says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is established in an authentic hadith that Allah said: “I have done so.” And the Exalted says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”

And it is reported from the Prophet

---

## Page 3720

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that he said:

“Allah has, for my sake, pardoned my community for mistakes and forgetfulness.”

This is a sound hadith narrated by Ibn Mājah and others. The Companions and all the other imams of the Muslims unanimously agreed that not everyone who makes an erroneous statement thereby becomes an unbeliever, even if his statement contradicts the Sunnah. Declaring everyone who errs an unbeliever therefore contradicts scholarly consensus. There are, however, disagreements concerning questions of declaring people unbelievers, which have been discussed at length elsewhere.

And (the point here is that no group affiliated with a particular shaykh or imam is entitled to declare those outside its ranks unbelievers. Rather, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If a man says to his brother, ‘You unbeliever,’ one of them has incurred that charge.”

He also said:

“A Muslim is a Muslim’s brother: he neither wrongs him nor abandons him. Everything belonging to a Muslim is inviolable to another Muslim: his blood, his property, and his honour.”

And he said:

“Do not sever ties with one another, turn your backs on one another, hate one another, or envy one another. Be brothers, O servants of Allah.”

And he said:

“The believers, in their mutual love, mercy, and compassion, are like a single body: when one part suffers, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness.”

Those affiliated with Ibn Marzūq are not entitled to prohibit intermarriage with those affiliated with al-Awfī on the grounds that they consider them unsuitable matches. Rather, the most honoured people in Allah’s sight are those most mindful of Him, whatever group they belong to, whether these groups or others. As the Exalted says:

“O mankind, indeed We created you from

---

## Page 3721

a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most honoured of you in Allah’s sight is the most mindful of Him.”

It is reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “Who are the most honoured people?” He replied, “Those most mindful of Allah.”

It is also reported in the Sunan that he said:

“No Arab is superior to a non-Arab, nor any non-Arab to an Arab; no white person is superior to a black person, nor any black person to a white person, except through mindfulness of Allah. All people descend from Adam, and Adam was created from dust.”
